Offering distance learning as a way for pupils to attend lessons from home through the internet or video‑conferencing may sound attractive, but I firmly believe that it does not help students succeed. Several problems make remote classes ineffective.

First, many learners lose focus when they study at home. Mobile phones and other gadgets are always within reach, and it is difficult for students to resist checking them. In addition, family members—parents, brothers or sisters—can create interruptions that pull attention away from the lesson. When concentration is broken, students fall behind, waste time and may ultimately fail. For example, my cousin moved to the United States with his siblings and was allowed to take one of his courses online. At home he was constantly disturbed by his brothers, which caused him to lose interest in the subject and eventually fail the class.

Second, studying alone often feels tedious and confusing. Without a teacher’s immediate explanations, pupils struggle to grasp difficult concepts, and the lack of verbal interaction makes the experience dull. Some students need an active, engaging environment; when they cannot get it, they tend to skip material or even fall asleep. A friend of mine experienced exactly this: he found distance lessons boring, felt sleepy quickly, tried drinking strong coffee, and eventually turned off the computer and went to bed, which harmed his grades each year.

Finally, fatigue is a common issue for remote learners. Many have to complete after‑school jobs or chores before they can log on, leaving them exhausted when the lesson starts. I know this personally: after walking a half‑mile home, doing homework and showering, I still have to sit in front of a screen for an online class late at night. The tiredness makes it hard to concentrate and slows down my learning.

In sum, the numerous drawbacks—distractions, lack of teacher support, boredom, and fatigue—show that distance learning does not benefit students and can even lower their academic performance.

Success depends largely on the attitude you adopt. Research indicates that a person's outlook is the main driver of achievement, because it reflects who they are. A positive mindset is essential for success, as it helps you achieve more, earn respect and makes a strong first impression.

Firstly, maintaining optimism enables you to reach a greater number of goals. A constructive attitude can assist you in securing employment, completing academic assignments and gaining admission to university programmes.

Secondly, possessing a hopeful outlook smooths the course of everyday life. When you believe in yourself, you are more likely to accomplish whatever you decide to pursue.

Thirdly, a positive disposition signals that you value those around you. This creates a favourable image in any setting, and people are more inclined to offer you opportunities, including jobs. Demonstrating respect and a good attitude therefore contributes directly to a successful life.

In the job market, presenting a positive attitude is crucial for making a good first impression on potential employers. First impressions shape how others view you and can determine whether you are hired. Lacking a positive outlook may result in a poor impression and a missed opportunity.

In summary, your attitude is the key factor in achieving success, and it is entirely within your control. Studies confirm that a positive mindset leads to greater accomplishments, earned respect and strong first impressions, all of which pave the way to a successful life.

People ought to decide for themselves rather than rely on the advice of so‑called “experts.”  

First, individuals understand their own preferences and needs better than anyone else. They know what they enjoy, what suits them physically, and what will make them happy. Imagine someone buying a gift for a friend without considering the friend’s tastes; the present would likely be unwanted or even useless. If the buyer had taken the friend’s wishes into account, the mismatch would have been avoided.  

Second, making personal choices allows us to learn from our own errors. Many people order clothing online and receive items that don’t fit because they never tried them on or measured themselves first. After such a disappointment, they are more likely to visit a store or get accurate measurements before the next purchase. Likewise, shoppers often ignore product descriptions, receive something different from what they imagined, and then realize the importance of reading the details. These experiences teach valuable lessons that cannot be gained by simply following someone else’s recommendation.  

Finally, not every “expert” is capable of providing useful help for every situation. A lawyer may charge a large fee yet lose a case, a doctor might dismiss a genuine problem and prescribe an expensive medication that the patient already has at home, and some therapists may offer unnecessary drugs simply because they can. While there are competent professionals, many are more interested in profit than in the client’s well‑being.  

Consequently, relying on experts can lead to poor guidance, whereas making one’s own decisions—even if it involves occasional mistakes—promotes personal growth and better outcomes. It is therefore wiser to trust oneself and decide independently.

Everyone has different opinions about the benefits of working in a group or working alone; some people prefer working alone and others prefer working in groups. I believe that the best way for people to improve is by working in groups because they learn more and understand better.

First, working in groups helps people improve in school or at work because they learn new things—for example, listening to other ideas and points of view from their partners. One day my English teacher made groups of four in class and gave each group a piece of paper. Then he put some questions on the board and told us that we needed to answer them as a group. When we finished, the teacher told us that we were going to discuss them. As each group discussed their answers with the class, we all realized that each group had different opinions, ideas, and points of view. Each group learned something new from each other.

"Every day we all learn new things in life."

Second, working in groups helps people improve because they will understand better. For example, asking their partners if they have a question or didn’t understand something well. My history teacher gave the class an assignment that we needed to complete by the end of the class. When the teacher gave the instructions, I didn’t understand them really well, so I asked one of my partners if he could explain them to me again in order for me to understand, be able to give my opinions, and help my group.

"We could do more if we all help each other."

Many people believe that it is better to work alone because they will concentrate more. For example, they will not get distracted by anyone and will finish the work faster. A friend of mine has always worked alone because she said that when people are working in groups they tend to start talking, distract others, don’t do their work, and by the end of the hour only get a couple of questions done. However, this argument is meaningless because if they don’t understand something well, then they would not have a partner who could explain to them what they are doing. For example, they might not finish their work because they get stuck on a part. Not having someone to discuss the work with can be hard sometimes.

In conclusion, there are a lot of benefits when working with a group. Some of the other benefits that working in groups has are making new friends, having the opportunity to learn more about your partner, and learning more about yourself. Having to work with someone is a good idea because you don’t have a lot of pressure about having to finish the work on time or not having any idea what to do. Even though some people say the opposite, I believe that working in groups is better than working alone.

People often wonder whether it is more advantageous to work alone or in a group. Opinions differ: some individuals prefer solitary work, while others enjoy collaborating with others. I am convinced that teamwork is the better option because it promotes greater learning and deeper understanding.

His explanation helped me grasp the requirements, voice my own ideas, and contribute to the group’s work. As another proverb notes, “We can achieve more when we help each other.”

Without a partner to discuss problems with, a lone worker may remain confused and unable to progress.

In conclusion, teamwork offers many advantages. It enables us to make new friends, learn about our peers, and discover more about ourselves. Working with others reduces the pressure of having to finish everything on time or figuring out everything by ourselves. Although some claim the opposite, I maintain that collaborating in a group is far more beneficial than working alone.

Homework is often difficult, and many students need extra help to complete it. While an after‑school homework club might sound enjoyable and useful, it is not the best solution for most learners. Such a club could help children who cannot finish their assignments or who do not understand the material, but it also creates several problems for those who already have full schedules.

For many pupils, the period after school is already packed with other commitments. They may have sports practice, dance lessons, choir rehearsals, music lessons, or other activities that take up their evenings. Even when they get home, they often still lack the time to sit down and work on their homework. A homework club would only benefit students who have nothing else to do after school, allowing them to stay at school and finish the tasks they missed that day.

I personally oppose the idea of an after‑school homework club. My own schedule includes regular practice sessions, so I rarely have time to complete assignments after school; I usually try to finish them later and hand them in the next day. Teachers also face time constraints—they have personal responsibilities such as feeding pets, caring for their families, or handling other duties that prevent them from staying late. This is another reason why an after‑school club is impractical.

Transportation is another concern. Many students rely on parents who may be working, ill, or otherwise unavailable, leaving the children without a way to return home after a late‑day club. It is unlikely that the school could supervise all those students, provide meals, or address other basic needs. If a school wants to offer extra help, it would be better to schedule it during the last period of the regular timetable, giving students a dedicated block to finish homework before they leave.

Placing the homework session in the final class would help students who have extracurricular activities later in the day, preventing them from worrying about unfinished work. It would also give teachers a short break and time to grade papers or check assignments. Another possibility would be to schedule a similar session at the beginning of the day, allowing pupils who missed homework the night before to catch up before lessons start.

Overall, I prefer the idea of a homework period at the end of the school day. It provides a brief pause for everyone, lets students complete their assignments, and frees up the afternoon for other activities without the logistical and personal difficulties associated with an after‑school club.

People all over the world constantly acquire new knowledge—about animals, cultures, objects, and ideas. While some claim that Ralph Emerson’s warning “unless someone tries to do something beyond what they have already mastered, they will not grow” is true, I disagree. I think that attempting tasks far beyond one’s current abilities often hinders growth because the person lacks the necessary experience and knowledge.

First, everyone dreams of achieving a certain career, and most people believe that studying or taking part in relevant activities will help them reach that goal. Effort, however, is not enough if it is directed at something completely unfamiliar. Take my friend, Maria, for example. She has worked as a server in a restaurant since she was seventeen. At nineteen she knows every menu item, how to restock supplies, and the routine of the job. Yet she feels bored and refuses to try anything new. Because her experience is limited to one type of work, she lacks the broader perspective that different jobs could provide. If she never applies for another position, she will not develop the confidence or self‑esteem needed to move forward, and she will miss out on alternative career paths.

Second, some basic knowledge is essential before attempting something beyond one’s current mastery. When I was in eighth grade, my teacher, Mr. Lee, often ate lunch with me and we talked about many subjects. As I prepared to enter high school, I asked for advice. He warned me that the years ahead would be harder and that I needed to take my studies seriously, pass exams, and keep a high GPA. He explained that these steps would help me decide on a future career. This conversation showed me that having at least a foundation of knowledge is crucial for growth; merely jumping into an unfamiliar field without preparation does not lead to improvement.

Critics might argue that staying within one’s comfort zone prevents progress, and that venturing beyond familiar territory is the only way to learn. Yet without experience, a person remains stuck in that comfort zone, and without sufficient knowledge, they become confused and ineffective. My father’s story illustrates this point. He arrived in the United States at fourteen with only a handful of English words. He dedicated himself to learning the language step by step, and each small success allowed him to move beyond his initial limitations. His growth came from gradual learning, not from leaping into a task he was wholly unprepared for.

In conclusion, both experience and knowledge are necessary for personal development. Imagine conducting a science project on an unfamiliar animal that can change its colour, size, and shape. Would you simply note the basic facts, or would you invest time in understanding how it lives and behaves? The latter approach—building on what you already know while slowly expanding your skills—leads to genuine growth, whereas trying to do something entirely beyond your mastery usually leaves you stranded.

My friend began homeschooling after she was constantly bullied and could no longer tolerate the situation. Her counselor suggested she take online courses because she already had good grades and wanted to ensure she would graduate and have a bright future. Many schools now provide distance‑learning options, allowing students to attend lessons from home through the internet or video calls. I believe homeschooling is a valuable choice for students who face difficulties at school, for those who are considering dropping out, and because it is often simpler and faster.

The main advantage is that it protects students from negative school environments. If a pupil is constantly involved in fights, suffers harassment, has conflicts with teachers, or feels that staying in school is a waste of time, online classes can keep them out of trouble and allow them to continue their education. This not only removes them from the problematic situation but also helps them graduate without obstacles. Anyone dealing with such issues should speak with a counselor or ask their parents about the possibility of homeschooling.

A second benefit concerns students who are about to leave school. Many drop out for financial reasons—perhaps they need to work to support their families—or because of personal circumstances such as an early pregnancy and a lack of parental support. Homeschooling lets them keep learning and improves their chances of obtaining a better job later. It also brings relief, knowing they can still earn a diploma despite having decided to quit traditional school. I recall a time when I worked as a student‑counseling aide; a distressed teenager asked where to store his laptop because he planned to drop out. When I suggested online classes, he was surprised that this option existed and left much happier.

Finally, homeschooling is often easier and quicker. Learners can study at any time that suits them, pause when needed, and resume whenever they are ready. The flexibility reduces stress compared with the rigid schedule of conventional schools. Research shows that a high percentage of students feel pressured by homework and deadlines, whereas only a small fraction of homeschooled students report stress. A science teacher at my former school explained that while about 88 % of students feel stressed about schoolwork, only roughly 5 % of those who are homeschooled experience such pressure. This freedom allows students to wake up when they wish, take breaks whenever they need, and enjoy a more relaxed routine.

Some critics argue that homeschooling lacks immediate teacher assistance when questions arise, but many programs offer one‑on‑one instruction, giving students direct access to an instructor without the distractions of a crowded classroom. In my view, online schooling is a strong advantage for those dealing with difficult school situations, for those who might otherwise drop out, and for anyone who wants a faster, less stressful path to completing their education.

Problems are not merely obstacles; they can reshape our lives and teach us valuable lessons. I once witnessed a scene in a supermarket where a man with short legs was being mocked for the way he walked and talked. When the bully, whom I will call Alex, challenged him to a bike race, the man with short legs accepted and ultimately won. After that experience, Alex never ridiculed anyone again. This episode shows how a problem can become a turning point that changes behavior and perspective.

First, a problem can dramatically alter the course of one’s life. A few years ago, a man named Mark recounted his troubled past. He admitted that he had stolen, lied, ignored advice, and avoided work. During a family vacation, their car was struck by a truck; Mark was the sole survivor. Overwhelmed by guilt, he fell into deep despair and even contemplated ending his own life. Six months later, while walking on a beach with the intention of jumping into the sea, he met a stranger who asked his name. The stranger, also named Mark, listened to his story and reminded him that his survival meant his life still had purpose—there were people who would wish they could breathe without assistance. Those words sparked a change; Mark began to rebuild his life, honoring his family and finding new meaning. This narrative demonstrates how a sudden crisis can force a person to reevaluate priorities and move forward.

Second, confronting difficulties can teach us important lessons. Consider the story of Daniel, a devoted father of eleven children who always helped those in need. One day a messenger arrived with terrible news: a fire had destroyed Daniel’s home and his children were trapped inside. All his possessions vanished, and his wife urged him to curse God, believing the tragedy was a punishment. Daniel refused to blame anyone and, in a moment of anger, shouted at God, recalling a promise he had made years earlier to provide food for a needy family—a promise he had repeatedly forgotten. Realizing his negligence had contributed to the loss, Daniel sought forgiveness. God granted it, and Daniel’s life was restored. This account shows how facing hardship can bring awareness of personal responsibilities and lead to spiritual growth.

In conclusion, problems present opportunities to improve ourselves. They can change our direction, reveal the value of our existence, and teach us to keep our commitments. When faced with a challenge, remember that life matters, honor the promises you make, and use the difficulty as a chance to become better.

No two people are identical, and we should not always be instructed to emulate what everyone does. It is crucial that we make decisions autonomously because doing so strengthens us as human beings, bolsters self‑confidence, and encourages self‑reliance.

For instance, growing up, your guardians could be anyone—they might be virtuous, or they might be less admirable. It is our responsibility to apply common sense and determine for ourselves what is right and what is wrong. It is always wise to engage your intellect and judge whether something is morally sound. Not only does it foster personal development, but it also strengthens the mind.

All of these reasons underscore why we should mature by making our own choices and decisions instead of mindlessly doing what everyone else does. People possess all the power within themselves to become who they wish to be. You are no one other than yourself, after all, and that is the most important consideration when choosing our own character traits.

Imagine stepping onto a paradise unlike any other—that’s the Bahamas. Its crystal‑clear seas teem with vibrant fish, its shores are lined with striking cliffs, and the gentle trade‑winds add a refreshing feel to every day. The local cuisine bursts with colour and flavour, and there’s no shortage of things to do: mountain climbing, food festivals, dancing, swimming, and more. Many destinations simply can’t match such a blend of natural beauty, pleasant weather and diverse activities.

Although the Bahamas is known for being pricey, the experience it offers makes the cost worthwhile. Some travelers might prefer to spend their money in places like Paris, Germany or Italy, but I’m drawn to the islands for their rich culture. I would love to explore that culture first, then spend hours hiking the hills to enjoy the panoramic views and the kaleidoscope of tropical plants. A trip there would be a perfect way to unwind, reduce stress and broaden my understanding of different customs and languages.

Visiting a new country often teaches useful skills. While abroad, people pick up cooking techniques, learn to ski, or become comfortable on a bike. Biking, in particular, appeals to me; I enjoy it so much that I hope to join a team someday. The Bahamas’ wide, safe streets would provide an ideal setting for practicing, allowing me to ride around the city without worrying about traffic hazards.

Living in the Bahamas is another tempting idea, even though the cost of living is high. Those who reside there either earn good salaries or come from affluent backgrounds. While beachfront living can be risky because of storms, I would choose a home farther inland for safety. The islands’ abundant colourful flora and fauna are a big part of why I want to experience them.

In short, the Bahamas stands out as one of the world’s most beautiful and lively destinations, offering countless activities, cultural richness, and opportunities to learn new skills—exactly why I hope to visit soon.

Many companies assign jobs to more than one person because they know a team works more efficiently than an individual, and teachers should do the same in their classes to help students raise their grades and submit work on time. Group work should be allowed in classes to improve cooperation and to provide different points of view for the best outcomes in the subject.

Working alone means students never have to argue about project decisions or collaborate with unfamiliar classmates. Yet most learners prefer group work because it lets them divide tasks, exchange ideas, and support one another. Collaborating in a team generally makes the work more efficient, and based on my own experience and the reasons outlined below, I would choose group work for its many advantages.

First, students are often assigned numerous projects each term, and a single large assignment can represent a significant portion of the final grade—sometimes up to ten percent. Handling such a workload alone can be overwhelming. When students form a group, the project can be split among members, allowing each person to tackle a portion that suits their strengths. Everyone brings different skills and talents, which can make challenging parts of the assignment easier to complete.

Second, group work teaches valuable cooperation skills that are essential in the workplace. Many companies assign tasks to small teams because each member contributes distinct knowledge and expertise. The common corporate mantra, “Work as a team,” reflects the belief that collaboration boosts productivity. Teachers should view group projects as a way to give students real‑world experience in teamwork, while also exposing them to diverse perspectives and ideas.

Allowing students to collaborate can also increase their confidence. When classmates discuss the material together, they can compare approaches and choose the most effective solutions. Schools often keep facilities open after regular hours, which helps students who cannot meet at a teammate’s house. Moreover, a group can help members who struggle to meet deadlines by providing motivation and shared responsibility, leading to higher overall productivity.

In conclusion, no student should have to face a major project alone when time is limited. Businesses recognize that teams accomplish tasks more efficiently than individuals, and schools should adopt the same principle. Permitting group work in classrooms not only improves grades and timeliness but also fosters cooperation and exposes students to multiple viewpoints, ultimately helping them succeed in the subject and beyond.

Churchill’s words are still relevant to people today, especially in the United States. Many individuals who experience failure manage to pick themselves up and keep pursuing their goals, yet some think that a setback means they should quit. It is worth examining both viewpoints, but ultimately the message that we must not give up remains crucial.  

First, perseverance allows us to learn from our mistakes. Failing does not signal the end of the world; it simply provides information about what did not work. When we understand why we went wrong, we are better prepared to succeed the next time. Recognizing that setbacks are part of the process helps us stay focused on our objectives, and defending what we believe in keeps us moving forward.  

Second, abandoning our efforts prevents us from achieving our highest aspirations. To obtain what we truly want, we must fight for it. Some people, after a failure, claim that they have wasted their time and give up. Life, however, does not guarantee constant victories; failure is inevitable and often uncomfortable. Still, we must continue to push forward because success brings confidence and satisfaction, proving that we did not surrender.  

Conversely, those who give up often miss out on opportunities. Individuals who think they can easily secure a good job, attend a prestigious school, or realize their dreams without encountering obstacles are likely to quit at the first sign of difficulty. The people who attain impressive positions or admissions have persisted despite hardships. When failure makes us doubt our intelligence or abilities, we should remember that help is available from friends and family, who can assist us in overcoming challenges.  

In conclusion, whenever we set a goal, giving up should never be an option. Hard work and determination make it possible to reach our aims, and support from loved ones can guide us through any setbacks. By refusing to quit, we build self‑confidence and develop the resilience needed to succeed throughout life.

I have back problems because I was arched a lot as a kid; it is only a matter of time before everyone has an arched back and the few with straight backs will be in charge. You cannot stand tall if your back is arched.

Technology also has positive effects; it can help you find answers to your homework. You can find love, start a new life, or even locate a new home. Technology is not that bad—it’s just that people misuse and abuse it. It helps us, but it hurts us at the same time, and people don’t see that.

Have you ever looked up from your phone just to watch the sky? Most of us reach for our devices the moment we wake up, and our lives have become inseparable from technology. The tools keep advancing, but have we? We entrust everything to the internet, constantly comparing ourselves with others online. It’s no surprise that many feel depressed, seeing what other people possess while ignoring what they already have. The same world is visible to all, yet each person views it through a different lens.

One of the biggest problems is wasted time. People stare at their personal screens as if they were glued on, becoming “sheeple.” They chase the newest gadget, the flashiest outfit, or the highest number of likes, building a fake online persona that matters more than real interaction. Conversations are reduced to brief FaceTime calls, never face‑to‑face. Fear of not fitting in drives the desire for the latest, most expensive items, as if price equals worth. All of this stems from excessive screen time. It affects both mind and body: many develop slouched postures and curved backs, leading to chronic back pain. I, too, suffered from a hunched spine as a child, and I notice more people with similar problems. Those who can stand tall will eventually lead, because a straight posture reflects confidence and health.

Of course, technology also brings benefits. It can help you solve a homework problem, find a romantic partner, or locate a new home. The tool itself isn’t evil; it is the way we use—and sometimes abuse—it that creates harm. Technology can be both a help and a hindrance, and we often fail to see both sides.

Schools ought to form partnerships with businesses. While some people argue against this idea, the benefits for students seeking future employment make it clear that such collaborations are worthwhile.

Critics often ignore the fact that many students are not even aware of the career options available to them. Without connections to companies, pupils may struggle to discover the kinds of jobs that suit their interests and abilities. Partnerships give schools the chance to expose learners to real‑world work environments, helping them to identify fields they might enjoy.

When schools work together with firms, students gain access to internships, apprenticeships and mentorship programmes that smooth the transition from education to employment. This direct exposure reduces the difficulty of job hunting, as students already have contacts and experience in their chosen sector. As a result, they are more likely to find a position they are passionate about and to succeed in their careers.

In short, establishing school‑company partnerships enables learners to explore vocational possibilities, acquire practical skills and enter the job market with confidence. Therefore, schools should indeed partner with companies so that students can secure work that matches their talents and interests.

Choosing a career is one of the most important decisions in a person’s life. With countless occupations to explore, many young people take the idea of work very seriously and want to understand it better. Encouraging students to commit to a career path early has several advantages: it gives them a realistic picture of the job, helps them discover enjoyable activities, and reduces anxiety about employment later on.  

First, early commitment lets students see what a profession really involves. Many pupils have only a vague idea of what it takes to become a doctor, a dentist, or any other specialist. By taking part in related programmes or shadowing professionals, they can observe daily tasks, learn basic skills, and gather reliable information. Researching a field online also becomes easier when they already have a concrete goal in mind. In short, early exposure provides the knowledge and resources needed to make an informed choice about a future career.  

Second, involvement in a career can turn work into a source of fun and personal satisfaction. A large number of teenagers spend their free time without a clear hobby or purpose, which can lead to boredom and unhappiness. After‑school clubs or career‑oriented activities give them something engaging to do, allowing them to develop interests that may later become lifelong passions. Discovering a rewarding pastime through early career experiences helps students feel more motivated and less idle.  

Finally, deciding on a career path while still in school eases the pressure of finding a job after graduation. Many young adults wander through adulthood unsure of what they want, making the job search stressful and uncertain. Students who have already explored a profession, gathered information, and perhaps even gained some experience are far more confident about their future choices. Consequently, they face less anxiety when entering the workforce and can transition more smoothly into employment.  

In conclusion, students benefit from committing to a career early because it offers realistic insight, lets them enjoy meaningful activities, and eliminates much of the worry associated with adult job hunting. Even those who are initially unsure should spend time researching and participating in career‑focused programs, as this early involvement ultimately leads to a clearer, less stressful path forward.

Ralph Waldo Emerson once said, “To be yourself in a world that is constantly trying to make you something else is the greatest accomplishment.” If you doubt that individuality is valuable, consider why it truly matters. Each person ought to have the freedom to choose for themselves and to think and act independently.

It is natural to want to please loved ones and to fit into a group, because belonging can give a sense of moral direction and help define who we are as members of a community. Shared values, common interests and traditions can be a source of pride—much like patriotism or nationalism—when we identify with the larger whole.

Nevertheless, we must also feel entitled to question the ideas and practices of that community, especially when they rest on unsound reasoning. When a belief is treated as absolute truth, it becomes dogma, and blind acceptance can be dangerous. Even the advice of friends and family should sometimes be examined critically, since they may unintentionally steer us wrong, though we can still trust them in most other matters.

In short, you should be yourself, think for yourself, and combine the traits that set you apart while asserting your own will and personality.

These factors have supported human life for a long time, and they continue to do so. Everyone in this world must care for them, because these resources help us survive and support our lifestyle. This writing will give advice, discuss benefits and disadvantages, and outline plans for caring for our resources.  

Let us talk about the benefits we will get if we save our resources. First, there is a recommendation to adopt a four‑day work week, with each day consisting of ten hours of work, and school days limited to two hours. This is a way to save resources and obtain the following benefits: we will save energy, food, internet, water, and time (time that can be spent with family or on other activities); we will reduce the deterioration of our clothes and shoes; we will help the environment stay safe from pollution; we will create a better lifestyle for humans; and we will preserve resources for critical moments in the world. As you can see, there are many resources we could save if we adopt this plan.  

In this plan there are many benefits, but also disadvantages. I will now discuss the disadvantages of implementing this project. Several problems could arise, such as loss of learning time, reduced work time, and a diminished social life both at school and at work. Becoming a professional could become harder and more delayed. Technological advancement would slow, which could affect human evolution. Consequently, we would lose many important things and resources that support life and make it easier.  

In conclusion, many people will benefit from this project, but at the same time it will create many problems because of its disadvantages. If we implement this plan, we must understand that we are taking a risk. Moreover, we must think about the risks involved and try to prevent more problems than we already have. I recommend that we stop wasting time and start creating a better world with a better lifestyle, and that we develop new projects to save resources. Now caring for our resources has become a new goal for me after reflecting on a topic like this. We must understand that protecting our resources is necessary, because they are indispensable for keeping us alive and moving forward in the twenty‑first century.

Energy and natural resources are essential for human development and survival. They include not only oil, gas and electricity but also money, manufactured goods and other commodities that support our modern way of life. Everyone depends on these assets, yet many people either do not understand the consequences of wasting them or simply ignore the problem. It is therefore crucial to change our habits and protect what we have. The following paragraphs discuss some suggestions, the advantages they could bring, possible drawbacks, and the steps we should take to preserve our resources.

One proposal that could help conserve energy and other supplies is to introduce a four‑day work week, with ten‑hour days, and to shorten school days to two hours. By reducing the amount of time people spend in offices and classrooms, we would cut down on electricity use, heating, water consumption, food preparation, and even internet traffic. Employees and students would also gain more free time for family, leisure or personal projects, and wear and tear on clothing and shoes would decrease. In addition, fewer commuting days would mean lower emissions, which would benefit the environment and leave more reserves available for emergencies. In short, a shorter schedule could save a wide range of resources while improving quality of life.

However, the plan is not without disadvantages. Critics argue that a condensed schedule could limit the time available for learning and for completing work tasks, potentially harming professional development and social interaction. Some fear that slower technological progress and reduced productivity might impede overall human advancement. If people feel rushed to finish duties within longer days, the quality of work and education could suffer, leading to a loss of valuable knowledge and efficiency—resources that are just as important as physical ones.

In conclusion, while the four‑day work week could bring substantial benefits, it also carries risks that must be carefully weighed. Any decision to implement such a system should involve a thorough assessment of possible problems and strategies to mitigate them. Governments, which have the authority to shape national policies, should lead the effort to develop and fund projects that promote resource conservation. Protecting our energy, materials and other assets is indispensable for maintaining a sustainable, comfortable life in the twenty‑first century.

One of the biggest benefits of homeschooling is its flexibility in both place and time. With a good night’s sleep, students can start the day feeling refreshed and organise their day as they wish. In the first place, attending classes from home is not the same as being in school, because at school students take their homework, quizzes, and exams more seriously than they can at home. When students are in class and have a question about the topic they are learning, they can freely ask their teacher, who will give a clear, explained answer and examples so the students understand everything being taught. In addition, if students attend classes online they will not have the opportunity to stay after school for extra help, to retake a quiz or exam, to go to a learning center where other students can help with their homework, or simply to study with the company of another student. As a matter of fact, students' grades will decline due to unanswered questions and unresolved problems.  

Secondly, if attending classes online becomes common, students will not practice their communication skills because they will not build relationships with classmates, discuss concerns, or have fun with friends during lunch. They would not feel the same way, since at school students sometimes get inspired by peers; they see classmates not just as peers but also as friends, even as family. Over time, students come to view the school as another home where they know people can help with schoolwork and give personal advice, just as counselors and teachers do. Moreover, when students receive classes online at home, they will feel bored and lonely because there is no one to discuss questions or doubts with. In addition, a large percentage of teenagers today deal with psychological problems such as stress, anxiety, and depression; being at school distracts them from problems at home or work and provides a great way to receive help and advice from counselors, teachers, and friends. Being in school is better than being at home alone just studying.  

Lastly, attending classes online is not the best idea for students who tend not to take their studies seriously. While they are at home they do not feel the presence of a teacher standing nearby, telling them to get their work done, to pay attention, or not to fall asleep during class. They also do not feel the obligation to complete homework for submission the next day. When students work in groups they learn many things from teammates that they did not know before; group work is an awesome way to inspire each other and have fun, as students see peers working hard toward their goals and follow suit. If students work alone, the opposite occurs, and they may think they can do whatever they want without taking their courses seriously.  

In conclusion, attending classes online is not a favorable way for students to learn because they will not learn the same way they do while in school. Students will not develop their communication or social skills, and they will not take their courses with the seriousness required for good grades.

Studying from home through online platforms or video‑conferencing is not an especially effective way for pupils to learn, because it cannot replace the experience they receive in a physical school. If remote classes become the norm, students will lose the chance to form solid friendships with classmates and teachers, and they may not treat their coursework with the same seriousness they do when they are supervised in a school environment.

First, learning at home differs greatly from learning at school. In a classroom, homework, quizzes and examinations are taken more seriously than when a student works alone at home. When a concept is unclear, a pupil can raise his hand and receive an immediate, detailed explanation from the teacher, often accompanied by examples that make the idea easier to grasp. Online lessons rarely provide the same immediacy, and they also eliminate the possibility of staying after school for extra help, retaking a test, or visiting a learning centre where peers can assist with assignments. As a result, many students see their grades slip because their questions remain unanswered and their problems unsolved.

Second, if online learning becomes widespread, students will miss out on practicing their communication skills and building relationships with fellow pupils. Face‑to‑face interaction during lunch breaks, group projects, or casual conversations can inspire students and create a sense of belonging that makes school feel like a second home. These social ties also give access to personal advice from teachers and counselors. Studying alone at a computer can feel boring and isolating; teenagers already face high rates of stress, anxiety and depression, and the school environment often provides a distraction from home problems as well as a network of support. Without that environment, young people may feel lonely and less motivated to seek help.

Finally, remote classes can encourage a lax attitude toward study. At home, the physical presence of a teacher who can remind a student to stay focused or discourage dozing off is absent. The sense of obligation to complete and submit homework on time weakens, and opportunities for collaborative work—where teammates share ideas and motivate each other—are greatly reduced. Students who are accustomed to working alone may begin to think they can ignore deadlines or lower their effort, which undermines the seriousness required for academic success.

In summary, online schooling is not a favourable approach for students because it does not provide the same quality of instruction, social interaction, and accountability found in a traditional school setting. Learners miss out on essential communication and social development, and they are more likely to treat their courses with insufficient seriousness, leading to poorer academic outcomes.

Some school districts now let high‑school pupils finish their studies a year ahead of the usual four‑year schedule. I think most teenagers who choose this route do so simply to get out of school as quickly as possible. Instead of spending the summer on a beach vacation or hanging out with friends, they sign up for extra classes just to shave a year off their timetable. It may sound attractive at first, but in the end the shortcut is hardly worthwhile.

Education is not always fun, yet the knowledge and skills acquired in school can open many doors later in life. Graduating a year earlier does not make a student any smarter or more capable than his peers; it is merely a way of skipping part of the high‑school experience. The extra year that most students spend in senior year brings valuable new experiences that help shape their future.

During the senior year students can attend college fairs, receive guidance on building their resumes, and take part in activities that prepare them for adulthood. Many people describe senior year as the “best” year because it offers a final push toward a successful future. Leaving school early means missing out on these enriching events, the camaraderie of classmates, and the traditions that mark the last year of high school. That final year serves as a bridge to adult life, giving students clearer goals and a stronger sense of direction.

Another reason I oppose early graduation is that the students who opt for it are often those who are disengaged from school. The type who skip classes, turn in assignments late, or chronically arrive tardy are the ones most likely to want an easy exit. High school is not a race, and success is earned through hard work, not by cutting corners. Some of these students head straight into low‑pay jobs such as fast‑food work, where earnings are modest and job security is limited. A solid education provides the foundation for better‑paying and more stable occupations, reducing the need to hop from one temporary job to another.

For the youngsters who really want to finish in three years, careful planning is essential, especially if they intend to apply to college. Many universities expect four years of high‑school coursework and may view a shortened record with suspicion, possibly rejecting the applicant. Colleges also look at the overall academic profile, and a three‑year transcript might raise questions about the student’s preparedness. Those who do not plan to attend college must also have a realistic plan for entering the workforce, rather than assuming that an early diploma will automatically guarantee a good job.

If I were to support the idea of allowing students to graduate early, I would limit it to those who truly excel academically—students with perfect attendance, high grades, and a clear career plan. Only individuals who have demonstrated exceptional readiness should be given this option, not those who simply want to escape school.

In conclusion, high schools should not readily permit students to finish a year early. The senior year offers essential experiences, guidance, and a final opportunity to mature before adulthood. While school may have its drawbacks, it remains the most reliable pathway to a rewarding career and a stable future.

School is a very important part **of** a person's life; however, it takes away most of **students'** and **teachers'** day. In a normal public middle school in Maryland, a student's first class starts at 8:15 in the morning and the last class ends at 3:00 p.m., which means that a student spends 7 hours and 25 minutes in school— a long time for a person to be receiving information nonstop. The school board should not extend the school day, because that would take time away from activities that students need or will need in the future, such as: students would have less time to do homework or study, students would have less time to participate in after‑school activities like sports, and students **would** have less time to volunteer in community events.

Students would have less time to do homework or study. Students already **spend** more than seven hours at school and usually **have** 6–8 classes that last 45 minutes each. From those 6–8 classes, at least **three** would have assigned homework, which means that the students would need time to complete their homework with accuracy. If the school days **were** extended, students would have less time to complete their homework, which means that their grades might **decrease** for missing assignments.

Students would have less time to participate in after‑school activities such as sports or clubs.

Every healthy person should exercise for at least 1 hour per day, and at school not every student takes physical education (P.E.) as a course, which leads to the thought that students might not **be** getting the necessary amount of exercise per day. Even if a student does take P.E., a normal class lasts 45 minutes, which is not enough for a healthy person. If the school board were to add one and a half hours to the school day, students would have less time to practice in an after‑school team. Clubs, just like sports, are a very big part of a school; clubs **show** students opportunities they usually would not get in a school day. If the school board were to extend the school day, students **who are part** of clubs would probably get less time to spend in those clubs.

Students will have less time to volunteer in community events. Community service is usually a requirement in most **curricula**. In past experiences I have had to complete 75 hours of community service; those hours were earned for volunteer work, like helping a teacher with younger students or helping a teacher organize her classroom before the school year, etc. Those acts were usually done after school and usually took around 2 hours. If the school board were to extend the school day, **students** would have less time to finish their community service and could eventually fail **because** of not enough volunteering hours.

Overall, it is just more **convenient** for the school board to not add any more hours to the school day so students can have more time for their other activities like sports, clubs, and community service.

School plays a central role in a person’s development, yet it occupies most of the day for both pupils and teachers. In a typical public middle school in Maryland, classes begin at 8:15 a.m. and finish at 3:00 p.m., meaning students spend roughly seven hours and twenty‑five minutes inside the building. That is a long stretch of continuous instruction, and extending the school day would cut into the time students need for other important activities. For this reason the school board should keep the current schedule, because a longer day would reduce the time available for homework, extracurricular pursuits such as sports and clubs, and community volunteering.

First, a longer school day would leave students with less opportunity to complete homework and study. Most learners already attend six to eight 45‑minute periods each day, and a large number of those courses assign regular homework. If the school day were lengthened, pupils would have even less time at home to finish assignments accurately, which could cause grades to slip and increase the likelihood of missed work.

Second, extending the schedule would impinge on after‑school activities. Health experts recommend at least an hour of exercise daily, yet not every student takes physical education, and the standard PE class lasts only 45 minutes—insufficient for a healthy routine. Adding an extra ninety minutes to the school day would mean less time for practice with sports teams. The same would happen with clubs, which provide valuable experiences that most cannot be accommodated during regular classes. A longer day would force club members to sacrifice the time they spend developing skills and building friendships.

Finally, community service would suffer. Many curricula require a certain number of volunteer hours; for example, I had to complete 75 hours by helping teachers, assisting younger pupils, or organizing classrooms. These activities usually take about two hours after school. If the school day were extended, students would have fewer evenings available to fulfil these obligations, potentially jeopardising their ability to meet the required service hours.

In sum, keeping the current length of the school day is the most practical choice. It allows students to balance academic work with sports, clubs and community service, all of which are essential for a well‑rounded education.

I know a girl whose father confiscated her phone for an entire school year, hoping it would improve her grades. Instead, she became rebellious, spent the time socialising, and ended up failing every subject. This example shows that outright bans can be counter‑productive, while controlled use supports the teaching‑learning process.

Cell phones also serve an important safety function. If a threatening situation arises—a lockdown, an intruder with a weapon, or a fire—students can call emergency services immediately. In more routine emergencies, such as severe weather, a quick call to family lets loved ones know the student’s condition. Prohibiting phones does not stop students from using them secretly; it simply pushes the behaviour out of the teacher’s sight and makes it harder to monitor.

In summary, permitting mobile phones in classrooms for educational reasons brings clear benefits that outweigh the potential drawbacks. While some still argue for a total ban, the advantages for learning, safety, and communication make a controlled allowance the wiser choice.

Moreover, some students have personal issues; for example, I sometimes cannot focus on my homework because a problem clouds my mind, making me feel stressed and unable to work. Also, some students have jobs after school. I have a job after school, and sometimes my tiredness is so great that it prevents me from finishing my homework. Having this experience, I think it would be really good for schools to allow students to use their cellphones for educational purposes.

Another reason is that students will have the chance to check their grades or assignments. Some students miss school and probably do not know if they have assignments, or they do not have time to check them at home. Most students forget easily that they have homework; for example, when I get home and start doing some chores, I may realize it is already time to sleep, so the next day I have no time to finish it. Therefore, it will be good for most students to check what they are missing during class, and they can ask the teacher for permission to work on it. They can also ask the teacher for help if they do not know how to do it. For instance, I had a friend for whom math is hard, so he checked his assignments in the classroom and asked the teacher for help to understand better; this would help students improve their grades.

Some people say that allowing the use of cellphones can have a negative effect because it will distract students; for example, some teachers claim that students will be texting or playing video games, so they will not pay attention in class. This is incorrect because students can learn in a better way that makes them feel comfortable. The point is to make them feel that they can learn in an interesting way. Some teachers let students play trivia games on their cellphones, so students can learn and have a good time doing it. They will learn better because most of the things students look up on their phones they are able to memorize. Perhaps previous generations think that too much technology, such as allowing cellphones in classrooms, is a bad idea because it will make our brains slow; this is not true—it just helps us learn in a better way.

In conclusion, allowing the use of cellphones in the classroom will have a positive effect because it will help students finish their school work or homework, check their grades and assignments, and learn better. We are the new generation and the future of the next one; we have the help of technology to gain better knowledge. The future is in our hands, and making it easier is our decision. educators are just finding better ways for us to learn and succeed in school and in life.

Allowing students to use their cellphones in class can have a beneficial impact on their learning, especially for those who rely on their devices every day. In other words, permitting mobile phones can make pupils feel more comfortable while completing their assignments, help them keep track of grades and tasks, and ultimately improve their academic performance.

One advantage of this policy is that it gives students more opportunity to finish classwork or homework during school hours. Many pupils receive a large amount of homework and simply need extra time to complete it. In addition, personal problems can distract a student’s mind and cause stress, making it hard to concentrate on schoolwork. Some learners also have part‑time jobs after school, which leaves them exhausted and short on time for their assignments. From my own experience, I believe that allowing the use of cellphones for educational purposes would help students in these situations to catch up on their tasks while they are still at school.

A second benefit is that phones enable learners to check their grades and assignment status instantly. Students who miss a lesson often do not know what work they have missed, and they may not have the chance to look it up at home. Forgetfulness is common; for example, I sometimes return home, start my chores, and then realize it’s already bedtime, leaving me no time to do my homework. If they can use their phones during class, students can quickly see which tasks are pending and ask the teacher for permission to work on them. They can also request help on topics they do not understand. A friend of mine, who struggles with mathematics, used his phone to look up the assigned problems and then asked the teacher for clarification, which improved his grades.

Critics argue that cellphone use in class is a source of distraction, claiming that pupils might text or play games instead of listening. However, this view overlooks the possibility of using the devices as learning tools. When teachers incorporate educational apps or trivia games into lessons, students can enjoy the material while reinforcing their knowledge. Modern students are adept at remembering information they encounter on their phones, and the old belief that technology “slows the brain” is no longer accurate; instead, it can enhance the way we process information.

In conclusion, permitting the use of cellphones in the classroom can positively affect education by helping students complete their work, monitor their progress, and learn more effectively. As the generation that will shape the future, we benefit from technology that supports our learning. The decision to integrate phones into school life is a step toward more efficient and engaging education, helping us succeed both academically and beyond.

Almost everyone spends time at the beach or in a swimming pool, and I have often thought about which activity is the most enjoyable. For me, joining a swimming club is the best choice. Swimming is enjoyable because it calms me when I am angry, because I can share the water with friends, and because it makes exercising feel easier and more exciting.

First, swimming helps me relax whenever I feel upset or down. Last year, after school had finished and everyone had gone home, I jumped into the pool and started swimming. The sound of the water splashing against my feet, the gentle waves hitting the side of the pool, and the rush of water as I emerged all made me feel happy and alive. Another time, during a field trip to the beach, I felt sad because I didn’t want the vacation to end. I changed into my swimwear, took my camera, and walked along the sand. The sound of the waves crashing and the birds singing created a peaceful atmosphere, and I spent a very calming and enjoyable day. These experiences show how swimming can soothe my mood.

Second, swimming is fun because I can do it with friends and even meet new ones. When I swim alone I am fine, but the moment my friends join me the water becomes a place for laughs and games. We try tricks, race each other, and sometimes bump heads while swimming underwater, which always ends in laughter when we surface. Having a buddy also makes learning to swim easier; a friend can help you stay afloat or correct a technique, turning a difficult skill into something enjoyable. Practicing together is far more pleasant than doing it alone, and that is another reason why swimming is a great activity.

Finally, exercising in the water feels more exciting than other forms of fitness. I took swimming lessons every Friday after school. At first I wasn’t enthusiastic, but by the third session I started looking forward to it. I used to weigh 145 pounds at ten years old, and after regular swimming my weight dropped to 111 pounds. The progress was not obvious at first because I was focused only on losing weight, not on improving my strokes. As I became more passionate and determined, my swimming skills improved and the pounds fell off. The fun I had in the water kept me motivated, and swimming has since made me happier overall.

In summary, swimming is more exciting and easier as a form of exercise, it allows me to have fun with friends, and it helps me calm down when I am angry. These are the reasons why I consider a swimming club to be an enjoyable activity, and I hope more people discover how beneficial it can be.

To achieve a better life we inevitably encounter difficulties—failures—that can make us want to quit the very things that could lead us to success. The key role of failure is that without it we would not learn. When we mess up, we discover what went wrong, and that knowledge helps us avoid the same mistake later. In other words, each error becomes a lesson that moves us closer to the right path.

Then I told myself, “You will be okay; you will do what you love and make your parents proud.” By adopting a positive mindset and correcting my actions, I overcame the depression, even though some anxiety remained. This experience showed me that failure can bring hopelessness and a loss of drive, but if you keep believing in yourself, those feelings can be turned into hope, enthusiasm, and faith that nothing will stop you from succeeding.

Failures are essentially extra challenges on the road to the summit. To reach the top of a mountain and see the ocean beyond, you must keep climbing despite the obstacles, traps, and even people who want to see you fall. Some individuals cannot comprehend the purpose of failure, so they let it halt their progress.

In conclusion, I agree that success consists of moving from one failure to the next. Even when hope or enthusiasm wanes, we must persist in pursuing our goals. When we view failure as a necessary part of the journey, it becomes a stepping stone toward a successful life.

They claim that what you do, the words you choose, and the way you look reveal exactly who you are, and that these factors are difficult to change once a judgment has been made. When you encounter someone for the first time, your conduct is paramount. Actions speak louder than words, and the way you behave cannot be erased from that initial encounter. If you act rudely or are unkind, the other person will quickly label you as unpleasant and will likely avoid further interaction. Therefore, it is essential to present yourself politely from the start.

The language you use also influences the impression you make. Swearing or using harsh expressions can suggest that you lack social skills, whereas speaking clearly and respectfully helps build trust. Even if you tend to stutter, trying to speak calmly can improve the perception others form of you. Occasionally, people are generous enough to give a second chance, but it is better not to rely on that generosity. Likewise, gestures such as talking with your hands should be kept moderate, as they can distract from the conversation.

Appearance is perhaps the most immediate factor in a first impression. What you look like on the outside—and, to a lesser extent, the confidence you project—often determines whether someone deems you approachable. A sloppy or disheveled look may cause others to assume you are careless or untrustworthy, while a neat appearance can make a positive impact. Although inner qualities matter, most people form a quick judgment based largely on what they see.

There are occasions when a first impression can be revised. Bad days happen, and a single mishap does not necessarily define a person. Some individuals understand that a poor initial encounter may not reflect the person’s true character and may be willing to reconsider. Nonetheless, the original impression tends to linger, making it hard to overturn completely.

In conclusion, many believe that first impressions are virtually impossible to change, and I share that opinion. Our actions, the words we utter, and our appearance all contribute to the image that sticks in someone’s mind. Because people constantly meet new individuals, it is wise to be mindful of how we behave, speak, and look, ensuring that the first impression we give is a favourable one.

Thomas Jefferson once observed that “wonderful things may be accomplished if we are constantly active.” I disagree with that idea; I believe that inactivity always has a purpose. To complete any task we need regular breaks, and without them our bodies would simply shut down.

First of all, modern life already recognizes the need for rest: we have weekends—Saturday and Sunday—to recover. Our bodies cannot operate indefinitely without a pause; without downtime we would quickly become exhausted and unable to sleep, as the pressure builds up. Even animals take time off after a hard day's work before they can move again, showing that rest is natural and essential.

Secondly, continuous activity can be dangerous. While we might be working, we can start to drift off or make mistakes that lead to accidents. Depending on the nature of the job, fatigue can cause injuries, and in extreme cases it can even result in loss of life—whether while driving or performing other tasks.

Some people argue that nonstop effort yields more results because it allows us to finish projects faster. They claim that constant work helps us learn quickly and that, for example, a construction crew could complete a building in less time if they never stopped. Realising the importance of face‑to‑face interaction, Alex decided to return to a normal classroom, where the possibility of making friends is built into the daily routine.

Second, schools give access to clubs and extracurricular activities that are rarely available through remote lessons. Whether it is sports teams, music ensembles, debate clubs or science societies, these groups not only provide enjoyment but also help students discover future career interests and develop teamwork skills. A teenager who loves football, for instance, can join the school team, improve his abilities, and possibly earn a scholarship. Such experiences are crucial for personal growth and for exploring paths that might shape a future profession.

When a concept is difficult, a student can ask questions on the spot and receive explanations tailored to their needs. I firmly believe that extending the school day is a bad idea. My opposition is not based solely on being a pupil; it concerns the impact on every student, as well as on teachers and the school itself.  

First, longer days would make students exhausted. Spending many continuous hours in the same building drains energy and makes it difficult to stay focused. When fatigue sets in, learning suffers and grades are likely to drop. Moreover, an extended timetable would leave little time for homework, test preparation, or extracurricular activities, which are essential for a balanced education.  

Teachers would also feel the strain. Many educators have families and responsibilities outside of work, and a longer day would reduce the time they can spend with their own children or attend to personal matters. This could lead to increased stress and lower morale among staff, which in turn affects the quality of instruction.  

Students often have appointments that cannot be moved to the afternoon. For example, I must see my orthodontist every month in the morning, which means I miss several classes and then have to catch up on a large amount of work. Adding extra hours would make it harder to arrange such appointments at convenient times, causing more missed lessons and a heavier workload later on.  

Health issues present another problem. When a student falls ill and has to stay home, they already miss valuable instruction; a longer school day would only increase the amount of material they need to recover. This places additional pressure on teachers to provide extra support and on the school to supply more resources—more meals, more paper, more bathroom supplies, and even more administrative paperwork such as updated agendas and pass slips.  

Finally, extending the day would create practical difficulties for the community. All students would leave school at the same time as younger pupils, leading to heavier traffic, more bus congestion, and a higher risk of accidents on the roads.  

In summary, lengthening the school day would tire students, lower academic performance, burden teachers, and generate logistical and safety concerns for the entire school system. The board should reconsider this proposal and listen to the opinions of students, parents, and staff before making any changes.

When it comes to choosing between working alone or working in a team, I firmly believe that collaboration offers far more advantages. First of all, a group allows you to share the workload, assign different tasks to each member, and gain a deeper understanding of the subject matter. If you encounter difficulties, a teammate is likely to notice and offer assistance, explaining the problem in a way that helps you grasp the solution. Because everyone had a clear role, we completed the work by the end of the lesson and earned an A.

Your teammates may discover sources or insights you had not considered, making the topic clearer and enriching your overall knowledge. This broader perspective is also useful when preparing for tests or quizzes, as the discussion and shared discoveries reinforce learning.

In short, working in a group lets you learn more about the subject, reduces the amount of work you have to do by yourself, and provides helpful support when concepts are unclear. These reasons show why teamwork is far more beneficial than solitary study.

The question of whether teenagers should be subject to a curfew is a hot topic in our city council. Many parents and officials argue that keeping young people safe after dark is essential, especially because the world does not feel as secure as it once did. The council is currently debating whether to introduce a legal curfew for minors, and the discussion raises several important points: will a curfew make teens break the law simply by being out after a certain hour, and will such a rule actually protect them or merely restrict their freedom?

One reason the council is considering a curfew is the desire to prevent teenagers from getting hurt or putting themselves in danger at a young age. Officials also want to shield youths from the negative influences that can be found in the streets at night. Finally, they hope to reduce incidents of under‑age drinking and other risky behaviours that some teens engage in when they are unsupervised. These concerns form the core of the council’s argument for a curfew.

If a curfew were enacted, does that automatically mean any teenager on the streets after the set hour is committing a crime? Opinions differ. In my view, the legality depends on the reason for being out. A teen who is working late or responding to an emergency would not be violating the law, nor would a young person who is accompanied by an adult. However, a teenager who is simply out socialising, partying or hanging with friends without adult supervision would be breaking the curfew. Thus, whether a teen is breaking the law after dark hinges on the purpose of their outing.

Do curfews actually keep young people out of trouble, or do they unfairly intrude on their lives? Many teenagers would argue that a curfew limits their independence and prevents them from enjoying normal social activities. On the other hand, a curfew can provide a safety net, because nighttime can bring unpredictable dangers. A lot of teens tend to leave the house at night without telling their parents, which is risky. They need to consider whether the potential benefits of staying out late outweigh the possible hazards. Even if a teen feels that nothing bad will happen, there is always a chance they are wrong, and a curfew can help reduce that risk.

In summary, the council’s debate reflects two opposing views. Some citizens believe a legal curfew is necessary to protect adolescents from injury and trouble, while others think it infringes on personal freedom. Whether a teen who is out after the curfew is breaking the law depends on the circumstances—work, emergencies, or adult supervision are acceptable reasons, whereas attending parties or simply hanging out with friends is not. Ultimately, the purpose of a curfew is to keep young people safe, but it must be balanced against the desire for independence that teenagers naturally seek.

Who doesn't want to be left in the house all day using an electronic device with online access? Although students save money and time by taking classes from home. It is not beneficial to learn online because students lose focus of what they are learning and tend to easily get distracted when they're in their house, students can't have a one on one conversation with a teacher nor discuss with classmates, and students could also face technical difficulties when attending online classes from home.

Losing focus has a big impact in learning. For example, my friend Generic_Name sent me a text message last month, right when I started studying for my history mid-term exam. I responded back to Generic_Name's text, and without realizing we kept on messaging past midnight. This shows how easily students get distracted at home with a cellular device and how easy it is to lose focus. The next morning I decided to get to school an hour early and review one on one with my teacher.

Secondly, taking classes online doesn't just mean you don't have a physical teacher or instructor that you can question lively, but also means that it will be challenging to find answers to your questions. I remember in my sophomore year a kid in our econ class named Generic_Name was really sick for a while so he had ended up taking classes online. Generic_Name was a straight A student, always was first to answer the teachers questions and he also used to ask questions. Thankfully Generic_Name healed towards the end of the year and I asked him if he benefited and if he recommends attending classes from home. The straight A student Generic_Name said it was a real challenge to take the class online and he finished the class a month after he should have with a B- average. Generic_Name had also said that one of the most difficult parts about attending a class online was his laptop not functioning at all times, and not having a teacher you can talk and converse with one on one.

Finally, using your personal computer and internet connection can always be an issue. You can't always depend on your computer, not just the computers but even people aren't perfect. Another main problem Generic_Name had when attending classes online was his laptop and network connection. Generic_Name explained that he always faced technical difficulties. When his laptop wasn't functioning right, the only thing he could do was to stop the lesson and wait for his dad to get the laptop repaired, which took time. Each month, either his laptop or internet connection would not cooperate, so he finished the class a month later than everyone.

In conclusion, Everyone would like to save money and time by taking classes from home. But getting distracted, not asking your teacher questions when you need to, and wasting money on laptop repair is not worth it at all. Learning from a far distance could also be an option but when asking if it is beneficial, we can say that it is not by looking at the listed reasoning.

However, studying over the internet is not as effective as traditional classroom teaching. The incident showed how easy it is to become distracted by a phone or other devices when you are not in a classroom setting.
