They say the you should never judge a book by its cover and, especially regarding people, its true. In this case, the cover is not necessary meaning the appearance, but the first impression of another person. Like the cover of a book, first impressions are not always as appealing as what is really there. its not until after you start "reading" or get to know someone, when you really find out that what you see is not always what you get. There are several factors that can affect the first impression that one receives from another. Differing personality, situations and representation of a person, make impressions often the worst means of judging people.

A person's personality has a big effect on the first impressions that they emit. Everybody is different but when it comes down to it first impressions are really based off of whether you are shy or not. I met my best friend after moving during my junior year, at my new high school. Before i knew her, she never said a word to me or anyone else in the classes that she was kind of odd, but then realized that I was the same way, i didn't talk to many people either because of my personality. I knew that I was shy person and after I get to know someone, I put down my front and show my true colors. I thought that maybe she would be same way. After starting to talk to her a little more each day, our friendship grew and I learned that she wasn't odd at all, but just like me an outgoing person hidden by their shyness. Some people like me and my friend, are shy and put up a reserved and quiet front when facing new people. Based on my first impressions of my friend, I thought something that was far from the truth. One who has a shy personality might in reality be outgoing, but uncomfortable showing it at first, making the first impression of that person a mistaken one.

Your first impression of someone is not suitable because you do not know the situation they may be in. When seeing or meeting someone new, you have no idea the kind of day,

difficulties or kind of disappointment that person may be experiencing. People often repeat the saying that you should never judge a book by its cover, and this is especially true when it comes to judging other people. In this context, “cover” does not refer to physical appearance but to the first impression we form of someone. Like a book’s cover, an initial impression can be misleading; only after we start “reading”—that is, getting to know the person—do we discover the real substance beneath. Several elements influence those first impressions: personality traits, current circumstances, and the way a person presents themselves. Because of these factors, first impressions are frequently an unreliable way to assess others.

A person’s character heavily shapes the impression they give off. Everyone is unique, yet many first impressions are rooted in whether someone is shy or confident. I met my best friend after moving to a new high school in my junior year. At first, she never spoke to anyone and seemed a bit odd, but I soon realized that I was the same way—quiet and reserved. Knowing that I was shy, I lowered my guard once I started talking to her, and I discovered that she was not odd at all; she was simply an outgoing person hidden behind shyness. Both of us tend to present a calm, silent front when meeting new people. My initial judgment of her was far from the truth; a shy demeanor can mask an otherwise lively personality, leading to a mistaken first impression.

Another reason first impressions can be deceptive is that we rarely know what the other person is experiencing at the moment. When we meet someone new, we have no insight into their day, their recent losses, or any personal struggles they may be facing. They might be dealing with grief, new responsibilities, or everyday stressors that occupy their mind. These circumstances can create a barrier to social interaction, making it unlikely that a positive first impression is a priority for them.

I experienced this personally on the first day of my senior year. I rushed into my first class, focused solely on finding a seat, even though I had plenty of time. At lunch I ate quickly and alone, eager to get to my next class. My main concern was not being late or making a good impression; I was simply trying to manage my schedule. As a result, my classmates assumed I was nervous and unsociable, when in fact my behavior was driven by the pressure of the situation, not by my personality.

In summary, many factors shape the way we perceive others at first glance: personality, current circumstances, and the manner in which a person happens to present themselves. Because these judgments are based on limited information, they are often inaccurate. If friendships depended only on first impressions, far fewer would exist. True understanding comes from getting to know someone beyond the initial “cover,” allowing us to appreciate their real values and character.

However, this type of studying carries the risk that students will forget what they have learned during the break because they tried to cram too much information—math, science, English, and history—into a short time. Even though students who cram for tests or assignments can earn good grades, they must review the material again shortly afterward. Therefore, a long summer vacation is better than a short one.

As I mentioned, summer break is the best time for students during the whole year. Almost every student makes their own plans for what they should do. However, students often feel uneasy before the summer vacation, so some want to reduce the summer break and lengthen the other breaks. It is not a bad idea to make such changes, but they must understand that longer winter and fall breaks would affect their entire summer plan. They also need to realize that they can do many more things with a longer break. How people use their time varies, but a longer break provides a wider range of opportunities.

Students usually look forward to a long summer break, hoping it will be the most enjoyable part of the school year. While some argue that the vacation should be shortened and the other holidays extended, I believe that a lengthy summer holiday combined with shorter pauses in winter and spring is the better arrangement. My position rests on two main points: a long break makes it easier for students to plan extended activities, and a short school term followed by a brief holiday is less effective for learning.

First, a long vacation gives students the chance to organize trips and visits that require considerable preparation. Many youngsters want to travel abroad or spend time with relatives who live far away. When the break is short, they must worry about unfinished assignments and looming exams, which limits how much they can enjoy the experience. A brief holiday often forces families to rush, leaving them dissatisfied and wishing they had more time. If a student’s family lives in another country, the opportunity to stay together for an extended period becomes especially valuable, because the next meeting might not happen for months or even years. The ability to make the most of these moments is a strong argument for keeping the summer vacation long.

Second, a short school term followed by a quick break disrupts the rhythm of learning. Just as athletes follow a regular season without an abrupt pause, students benefit from a continuous schedule. Those who study music, for instance, improve by practicing a little every day; a week off after a short term does not help them retain what they have learned. Maintaining a steady routine during the school months helps students keep their knowledge fresh and their skills sharp. Returning to class after a long break may be challenging, but it is preferable to the inefficiency created by a compressed academic period and a fleeting holiday.

Admittedly, some learners thrive on intensive study sessions and prefer brief vacations. However, this approach carries the risk of information loss. When large amounts of material—math, science, language, history—are crammed into a short span, students may achieve good grades initially but soon forget much of what they have studied. A lengthy summer break reduces this risk by allowing material to settle and giving students time to review at a more relaxed pace.

In summary, the summer holiday is the most valuable part of the academic year for the majority of students. While restructuring the calendar to lengthen winter and fall breaks might seem appealing, it would inevitably compromise the benefits that a long summer vacation provides. Longer breaks give students the freedom to travel, to spend meaningful time with family, and to maintain a more effective learning rhythm throughout the rest of the year.

The most reasonable approach is to choose our own character traits, because it makes the most sense and most people can regulate their emotions.

There are different types of character traits, for example funny, exciting, joyful, and many more. Our character traits are formed by our own influence and actions, which cause them to react to different emotions. For the most part we are able to control our emotions, but sometimes they become unmanageable.

Character traits can be used in many different ways. However, some traits we can’t control; they happen to us because we sometimes lack self‑control. For example, anger, sadness, and depression can make us lose control because we are unable to regulate them. These emotions can be dangerous when we are out of control; we may do something terrible without realizing it. That is why character traits can be good or bad.

Some people support the idea of picking their character traits for themselves, while others think traits are not under our control. Those who decide to choose their traits say that when they act they can feel their emotions in control and do what best fits them. On the other hand, people who think character traits are not under their control say that when they are working or doing anything, their emotions just happen and they can’t regulate them, often because of bad emotions like anger or sadness.

There are many reasons people discuss character traits. Not all traits are good, nor are they all bad; it mainly depends on the person who is controlling them. For those who are unable to control their traits, a few simple actions can prevent their emotions from taking over. That’s why controlling your own character traits is different from having them shaped by external influences.

There are several ways in which we acquire our character traits. One possibility is that we deliberately select the qualities we want to develop, choosing them for ourselves. Another view holds that our character is shaped by forces beyond our control, so we cannot decide what we become. The most convincing position is that we should take responsibility for our own traits, because most people are able to manage their emotions and direct their behaviour.

Character traits come in many forms—humorous, lively, cheerful, and countless others. They are largely the result of personal influence and the actions we take, which in turn affect how we respond emotionally. Generally we can keep our feelings under control, although there are occasions when emotions slip away from us.

These traits can be applied in various situations, but some aspects of our character seem to resist conscious regulation. For instance, feelings such as anger, sadness or depression often arise without our permission and can make us act irrationally. When these emotions dominate, they may lead to dangerous or regrettable actions. Consequently, character traits can have both positive and negative effects.

Supporters of self‑determined character argue that when people deliberately shape their traits they can experience emotions in a manageable way and act in accordance with their goals. Opponents claim that personality is dictated by external influences; they say that emotions simply appear while they work or engage in activities, leaving them powerless to control them. In many cases, negative emotions such as rage or sorrow are blamed for this lack of control.

Overall, discussions about character traits reveal that they are not inherently good or bad; their value depends on how the individual handles them. Those who struggle to manage their feelings can improve by adopting simple strategies and preventing emotions from taking over. This is why deliberately guiding one’s own character differs from letting it be shaped solely by outside forces.

The discussion centres on whether students should be allowed to use mobile phones in class for learning. Some argue that phones are a distraction because once students have them they immediately start texting friends. Others claim that phones can be useful educational tools that help students complete their work. I side with the view that allowing phones in the classroom will mainly divert attention, reduce concentration, and hinder productive work.

First, phones tend to pull students away from the lesson by providing easy access to music and social media. Young people often open Snapchat, Instagram or Facebook the moment a teacher asks them to take out their devices. Personally, the first thing I do is send a message to a friend, which quickly leads to laziness and a loss of motivation for the tasks at hand. When I do not have a phone, I feel more responsible for completing homework and class activities. In a recent group project, one of my teammates kept his phone on, listening to music. While the rest of us followed the teacher’s instructions and presented our part, he was clueless and ultimately received a failing grade for the assignment.

Second, having phones in class makes it harder for students to listen to the teacher. The constant temptation to check notifications or watch a video means many pupils stop paying attention, which frustrates the teacher and slows the lesson down. I have found myself distracted by a favourite TV show during a lecture, and I know most classmates would only stay focused if their parents exerted pressure. Without that external push, I doubt anyone would follow the teacher’s directions, leading to poor performance and possible failure in the course.

Third, the presence of phones can discourage students from doing their work altogether. Knowing that a device is available often encourages procrastination and a lack of effort. In my junior year, I used my phone while conducting a chemistry experiment; I accidentally spilled a chemical on it, ruining the phone and drawing my parents’ ire. They scolded me for being irresponsible and warned that my careless use of the phone would hurt my grades.

In summary, permitting mobile phones in classrooms is unwise because it fosters distraction, reduces attention, and prevents students from completing their assignments. Phones do not make students smarter; dedication to studying and listening to teachers does. Education remains the key to success, and staying focused on learning is essential for a responsible and prosperous future.

Should schools control how many extracurricular activities you take? There should be a certain extent to which schools can control how many out‑of‑school activities you are in. The student's family should be the deciding factor in whether you leave or not. If you start to fail classes, your parents can ask the school to take you out of some activities, or if your attendance at the meetings looks poor, the school helps decide what happens to the student.

First of all, I think there should be a limit on what you can enroll in, but it should always be up to the student and their family since that is a major factor in deciding what to do. If the family thinks the child has no time for homework or to study for an upcoming test, they should talk to the student about the issue and hear what the student has to say. If the family decides to let the child continue, that decision is theirs; but if they choose to take their child out of the extracurricular activities, they must notify the child's guidance counselor and the main person in the activity.

However, if the student starts to fail classes or most of the grades keep dropping, the student's guidance counselor should talk to the student and see why. If they see too many extracurricular activities, there should be a discussion with the student to determine which ones can be dropped until the grades improve. This should encourage the student that, if they want to be part of the activities, they must be able to maintain their grades.

Lastly, if the child's attendance at the meetings is poor and inconsistent, they should not be allowed to participate in the extracurricular activities. The child should be allowed to miss up to five meetings per month without any consequences. By making the child leave the club and notifying their parents of the reason, the child can then be removed from the activity. Without further justification, the child could be suspended from attending meetings for a certain amount of time.

In conclusion, the school should have very little say in the decision of a student being a part of an extracurricular activity. In other words, the families have the most say in the deciding factor unless the student's grades are dropping or they start to fail some classes, their attendance at meetings is poor, or they simply do not attend any meetings.

Schools can set some limits on the number of extracurricular activities a pupil takes, but the main decision should rest with the student and their family. Parents are the ones who know best whether their child has enough time for homework and test preparation, and they should discuss any concerns with their child. If a family decides that their child should continue with the activities, they must inform the guidance counselor and the leader of each activity. Conversely, if they choose to withdraw their child, the same parties should be notified.

When a student’s academic performance begins to slip and grades start to fall, the guidance counselor should intervene. By meeting with the student, the counselor can determine whether the extracurricular load is the cause. If it appears that too many activities are affecting study time, the counselor can suggest dropping some until the grades improve. This approach motivates students to keep a balance between participation and academic achievement.

Regular attendance is another important factor. If a pupil frequently misses meetings or shows unreliable attendance, they should not be permitted to stay in the activity. Missing a few sessions—up to five per month—might be acceptable, but consistent absences should lead to a discussion with the parents and possibly removal from the club. In serious cases, the student could be suspended from attending meetings for a set period.

In summary, schools should have only a limited role in deciding whether a student can join an extracurricular activity. The primary authority belongs to the family, unless the student’s grades start to decline, their attendance becomes poor, or they fail to attend meetings regularly.

Most people would prefer to finish high school a year early and move on to college or work, but some argue that a full four‑year programme is essential. Young people need time to mature, and completing the standard four years of secondary education should be compulsory for several reasons.

Firstly, school equips students with the skills they will need in adulthood, and many of them benefit from an additional year to solidify their plans for the future. If they were to leave after only three years, they might have to abandon sports or other extracurricular activities, devoting all of their energy solely to passing the required classes.

Secondly, a four‑year experience helps teenagers become more independent. During this time they learn how to organise their study time, balance homework with hobbies, and become reliable and confident in meeting deadlines. A three‑year schedule leaves little room for breaks, so students may not get enough rest to perform well and stay healthy.

Some people claim that three years of high school provides sufficient knowledge for entering the real world. However, those who stay for the full four years gain a clearer sense of their future goals and are better prepared for the challenges that await after graduation. In short, completing the four‑year high school programme gives students a deeper understanding of what lies ahead and equips them more effectively for life after school.

Having school lessons at home rather than attending a physical campus offers several advantages for students. First, learners can study at a speed that suits them, without being forced to keep up with a class timetable. They no longer have to rise early in the morning, which often leaves them feeling tired; when students arrive at school exhausted they are less likely to concentrate and complete assignments.

Schools would also be insulated from disruptions such as snow days, since learning can continue uninterrupted online.

Parents can also monitor progress more directly, seeing the work their children complete each day. I think students gain more from working in groups than from tackling tasks alone.  

Even my friend, whom I’ll call Alex, is very capable of handling schoolwork by himself, but he still sometimes needs a hand to grasp certain concepts. I, too, can manage a project on my own, yet I often appreciate another person’s viewpoint.  

These experiences show why collaboration is valuable. Take Alex, for example. He is one of the top students in our class, consistently earning high grades, yet he once tried to complete a teacher‑assigned project solo. He handed it in on time, but the teacher marked it as a failure because he had misinterpreted the question. After discussing it with her, Alex learned that his misunderstanding cost him points. Two weeks later, the teacher gave us another project and explicitly told Alex to work with someone. Reluctantly, he paired up with a classmate. On the due date, their joint effort earned a perfect score. The teacher explained that the success came from combining different perspectives, which clarified the task and filled gaps in each student’s knowledge.  

A similar situation happened to me in high school. We first completed a two‑part assignment individually. After turning in our work, the teacher asked us to choose partners and compare our papers. My partner, Alex, and I discovered that—even though we wrote on the same topic—our papers were very different. The teacher then instructed us to rewrite the assignment together. When all groups finished, she had us rotate the papers and choose the one that made the most sense. Every group selected the collaborative version, noting that single‑author papers felt one‑sided and lacked balance.  

Some people argue that working alone is better, but both Alex and I have learned that many problems benefit from at least two viewpoints. If I had continued to rely solely on my own ideas, my understanding would be narrower, and Alex’s academic path would likely have taken a different turn.  

Developing teamwork and listening skills lets us make decisions with others rather than in isolation. I suggest you speak with your teachers about increasing group projects, and discuss with your parents how these abilities apply outside school. You’ll be surprised at how often you use them and how much smoother life becomes when you don’t have to decide everything on your own.

Technology brings both benefits and drawbacks, but its influence on human interaction has become increasingly harmful. I believe that the way we rely on gadgets and online platforms has led to a decline in real‑world contact, which in turn contributes to depression and isolation, distorts our sense of reality, and damages both physical and mental health.

One of the most serious consequences of excessive technology use is the rise of loneliness and depressive feelings. Many young people are bullied on social‑media sites, and the constant stream of negative comments can push them into emotional crisis. Some teenagers withdraw from school and avoid friends, preferring to stay hidden behind a screen. Video games are another common trap; countless individuals become so absorbed that they neglect their relationships and responsibilities, spending hours alone in front of a console. Even simple habits like checking a smartphone all day limit opportunities for face‑to‑face conversation, reinforcing a cycle of isolation that fuels depression.

A second problem is that technology can blur the line between the virtual world and reality. The internet makes it easy for anyone to spread misinformation, and many children absorb misleading videos on platforms such as YouTube without questioning their truthfulness. Some adults also fall prey to conspiracy theories that claim governments are using advanced devices to control minds. Moreover, immersive games can lead players to believe that the actions they perform online are acceptable in real life, which can result in risky behavior when they try to imitate virtual stunts or scenarios.

Physical health suffers as well. Ophthalmologists warn that prolonged screen time strains the eyes and may lead to long‑term vision problems. Constant exposure to digital media also influences how people dress, speak, and act, as they attempt to emulate online personalities. This can erode personal identity and promote anxiety about fitting in. In extreme cases, individuals have tried to replicate dangerous stunts they saw on video, only to end up injured and hospitalized. The sedentary lifestyle encouraged by gadgets further reduces exercise, contributing to obesity and cardiovascular issues.

While technology undeniably provides conveniences—saving lives in emergencies, improving communication, and streamlining many tasks—its drawbacks outweigh these advantages when it replaces human contact. Machines can fail, leading to accidents, and the environmental toll of manufacturing and disposing of electronic devices adds to global pollution. Relying too heavily on technology diminishes our ability to solve problems independently and can make everyday life more stressful, not less.

In conclusion, the over‑reliance on technology has a profoundly negative impact on society. It encourages isolation and depression, disconnects people from reality, and harms both mental and physical well‑being. Although we cannot eliminate technology entirely, we must recognize its risks and strive to maintain genuine human interaction alongside its use. Ignoring these issues will only allow the problems to grow deeper.

I strongly disagree with Emerson’s claim that individuality is inherently valuable. My experience shows that close relationships—parents, siblings, and close friends who feel like family—are essential. They make life easier and allow us to grow and adapt. Without these connections, a person would likely end up isolated and lonely. Trusting one another is crucial for getting through life’s challenges.

When I was about twelve or thirteen, I constantly struggled with my schoolwork and felt a deep sense of unease each morning. I doubted my ability to improve academically or to make friends, and I spent most of my time caring only for myself. After school I would come home feeling depressed and worthless. Eventually I realized that I needed the support of others. With the encouragement of teachers, classmates, and family members, I began to change. My improvement was not caused by some external force reshaping me; rather, living among people gave me the chance to develop on my own. That gradual transformation proved that anyone can change when they are surrounded by supportive others.

Another problem of complete isolation is boredom. When you are alone, you have no one to talk to, no one to share activities with, and life can feel dull. In contrast, having many friends allows you to enjoy a wide range of experiences—playing games, traveling together, and learning new lessons from each other. Some people claim that society is indifferent and uncaring, but that view ignores the fact that relationships can have both positive and negative effects. Negative people can drag others down, which often leads them to become lonely because they push people away. Yet this cycle can be broken simply by choosing to seek help and surrounding yourself with supportive individuals.

In summary, extreme individuality can be harmful and steer people toward an undesirable path. Human connections are necessary because we lift each other up; no one is worthless. Leaving someone to fend for themselves is tragic, while offering help makes both the giver and the receiver stronger and makes life smoother. At the same time, you should not allow anyone to force you to become someone you are not—being yourself is important, but being completely alone is not. You are the main character of your own story, and your life belongs to you.

Imagine being able to join your lessons without leaving the comfort of your own home. While some argue that online education offers little advantage, I contend that distance learning can be highly beneficial. It not only supports students with disabilities but also provides an alternative learning environment for those who struggle with traditional schooling.

Critics of remote education often point to potential drawbacks. They worry that students might miss out on face‑to‑face social interaction, which could affect their future relationships. Others claim that relying on virtual platforms may make learners too dependent on technology. For instance, a friend of mine prefers to attend classes online and spends most of his free time playing video games instead of interacting with family or friends.

Nevertheless, remote learning can be a lifeline for pupils with physical impairments. When I lived in Honduras, I knew a girl named Ana who could not walk because of a leg condition. Every morning her mother had to push her wheelchair 30 minutes from home to school, and throughout the day Ana had to maneuver the wheelchair to reach each classroom, the bathroom, and the playground. Even after waking up early, she often arrived late and was exhausted, which made it difficult for her to concentrate. Her tardiness was not her fault; the commute drained her energy and sleep. If Ana had been able to study from home, she could have rested properly and focused better on her lessons.

Distance education also opens up new perspectives for students who feel disconnected from conventional classrooms. My cousin Luis, for example, was disengaged and received poor grades at the start of the year. He complained about early wake‑up times, school lunches, and believed he wasn’t cut out for school. After speaking with his counselor, he switched to online classes. Since then, his grades have improved dramatically, and he describes the experience as “amazing.” Luis simply needed a different teaching approach, and remote learning provided it.

In summary, online learning offers valuable support for students with disabilities, ensuring their needs are recognized, and it gives those who feel out of place in a traditional setting a chance to thrive. By embracing distance education, we can create a more inclusive and flexible system that serves all learners, regardless of how they best absorb knowledge.

For example, when you meet someone, your first impression might be that she is haughty and slightly mean. However, when you get to know her better you will discover that she just had a bad day and that she is pleasant and sociable. Occasionally the reverse occurs: a person appears affable but in reality is not, so your first impression was erroneous. It is unwise to cling to a first impression because it is frequently mistaken.  

Moreover, appearance, behavior, or demeanor can alter an impression. If a person does not smile and seems rude but in fact is the kindest individual, the situation will feel awkward because you presumed she was unkind. Sometimes a person acquires a poor reputation because of the first impression he projects, and it is not his fault; some individuals simply do not smile often. You may feel disappointed because you never got to know the person beyond your initial impression.  

First impressions are not limited to people; they also apply to situations or objects. For instance, if you are in a library and want to purchase a book, the first thing you will do is glance at the cover. If it is attractive, you will more readily select it over a volume with a plain black cover and only a title, because of your first impression. Yet that impression may be wrong because you did not take the time to read the synopsis, and you will soon find that the attractive book is actually dull, whereas the modest black book is genuinely engaging. An object can look appealing yet possess inferior quality. The first impression consists of the color and shape of the object, much like the appearance and attitude of a person.  

In conclusion, I would say that the first impression is sometimes accurate but most often mistaken. In my view, you should not rely on your first impression of a person, as it is usually faulty. You must get to know the individual to form your own judgment. It is natural to have a first impression, akin to judging, but you should not make a habit of clinging to it.

If others dictate choices, satisfaction drops because the selected options serve the decision‑maker’s agenda rather than the individual’s desires. This reliance can lead to numerous problems in life, as the person never learns to assess situations or make judgments on their own.

The idea of shortening the summer holiday and extending the winter break raises several questions. Would such a shift be welcomed by pupils? Would it benefit their learning? 

Many students would probably oppose the change. Winter weather can be extremely cold, making it difficult to spend time outdoors, go for walks or play sports. While the summer break allows children to enjoy the sunshine and visit various places, a longer winter vacation could keep them inside for most of the day. Prolonged exposure to the cold might also lead to illnesses, causing students to miss school and fall behind in their studies.

On the other hand, some youngsters might see advantages in a longer winter holiday. Summer days can become sweltering, and excessive heat can lead to dehydration. Although warm weather offers pleasant activities such as trips to the beach, amusement parks, camping and traveling, a cooler break could provide a different kind of recreation. More days off in winter would give students extra time to relax, use indoor facilities, and perhaps reduce their reliance on electronic gadgets.

Personally, I would not welcome this adjustment. I prefer warm weather and enjoy being outside during the summer; having fewer sunny days and a longer cold break would be unpleasant for me. I also dislike the idea of school closures because of snow, which can disrupt the routine.

Overall, I think the current holiday schedule works well because it offers a balance that most students appreciate. Most pupils are likely to prefer keeping the existing arrangement rather than swapping a generous summer vacation for a longer, colder winter break. If any changes are considered, it would be sensible to consult the students first and find a solution that meets everyone’s needs.

During high school I once met a teacher who seemed hostile and unwilling to discuss his lessons again. I even asked my counselor whether I could switch classes, but she refused. After spending several weeks in his class I discovered that he was actually an excellent and kind instructor; whenever I asked for help he patiently explained the material and helped me improve my quiz scores. A person who appears unfriendly at first may just be struggling with something unrelated to you. Therefore, it is unfair to label someone based solely on that brief encounter; we should learn more about their character before forming an opinion.

The old saying “don’t judge a book by its cover” reminds us that outward appearances do not always reflect what lies inside. Some people look friendly and trustworthy yet may disappoint us later, while others who seem harsh can turn out to be caring and helpful when we get to know them. Relying only on looks or a single action can lead to misunderstandings and missed opportunities for valuable connections.

In summary, first impressions can indeed change because a person might be having a temporary bad day, and because deeper knowledge of their character often reveals a different picture. It is wise to reserve judgment until we have a clearer understanding of who someone really is, as the individual we dismiss early on might later become the one we need most.

Even a brief conversation with a lonely person can make them feel valued and less isolated.

When you act kindly, you not only improve the other person’s situation but also feel better yourself. The satisfaction that comes from doing something helpful can enhance your own mood and reinforce a positive self‑image. Whether you pick up trash, help with school work, or simply talk kindly to someone who is upset, each small act contributes to a kinder community and a more rewarding life for everyone involved.

Something that students hate most is waking up in the morning to get ready for school. Having to rise early just to attend school for about eight hours can make a student lazy and tired.

Unfortunately some students are born with or are diagnosed with a disability that prevents them from attending school. However, those students have a right to an education. Distance learning will benefit them by allowing attendance from home. There are many reasons why students benefit from distance learning, but helping a child with a disability receive an education is the most important reason.

If students don’t attend a physical school, there will be fewer problems. Some students are treated badly, many are bullied, and some act like drama queens. Attending school at home will benefit a child because they won’t have to see other students, resulting in less drama and more focus on education. Schools will experience fewer bullying incidents.

On the other hand, many will disagree and say that if students stay at home to pursue their education, they will become irresponsible and lazy. Students should be allowed to attend school however they choose. If a student becomes lazy because of distance learning, the problem lies within the student. Many will argue that distance learning can make a student less lazy and more responsible.

Supporters often argue that distance learning is an excellent alternative for pupils. They claim it can improve attendance, reduce a number of difficulties, and provide a valuable solution for students with disabilities or health issues. Critics, however, contend that studying away from a physical school may encourage laziness and irresponsibility. Overall, remote education can bring benefits both to learners and to schools.

One clear advantage of online schooling is higher attendance. When pupils can study from home, they are less likely to skip classes. Many young people dislike the early‑morning ritual of getting ready and traveling to school for a full day; this fatigue can make them feel sluggish and unmotivated. By eliminating the commute, distance learning removes a major obstacle to regular participation.

A second benefit concerns students who have certain disabilities or medical conditions that make it hard for them to be present in a traditional classroom. These learners still have the right to an education, and remote lessons allow them to study without leaving their homes. While there are several reasons to favor distance education, the ability to include children with special needs stands out as the most compelling.

Finally, studying remotely can lessen some of the social problems that occur in schools. Bullying, peer conflict and unnecessary drama are common in many classrooms. When learners attend lessons from home, they avoid these negative interactions, which can create a calmer environment focused on learning.

Opponents maintain that home‑based study may foster irresponsibility and sloth. They argue that the onus lies with the student, and that if a pupil becomes lazy, the problem is personal rather than methodological. Nonetheless, many agree that, when managed well, distance learning can actually promote greater responsibility and engagement.

Education plays a crucial role in shaping people for an ever‑changing world. It influences how future workers respond to problems and devise solutions. Whole generations have relied on education; basic skills such as mathematics and language have enabled humanity to reach the Moon and tackle global challenges. Because of this importance, I believe school boards should not lengthen the school day. The present schedule already provides about seven hours of learning and growth, extending the day would add unnecessary stress, and it would create scheduling conflicts for students, families and staff.

First, the current seven‑hour day is already demanding. A typical student may arrive late because of a delayed bus or be early and have to wait. Throughout the day they must grasp new concepts, finish homework, manage locker issues, and coordinate with friends on upcoming projects. By the end of the day many are still wondering how to balance assignments and personal responsibilities. In other words, a normal school day already contains many pressures that can be overwhelming for students.

Second, making the day longer would amplify existing problems and introduce new ones. More class time often means more worksheets, more homework, and longer periods of concentration, which can lead to boredom and fatigue. To accommodate the extra hour, some subjects might be shortened, reducing the quality of instruction. The additional time could feel forced and unproductive, making it harder for students to stay engaged throughout the extended schedule.

Finally, a longer school day would clash with the timetables of teachers, parents and extracurricular activities. Many students participate in sports, music, or clubs that require time after school. Extending the day would cut into these important activities. Parents who work full‑time might find it even more difficult to pick up their children or be involved in their education, potentially harming family routines. Teachers would also have to stay later to plan lessons and grade work, increasing their workload and stress.

Although some argue that a longer day could allow deeper study, more time for homework, and extended social periods, these benefits do not outweigh the drawbacks. The current schedule already offers a full range of lessons, activities and interaction. Adding extra hours would likely create more negativity than improvement.

For these reasons I remain opposed to extending the school day. The existing schedule, while demanding, balances learning with personal time and extracurricular commitments. Extending it would increase stress for students, disrupt families and staff, and offer few clear advantages.

In fact, attending a public school offers several advantages: it encourages students to be active, provides them with ample information, and creates opportunities to exchange ideas.

Public schools motivate pupils to move and participate. Teachers play a key role in this, often designing lessons that are enjoyable and physically engaging. For instance, physical education classes give children a chance to exercise, whether they play inside the gym or outdoors on the field, and teachers usually encourage even reluctant students to join in.

Beyond promoting activity, schools supply the information learners need to succeed. Access to knowledgeable teachers and extra‑class support helps students grasp the material more fully. Many schools offer after‑school tutoring, allowing pupils to review content and prepare for exams. If a student is confused, they can simply ask the teacher, who is there to clarify doubts and deepen understanding.

Another important benefit is the chance to share ideas with peers. Group work and collaborative projects let students discuss their thoughts, debate different viewpoints, and learn from one another. Working in pairs or small teams not only makes problem‑solving more enjoyable but also teaches students how to listen, negotiate, and respect diverse opinions.

In summary, public schools enable children to stay active, acquire needed knowledge, and communicate their ideas with others. Homeschooling can be isolating, leaving a student without partners, limited physical activity, and fewer sources of information. Picture a child learning alone at home—how discouraging that would be. By contrast, a public school environment offers daily opportunities for growth and learning, paving the way for a brighter future for every student.

Most students enjoy summer vacation, but some educators think that summer break is too long and students do not retain information as easily as they would in the fall. Because of this a lot of educators think we should have year- round school years. This would be shorter breaks in the summer (3-4 weeks) and longer more spread-out breaks throughout the year. I disagree with this statement and believe that summer break should stay the way it is.

The first reason I disagree with this statement is that it would ruin certain summer activities or even business plans. Think about all the activities in the summer that kids usually take part in, this could be sports, some sort of trip, etc. All of these activities students would preferably do during summer break. They have this preference because they see the summer as a perfect time to do all these activities without having to balance their education as well. They can put most of their time on this activity. The same preference applies to things like summer jobs or internships. During the summer they can learn important values like how to save and earn money. Or if a certain student has a chosen career path they can explore this career path by going in a internship for that spesicifc job. For all of these activities students at the very least would be discouraged to participate in if there was a year-round school year.

The second and probably most important reason is pertaining to the students mental health. An article, by Complex News writing about kids mental health stated, that over 40% of kids by the end of their freshmen year in high school are depressed or overall feel exhausted and depleted mentally. The article continues to say that this number from the time of their freshmen year only increases after each school year. Students use the summer break as a way for their brain to refresh from the long almost ten month school year. Students need this time to relax their brain and get ready for the next year of education. As a student, I can say that during school my brain goes into this state where I am mostly just focused on school work. And I can admit that my brain at multiple points during the year is worn down and damaged by always be in this state. My brain does not get a chance to heal from this until the summer, when school is over. So if we were to hypothetically have a year-round school year, this would mean that the brain would also be in this damaged state year round. If this were the case than the brain of the student would eventually just break and shut down. No student should have to experience that because of a year- round school year.

Although the strongest reason for this year-round school year is that students cannot properly retain enough information for the next school year, I think I have a much stronger counter claim and solution to this problem. A very simple way to take care of the problem of retaining information, is to make mandatory (but simple) assignments from the previous year for the student to complete so that they don't forget this information. This way students can have their long summer break to refresh their brain and do their activities, without them having to forget any information. You get the best of both worlds with no need for a year-round school year.

In conclusion I think my assertions for the summer break to stay the way it is is much stronger than year-round school year argument. Having a year-round school year would be unnecessarily tedious and dangerous as it would negatively affect summer activities and mental health. As someone said once upon a time "Don't fix it if it ain't broke."

The article continues that this figure only rises after each subsequent school year. Students use the summer break to let their brains refresh after the nearly ten‑month school year. They need this time to relax and prepare for the next year of education. As a student, I can say that during school my brain is almost constantly focused on school work, and at multiple points throughout the year it feels worn down and damaged. It does not get a chance to heal until the summer, when school is over. If we were to adopt a year‑round schedule, the brain would remain in this damaged state year‑round, eventually breaking down. No student should have to experience that because of a year‑round school calendar.

Although the strongest argument for a year‑round schedule is that students cannot properly retain enough information for the next school year, I have a stronger counter‑claim and solution. A simple way to address information retention is to assign mandatory, low‑stakes assignments from the previous year for students to complete during the break. This approach prevents forgetting while still allowing students to enjoy a long summer break to refresh their brains and pursue activities. In this way we get the best of both worlds without needing a year‑round school year.

In conclusion, my arguments for keeping summer break as it is are stronger than the case for a year‑round school calendar. A year‑round schedule would be unnecessarily tedious and harmful, negatively affecting summer activities and mental health. As someone once said, “Don’t fix it if it ain’t broke.”

Many students look forward to the summer holidays, yet some teachers argue that the break is too long and that pupils forget what they have learned once school resumes in the fall. Because of this belief, a number of educators propose a year‑round school calendar, with shorter summer vacations of three to four weeks and several longer breaks spread throughout the year. I disagree with that idea and think the traditional summer break should remain unchanged.

First, a shortened summer would interfere with numerous activities and plans that families and students rely on. Think of the camps, sports leagues, trips and other programs that take place during the warm months; these are usually scheduled for the long break so that children can devote their full attention to them without worrying about schoolwork. The same applies to summer jobs or internships, which allow teens to earn money, learn responsibility and explore possible career paths. If the school year were continuous, many young people would be forced to abandon or limit participation in these valuable experiences.

Second, and perhaps more importantly, the extended break is essential for students’ mental health. A report from Complex News noted that more than 40 % of high‑school freshmen experience depression or severe mental fatigue by the end of their first year, and that the figure rises each subsequent year. Summer provides a chance for minds that have been under constant academic pressure for ten months to rest and recover. From personal experience, I can attest that staying in “school mode” for most of the year wears me out; my concentration wanes and I feel mentally exhausted. Without a genuine break, this chronic stress would continue all year, potentially leading to burnout. No student should have to endure that.

Those who support year‑round schooling often claim that the main problem is the loss of knowledge over the long vacation. A simpler solution exists: assign brief, mandatory review tasks during the summer so students keep key concepts fresh. This approach preserves the benefits of a long break—relaxation, extracurricular activities, and mental recovery—while addressing the issue of retention. In other words, we can enjoy the best of both worlds without overhauling the school calendar.

In conclusion, my arguments for keeping the traditional summer vacation outweigh the case for a year‑round schedule. Cutting the break would disrupt valuable activities and jeopardize students’ well‑being. As the saying goes, “If it isn’t broken, don’t fix it.”

Hopefully, future teaching practices will focus on rewarding real effort rather than rewarding minimal attempts.

Imagine spending a whole school day confined to a room with four walls, already having endured a stressful day filled with demanding teachers, difficult classmates and endless assignments, only to be told you must remain there for another ninety minutes. Moreover, when students finally leave school they often do so after dark, which raises safety concerns for those who travel home in the evening.

Homework and projects would spill over, leaving little opportunity for relaxed interaction. Teachers would face the same problem, as they would have less time for grading and preparing lessons, and might feel pressured to work late into the evening. Consequently, students would lose motivation for play and leisure, as school would dominate their thoughts, and they would also get less sleep.

Finally, the cumulative effect of an extended day could sap students’ energy and affect their mental health. Fatigue and a negative mood could lead to disengagement from school altogether, increasing the risk of depression and causing some pupils to dread attending classes.

In conclusion, adding an extra hour and a half to the school day would harm students’ performance and well‑being. It would interfere with extracurricular commitments, create safety issues after dark, reduce family and social time, diminish motivation for recreation, and ultimately drain the energy needed for learning. Therefore, the school board should keep the current length of the school day.

Even with great talent and a brilliant mind, he will never succeed without the ability to express himself. High school is often seen as the final playground before college, especially by many middle‑schoolers. We are required to take a long list of subjects that are meant to steer us toward our future goals. Yet classes such as art, music or drama offer something the core curriculum cannot: a chance to step away from essays and equations and simply enjoy creating, singing, painting or acting with friends. These subjects also teach us how to interact and communicate with others.

The reality of high school is far from easy. Students frequently feel overwhelmed as they try to pass their courses, prepare for standardized tests and think about college all at once. Creative electives can provide a much‑needed break from that pressure. The atmosphere in these classes is usually lively and enjoyable, allowing learners to develop social skills while having fun. A pupil who never imagined an interest in music might, after several months of lessons, discover a real passion and even consider a career as a musician; the same can happen with visual arts or theatre. Thus, these courses not only lessen stress but also impart unexpected lessons.

Consider a shy student who never feels comfortable asking a question in a math class. While a single query per unit might seem routine, the ability to speak up later—delivering presentations or advocating for oneself in a corporate setting—depends on having practiced communication. Even a brilliant mind can fail to succeed without the skill to express ideas clearly. Being able to articulate thoughts is essential for personal progress; it is a social competence we must develop.

Critics may argue that arts, music and drama are wasted time, claiming they merely give students a place to chat with friends for ninety minutes. But what about those who have no friends, who sit alone in a corner and never get a chance to speak? Should schools not nurture these quiet learners, helping them find their voice and take advantage of future opportunities?

In today’s competitive world, people are expected to master many skills, yet most prefer to stay in the comfort of familiar jobs. Consequently, they rarely try something different from what they already do. The best advice for personal development, as Ralph Waldo Emerson suggests, is to venture into new areas; otherwise, growth stalls.

Firstly, many professions require expanding into unfamiliar territory in order to improve. A photographer, for example, may be accustomed to taking still images, but learning how to shoot video opens doors to cinematography or journalism. By exploring these related fields, the photographer advances professionally. Similarly, leaving one’s comfort zone fosters personal growth: a student who studies abroad or a doctor who investigates new branches of medicine both gain knowledge that would be impossible if they remained within their usual limits. Exploring unfamiliar domains therefore promotes development for everyone.

Secondly, stagnation prevents progress. Even highly skilled individuals, such as carpenters or construction workers, may hesitate to start their own businesses because they fear failure. Though they are experts in their trade, they often avoid the new challenges of managing a company or investing in modern equipment. Without such change, a business cannot grow. Some argue that repeating the same actions makes one a specialist—like an athlete who practices the same routine. Yet even elite athletes must vary their training to improve; doing the same thing continuously will not keep them at the top. This principle applies to many fields where success is the goal.

In conclusion, Emerson’s statement reminds us that achieving our aims is difficult when we keep repeating the same actions. To truly grow, people must step beyond what they are accustomed to and dare to try new things. Embracing change brings benefits, and it is better to develop a range of abilities rather than mastering only one.

In my view, I am largely opposed to schools providing distance‑learning options that let students attend classes from home through the Internet or video calls. This position is not tied to the fact that I attend a public high school; there are several reasons why I think online schooling is not the best choice.

First, studying online can impair students’ communication abilities. When lessons take place in a virtual setting, pupils are isolated in their own homes and interact mainly with the teacher. They miss the chance to engage with classmates, ask peers for clarification, or share ideas in a group. For people who thrive on collaboration, this lack of social contact can be a serious drawback, because fellow students often help each other understand material that one individual finds difficult.

A second concern is that online classes tend to weaken participation skills. In a physical classroom we take part in hands‑on activities, discussions, and experiments that reinforce what we are learning and make the information stick. Asking questions face‑to‑face also tends to be quicker and more effective than sending an email or waiting for a reply in a chat. Delays in teacher responses can hinder comprehension and may even affect grades, which is why direct interaction is preferable.

Finally, studying from home can lead to laziness and missed lessons. Without the structure of a school day, it is easy to fall asleep, become distracted, or skip sessions altogether. This lack of discipline can damage academic performance, especially for students who are not highly organized. While some very disciplined learners might succeed in a virtual environment, most people benefit from the routine and accountability that a traditional school provides.

These points explain why I do not support distance learning as a regular option. It may be useful for students who have a genuine reason to stay away from school, but for me and many others, attending classes in person remains the better choice.

I support the introduction of a 10 p.m. curfew on weekdays and a midnight curfew on weekends. Such a rule would ease parents’ constant anxiety, help teenagers concentrate more on their studies, and teach them greater responsibility. Young people often want to stay out late with friends, and when they are denied that freedom they can become resentful or even disrespectful toward their parents. A curfew would remind them to be thankful for the limits placed on them.

Parents worry about where their children are because today’s society is filled with risks that were less common in the past. For this reason many parents would welcome a city‑wide curfew law. Usually, when a parent lets a teen out, they set a return time, but adolescents frequently ignore the deadline and come home whenever they please. A legal curfew would give parents peace of mind, knowing that their children must be home by a certain hour or face police intervention. This would likely make youngsters more inclined to follow the schedule set by their parents, rather than acting as if there were no rules at all. With the increase in kidnappings and violent crimes against teenagers, a curfew provides an extra layer of protection; youngsters out after 10 p.m. would be stopped by authorities and reminded of the consequences of staying out too late.

If the 10 p.m. curfew were enforced, teenagers would return home earlier and be able to get enough sleep. Proper rest would reduce the number of students who fall asleep in class and improve their overall attention and performance. Some teens think school isn’t important and prefer to spend the night with friends, forgetting about the next day’s lessons. However, education is essential for personal growth and future success, and a curfew would help them prioritize school over late‑night outings.

A curfew also encourages teens to become more responsible. They must learn to manage their time and ensure they are home before the limit, knowing that missing it could lead to trouble with the police. Being out after the designated hour usually indicates that a young person is involved in unsafe activities; staying home eliminates that risk. When teenagers repeatedly ignore warnings, they eventually have to face the consequences, which reinforces the lesson that following rules protects them from harm.

In conclusion, a 10 p.m. weekday curfew—midnight on weekends—could encourage adolescents to respect their parents’ wishes, improve their school performance, and make them more accountable for their time. It would also help them understand how much their parents worry when they are out late. Ultimately, the curfew aims to keep teenagers safe and steer them away from trouble while fostering better habits and greater responsibility.

Supporters of online schooling point to data indicating that around 80 % of high‑school students hold jobs after school hours. They return home late, still have homework to finish, and must rise early—often by 7 a.m.—to attend class. Fatigue leads to dozing off and a lack of motivation. The ability to study online at any convenient time would alleviate these pressures.

Moreover, some learners have to travel long distances on foot to reach school. During winter the cold and icy sidewalks can cause injuries, as I have witnessed when a student slipped and broke an arm, and another was attacked on his way home. If classes were available online, these hazardous commutes would be unnecessary, improving safety for students.

Finally, research shows that about 70 % of students who have taken online courses achieve success, suggesting that remote learning is effective. Learners can rest more at home and no longer need to rise at dawn each day.

In sum, schools should adopt online classes, just as colleges and universities already do, because the majority of participants succeed. Providing this option would be the most advantageous step schools can take for their students.

While some argue that studying remotely can make learners careless, there are clear advantages: studying from home saves the time usually spent traveling to school and helps students become more adept and efficient with technology.

First, attending classes online allows pupils to avoid the commute, which can take anywhere from ten to forty minutes each way. This travel consumes valuable time that could otherwise be used for study or other productive activities. No one wants to waste hours on transportation when that time could be devoted to learning.

Second, learning from home encourages greater competence with digital tools. Students who regularly use technological resources become quicker at completing tasks that involve computers and the internet, compared with peers who have little exposure. This familiarity not only supports their current studies but also prepares them for further education, where tech skills are increasingly essential.

In summary, remote learning benefits students by eliminating unnecessary travel time and by enhancing their technological proficiency. Schools should therefore provide distance‑learning options so that learners can enjoy these advantages while studying from home.

Ultimately, adopting an optimistic demeanor can bring great rewards, turning you into the kind of person who naturally attracts success.

All children deserve equal access to education and to a variety of programmes, without discrimination. They should have the freedom to explore their interests while receiving guidance that prevents them from making harmful choices. The American education system illustrates this balance: students can study core subjects and at the same time choose electives that match their passions. This flexibility allows them to acquire knowledge relevant to future careers, reduce stress, and focus on shaping their own futures.

Many teenagers choose this route because their parents pressure them to enter college or the workforce sooner, not because they truly want to. Pushing children into accelerated programs deprives them of valuable leisure time and the chance to enjoy their teenage years. Higher grades alone do not guarantee happiness or competence; what truly matters is how well we can apply the knowledge we acquire later in life.

To graduate early, students must take summer courses and study late into evenings, leaving little room for rest. Without downtime, concentration suffers, and the learning process becomes a chore. Allowing students to select electives they enjoy can nurture skills that will be useful in their future professions.

Although he succeeded academically, he now regrets missing the final year’s experiences, which would have better prepared him for university life. Therefore, adolescents should not be forced into paths they dislike; they should be encouraged to follow their genuine interests.

introduction

The people who value self‑reliance should seek guidance from experts and authorities instead of making every important decision on their own. When we say “experts,” we mean people who know a lot more about the topic than we do—think of a teacher and a student.

Teachers have graduated in the subjects they teach, such as a science class, and they have had to do a lot to become educators in that field. This is why, if we value self‑reliance, we still need help from experts; that way we can succeed in life. However, there are some decisions we can make ourselves. For example, we can choose whether to drink alcohol or smoke. For those kinds of choices we only need to consider who we might hurt—ourselves and nobody else. If we don’t think about ourselves and the decisions we make, nobody else will.

Reason 1

In my opinion, self‑reliance is important for every person’s life. Self‑reliance is about decision‑making. Sometimes we think we are right in every decision we make, but we must remember that no human is perfect, so we sometimes make bad choices. A good example is when we are teenagers. At that age we need more help than ever because many things can influence us easily. This is the time we need help from experts, and who better than our parents? They want the best for us, so they will teach us what could be best, and what really matters in life is that they love us. I am not speaking in general, because some parents don’t care about what their son or daughter is doing, but many do. We can also look for other types of experts who are professional and have a diploma in their field. It can be very helpful for us to succeed because they have studied their careers for years. Their guidance can help us make better decisions throughout life and become better people.

Reason 2

Bad decisions can hurt ourselves. Decision‑making is something we all face. A decision can be good or bad, and sometimes a decision that looks good can lead us to do something harmful. For example, a person might want to invest money to open a restaurant. At first it sounds appealing because many think such a business guarantees profit, but the reality is that it can be a challenge. Some people do not take the time to consider the consequences of opening a restaurant. They fail to think about the expenses they must cover with the restaurant’s income, or that they could lose all their money if the restaurant fails. When people lose everything, they can become depressed, and some even take their own lives. This is when we need help from experts rather than deciding to open a restaurant on our own. Experts know a lot more than we do because they have graduated in the field; they understand business and what is best for us. With their help, we can succeed in business and avoid losing money.

Counter‑argument

Someone might argue that making decisions ourselves is better because we won’t have anyone to blame if we fail, and we can learn responsibility. However, we don’t need to wait for failure; it is better to look for experts who can help us make good decisions. Two heads are better than one.

Conclusion

In conclusion, help from experts is the best way to accomplish things. They can teach us how to improve, which is why they exist—to be consulted for assistance. Sometimes we need to accept that we can handle certain tasks ourselves, but we also need help from experts or our parents. We must seek different sources to succeed in life. At times we must be strong, but to make any decision we need to be social—that is, to ask for help and make good choices.

People who place great importance on self‑reliance should still turn to specialists and authorities rather than handling every major life choice alone. By “experts” we mean individuals who possess far more knowledge about a particular subject than we do—much like a teacher compared with a student.

Teachers have spent many years studying their discipline, for example science, before they can teach it. Their extensive training shows why, even if we value independence, we benefit from consulting knowledgeable people. This guidance can help us succeed in life. Of course, there are personal matters where we can decide for ourselves, such as whether to drink alcohol or smoke. In those cases we simply need to consider the impact on ourselves, because the consequences affect no one else.

Self‑reliance is indeed a vital quality for everyone. It is closely linked to the decisions we make. At times we may feel certain that our choices are correct, yet we must remember that no one is infallible. Poor decisions are inevitable, especially during adolescence, when young people are especially vulnerable to outside influences. In that stage of life, help from experts—most notably parents—becomes crucial. Many parents genuinely want the best for their children and can offer valuable advice because they care. When parents are unavailable or unsupportive, we can also seek professional experts who hold formal qualifications in their fields. Their years of study enable them to give advice that can improve our decision‑making and help us grow as individuals.

Bad decisions can also harm us directly. Every person must make choices, some of which appear attractive but may lead to negative outcomes. Consider someone who decides to invest a large sum of money in opening a restaurant. At first the idea seems promising, yet the venture entails many hidden costs and risks. If the business fails, the investor may lose everything, fall into depression, or even contemplate suicide. Here, consulting experts—business advisors, accountants, or experienced restaurateurs—could prevent such disastrous results. Professionals understand the market, the financial obligations, and the pitfalls, allowing us to avoid costly mistakes and increase the chances of success.

Some might argue that making decisions alone is better because it prevents us from blaming others for failures and forces us to become responsible. While personal responsibility is important, waiting until we make a mistake before seeking advice is unnecessary. Two heads are often better than one; expert input can steer us toward sound choices before problems arise.

In conclusion, seeking help from experts is the most effective way to handle many of life’s challenges. Specialists can teach us how to improve, and they exist precisely for us to consult. At times we must rely on our own judgment, but in most important matters we should draw on the knowledge of professionals or trusted parents. Combining personal strength with external guidance leads to more successful and balanced decisions.

The constant need to check messages or social media pulls attention away from the subject, so the learner misses important points and ends up confused about what has been covered. The frequent vibrations and notifications create a habit of looking at the screen, which makes it difficult to stay focused on the lesson.

Second, when a phone is used for purposes unrelated to education, it does not contribute to learning at all. Students who browse the internet for entertainment or chat with friends are not acquiring the knowledge they need for their courses. If a device is required for a specific assignment, the teacher should give explicit permission; otherwise, the phone should remain out of sight. Misusing the device therefore hampers academic progress and can even lead to penalties.

Third, the presence of cellphones can disturb other pupils. A ringing or vibrating phone draws the attention of the entire class, interrupting the flow of instruction. Such interruptions prevent classmates from following the lesson and completing tasks, which ultimately undermines their chances of succeeding in school and later in life. It is unfair to let one person’s misuse of a device affect the learning of others.

In conclusion, having cellphones in the classroom interferes with the teacher’s instructions, diverts students from educational activities, and creates unnecessary disruptions for peers. Phones should only be used when the teacher explicitly allows them for a school‑related purpose. By keeping cellphones out of the learning environment, we protect both individual focus and the collective ability of students to succeed.

This essay examines the advantages and disadvantages of working in a team compared with working alone, focusing on how each approach affects the individual rather than the group as a whole. First, we will look at the nature of group dynamics versus solitary work, then explore the specific issues that arise when a person participates in a group, and finally evaluate whether these factors help or hinder personal development.

Think back to the last time you had to complete a project. You probably considered several options, and one of the first decisions was whether to tackle the task by yourself or with others. Everyone is familiar with the concept of individual work: a single person takes responsibility for the whole assignment. But what exactly constitutes a group, how does it form, and what dynamics come into play?

A group can be defined as a collection of people who come together to achieve a specific goal. The way a group is organized, its structure and its processes determine how it functions. These aspects of group dynamics are relevant for both formal and informal groups and are a key subject in the study of organisational behaviour, where groups appear in almost every setting.

Group dynamics concerns the reasons why groups are created and how they develop over time. Numerous theories have been offered to explain these processes. While cooperative work offers many benefits, it also has some drawbacks. For instance, individual members often have less control over the task than a single person working alone, and in many groups some participants dominate the discussion while others remain passive. Although the group may still reach its objective, the quieter members may miss out on valuable learning experiences. On the other hand, when a team collaborates effectively it can accomplish far more than isolated individuals. A wider array of skills can be applied, and exchanging ideas usually deepens each member’s understanding of the subject matter.

Being part of a team also helps a person develop interpersonal abilities such as speaking, listening, and cooperating, as well as leadership and motivational skills. These competencies are useful throughout one’s academic life and beyond, adding lasting value.

To reap these advantages, it is essential to manage group work well, ensuring that every member can contribute and benefit from the collaborative process.
