Is setting an example by your own behavior the best way to influence other people? Sometimes it is not the best idea to mirror other people's behavior because some people do not always have a positive behavior. There could be time's that someone could be in a negative place of mind, reckless, and does a lot of horse play; other time's people can be charming, properly mannered, and influential.

Growing up in the Generic_City area, I have been able to witness a lot of drugs, gangs, and violence. The example these group of people decide to display is not a very positive act on their behalf; this is not a pathway you would want to be taking because of the bad outcomes from it. I remember I had a friend who's father shot himself due to the poor choice he made which made him reflect and he figured that was the only solution.

On the other hand, some people decide to be very influential to society in a positive manner. Out of my three years of high school I was able to see some students making their way for others by not being selfish; a lot of them did volunteer work as well to help the community and to hopefully inspire others to do so as well. I actually got the opportunity to throw a kids halloween party at a church: I enjoyed it, it was a lot of fun.

Honestly, I do not feel like I am a good example nor do I feel like I am a bad one either. I make mistakes: it is how I was taught. Growing up I believed that the only way you are ever going to learn is by making mistakes and being able to evaluate the error of your mistake; only then you can truly improve yourself and help insipre other people as well.

In conclusion, I am mutual about examples being the best way to influence other people because of it not always being a positive thing due to the poor decisions some people choose to make. Truthfully I think it is a better idea to be the best you that you can be because at the end of the day there is only one of you and so many of us; it is best to stay unique.

Honestly, I do not feel that I am a good example, nor do I feel that I am a bad one. I make mistakes; that is how I was taught. Growing up I believed the only way to learn is by making mistakes and evaluating the error, because only then can you truly improve yourself and help inspire other people.

In conclusion, I am ambivalent about examples being the best way to influence other people, since they are not always positive due to the poor decisions some choose to make. Truthfully, I think it is better to be the best you can be, because at the end of the day there is only one of you. Since there are so many of us, it is best to stay unique.

Is leading by personal example truly the most effective way to influence others? Not always, because not everyone behaves positively. At times a person may be in a bad mood, act recklessly, or engage in childish mischief; at other moments they may be charming, well‑mannered, and persuasive.

The behavior that these groups display is far from admirable; following that path inevitably leads to harmful consequences. I remember a friend whose father took his own life after making a terrible decision, which forced the young man to reflect on how he saw that as the only solution.

Conversely, many individuals choose to make a positive impact on society. During my three years of high school I observed numerous classmates who acted selflessly, taking part in volunteer projects to help the community and, hopefully, inspire others to do the same. I even had the chance to organize a children’s Halloween party at a church – an experience I found both enjoyable and rewarding.

I have always believed that learning comes from erring, recognizing those errors, and then improving. Only then can we truly develop ourselves and set an example for others.

To sum up, I am ambivalent about the idea that examples are the best way to influence people, because the influence can be negative when people make poor choices. Ultimately, I think it is more important to be the best version of yourself – there is only one you, and many people like you – so staying authentic and unique is the wiser path.

Minister Churchill’s message is that moving from failure to success is rarely simple, but perseverance can eventually lead to achievement. Many would agree that not everyone will reach the top immediately; mistakes are inevitable, and success often demands years of effort. Failure does not spell disaster—people must discover the paths that suit them best and keep striving toward their goals.

First, some people view the transition from failure to success as a positive challenge. My friend once told a classmate that basketball was not his strong suit, yet with continued practice he improved dramatically. The saying “practice makes perfect” reflects this belief. Another example involves my sister, who dreamed of attending the University of Virginia. She studied intensely, and although our family doubted her chances, she received an acceptance letter a few weeks later. These stories show that progress is rarely easy, but determination can turn setbacks into triumphs.

On the other hand, difficulties are a universal experience. No one goes through life without encountering problems, and even in school it is rare to find a student who never struggles with coursework. Intelligence is not innate; it develops through effort. For instance, I earn high marks in mathematics and history, but my grades in English and science are lower. This illustrates that everyone has strengths and weaknesses, and success requires work in the areas where we are less proficient.

Some critics argue that the pursuit of success is a waste of time, claiming it offers little benefit for future careers. They emphasize the burden of paying for housing, bills, insurance, and supporting family, suggesting that endless studying and training may not be worthwhile. Often, those who adopt this pessimistic view feel stuck or lack direction.

Ultimately, striving to move from failure to success is valuable because it builds self‑esteem and reduces future stress. When people accomplish the requirements of their chosen profession early, they avoid later crises. Diligent study and hard work increase the chances of reaching one’s goals, and even if success does not come immediately, continued effort leaves room for improvement. By committing to learning and perseverance, individuals are less likely to regret missed opportunities later in life.

Some people may say that students finishing high school in three years and entering college or the workforce one year early is a good idea. However, it can be very stressful for students. They have to study for all of their classes, do homework at home, and keep up with their classwork so they won't fall behind. Additionally, students have to complete projects and presentations. All of these can stress students a lot and leave no time for their own interests.

It is not a good idea for students to finish high school and enter college or the workforce one year early. They would need to take classes during the summer or in the evenings and would not be able to take elective classes. Finishing one year early can also be stressful for students. Schools should not offer students the option to finish high school in three years and enter college or the workforce one year early.

Finishing high school in three years and moving on to college or a job a year earlier may sound appealing, but it is not a wise choice for most students. The compressed schedule forces learners to take courses during summer or evenings, limits their ability to choose electives, and creates a high level of stress.

To complete all graduation requirements in three years, students would have to enroll in summer classes or attend night school. Many teenagers work during the summer to earn money, and adding coursework would leave them with little time for employment. Likewise, evening classes would clash with extracurricular activities such as sports, clubs, or other after‑school commitments, preventing students from taking part in them.

A shortened high school program also reduces the chance of studying elective subjects. While core classes are essential for graduation and for college admission, students also benefit from courses like art, drama, music, or photography that develop creativity and well‑being. When the timetable is already packed with required subjects, there is little room left for these valuable electives.

Some argue that graduating early gives students a head start, but the reality is that the workload becomes overwhelming. Pupils must keep up with daily homework, study for tests, complete projects and deliver presentations—all within a tighter timeframe. This pressure can lead to burnout and leaves little opportunity for personal time or relaxation.

For these reasons, schools should not promote a three‑year high‑school track that pushes students into college or the workforce a year ahead of schedule. The need to attend summer or evening classes, the loss of elective options, and the heightened stress all outweigh any perceived benefits. Keeping the traditional four‑year program better supports balanced academic growth and overall student well‑being.

I think that every person ultimately decides what kind of character they will have, even though outside forces can sometimes sway us. Friends, family, acquaintances and even strangers can try to shape our habits and attitudes, for better or for worse. Still, many people manage to follow their own positive values, and those values often lead to a successful and satisfying life. It is also true that not everyone is dominated by negative traits; some individuals receive good influences that guide them toward the right choices, and it is up to each person to judge whether a particular influence helps or harms their own path.

First, I believe each individual possesses a set of personal traits that guide their behavior. Some of these traits are constructive, while others are detrimental. Negative traits often develop because of the people surrounding us—friends, relatives, or even casual contacts—especially when a person grows up in an unstable or unhappy household. Conversely, those raised in supportive, loving families are more likely to adopt positive habits and attitudes. Nevertheless, even a person with a solid foundation can be harmed if they spend too much time with someone who carries harmful traits.

Second, the traits we hold can determine how successful we become. People who own large homes and expensive cars usually exhibit positive qualities such as hard work, perseverance, and ambition, which have paved the way for their achievements and set a good example for future generations. On the other hand, negative traits often lead to unfulfilling lives. When a person with good habits forms a close friendship with someone who has bad habits, the latter can start to control and influence the former. Relationships can also have a powerful impact: a toxic romantic partnership, for instance, can bring constant arguments, self‑blame and emotional wounds that may scar a person for years, fostering harmful traits that affect their future.

Finally, not everyone is completely under the sway of others. Intelligent and determined individuals can recognize when others are trying to drag them down. When success attracts envy, some people will attempt to sabotage it, but awareness of those negative influences allows a person to protect themselves. My advice to anyone who feels trapped by external pressure is to remember that you have the power to choose your own character. Reflect on whether your traits are helping or hurting you, and commit to cultivating the positive ones that will shape the life you want.

A large proportion of students finish high school early in order to start college sooner. I think that young people should instead take three years to graduate and then enter the workforce before attending university. Doing so would allow them to save money for tuition, develop greater maturity, and acquire valuable time‑management abilities, all of which open up many opportunities before they begin their studies.

First, working after high school gives students a chance to accumulate funds for college. Many youngsters rely on student loans because they lack personal savings and their parents cannot fully support them. However, loans must be repaid after graduation, adding financial pressure. If a student leaves school after three years and spends a year working, they can earn and set aside enough money to cover tuition without borrowing. This reduces the financial burden on families and forces the student to become more responsible, which in turn demonstrates maturity and makes their parents proud.

Second, a year of employment helps students become more mature. When they have to support themselves, they assume many responsibilities and gain a clearer understanding of how the adult world operates. Some early graduates are only 17, and the sudden transition to college can be overwhelming. By working for a year, they earn income and grow emotionally, learning to meet deadlines and manage obligations. Maturity also means being taken seriously by peers and professors, and it can protect younger students from being bullied or feeling isolated. With work experience, they will enter college alongside their friends rather than feeling out of place.

Finally, the workplace teaches essential time‑management skills. Employees must arrive on time, complete tasks promptly, and adhere to schedules. These habits translate directly to academic life: turning in assignments on time, arriving to class punctually, and maintaining a healthy sleep routine. Good time management also helps students allocate periods for studying, leisure, and rest, reducing stress and preventing missed deadlines. Having already practiced these skills, students will find the academic schedule easier to handle.

Some people might argue that students should proceed directly to university, but I respectfully disagree. Gaining work experience before college provides financial security, strengthens personal discipline, and fosters the maturity needed to succeed in higher education.

In summary, taking a year to work after high school equips students with money for tuition, better time‑management abilities, and a higher level of responsibility. These advantages make the transition to college smoother and set the foundation for a more successful academic and professional future.

Joining a gang is extremely dangerous and can lead to a needless death, leaving loved ones in grief. Drunk driving not only endangers the driver but also puts other families at risk, as an accident may send someone to the hospital or worse. Drug use is harmful in every respect; the only way to avoid its damage is not to start in the first place. Unsurprisingly, families and friends are rarely pleased with such behavior. In contrast, there are many positive decisions that people can make.

Good choices help you determine what you want to do after high school—whether it is a particular career, a field of study at university, or the desire to start a family. These are all examples of constructive decisions for the future. Finding a job is difficult without experience, and employers prefer candidates who are prepared and motivated. If you finish college and already know the profession you aim for, you can choose the right subjects to study, which in turn makes it easier to secure employment and later support a family financially.

While many adults are sorting out these plans, younger people also begin to test their independence by making their own decisions. Their parents may wonder whether their child truly needs assistance, but allowing a teenager to decide for themselves shows that they are growing into an adult. Parents recognize that this freedom helps their children think independently and develop as individuals, proving that they can handle situations on their own.

All of these points illustrate that decision‑making can be challenging, yet it is essential for gaining independence. Both youngsters and adults must learn to make choices in order to move forward. Independence is something many people desire; once you have it, the question becomes: what will you do with it?

Thomas Jefferson once advised, “Determine never to be idle… It is wonderful how much may be done if we are always doing.” The idea is simple: staying active helps us achieve more, while doing nothing rarely leads to success. When we keep ourselves busy, we learn new skills, meet people who can support our goals, and discover how much we are capable of accomplishing.

Being productive expands our knowledge. For instance, my mother enrolled me in a soccer team even though I had never played before. At first I was hesitant, but through regular practice I learned how to control the ball, improve my speed, and even understand the role of a goalkeeper. Another occasion was an English vocabulary test; I knew only a few of the required words, so I devoted extra time to studying until I mastered them. These experiences show that effort directly translates into learning.

Active involvement also introduces us to new people who can help us reach our objectives. Although I usually prefer indoor activities, joining the soccer team forced me to interact with teammates, coaches, and other players. Their feedback pushed me to become a better teammate and to work on my speed and mindset. Likewise, when I struggled with a math equation, I approached a new teacher for assistance. He explained the problem clearly and has since become a reliable resource whenever I need help. Building these connections is often a by‑product of staying engaged.

Consider how much can be achieved when we constantly do something worthwhile. Rather than spending the whole day on the couch watching television, we can use free moments to work on projects that will benefit us later, such as reading, exercising, or practicing a skill. Even when we think we can manage on our own, asking for guidance can open up new perspectives and improve our understanding.

Of course, not everyone has ample time or resources, and occasional rest is necessary. Some people may need to pause due to financial constraints or lack of transport, and a period of inactivity can be a strategic part of a longer‑term plan. However, simply waiting for opportunities to appear without any effort is rarely effective.

In conclusion, consistent activity is a key driver of personal achievement. By staying busy we learn more, form valuable relationships, and realize the many possibilities that would remain hidden if we were idle. Jefferson’s words still ring true today: avoiding idleness opens the door to countless accomplishments.

In scientific experiments we form hypotheses by imagining what will happen, and when signing a contract we consider the possible consequences of agreeing or refusing. Have you ever had a really important decision you had to make? Did you feel overwhelmed because you didn't know what you should do? Asking for help or advise from people such as friends and family around you can really help alleviate all that stress. Most people encounter big decisions often throughout their lives, so getting advise from numerous people can help you get more input on something, and may end up helping you make a final decision. Seeking multiple opinions can really help someone make a better choice when dealing with decision making.

One way seeking multiple opinions can help someone make a better choice is that by asking more than one person, they can get more input. Asking numerous people can be a huge help when making an important decision. Not only are people getting different ideas of what they may want to do, they can also get advise from people who may be more experienced than themselves. For example, if someone was debating on which college they should apply to, they may end up asking people such as older siblings or parents for advise because they may have more experience with that matter. By asking multiple people, you can get multiple ideas, each of them being different in their own way. By getting more people's input, you may be able to start to make your own choice about the matter because of the advise you've gotten.

Another way seeking multiple opinions can help someone make a better choice is by not getting any biased opinions. By asking more than one person for advise on a subject, they can get more than one new idea that isn't one of their own. This way, they can get more than one person's thoughts on the decision, and have different ideas on it. For example, if someone were trying to make a decision on what sport they may want to tryout for at school, they could possibly ask their friends and family about which they should choose. However, they should also ask people like classmates and teachers, as they may have their own ideas, and won't give the person any biased ideas or information. Friends and family can have a great deal of influence on people, so it's important to always get people's thoughts that are on the outside. This will make it to where there's a greater chance of the decision maker not being biased, as they've heard numerous people's thoughts, and can make their own decision off of that.

A final way seeking multiple opinions can help someone make a better choice is by being more prepared about the choice they're going to make. The decision maker can use all the advise they've gotten from different people to make their own choice, and feel better prepared. They will be more focused as they know what they want to do, and will feel more confident and less overwhelmed. Feeling less overwhelmed can be a big help as the person doesn't have to be so worried, so they won't have any distractions from making the best possible decision. For example, if someone is trying to decide what kind of car they want to get, and they've gotten advise from numerous people, they can make a better choice when picking. They'll know exactly what they want, as they've heard many thoughts from the people around them, and so they can make their final decision.

After getting advise from multiple people around them, the decision maker may be able to make the best choice possible, as they've gotten new thoughts and ideas. Asking for help or for some advise from those around you can help you make the best possible choice because you've gotten a lot of new information and opinions that you wouldn't have gotten if you had only asked one or no one at all for advise. Making an important choice can seem a little bit easier and less stressful after seeking advise from multiple people. Getting help from others around you can help you make the best choice you can.

I want to begin with a question that we rarely consider: how does technology affect our health? It is a crucial issue that deserves attention.

From the moment we wake up until we go to sleep, we interact with countless devices, apps, and digital tools. Modern technology lets us accomplish many tasks without meeting anyone in person—buying books, shopping, playing games, even chatting with friends or family can all be done behind a screen. This reduction in face‑to‑face contact can have harmful consequences for our well‑being.

Some may argue that the convenience of technology brings benefits, but the prevailing view is that the loss of human interaction is detrimental. If we compare two people—one who relies on technology for everything, from buying clothes to doing homework and contacting relatives, and another who prefers to go out, shop in stores, and meet friends in person—the first is much more likely to experience health problems. Heavy use of computers and gadgets encourages a sedentary lifestyle and promotes poor posture, neck strain, back pain, and even hearing loss. Over time these issues can develop into chronic discomfort that is difficult to treat.

Returning to the original question—how is technology impacting our health?—the answer is far from positive. Frequent device use is linked to increased stress, eye strain, back problems, hearing damage, and a range of other negative effects. Moreover, excessive screen time often leads to social isolation; people spend so much time at home on their devices that they miss out on real friendships. Research shows that humans need regular social contact to maintain mental health, and the lack of it can contribute to depression.

In summary, while technology enables us to perform many tasks without direct contact, this very convenience reduces human interaction and harms our physical and mental health. If we do not learn to balance our digital lives with real‑world activities, future generations will inherit the same issues. Although technological progress is now the norm, we can still mitigate the damage by managing our screen time and ensuring we maintain personal connections. Only then can we prevent the worsening of back pain, illness, and depression associated with over‑reliance on technology.

By offering this support, students will not be held back from remote learning simply because they do not own a computer.

Having the choice of doing classes from home can be very beneficial to students. It gives them the opportunity to complete more classes without the excuse of being absent from school. Providing the chance to learn from home can increase the passing rate for many courses. The option of at‑home classes can help students who need it and encourage those who prefer this format to actually complete their coursework. I think all schools should have an option that allows students to take classes from home.

Allowing students to attend classes from home is a highly valuable option for schools. Learners differ in the ways they absorb information and in the speed at which they progress. When pupils can study in an environment that suits them best, their academic performance often rises. Moreover, students who are ill or otherwise unable to be physically present can keep up with their assignments online, eliminating the excuse of falling behind because they could not attend school.

Frequent illness or personal circumstances that keep students away from school would no longer be a barrier if remote learning were available. With the chance to study from home, learners would not have to worry about returning to a mountain of missed work. Consequently, absences would not automatically translate into failing grades. I experienced this personally: after undergoing surgery last year, I struggled to catch up because the only way to obtain my assignments was for someone to collect them from school. My parents both worked, so I had no means of completing the work at home. The lack of an online option made it extremely hard to maintain my grades, and an internet‑based solution would have helped enormously.

Senior students often need extra credits in order to graduate on schedule. Having to rely solely on morning or evening classes can make it difficult to finish the required courses in time, adding stress and discouragement. Many seniors also hold part‑time jobs, and a full day of in‑person schooling combined with work can become overwhelming. When the workload becomes too heavy, more students risk failing. Providing the possibility of taking some courses online would lessen the pressure and enable a larger number of seniors to graduate successfully.

It is true that some learners prefer face‑to‑face instruction, feeling that they understand concepts better when a teacher explains them directly. Schools can still accommodate these students by offering virtual lessons that include live explanations and interactions. A practical obstacle, however, is that not every household owns a suitable computer. To overcome this, schools could lend laptops or tablets to students who need them, ensuring that lack of equipment does not prevent anyone from participating in remote classes.

Overall, giving students the option to study from home brings many advantages. It allows them to complete more coursework without the excuse of absenteeism, raises pass rates, and supports those who genuinely need a flexible learning environment. For these reasons, I believe every school should make home‑based classes an available choice for its students.

Working in a group can bring a lot of advantages. When you discuss a task with several people, you are exposed to a wider range of ideas and knowledge, because each member contributes a different perspective. This exchange often leads to more creative solutions than you might reach on your own.  

Nevertheless, I usually prefer to work alone. My personal experience with group projects has often been disappointing. Frequently I end up doing most of the work while others contribute little or submit sloppy, hard‑to‑read material. When group members are careless, spend too much time on their phones, or miss deadlines, the whole project suffers and the final grade is lower for everyone. In those situations I feel that the only person I can rely on is myself.  

Even though I favor solo work, I recognise that group work has its merits. It forces shy people like me to speak up, share opinions, and interact with classmates, which can lead to new friendships and help us step out of our comfort zones. If the group members are committed, communicate well, and share responsibilities, the collaboration can be very productive.  

The reasons I choose to work alone are straightforward. I can concentrate fully on the task at hand, I am the one who must meet the deadline, and any mistakes or low grades are entirely my responsibility. I also receive all the credit for the work I complete, which motivates me to maintain a high standard.  

On the other hand, group work often fails when some members do not fulfil their part, produce messy work, or treat the project as free time. Delays and uneven contributions can lead to late submissions and reduced marks, while the effort of the diligent members is diluted by those who do little.  

In the end, group projects can be beneficial, but only when the participants are reliable and care about the outcome. If the team consists of motivated, responsible people, collaboration can be rewarding. Conversely, if the group includes indifferent members who merely coast along, the experience becomes frustrating and unproductive.  

Therefore, for me, working alone remains the better option. It allows me to focus, take full responsibility for my results, and avoid relying on others who might not pull their weight. Each person must decide which method suits them best, but personally I find solo work more advantageous than group work.

This is the question many students face when deciding whether to enrol in online courses. Because many learners balance part‑time or full‑time jobs with their studies, their time is precious, and understanding the pros and cons is essential. I contend that online classes provide a valuable opportunity for students because they offer flexibility, a wide range of subjects and greater access to instructors, and they often allow accelerated learning.

First, flexibility is perhaps the greatest benefit of online education. Learners can usually attend lectures and complete assignments at any time that suits them, whether during the day or late at night. This means that a student who works in the afternoon can schedule study sessions around his or her job. Traditional, face‑to‑face courses often cannot accommodate such irregular timetables, making it difficult for working students to attend.

Second, the variety of courses available online is impressive. Distance‑learning programmes are offered by many colleges and can be found with a simple Google search. While some people argue that online learners have limited contact with teachers, the opposite is often true: many platforms provide prompt communication with faculty members, allowing even shy students to ask questions and receive quick answers.

Finally, online courses are especially convenient for both undergraduate and graduate students who need to fit study around other responsibilities, such as work or family. The ability to set one’s own schedule and finish assignments when it is most effective helps many learners stay on track. Moreover, accelerated or “fast‑track” options are common online, enabling motivated students to complete a program more quickly than they could in a conventional classroom where the pace is set for the whole group.

In summary, online classes let students work at their own speed as long as they meet deadlines and participate appropriately. Because there is less direct supervision, e‑learning also encourages greater self‑motivation and time‑management skills—qualities that are highly valued in the workplace. Studying online not only imparts knowledge in subjects such as geology or poetry, but also fosters independence and open‑mindedness, preparing both learners and educators to make informed, mature decisions.

Trying to change a creature’s nature meets resistance—after thousands of years of evolution, we cannot simply rewrite it. All I’m trying to point out is that technology is a beneficial element of our lives, but it does not benefit our social life.

Technology is often hailed as the greatest achievement of the 21st century, and most people seem to love it. But is it really all that wonderful? When I was a child, adults warned me that “technology will ruin our social lives.” I dismissed the comment at the time, yet now I understand what they meant.

The main purpose of technology is to simplify tasks, not to make us antisocial or unhealthy. In my view it still has huge potential that we are far from exploiting fully. Instead of using it to make everyday chores easier, many people misuse it: we order fast food from a restaurant rather than cooking at home, which is far less nutritious. Moreover, many individuals build their entire existence around gadgets; if those devices fail, they feel as if they cannot survive. The prevalence of social‑media apps on phones is a clear example, as they encourage people to choose virtual interaction over face‑to‑face conversation.

Of course, technology has both advantages and disadvantages. One of its greatest benefits is the saving of time in routine activities. In the past, people relied on letters that could take weeks to reach their destination; today a message can be sent and read within minutes. Technology also enables the creation of low‑waste homes, cars, aircraft, and other machines by replacing fossil fuels with electricity, which can be generated from solar panels, wind turbines or hydroelectric plants. These renewable sources are virtually limitless, provided no catastrophic event—such as a sudden loss of sunlight or wind—occurs.

Overall, I consider technology a remarkable invention for humanity. Although it brings several harmful effects, the solutions are relatively simple. If we stop letting social media dominate our lives and treat technology merely as a supplementary communication tool, many of the negative impacts would disappear. Technology has come a long way: from lighting a single bulb to powering cars, homes, phones, and entire cities—everything we build now contains some form of technology.

Nevertheless, these dazzling innovations have also drawn our attention away from one another, isolating us. I believe technology is brilliant but also dangerous for our social existence. Humans are inherently social beings; when something hinders our natural tendency to connect, the result is inevitably poor. Trying to change a species that has evolved over millennia is bound to meet resistance. In short, technology is a valuable part of modern life, but it should not replace genuine human interaction.

It is often argued that a person who has mastered a particular skill can still develop, even if they never venture beyond that area. Many people, however, think that once someone becomes proficient in one field, there is little point in pursuing anything else. They assume that mastering a single profession is enough, but they also recognise that personal growth will stall if one does not try new things. In other words, if a person limits themselves to what they already know, their knowledge will expand only within that narrow scope and they will not continue to grow.

Sticking solely to what one has mastered inevitably hampers further development. Take the example of Ms. Generic Name, a charming plant‑shop owner who also teaches about horticulture. One day she gathered a group of children to explain that plants do not grow by themselves; they need human care. She showed them an apple seed and recounted how, after the seedlings grew a little, she stopped looking after them, believing that once they were big enough her job was finished. She left the plants to stand there, assuming they were fine, not realizing that without continued attention they would not develop further. This mirrors the behaviour of people who become experts in a single area, then cease to explore anything else: they become static and cease to grow. Consequently, those who are satisfied with a single mastery and make no effort to try new things will eventually stop advancing.

Knowledge is a key driver of personal growth. Ms. Generic Name eventually realised that caring for plants required ongoing effort, and over the years she accumulated extensive expertise. Rather than remaining confined to what she already knew, she pursued further study, enrolling in a university program that examined plant species from around the world. Her enthusiasm turned her into one of the most respected plant specialists globally. Her story shows that comfort with limited knowledge is a barrier; we should continually seek new information, just as she did.

Some might argue that mastering one discipline is sufficient for growth, especially if it aligns with one’s passion. For instance, a man named Generic Name entered college dreaming of becoming an architect. He graduated as a construction manager instead—still within the building field, but not his original ambition. Even though he achieved a level of mastery, his example illustrates that limiting oneself to a single role can prevent fuller development. After attaining expertise, it remains important to stay open to learning new skills and ideas every day.

In summary, personal growth ceases when we stop trying new things. Knowledge expands in proportion to the time and curiosity we invest in it, and it is a fundamental factor in development. While mastering a subject is valuable, it is far better to remain receptive to further learning and to keep expanding our horizons.

Many people believe that setting ambitious goals is the smartest approach, while others argue that modest targets are safer. Even though some individuals dislike aiming high because falling short can be discouraging, they overlook the fact that achievements come in many forms and sizes. In reality, striving for high goals is beneficial because it enables greater accomplishment, boosts motivation, and enhances the sense of success.

Critics claim that overly lofty goals can demotivate a person when they are not reached. They think that failure after aiming high may lead to giving up and a feeling of emptiness, which can discourage future attempts. This viewpoint highlights a fear of failure, but it ignores several important advantages of setting high aspirations.

One reason to aim high is that it encourages people to accomplish more. When a person sets a challenging target, they often create several sub‑goals rather than focusing on just one. Reaching multiple milestones not only improves performance but also generates pride and satisfaction. Even if one objective is missed, it does not prevent the individual from succeeding in other areas. Different goals have different levels of difficulty, and higher challenges can still be attained with effort.

Another benefit is the increased feeling of success that comes from tackling ambitious goals. Completing a demanding achievement gives a strong sense of triumph, builds confidence, and reduces anxiety. Knowing that one can meet tough objectives provides a lasting boost that can help in future endeavors, making life feel purposeful rather than unfulfilled.

Finally, setting high goals tends to raise motivation. A clear, challenging target demands focus and hard work, concentrating the mind on what needs to be done. This mental concentration creates energy and drive, prompting people to keep pushing toward their objectives. The excitement of working toward a significant goal fuels persistence and determination.

In summary, aiming for high goals is advantageous because it leads to greater achievement, stronger motivation, and a deeper sense of success. Although fear of failure is natural, everyone experiences setbacks, and overcoming them is part of personal growth. By confronting those fears and striving for ambitious targets, individuals can enrich their lives and reach their full potential.

Students work hard; there is no arguing that. They have schoolwork, homework, extracurricular activities, and maybe a job. All these things make a student's life stressful, so it is important that they get a break every once in a while. I believe that students should get a long summer break instead of a year‑round school year because, firstly, there are other activities that can be done during the summer that keep students' minds active; secondly, their health is at risk; and lastly, summer break is beneficial to school staff as well.

From time to time, people need a break from their day‑to‑day life. They need a moment to relax, enjoy life, and perhaps discover an interest they may have. Although school is important and necessary for success later in life, outside experiences also contribute to the development of a student's “real‑life skills.” During summer break there are multiple activities that can keep a student's mind active, whether sports, summer camps, summer jobs, etc. All these activities allow their minds and bodies to stay active. Even though they are not engaging in schoolwork or studying, they are exposing themselves to new activities that might require critical, open‑minded, and collaborative thinking, which I feel is essential for real life. For example, a student at a summer camp might be placed in a group with four strangers and given a challenging task that requires collaboration, critical analysis of the situation, and openness to the perspectives of peers. This mirrors the school environment; therefore, it can be said that they are keeping their minds active while outside of school.

Although not all students might be involved in activities outside of school, some are simply taking a break from the stress of life itself. Because of the many demands during the school year, summer break is a good way to take a breather and care for themselves mentally. Depression has become very common among teenagers in recent years, and although it may not be entirely due to school stress, school does contribute to the deterioration of their mental health. In addition, over‑working oneself has negative impacts overall, whether one is depressed or not. Too much stress can have harmful effects on health: high blood pressure, hypertension, and severe weight loss are a few examples. Furthermore, when stressed the body releases a neurotransmitter called cortisol; excess cortisol can impair a person's thinking and reaction time, which is crucial for students who need to complete schoolwork and homework. Therefore, if they don’t take breaks, their grades are likely to drop due to an inability to think effectively, further contributing to their deteriorating mental health.

Lastly, summer break is an essential time for everyone involved in schools—teachers, administrators, counselors, etc. Although schools are intended to educate students, it is the school staff who make this possible. This is why we need to give our school staff a break, because all the points I stated above also apply to them. In addition, with a long summer break teachers have more time to thoroughly think about lesson plans and an extended period to live their lives and enjoy time with family and friends. After all, teachers are humans too; they need to live their lives and not feel that they are required to do so much for such little pay.

To emphasize further, I believe that schools should give students a long summer break instead of a year‑round schedule because a student's mind will stay active during the summer through various activities that require open‑minded, critical, and collaborative thinking. Students also need a break to de‑stress for the sake of their mental and physical health. Lastly, a long summer break is needed for school staff as well, because they too need time away, just like the students.

There is no doubt that students lead very busy lives. Between classes, homework, extracurricular activities and often a part‑time job, their days can become quite stressful, making regular breaks essential. I argue that a long summer vacation is far preferable to a year‑round school calendar because it allows students to stay mentally engaged through diverse activities, protects their health, and also benefits the staff who work in schools.

Everyone needs occasional downtime to unwind, relax and perhaps discover new interests. While formal education is crucial for future success, experiences outside the classroom help develop practical life skills. During the summer months students can take part in sports, camps, summer jobs and similar pursuits that keep both mind and body active. Even though these activities are not academic in nature, they often require critical thinking, openness and teamwork. For instance, a camper might be placed in a group with strangers and tasked with solving a challenging problem; the group must analyze the situation, listen to each other’s ideas and collaborate to find a solution. Such experiences mirror the collaborative environment of school and therefore keep students’ minds sharp while they are away from lessons.

Not every pupil will fill their summer with organized activities, but many simply need a pause from the constant pressures of the school year. Teen depression has risen sharply in recent years, and although many factors are involved, academic stress is a significant contributor. Prolonged stress can lead to health problems such as high blood pressure, severe weight loss and an over‑production of cortisol, a hormone that hampers thinking and reaction time. When students do not get a chance to rest, their ability to concentrate on homework and exams suffers, which can cause grades to fall and further damage their mental well‑being. A substantial break therefore helps safeguard both their physical and psychological health.

School staff—teachers, administrators and counselors—also need a break. They are the ones who make education possible, and they deserve time to recharge. A long summer recess gives teachers the opportunity to reflect on their curricula, design better lesson plans and enjoy personal time with family and friends. After all, educators are humans too, and they need periods of rest, especially given the heavy workload and modest pay they often receive.

In summary, a lengthy summer holiday is far more advantageous than a continuous school year. It allows students to stay mentally active through varied experiences, reduces stress and protects their health, and it provides essential downtime for the teachers and other school personnel who support them.

Many people have heard the saying, “The greater danger for most of us lies not in setting our aim too high and falling short, but in setting our aim too low and achieving our mark.” It is attributed to the great artist Michelangelo. While some may disagree, I believe that aiming high is far more beneficial. When we set lofty goals, we open ourselves to larger achievements, more original ideas, and a wider range of possibilities.

First of all, high ambitions create many more opportunities. People often decide what they will do before they even start thinking about it. Imagine two job‑seekers: one applies only for low‑skill positions such as washing dishes because they are easy, while the other applies to all the fields they are interested in. The second person obviously has many more chances of finding a better job. The same principle works in education. A young person who is uncertain about the future could either join the military, which offers limited options, or enrol in a university where a variety of career paths are available. By choosing the higher‑level route, the number of possible outcomes expands dramatically.

Secondly, setting high goals encourages more original thinking. Those who aim low tend to stay within their comfort zones and may even be unaware of their own potential. Because they do not challenge themselves, their thoughts remain ordinary. In contrast, people who pursue difficult objectives must solve harder problems, which stimulates the brain and leads to creative solutions. History is full of artists, writers and inventors who achieved greatness precisely because they refused to limit themselves. Their groundbreaking works would not exist if they had settled for mediocrity.

In addition, striving for high standards enables us to reach larger results. Consider an assignment: would you aim only for the minimum requirements or try to exceed them? Most likely you would choose the latter, because a higher effort usually yields a better grade. When we set low goals, we may give up before completing an important task; a higher aim keeps us motivated to finish what we started. Therefore, aiming high generally leads to greater success than settling for the easiest option.

Some argue that very high ambitions can cause stress or failure. While this may be true in extreme cases, it does not justify lowering our expectations. Balance is key, much like the advice to eat a well‑balanced diet. We should understand our abilities and set realistic yet challenging goals, rather than opting for the simplest path. A certain amount of pressure can even be beneficial. When I was a student in Japan, I felt lazy and avoided school, which only increased my anxiety and lowered my self‑esteem. Returning to classes forced me to confront that stress and improve my situation. Not all stress is harmful; a moderate amount can push us forward.

In conclusion, choosing the easy, low‑aimed route may seem safe, but it ultimately limits our potential. The real danger lies in forgetting that we can aim high and achieve remarkable things. No one needs to be perfect, but everyone should strive to do their best while they can, so that they live without regret.

In modern life many people claim that it is wiser to set a modest target and reach it rather than to aim high and fall short, but I disagree. The famous artist Michelangelo warned that aiming too low and succeeding can be dangerous, because he himself had experienced failure and error before he became renowned. He preferred to risk a great undertaking and possibly fail than to settle for a tiny achievement. I share his view: learning from past errors, daring to take risks, and pursuing larger objectives all contribute to personal growth.

Michelangelo’s greatness stems not only from his masterpieces but also from his willingness to keep moving forward after setbacks. By analysing what went wrong, anyone can improve. For instance, on the television program *MasterChef* contestants must impress the judges, and one chef is eliminated each episode. Although elimination can crush a dream, the chef gains the courage to continue, learns from the mistake, and becomes a better cook. A similar lesson can be seen when teenagers take their driving permit test. I failed the test by a single question, reviewed the mistakes, studied the missed material, and passed on my next attempt. These situations show that we can learn from our failures, develop as individuals, and that taking risks is often essential for progress.

Risk‑taking is most apparent in major decisions concerning work, education, and other important areas. I believe that embracing risk is preferable to making only safe, minor choices, even when the outcome is not as hoped. In the show *Shark Tank*, entrepreneurs pitch their ideas to investors; many do not receive funding, yet they persist and look for other opportunities. Over time, repeatedly facing risk makes a person more comfortable speaking publicly and expressing opinions. Likewise, meeting a potential employer face‑to‑face rather than online is more demanding, but it allows the interviewer to see you more clearly and increases the chance of getting the job. By confronting challenges, we become stronger and our mistakes turn into valuable lessons.

Thus, like Michelangelo, I maintain that striving for a big goal—even if it ends in failure—is more beneficial than setting a small aim and achieving it. Large ambitions boost confidence, focus attention, and force us to confront our shortcomings. Small goals require little effort and can encourage complacency, leading to laziness over time. Setting higher targets pushes us to expand our skills and knowledge, making us more capable individuals.

In summary, aiming high and risking failure is preferable to settling for easy success. Bigger goals teach us to learn from mistakes, to embrace risk, and to improve ourselves, whereas tiny aims serve only as an excuse for taking the easy route. Challenging ourselves prepares us for any obstacle that may arise, and even if we stumble on the high road, we are still able to try again.

First impressions also change in a work setting: you may think a job is easy and fun and make friends, but on the second day you meet a boss with a bad attitude, and your impression of the work shifts because you dislike the boss’s behavior. A first impression is a crucial moment because it forms your initial thought about a person or something, and that matters—if you have a good impression of someone, you can make a good friend.

In conclusion, first impressions can change depending on each person and on your attitude, but they do not always change because many people keep their original thoughts about something. Imagine if first impressions never changed—it would be bad, because when your impressions stay fixed simply because you think another person is not cool, you miss the opportunity to learn more about their life.

First impressions differ from one individual to another; each person reacts uniquely when encountering something for the first time. However, those initial judgments can shift once we learn more about the other person’s life. The importance of first impressions lies in the fact that they are our immediate responses, yet they are often subject to change after a short period—perhaps an hour or a day.

Consider a student who finds a class dull on the first day and forms a negative opinion. If the following session proves to be engaging and enjoyable, that opinion may reverse. One’s attitude also influences these initial judgments: a generally pessimistic mindset tends to produce negative first impressions. A poor reaction can reveal aspects of the responder’s character as well.

In some cases, first impressions are hard to alter because many people cling to their initial reaction. Likewise, a positive impression of someone can be undone if that person later behaves poorly.

Workplace examples follow the same pattern. An employee might think a job will be easy and fun, making friends quickly. Yet after meeting a boss with an unfriendly attitude, the initial enthusiasm can fade, and the perception of the job changes. A good first impression can help forge friendships, while a negative one may close that possibility.

In summary, first impressions are mutable and depend on both the individual and their attitude. Nevertheless, they do not always change; some people retain their original opinions. If first impressions never evolved, we would miss the chance to understand others more deeply, limiting our relationships and growth.

I believe strongly in individuality. It feels great when people follow their own wishes and live the way they want, without merely copying what others do. I have many friends, but they often act like everybody else, and that doesn’t appeal to me. I prefer to do what I think is right and follow my own preferences, even if I’m not always sure what those are.

My family tends to be negative and often refuses to listen to what I have to say. That makes me want to assert my own voice even more, because I need to be heard and to act according to my own decisions. I notice that many people rely too much on others, and I think that dependence is unhealthy.

In history class we learned that in the past societies did not value individuality. People sought attention by depending on others, and that still happens today. Modern life is very different from the past; now people care a lot about what others think of them—their appearance, what others say, and so on.  

I like who I am; I consider myself a nice person with good intentions, so I do whatever I want without worrying about others’ opinions.  

I came from Puerto Rico two years ago, and everything changed for me after I arrived. I have started to appreciate every opportunity because I now understand the value of hard work and sacrifice. Despite the difficulties—learning a new language and adapting to different customs—I keep trying to improve myself.

Meeting people from many backgrounds has been both rewarding and challenging. Some are very kind, others less so. I love learning new things and exploring new places, but it frustrates me that, even though we are U.S. citizens, many people treat Puerto Ricans as if we were undocumented simply because Spanish is our first language.

School has been one of my biggest obstacles. It’s hard to sit in a classroom feeling completely alone, unable to ask questions or communicate with anyone. After a few months I started to skip classes and make poor choices because I lacked support both at school and at home.

Now I sometimes feel that I don’t belong here, and the only reason I stay is because of my mother. I want her to succeed and to be able to give her the life she deserves. When we needed her, she was always there, even though life in Puerto Rico was difficult, and she always tried to give us the best she could.  

I continue to believe in myself, and I know that if I set a goal, I can achieve it, no matter how hard the path may be.

Thomas Jefferson said, “Do we accomplish more if we are always doing something, or does inactivity also serve a purpose?” Furthermore, not all the people agree with this statement. Of course, those two persons have different ideas. Furthermore, many people like to be lazy and they do not try to move on; others want to move and work hard to make more opportunities. I agree with this statement, because it represents three nice phases to make others’ opportunities: struggle, exploit, and related.

However, not everyone agrees. To begin, some people think they can't make more options than they already have for some reasons. For instance, a lot of people have not easy lives; some of them are not rich and do not have money to make more options. But we have to know something that’s true about this life: nothing is going to be easy to make or do. For instance, one day before my grandfather died he told me a story about how they were before his life. His life was really hard before; they were not a family, and his five children ate only one time on some days. But he always said these words: “One day everything is going to change.” He never stopped believing that. After this terrible day he found other opportunities to make a different life for his family. That is why every day I think carefully: if you want something, “I need to struggle.”

Moreover, we can accomplish wonderful dreams if we exploit the time. For instance, people can achieve many dreams so fast, also things you never believed you could get one day, like a beautiful car, a big house, and other beautiful things. But you can get all this if you work hard. In addition, other people can give a different life, because you have how to help others. All the persons who never stop work always make many things.

Finally, be related every day; this is something special. Because you are always looking for something more than one. That means you do not stop on one street; you always try to go the other way. For instance, one day I was thinking how to make my dream fast and how to get it. And I said, “If we are people who like to find different options, we are going to get them.” And that is all; this is a reflection to know how you can get everything in your life, but you have to know this: if you never go in, nothing is going to happen.

In short, the idea is to tell you how many opportunities or dreams you can make if you move from one side to the other side. For example, people who do not try to move farther away will never make something different, and that is so sad because you will never know how many special dreams you could have. But that will happen if you don’t move to the other side; if you work hard and always look for more, you will always have everything in your life. For instance, you want a car that costs one million; you will buy that car because you work hard and have the money. Struggle and you will have everything you want; explore, go outside, and find other opportunities. Do not lose your time; time runs very fast every day. You may cry one day because you were lazy, and that will be sad for you. The last try is to be related because there is a way you will find many options to make your life different. If you do all this, your life is going to be easy to live.

Thomas Jefferson said, “Do we accomplish more if we are always doing something, or does inactivity also serve a purpose?” Furthermore, not everyone agrees with this statement. Of course, the two parties hold divergent views. Moreover, many people prefer to be lazy and do not try to advance; others wish to strive and work hard to create more opportunities. I endorse this statement, because it illustrates three valuable paths to generate opportunity, struggle, and related growth.

However, not everyone concurs. To begin, some individuals believe they cannot generate more options than they already possess for various reasons. For instance, many people lead difficult lives; some are not affluent and lack the money to expand their choices. Yet we must recognize a truth about existence: nothing will be easy to achieve or create. For example, one day before his grandfather died he told me a story about his early years. His life was truly hard; his family of five children sometimes ate only once a day. Nevertheless, he always said, “One day everything will change.” He never ceased believing that. After that tragic day he discovered new opportunities to forge a different life for his family. That is why I think carefully every day: if you want something, “I must struggle.”

Moreover, we can realize wonderful dreams if we seize the moment. For instance, people can accomplish many aspirations swiftly, even those they never imagined—such as a beautiful car, a large house, and other splendid possessions. But you can attain all this through hard work. In addition, others can benefit because you know how to help them. Anyone who never stops working will constantly create many things.

Finally, the concept is relevant every day because it is something special. You are constantly seeking more than one option. That means you do not remain on a single path; you always try to explore another direction. For example, one day I contemplated how to achieve my dream quickly and how to obtain it. I concluded, “If we are people who like to discover different options, we will attain them.” This reflects how you can acquire everything in life, but you must understand that without effort, nothing will happen.

In short, the idea is to show how many opportunities or dreams you can achieve if you move from one side to another. For example, people who never strive to go farther will never create something different, which is sad because they will never know how many special dreams they could have. However, if you work hard and constantly seek more, you will eventually obtain everything you desire. Suppose you want a car that costs one million dollars; you will buy that car because you worked hard and amassed the necessary funds. Struggle, and you will obtain everything you want; explore, go out, and find other opportunities—don’t waste time, as time passes swiftly. One day you may mourn having been lazy, and that will be regrettable. The final aim is to stay engaged, because that is how you will discover many options to transform your life. If you do all this, your life will become easier to live.

Thomas Jefferson once wondered whether we achieve more by constantly staying active or if periods of inactivity also have value. Not everyone shares his view, and opinions differ greatly. Some people prefer to remain idle and avoid effort, while others strive to work hard and create new possibilities. I support Jefferson’s idea, because constant effort opens the door to opportunity, growth and personal development.

Nevertheless, not everybody agrees. Some argue that they cannot create additional options because of their circumstances. For example, many people live difficult lives and lack the financial resources needed to pursue new chances. Yet we must accept that nothing worthwhile comes easily. My grandfather told me a story the day before he died: during his youth his family was extremely poor, and his five children often went without food. He constantly said, “One day everything will change.” He never stopped believing in that sentence, and eventually he found ways to improve his family’s situation. His experience teaches me that success requires struggle and perseverance.

In addition, we can achieve remarkable dreams if we make good use of our time. Those who never give up tend to produce many achievements throughout their lives.

Finally, continually seeking new possibilities is essential. When we stop at a single path, we limit our chances for success. This reflection shows that nothing will happen if we remain passive; we must move forward to make our dreams a reality.

In summary, the message is clear: the more we strive and explore different avenues, the more opportunities and dreams we can fulfill. People who stay still rarely experience change, which is a missed chance to discover what they could achieve. When the teacher is teaching, some students may listen to music, which distracts others and prevents them from doing classwork. If a student wants to listen to music while the teacher does not, it can lead to conflict with the teacher. When one student repeatedly uses a cell phone in class, the school may decide to reject the student for repeated misconduct.  

Second, students shouldn’t have a cell phone in the classroom because they chat while the teacher is teaching. For example, when the teacher is delivering a lesson, students who are chatting pay no attention to what is being said, resulting in no learning. They are only playing with friends, which creates a bad image. A student might send rude pictures as a joke, and others may laugh in an inappropriate situation. This behavior harms their morals and can make students fear returning to school.  

Third, students shouldn’t have a cell phone in the classroom because they can cheat on tests. If a teacher gives a test and a student has a phone, they can use it to cheat and obtain a good grade, which is unfair to other students. This reliance on cheating reduces confidence in their own abilities and discourages studying for the test.  

Fourth, students shouldn’t have a cell phone in the classroom because it reduces participation and activities when the teacher asks questions. Time is wasted as students spend the entire day on their phones, which is bad for health; watching movies and listening to music constantly harms the brain and eyes. Constant phone use limits their ability to engage with others and pay attention to what people are saying.  

In conclusion, students shouldn’t use cell phones in the classroom because they cause disturbances, lead to chatting during lessons, enable cheating, and diminish participation.

Even though some people argue that pupils should be allowed to use mobile phones in class because they can access the Internet for school tasks, I believe that phones should be banned from the classroom. They cause disruptions, encourage chatting while the teacher is speaking, enable cheating, and reduce active participation.

First, having a phone in class creates disturbances. A student may play music or watch a video during a lesson, which distracts the whole group and prevents anyone from concentrating on the work. If a learner insists on listening to music while the teacher is speaking, it can lead to a confrontation with the teacher. When one pupil repeatedly brings a phone and causes trouble, the school may have to discipline him or her, possibly even sending the student away.

Second, phones encourage chatting during lessons. When the teacher is explaining a concept, many students will be typing messages to friends instead of listening. This lack of attention means they miss important information and the classroom atmosphere becomes noisy and unfocused. Sometimes inappropriate jokes or pictures are shared, which can embarrass classmates and create an uncomfortable environment. Such behaviour harms the moral climate of the class and makes some students reluctant to return to school.

Third, mobile phones make cheating easier. During a test a student could look up answers on the device, gaining an unfair advantage and lowering the grades of honest classmates. Reliance on cheating also undermines a pupil’s confidence in their own abilities and discourages genuine study.

Finally, phones reduce participation in classroom activities. When a teacher asks a question, many pupils are preoccupied with their screens instead of raising their hands. This wastes time and prevents meaningful interaction. Prolonged exposure to screens also harms health, straining eyes and limiting brain development, because students focus only on movies or music rather than engaging with the lesson and their peers.

In conclusion, allowing mobile phones in the classroom leads to disruption, chatting, cheating, and a lack of involvement, so they should not be permitted during lessons.

Distance learning is not an effective way for most students to study, and many schools rightly choose not to offer it as an option.  

First, learning from home can leave pupils without immediate help when they do not understand something. In a classroom a teacher or a fellow student can clarify doubts on the spot, but online the support is often delayed or unavailable, which hinders comprehension.  

Second, education requires interaction and structure that are difficult to replicate through a screen. Students need a school environment that provides guidance, resources, and a sense of community; without this, they may miss essential knowledge and skills.  

Third, while it is possible to acquire information at home, attending school in person remains the most reliable method for genuine learning. Face‑to‑face contact allows teachers to monitor progress, give feedback, and keep students motivated, which is much harder to achieve remotely.  

Some learners do benefit from online classes, especially those who have jobs after school or who have caring responsibilities such as looking after a child. For these individuals, flexible schedules can be an advantage. However, the majority of students face distractions at home—electronic devices, family members, and other interruptions—that diminish concentration and hamper study.  

Furthermore, video‑conferencing tools can deliver lessons, but they do not replace the personal interaction needed when a question arises. If a pupil cannot ask a teacher directly, misunderstandings persist.  

In conclusion, although distance learning may suit a small group of students with special circumstances, the traditional school setting provides the structure, support, and environment that most learners need to succeed. Therefore, schools that do not offer distance learning are making a sound decision for the overall quality of education.

When you need advice, it’s rare to rely on just one person. It’s usually wiser to consult several sources, which reduces the chance of missing better alternatives and lowers the opportunity cost of a single viewpoint. Most people seek out a few opinions so they can compare different options instead of basing a decision solely on one individual’s perspective.  

One advantage of gathering advice from multiple people is the variety of choices they present. By hearing several suggestions, you can weigh a broader range of possibilities before deciding. This can lead to a good outcome, but it also carries the risk of a poor one—every choice involves an opportunity cost. Your decision may influence many aspects of your life, from your mood that day to longer‑term consequences. Having more options simply means there are more potential paths to consider.  

Another benefit is that hearing others’ viewpoints helps you identify which ideas have worked well for them and which have not. You can adopt the useful parts of their advice and learn from their successes or mistakes. Over time this knowledge not only assists you in similar situations but also enables you to guide others who face comparable dilemmas. In this way, shared advice becomes a resource for personal growth and for helping friends or acquaintances in the future.  

A drawback of consulting several people is that the differing opinions can be confusing. Hearing many perspectives may make you question your original plan, and the abundance of options can increase the pressure you feel when selecting a course of action. The decision you finally make might turn out to be either a great success or a serious disappointment, and the uncertainty can be stressful. Nonetheless, despite the difficulty of choosing which advice to follow, seeking multiple opinions remains a valuable strategy for making more informed decisions.

People often change their behaviour once they get to know someone, and it is disappointing how many still resort to bullying without ever meeting the person they target. I have tried hard to get along with others, but not everyone is kind. Some individuals judge and attack strangers without any reason, which is why I often find myself alone; too many people spread rumors and gossip, and those who bully never seem to care about the feelings of their victims.

I try not to let what others say affect me. If they want to talk nonsense, that is their problem. When someone is hurt by a bully, however, they usually turn to you for help when they are in trouble. Whenever I feel angry or sad, I play soccer because it helps me forget my worries. If possible, I would organize soccer games so that anyone who wants to play can do so and leave their problems on the field. Sports give people a chance to have fun without fighting, and they also provide other ways to connect—going to the cinema, watching a football, basketball or volleyball match, or simply hanging out with friends. In my view, every problem has a solution; the main obstacle is a lack of respect for one another. If we treated each other with respect, life would be very different.

What everyone wants is to feel safe in a community where gangs do not thrive, because gangs only make people poorer and more vulnerable. Families need to work together to protect each other from those who cause harm. Many young people study hard because they want to lift their families out of trouble and find a stable job after high school. Even if the first job isn’t perfect, it provides a foothold and the chance to earn a decent living.

If someone tries to steal your belongings, you can call the police and report the incident; they may help you recover what was lost. People should not be afraid to ask for help, because showing fear can make others think they are easy targets. Although we are capable of great intelligence, we must use it wisely in all situations, not just in the areas where we excel. Being calm and respectful encourages others to treat you kindly, while anger often provokes more aggression.

Most people are good at heart, but anger can change them dramatically. To avoid conflicts, invite others to play sports or spend time together at the beach or another enjoyable setting. Sharing fun experiences can prevent hostility and turn acquaintances into lasting friends. At the same time, it is wise to keep your most vulnerable points private; revealing them can give others a reason to hurt you. This is my perspective on how to handle bullying and build safer, friendlier relationships.

Failure plays a huge part in becoming successful. By failing, people learn how not to make the same mistakes again. For example, let’s say that I was trying to become a professional soccer player. I played for the best clubs, I was named the best player on the team, and I had never been cut from a team. One day my coach tells me that there is a professional soccer try‑out next week and he wants me to get ready, so he gives me a schedule of what I should do to get fit. Every day I have to eat right and train hard. I did all of those things, although some days I did not want to train and I wanted to start eating unhealthy, but I fought through it. At the end of the day they gather everybody and call the people who made it. I am not one of them. I have failed to become a pro soccer player.

He is also a dad with one kid and lives in a motel. He gets kicked out of the motel because he cannot pay his bills, so he is homeless for a couple of weeks. Even though he is homeless, that does not stop him from trying to sell his machine. Still, nobody is willing to buy it from him. Finally, after his ups and downs, someone buys his machine.
