He becomes successful because he does not give up on his dream even though he is getting rejected every time he tries to sell it. Failure is the key to your success.

Failure plays a huge part in achieving success. When we fail, we learn what not to repeat. Imagine I wanted to become a professional soccer player. I had played for top clubs, was considered the best in my team, and had never been cut. One day my coach told me about a professional trial the following week and gave me a schedule to get in shape. Every day I had to eat well and train hard. Some mornings I felt lazy and wanted to eat junk food, but I pushed myself forward.

The trial day arrived and I felt as prepared as I could be. We began with warm‑ups and then moved on to drills. I performed strongly, thinking I was the best on the field. At the end, the coaches gathered everyone and announced the players who had made the cut. I was not among them. I had failed to become a professional soccer player.

Now enthusiasm becomes crucial. I could give up soccer altogether and choose a different path, or I could keep my head up and try again. Failure tests how patient we are and whether we are willing to keep trying despite repeated setbacks. A similar lesson appears in the book *The Pursuit of Happiness*. The protagonist creates a machine that he wants to sell, but no one is interested. He is also a single father living in a motel, and after he can’t pay the rent he is evicted and ends up homeless for a few weeks. Even while living on the streets he continues to try to sell his invention, but buyers remain scarce. Eventually, after many rejections, someone finally purchases the machine. That buyer tells others how good it is, and sales begin to rise. He becomes successful because he never abandoned his dream, despite constant rejection.

Thus, failure is not the opposite of success; it is a necessary step on the road to it.

If my school adds two more hours, kids could have three days off from school, which would save a lot of energy and water. Teachers could also get three days off a week if the school extends to 10‑hour days. There should be just four school days a week.

Some people have a hard time waking up early in the morning to do their homework. When students get enough sleep they can focus more on their studies and have more time on weekends to do their homework. That’s how students can achieve their goals in high school: with enough sleep they stay fresher and more active during school hours. In high schools most students struggle throughout the year because they don’t have enough time for homework; during weekends many students work 32 to 38 hours, leaving little time for homework on Saturday and Sunday.

I believe that a ten‑hour workday is far superior to an eight‑hour one because it saves a great deal of energy, electricity and personal time. By working ten hours each day for four days, a person still completes a 40‑hour week, and any extra hours can be taken as overtime on Friday or Saturday if desired.

The same idea can be applied to schools. If the school day ran from 10 a.m. to 10 p.m. instead of 8 a.m. to 4 p.m., we could extend the schedule by two hours and give students more sleep when they return home. With a longer school day, the week could be shortened to three school days, allowing both students and teachers to enjoy a three‑day weekend. This reduction would also cut down on electricity, water and other resources used by the school.

Many young people struggle to wake up early, which makes completing homework difficult. When they get enough rest, they are more focused during lessons and have extra time on the weekend to finish assignments. By granting a longer daily schedule and a shorter week, students would stay fresher and more active in class, helping them reach their academic goals. In high schools today, many pupils work between 32 and 38 hours a week, leaving little time for homework on Saturdays and Sundays. A four‑day, ten‑hour school week would alleviate this pressure and give them the balance they need.

Some people prefer to teach themselves, experimenting on their own, and they often find the experience rewarding because it allows them to discover their own style. In short, I use drawing mainly for enjoyment and as a mental escape, and I have honed my ability through art classes and continual practice.

John Lubbock, the British naturalist and politician, once said, “Your character will be what you yourself choose to make.” This statement invites us to consider whether our past merely shapes us or whether we have the power to decide who we become. While our experiences certainly influence us, it is ultimately our actions and choices that determine our character.

Take, for example, a person who grew up with abusive parents. One could assume that such a background condemns them to repeat the same patterns, yet many emerge stronger, using the hardship as a catalyst for personal growth. Society may hastily label someone as “mean” or “selfish,” but those judgments often confuse temporary behavior with deeper character. In truth, each of us builds our own character, and no one else has to approve of it. At the end of the day we are alone with ourselves, and that independence can be liberating because we are not constantly trying to satisfy others’ expectations. As the saying goes, you cannot judge a book by its cover; only when people get to know the story behind you can they truly understand the person you have become.

Consider a scenario where a family member dies after a long illness. Grief may plunge you into denial and sadness, but over time you may choose to honor their memory by living fully and making each day count. Even on the toughest days, pushing forward builds resilience and strengthens character, even if you do not always notice the progress yourself. Everyone faces moments of self‑doubt, when the mind insists that a goal is impossible. Yet, once you look back at what you have already achieved, those negative thoughts lose their power. Your character is not meant to be held back by fear; it is meant to break down the obstacles life throws in your way. Only you can decide to confront those “brick walls” and tear them down.

Therefore, do not let anyone’s opinion stop you from following the path you believe is right. Listen to your instincts, let your heart guide you, and turn what seems impossible into something attainable. Your uniqueness should be celebrated, and your character should shine because you chose to shape it deliberately.

Life is not about picking and choosing for others; it is about deciding what feels best for you. As Lubbock reminds us, “Your character will be what you yourself choose to make.” Embrace this freedom, enjoy the journey, and let every experience add strength to the person you become.

In conclusion, having a good attitude can help you in many areas, such as work, school, and family reunions. Now you know that the next time you feel bad or are having a rough time, the best way to handle it is to adopt a good attitude.

Having a positive attitude is the key to success. Attitudes can be divided into two categories: positive and negative. A positive attitude can help you in many situations. For instance, if you disagree with your boss about your salary, you can discuss the matter calmly and reach a compromise, whereas approaching it with a hostile attitude might get you fired. Likewise, a good attitude can lift the mood during difficult or boring moments. Imagine a family vacation that is going poorly; if you stay upbeat, you can improve everyone’s spirit.

There are many things that can foster a positive mindset: a good night’s sleep, sunny weather, receiving a gift, eating at your favorite restaurant, enjoying your preferred food, having friends over, visiting relatives, or simply having fun on a trip. All of these experiences can contribute to a constructive outlook.

Conversely, a negative attitude can lead you down the wrong path. People who are constantly irritable are hard to get along with and often end up with few friends. For example, if you arrive at school stressed and in a bad mood, and a teacher does something you dislike, you might yell at him, get sent to the guidance office, and receive a disciplinary note. Similarly, a person with a bad attitude who looks for a fight can create serious trouble.

Several factors can trigger a negative attitude: lack of sleep, an overwhelming workload, rain that keeps you indoors, encountering someone else’s poor mood, being angry with someone, or feeling hungry and being served unsatisfactory food. These situations can easily sour your disposition.

When I maintain a positive attitude, I always enjoy myself. Things that lift my mood include eating my favorite food, receiving a present, or spending time with family. Yesterday, for example, we celebrated my cousin’s birthday at an entertaining venue. I felt upbeat while playing with my cousin and eating delicious food. I also feel happy when my family and I travel, because exploring new places is exciting. Another instance is when my science teacher, in a good mood, gave us an extra day to submit a project, which was very helpful.

The benefits of a positive attitude are numerous. Take an important exam: if you study hard and feel confident, waking up with a good mood will help you approach the test calmly and likely earn a high mark. Overall, feeling happy is the best sensation a person can experience.

In conclusion, a positive attitude can improve many areas of life—work, school, and family gatherings alike. So the next time you feel down or face a difficult situation, remember that adopting a good attitude is the most effective way to cope.

A enjoyable way to spend time outdoors is to go biking, especially in summer, when you can see places such as stores, the river, birds, and cars, and you can bring food for a picnic. You also get to see other people who are biking, or you can buy food while riding and stop at a store. It’s an enjoyable activity that lets you see lots of wonderful spots—stores, famous locations, and many other sights—while you bike, and you can feel excited about it.

You can also ride with friends, making it even more fun, and have a picnic with them or with family members you choose. While biking you can admire beautiful art and designs, discover new places, and learn more about them.

Spending time outdoors on a bicycle is a delightful activity, especially in the summer. While riding, you can explore a variety of places such as shops, rivers, parks, and even stop for a picnic with food you bring along. The ride also gives you the chance to meet other cyclists and to purchase snacks or meals on the go, making the journey both social and convenient.

As you pedal, you may pass by well‑known attractions like museums, restaurants, or a zoo, and you can watch people enjoying these sites. The freedom of a bike lets you travel wherever you wish, revealing beautiful scenery such as riverbanks where people photograph the view, gardens filled with colourful flowers, and bustling streets lined with popular stores. Seeing others riding their bikes as well adds to the lively atmosphere.

The experience is especially enjoyable when you share it with family or friends. You can bring your children along, pack a lunch, and stop somewhere scenic for a picnic. Riding together makes the outing even more fun, and you can admire public art or interesting architecture as you pass by. In short, cycling lets you discover new places, enjoy the outdoors, and feel the excitement of exploring the world on two wheels.

Dear [Teacher’s Name],

I understand that we students are ultimately responsible for our own grades, but requiring a B average just to participate in sports or other extracurricular activities seems unreasonable. Most of us maintain C averages, and if this rule were changed, many parents and students would become upset—and I’m sure you don’t want to be seen as the bad guy in this situation.

Speaking for the whole school, I believe the minimum should be a D. As long as we are above an F, we are still passing our courses, which is the basic requirement for staying in any activity. It’s clear that academics must come first; without solid study habits we cannot succeed in any sport or club, and good grades open doors to future opportunities. 

Parents often argue that involvement in sports keeps kids out of trouble, and there is some truth to that. However, if the policy were tightened, we might see students who were once reliable turn into constant trouble‑makers, even resorting to calling patrol officers over imagined threats. Please consider how this change would affect both the student body and the wider community.

I disagree with school districts’ plans to let students complete their high‑school diplomas in three years. A three‑year schedule leaves far too little time for learning compared with the traditional four‑year program, and it forces pupils to study intensively during evenings and summer holidays. This relentless pace quickly exhausts their minds, leaves little opportunity for a proper break, and eliminates the chance to take elective courses that are valuable for personal development.

Finishing high school faster may seem attractive because it shortens the overall time before university, but it does not benefit the students. They would have to work excessively hard in the summer and after school, which can lead to fatigue and reduced concentration. Having four years allows learners to progress at a more reasonable speed, giving them the chance to think about their future direction and to choose subjects that match their interests.

A four‑year curriculum also provides the necessary space for students to prepare for higher education and the job market. With the extra year they can deepen their understanding of core subjects, explore electives, and develop the study habits they will need later. Moreover, the additional time means they can enjoy a healthier balance between schoolwork and personal activities, reducing stress and preventing burnout.

In summary, extending high school to four years is more advantageous for students. It offers a more manageable workload, opportunities for elective study, and sufficient time to reflect on future career paths, all of which better equip them for university and beyond.

First, students face more distractions at home, such as videos and other actions; many try to work while taking a class. In my view, students should not be allowed to attend lessons from home through online platforms or video‑conferencing. I do not believe that studying at home offers any real advantage.

First of all, the home environment is full of distractions. There are televisions, smartphones and many other temptations that make it difficult for pupils to concentrate on a lesson. When education is delivered remotely, schools must provide additional support to keep students on task, but this is often insufficient. In a classroom, teachers can interact directly with learners, answer questions instantly and keep the lesson focused, which leads to more effective learning than a distant, screen‑based session.

Secondly, studying from home is simply not suitable for many families. In my own household there are three brothers and a sister, and the noise and interruptions make it hard to follow a lesson properly. The same problem would affect countless other students who share their living space with siblings, parents working from home, or other sources of disturbance.

Finally, the timing of online classes can be problematic. Video sessions are often scheduled for the evening, a time when students are tired and less able to retain information. Morning lessons, on the other hand, correspond with higher alertness and better memorisation. Consequently, remote learning does not provide the same benefits as attending school in person.

In conclusion, I believe that students learn far more effectively when they go to school. Parents share this opinion, as they see the clear advantage of face‑to‑face teaching over distance education. Attending classes on campus remains the most productive way for students to acquire knowledge.

I recognize that some attempts at change may be misguided and lack mutual respect, which reinforces my decision to remain myself.

In conclusion, remaining true to who we are is a wise and beneficial choice. When society pushes us to conform, I will continue to act in accordance with my own values, because that is what makes me happy and fulfills my aspirations. Even if others suggest different ways, I know that staying authentic is the right path for me.

Individual projects tend to increase productivity, especially in a factory setting, and the higher output can bring additional resources for the workers.

Competition can reduce teamwork, but individual competition is a powerful catalyst for improvement. When a worker begins to earn more because his performance is superior, it can provoke jealousy among colleagues, leading to a competitive atmosphere in the workplace. This rivalry often raises overall production, as each employee strives to match or surpass the top performer. For example, if one worker finishes his assignment early and gains extra free time, others may feel compelled to find new ways to increase their output in order to obtain the same reward. Companies frequently encourage such competition by offering bonuses or extra leave to the most productive employees, which in turn motivates everyone to produce more. Thus, separating tasks and fostering individual challenges can be beneficial for the whole organization.

In real life, the leader is the person who works hard and supports teammates. Similarly, a company leader must out‑perform rivals who also aspire to rise to the top. Success therefore depends on making individual decisions and taking personal responsibility.

Doing my own work forces me to be dedicated and diligent, while group work can be hampered by disagreements. Those who possess distinct qualities can make a difference by excelling in competitive, high‑demand environments and influencing their fields. Individuality is crucial for success in any sector—government, industry, or nation. Consequently, I concur with Emerson: competition, driven by individual effort, brings benefits not only to the person but also to the progress of factories, governments, and countries as a whole.

I think that everyone should be allowed to decide for themselves rather than relying on experts or other people. My view is based on three main ideas. First, nobody is infallible; we cannot assume that others always know what is right. Second, only we truly understand our own goals and values, so the choices that affect our lives must come from us. Third, following other people’s examples—whether good or bad—does not guarantee that we will make the right decisions for ourselves.

Trusting other people’s opinions is risky because they may be mistaken or even dishonest. Would you let a best friend choose your path for you? Probably not, since you cannot be sure that they would act in your best interest. If we depend on others who are wrong, we may end up in trouble or make choices that do not suit us. When we succeed on our own—whether at school or elsewhere—we set a positive example for others and show that good decisions are possible without outside direction. Relying on someone else can create problems and place us in situations we would rather avoid.

In life there are countless possibilities, and the responsibility for picking one belongs to each of us. Other people should not judge or interfere with our choices, because everyone has the right to follow their own path. If a decision turns out badly, we must accept the consequences ourselves; we cannot blame anyone else for a situation we created. I have seen students who get into trouble simply because they imitate their peers instead of thinking for themselves. Those who resist that pressure tend to stay out of trouble and keep their education on track.

When you make a decision, you are the only one who truly knows what you want. If something feels wrong, you should not do it. Don’t let fear of making a mistake stop you from reflecting carefully before you act. Ask yourself whether a choice is sensible, because you are the one who will live with the outcome. No one should control your actions. For example, when I chose new friends at school, I selected them carefully so that I would not be swayed into making poor choices by their influence. Ultimately, the power to decide rests with each individual.

In summary, we should always make our own decisions rather than letting others decide for us. Nobody is perfect, and everyone makes mistakes now and then, but that is part of life. By taking the time to think about what we truly want, we can act confidently and avoid regretting our choices later. Do not let yourself be discouraged; trust your own judgment and own the decisions you make.

In a classroom setting, students may feel pressured by long days and heavy homework loads, whereas an online environment lets them study in short, focused sessions without the fatigue that a full‑day school schedule can cause.

I am in favour of establishing an after‑school homework club because it would give many pupils the chance to improve their performance at school and achieve better overall results.

Most students need extra assistance when the work becomes challenging, and a club would provide that help at a convenient time. Difficult assignments often discourage learners, causing them to abandon the task and turn to other activities. By offering a supervised environment after lessons, teachers could guide students through the problems they find most troublesome.

From personal experience, I sometimes require one‑on‑one help, which my family can only afford by hiring a private tutor. Not all parents have the means to pay for such support, so a collective club would relieve them of that financial burden while still giving children the guidance they need. Moreover, extending the session beyond a brief 45‑minute period would allow students to complete a larger portion of their work without feeling rushed.

In summary, a homework club would benefit many learners, reduce costs for families, boost exam scores, and make demanding tasks feel more manageable. Even if some teachers are unable to stay later, pupils can assist one another, ensuring the club runs smoothly and effectively.

This shows that staying positive after failures—even for a poor little boy—is not impossible. Not everyone can do it the same way, but we all seek happiness, and to achieve it, failure can become our right hand.

I completely agree with Winston Churchill: feeling enthusiasm for what comes next in life is more exciting than we think. If we believe in ourselves, stay positive, dream, and understand that failure is part of daily life, we will become more successful, knowing how life really works and that it is not as hard as we have imagined.

“Success consists of going from failure to failure without loss of enthusiasm.”  Although failure is often seen as the opposite of success, it does not have to destroy our drive. As Winston Churchill reminded us, we must not allow our enthusiasm to fade.

Everyone experiences failure at some point. In each stage of life there are setbacks that can feel discouraging, leading us to wonder why missteps occur precisely when we are pursuing something important—whether it is a job, an exam, or simply trying to keep our troubles in order. The question, however, is not why failure happens, but what role it plays in our everyday lives.

The true nature of failure is that it reveals what we did wrong, giving us a chance to improve. Each mistake becomes a lesson that helps us avoid repeating the same errors in the future. In this sense, failure is a stepping stone toward success, because every setback carries valuable experience.

Take scientists, for instance. They often conduct countless experiments that do not work before they achieve a breakthrough. Even when a trial fails, it can lead to unexpected discoveries that expand knowledge beyond the original goal. This demonstrates that no matter how many times we fall, there is always something new to learn.

Keeping a positive attitude can be difficult, especially after a disappointment. Yet feeling stress or insecurity is normal and can actually make us stronger. Many people become depressed after a setback, lose hope, and abandon their goals. It is crucial to recognize these feelings as part of the process rather than as reasons to quit.

A relevant example comes from a book that students at Generic School read last year, “The Life of an Indian.”  It tells the story of a poor boy living on a reservation who, after his teacher shows him a world beyond his circumstances, begins to believe in himself. He fails repeatedly, but each failure pushes him to confront his problems and keep moving forward. His journey shows that even someone with very limited resources can stay hopeful after failure.

Thus, failure can become a powerful ally in the pursuit of happiness. While not everyone reacts the same way, embracing setbacks and maintaining optimism can bring us closer to our goals.

In summary, learning from our mistakes is essential for achieving success. Every failure supplies a new experience and a fresh lesson, and regardless of how often we stumble, solutions will eventually appear. I fully agree with Churchill: sustaining enthusiasm for what lies ahead is more important than we often realize. By believing in ourselves, staying positive, and accepting failure as a regular part of life, we can become more successful and understand that life is not as daunting as it may seem.

The only topic that is frequently debated today is whether we should conserve energy and resources, especially since some businesses have adopted a four‑day work week with ten‑hour days. Should your school follow this model by extending the school day by two hours? Some people think that not only would extending the school day help conserve energy and resources, they also believe it would increase the amount of time students spend at school, which in turn would lead to higher energy use—such as electricity for lights, charging computers, electric blackboards, and other devices. Water is another resource that could be wasted; some students forget to turn off the faucet when they use the bathroom. I believe we should adopt this model and extend the school day by two hours because we need to take care of how we conserve energy and resources, and, last but not least, we will have more time to make the world better and act with conscience.

One reason I believe we should follow this model is that we can conserve more energy for the future. The school should also instruct each student to be careful about how they consume energy—for example, teaching the correct use of electricity at home and offering tips to keep light bills as low as possible.

Another reason is that water is a resource we can save at school. All students use the bathroom frequently and often leave the taps running. Students could create posters that show the importance of saving water, as well as other resources such as plastic and paper, which are purchased by the school. The money saved could make the school better, and students would become more careful with these resources.

The final reason is that, if the school adds two hours to the day, students and teachers will have more time to do additional things. For instance, they could produce a campaign to show society how to prevent climate change and teach others how to protect the world. Students could also create an online page to instruct other students and people outside the school on how to be careful with resources.

As you have read, I think the school should add two hours per day because everyone in the school can develop greater awareness of how to save energy and resources, ultimately benefiting the world. Only when we become conscious of the need for change will we have a better world.

The debate over conserving energy and resources is more common than ever, especially as some companies have moved to a four‑day work week with ten‑hour days. Should schools adopt a similar approach by lengthening the school day by two hours? Some argue that a longer day would actually increase energy use—more electricity for lights, computers, and electronic boards, and even more water waste when students forget to turn off taps. However, I think extending the school day is worthwhile because it can teach us how to use energy and resources more responsibly and give us extra time to improve our world.

One reason to support a two‑hour extension is that it provides an opportunity to teach students how to conserve energy for the future. Schools could include lessons on sensible electricity use at home, offer practical tips for lowering power bills, and encourage habits that reduce unnecessary consumption. By learning these skills early, students will be better equipped to make environmentally friendly choices later in life.

A second argument concerns water savings. Many pupils use the bathroom frequently and often leave taps running. If the school dedicates part of the extra time to campaigns—such as posters that explain the importance of turning off taps—students can become more mindful of water waste. The same principle applies to other resources like plastic and paper; by promoting recycling and careful use, the school can reduce costs and set a positive example for the wider community.

Finally, the additional two hours would give teachers and students more time to undertake projects that raise environmental awareness. They could create informational campaigns, produce online guides, or organize presentations that show how to combat climate change. This extra slot would allow the school to become a hub for sustainability education, reaching both the school community and the public.

In summary, extending the school day by two hours would not only increase awareness about energy and resource conservation but also give us the time needed to develop practical solutions. When everyone in the school becomes more conscious of how they use water, electricity, and other materials, we move one step closer to a healthier planet. Only by embracing such changes can we hope to create a better world for future generations.

Some schools offer distance learning as an option for students to attend classes from home by way of online video conferencing. Is it a good idea to take classes online, or not?

It is a great idea to take classes online; this is my opening argument because it saves the students’ time. Work schedules, family responsibilities, illness, and transportation can all affect students’ availability, and most workplaces do not give students the schedule they want. After work, students can take online classes from home, which makes them more relaxed.

Because focusing on classes after work is hard, studying from home allows students to eat and concentrate better. Online classes also free up time for other activities, such as sports or going out with friends.

If a student is very sick, they cannot attend school and may also infect others. Online classes can make a difference for sick students, especially those who cannot drive. Not all students have cars, and parking can be costly; sometimes the weather makes traveling dangerous.

Family responsibilities are another benefit of online learning. Some students have children, or are disabled and cannot travel to school on their own. Online classes allow these students to take time off when they feel unwell and keep up with their work. Parents who are students can care for their children while attending classes online, which eases their minds because they won’t miss lessons. Although they may feel busy, at least the option of online classes exists. For mothers or fathers who are also students, the time saved is valuable; they can spend time with their kids and check that they are doing well in school.

In the end, technology makes life easier and more helpful; it saves time and allows tasks to be done promptly. We can say that technology returns time to those who are always busy.

Offering distance learning through online video conferencing is a very good idea, and I firmly support it. The main reason is that it saves students a lot of time and gives them flexibility in handling work, family duties, illness, and transportation problems.

First, many students have jobs with irregular hours or responsibilities at home. Because employers rarely adjust schedules to fit a school timetable, it can be difficult for a working student to attend classes on campus. With online lessons, a student can finish a shift and then log in from home, which reduces stress and makes it easier to keep up with studies.

Second, studying from home helps concentration. After a long day at work it is hard to stay focused in a crowded classroom, but at home a student can take a short break, have a meal, and then return to the lesson with a clearer mind. The extra time saved can also be spent on other activities such as sports, meeting friends, or pursuing hobbies.

Third, health and travel issues are less of a barrier. When a student is ill, attending a physical school risks spreading germs to classmates. Online classes prevent this and also avoid the need to travel when someone feels too weak to drive or take public transport. Moreover, not having to search for parking or worry about bad weather eliminates additional hassles.

Finally, family obligations become much easier to manage. Some students have children, while others may have disabilities that make commuting difficult. Online learning lets them stay at home, look after their kids, or attend to personal health without missing lectures. Parents who are also students can watch over their children and still keep up with coursework, which relieves anxiety and improves their overall well‑being.

In summary, technology has made education more accessible and convenient. By allowing students to study from anywhere, online classes protect valuable time, reduce stress, and accommodate a wide range of personal circumstances. Therefore, distance learning is a beneficial option for many learners.

Ralph Waldo Emerson once said, “To be yourself in a world that is constantly trying to make you something else is the greatest accomplishment.”  While some people dispute this view, I fully agree.  Society constantly pushes us to adopt new opinions, abandon our traditions, and alter our beliefs.  To resist that pressure, we must never give up, continuously love and take pride in who we are, and never forget where we come from.  

First, the world may demand change, but we must hold firm to our own identity.  It does not matter whether others approve; the only person who truly needs to be comfortable with yourself is you.  Persistence in being yourself is essential, even when the path is uncomfortable.  

Second, we should always cherish and be proud of ourselves.  Mistakes are inevitable, but they do not redefine our core character.  By learning from errors we grow, and loving ourselves—our looks, our personality, our quirks—keeps us distinct from anyone who tries to force us into a mould.  

Third, we must keep our roots close.  Immigrants or anyone from a different cultural background often feel pressured to hide their heritage and pretend to be someone else.  Resisting that urge and staying true to one’s origin is a powerful way to demonstrate that we can surpass the expectations placed on us.  

In conclusion, do not let the world reshape you.  Keep fighting for what feels right, love and value yourself, and stay connected to your roots.  Every part of who you are makes you special, and staying authentic is truly the greatest achievement.

When we're born we come out of our mother's womb, the first thing we naturally do is screech and cry, and if we don't cry the doctor hits us on our backs and tries to make us cry. And from that cry on we develop our own kind of sound and our own screech with its own pitch. They take our fingerprints where there will never be two of the same; even when we're born with our twin it will never be the same no matter how much alike we are. From there on we start to learn and develop our own persona. After we're born our brain starts to function even with little stuff; babies learn to cry when they're hungry, want to be changed, when they're in pain or simply want attention. When children get older into the toddler stage they start to learn how to walk by observing everyone else; they learn to talk by listening to everyone else around them. We learn how to grab our bottle, pick up a fork or spoon, and practically our own daily doings. But we learn all that from observing and listening to everyone else. When we hit our 6‑12 years of age we have a tendency that we want to fit in, be in the cool kids group, and we watch TV, see celebrities, see that there are musicians, actors, painters, police officers, firemen, dentists, doctors, mayors, chefs, soccer players, basketball players, football players, baseball players, hockey players, tennis players, volleyball players, etc. The list could go on and on, but the point here is the fact that we are influenced. But as we get older in our teen years, 13‑19, we start to have our own kind of voice, at least until we're old enough to make them. We all take our own paths and we choose to make the decisions that we make; our parents don't go with us throughout the day telling us what to do or not do, making each and every decision for us. They sure do give us a hell of advice because they already went through that stage and they don't want to see us fail and get hurt, but sometimes it's good that we fail and make mistakes because then we learn what we can or cannot do. So honestly I don't think that we're born with labels; I feel like we all can make our own decisions of what we're going to make of life, if you're going to sit there and make everyone see you as a pity. A huge part of your character is your mentality; if you have a broken, down, weak mindset you're going to have negative vibes and a weak, dead‑beat character, but if you have a strong mindset and the will to get stuff done then you'll have a broad and respected character. In conclusion I'd like to think that we create and build our own character and that we're not given a label by any higher power of what our character is going to be in life.

When we're born we emerge from our mother's womb; the first thing we naturally do is screech and weep, and if we don't cry the doctor taps us on the back and tries to coax a tear. From that cry onward we develop our own kind of sound and our own screech with its own pitch. They take our fingerprints, which will never be identical; even when we are born as twins, they will never match no matter how alike we appear. From there we begin to learn and forge our own persona. After we're born our brain starts to function even with minimal input; babies learn to cry when they're hungry, need a diaper change, are in pain, or simply crave attention. When children grow older into the toddler stage they start to learn how to walk by observing everyone else; they learn to talk by listening to those around them. We learn how to grasp a bottle, pick up a fork or spoon, and manage our daily tasks. But we acquire all of that by watching and listening to others. 

When we reach the 6‑12‑year age range we develop a tendency to want to fit in, to be part of the cool‑kids group, and we watch TV, see celebrities, notice musicians, actors, painters, police officers, firefighters, dentists, doctors, mayors, chefs, soccer players, basketball players, football players, baseball players, hockey players, tennis players, volleyball players, etc.—the list could go on endlessly. The point here is the fact that we are influenced. 

As we age into our teen years (13‑19) we begin to find our own voice, at least until we are old enough to shape it fully. We each take our own paths and make the decisions we make; our parents no longer accompany us every minute, dictating what to do or not to do, though they do offer abundant advice because they have already traversed that stage and do not want us to fail or get hurt. Sometimes it is beneficial to fail and make mistakes, for that is how we learn what we can or cannot do. 

Now, as adults, that safety net we enjoyed while living under Mom and Dad's roof disappears; we no longer have that privilege, and we must grow up and formally create and develop our own persona. When you obtain a job it brings responsibilities, and from there we discover whether we are responsible or irresponsible, sociable or withdrawn, lenient or strict, patient or impatient, forgiving or unforgiving. I'd like to think we are all born to grow and learn about our rugged society, and based on what we've experienced we will act accordingly, because one can literally reside in a squalid place yet maintain the happiest attitude, surpassing a boy or girl complaining about not getting the car they wanted, versus the kid who saw his mother abused by a dead‑beat dad, or the child who stayed up all night wondering if his mother would return home, or even the child who fell asleep hungry. 

So honestly, I don't think we are born with labels; I feel we can each decide what we will make of life, rather than sit and allow everyone to view us with pity. A huge part of your character is your mentality: if you have a fragmented, weak mindset you will exude negative vibes and a feeble, lackluster character, but if you possess a strong mindset and the will to accomplish things, you will develop a broad, respected character. 

In conclusion, I'd like to think that we create and build our own character and that we are not assigned a label by any higher power dictating what our character will be in life.

From the moment we are born, we emerge from our mother’s womb with a natural instinct to scream and cry. Even if a newborn does not cry, a doctor will gently pat the back to stimulate a wail. That first cry marks the beginning of our unique voice, which later develops its own pitch and tone. Our fingerprints are taken at birth, and they will never be exactly the same as anyone else’s, even in the case of identical twins. From that point onward we start to form our own personalities.

Soon after birth the brain begins to function with very simple cues: a baby cries when it is hungry, needs a diaper change, feels pain, or simply wants attention. As children grow into toddlers, they learn to walk by watching the people around them, and they acquire language by listening to the speech of others. They also learn how to hold a bottle, use a fork or a spoon, and manage the basic tasks of daily life—all through observation and imitation.

When we reach the ages of six to twelve, we become more conscious of fitting in with our peers. Television, celebrities, and the variety of professions we see—musicians, actors, painters, police officers, firefighters, dentists, doctors, mayors, chefs, and athletes in many sports—show us the many possible roles in society. These examples influence our aspirations and the groups we want to belong to.

In the teenage years, roughly thirteen to nineteen, we begin to find our own voice. We start to make decisions independently, even though our parents continue to offer advice based on their own experiences. They try to protect us from failure, yet making mistakes can be a valuable part of learning what we are capable of and what we are not.

As adults, we no longer have the safety net of living under our parents’ roof. We must create and develop our own identity in a world that holds us responsible for our actions. A job brings duties that reveal whether we are responsible or careless, sociable or withdrawn, patient or impatient, forgiving or unforgiving. I believe we are born to grow and to learn from the roughness of society; our experiences shape how we behave. A person can live in a difficult environment and still maintain a cheerful attitude, while another may complain about a minor inconvenience because of a more comfortable background.

Therefore, I do not think we are born with fixed labels. Our choices determine the kind of life we lead. A weak, defeatist mindset breeds negativity and a fragile character, whereas a strong, determined outlook builds a respected and resilient personality. In short, we construct our own character through our decisions and actions; no higher power assigns us a predetermined label for who we will become.

Self‑reliance means that both students and adults are able to make their own choices and solve problems without depending entirely on others. To understand why this quality is so important today, we can start by looking at the challenges we face in our country. The recent government shutdown, for example, has not only affected individual citizens but also disrupted businesses, stores, farms and countless other sectors across the United States. In situations like these, seeking help and advice can make a huge difference. It is not enough for one person to voice an opinion; a variety of perspectives allows us to discuss issues more thoroughly and generate better solutions.  

We should not raise children to be mere followers. By teaching them how to think independently and to ask for guidance when needed, we are nurturing future leaders. Leaders, after all, also seek counsel; they begin with small steps, gradually acquire knowledge, and continue to ask questions even after they have mastered many skills. This habit of continual learning applies to families, workplaces, and everyday life.

Self‑reliance is not limited to students. Adults who combine personal initiative with the willingness to gather information become more effective at work and in their personal lives. While we are learning, we also pass these habits on to others, creating a ripple effect that benefits the whole community. Good decision‑making resembles leadership: we believe our choices are right, but we also recognize the value of hearing other opinions. By consistently asking questions and considering alternative ideas, we broaden our options and make more informed choices.

Even large‑scale matters, such as military service or national policies, require self‑reliance. Soldiers must be prepared mentally and skill‑wise to act when commanders issue orders, because lives are at stake. Boot‑camp training focuses on developing exactly this independence of thought. The same principle applies in civilian life—whether we are deciding about a career move, caring for children, or handling finances, we need to stay alert, seek information, and weigh our options carefully.

Regardless of age, race, gender or background, cultivating self‑reliance and the habit of asking questions is essential for the future. These skills help us teach the next generation about money, business, and civic responsibility. When we stay informed about what our government is doing, we can influence change and avoid repeating past mistakes, such as another stock‑market crash. Using our voice, our knowledge, and our willingness to help others strengthens both our communities and our nation.

Our jobs depend on the economy, which is largely supported by government revenue. A shutdown would threaten income, jeopardize businesses, and even put homes at risk. Therefore, instead of focusing on trivial decisions—like buying a new car—we should prioritize understanding the larger picture, seeking guidance, and offering fresh ideas. Never be afraid to ask for advice; asking questions does not hurt, it simply opens new perspectives. We learn every day, and no one is perfect, but by continually seeking answers and sharing our insights we grow together.

In conclusion, always pursue guidance, keep asking questions, and never stop learning. Thank you for your time.

The question of whether the reduced face‑to‑face contact caused by technology is beneficial or harmful does not have a simple answer; it depends largely on the individual.  

On the positive side, digital devices can help people who feel lonely. When someone has no one to talk to, being able to browse a book, shop online, play games, listen to music on platforms like Pandora, or watch a favorite series on YouTube or Netflix can be a lifesaver. These activities can prevent the darker outcomes that loneliness can bring, such as mental decline, unemployment, or even more severe consequences. In this sense, technology offers a useful outlet for those who would otherwise suffer from isolation.  

However, nothing is entirely perfect. As my grandfather liked to say, “there must be some bad things so that good things can exist.” Every advantage of technology is accompanied by a drawback. One of the most noticeable negative effects is that people increasingly lose interest in ordinary, real‑world interactions. Many individuals no longer value family gatherings or simple conversations; they prefer to stay glued to their phones. I have experienced this myself—my cousin and childhood friends used to spend afternoons chatting at my house, but now it is hard to have a normal conversation because most people are distracted by whatever is on their screens. This behavior can be interpreted as a sign of disrespect and can cause others to feel ignored or disliked.  

Technology is undeniably one of humanity’s greatest inventions. It has made communication faster, provided endless entertainment, and kept us informed about events happening anywhere on the planet, even in space. It spares us from having to read whole books for simple answers, lets us shop without leaving home, and allows us to order food with a few taps.  

Yet this convenience also breeds laziness. People begin to wonder why they should do something themselves when a phone or computer can do it for them. Why meet someone in person when a chat app can replace the encounter? Why engage in a real conversation when there are countless games or videos to watch? If this mindset continues, we may find ourselves alone, surrounded only by devices.  

In conclusion, technology is a powerful tool that can greatly improve our lives, but it should be used only when necessary and not allowed to dominate our thoughts or replace genuine human contact.

Besides that, choosing to sign up for an art class not only helps students clear their minds, making it easier to absorb information in the following block, but also increases efficient adoption. For instance, after a serious block with a lot of information in our brains, we need to clear it by singing, acting, or drawing; this helps our brain relax and become ready for more information. It also depends on our favorite form of entertainment, as your body and brain can feel relaxed when you are engaged in it.

We agree that every student should be required to take those classes, but if such classes are not electives that match students' natural abilities, a large number of students who are not serious about music, drama, or art will make others feel uncomfortable—like they are going to sleep or make noise, which affects everyone around them.

To sum up, we know students should take an arts class to feel fresh after a tired day or two to three blocks in a row, to recharge and improve their adaptive abilities; it helps students produce motivation for school and feel comfortable without pressure. However, art classes still need to be electives so that students can choose according to their own interests and avoid wasting time on a class they are not interested in.

As education advances, schools increasingly offer programmes that nurture each pupil’s innate talents, allowing those who are drawn to the arts to enrol and discover their strengths. In addition to academic work, students need a break after two or three hours of study to relieve stress. Such a pause lets them recharge and boosts their energy for the next productive session, especially when they then attend an art class. However, this time can feel wasted for students who have no interest in practising art.

High‑school life often becomes dull for many because they cannot pinpoint their interests or see a purpose in what they are doing. In this context, finding enjoyable activities is the most effective way to cut stress and refresh the mind between study blocks. Options such as joining a band, taking part in drama, or attending an art workshop can reignite motivation for learning. These activities should be compulsory, because they are also choices that students make for themselves.

Moreover, signing up for an arts class does more than clear the mind; it makes it easier for students to absorb new information in the following lesson. After an intense period of learning, singing, acting or drawing can relax the brain, preparing it for further input. The sense of relaxation varies with each person’s preferred form of entertainment, but the result is the same: a calmer, more receptive mind.

We agree that every student ought to take an arts class, yet if these courses are not offered as electives that match individual talents, many disinterested pupils may disrupt the learning environment—by sleeping or making noise, for example—affecting everyone’s enjoyment.

In conclusion, incorporating arts into the school curriculum helps students recover after long study periods, improves their ability to retain new material, and boosts motivation without adding pressure. Nevertheless, such classes should remain elective, allowing each student to choose the activity that best fits their interests and avoids wasting time on subjects they do not care about.

Technology shapes our lives in many ways, and its influence can be both helpful and harmful. In today’s world, technology is almost everywhere, and without it we would miss out on countless opportunities for learning and communication. Thanks to modern devices, we no longer have to meet face‑to‑face to have a conversation; a simple phone or an internet connection lets us text or video‑chat with people on the other side of the planet. Overall, I believe that technology mostly has a positive impact, and I will illustrate this with a few examples.

First, technology is essential in many jobs. Many people rely on computers and the internet to perform their duties, earn a living, and solve problems without constantly asking others for help. In schools, both teachers and students use technology every day. Assignments are often completed on computers and submitted online, and the internet provides instant answers to countless questions. In the United States, for instance, roughly half of all classroom activities involve digital tools, and books are used far less than they once were. Doctors also benefit enormously from technological advances. Modern medical devices enable surgeons to perform safer operations, and many clinicians now trust digital information as much as—or more than—textbooks. Even in factories, automation and digital equipment have reduced the need for strenuous manual labor, allowing work to be completed more efficiently.

However, technology can be used for both good and bad purposes. Most people employ it constructively: secretaries, teachers, doctors and many other professionals depend on it to communicate, store data and improve their work. Some parents even treat tablets and smartphones as “new babysitters,” using them to keep children occupied while they attend to other tasks. On the downside, a minority exploit technology for harmful ends. Cyber‑criminals commit fraud, hack bank accounts and harass victims through social media and online games. Older adults may be tricked by scams, and some youths use the internet to spread negativity. These examples show that increased access to technology does not guarantee that everyone will use it responsibly.

Technology also changes how we live and think. Modern security systems make homes feel safer, and platforms such as YouTube allow people to share their passions with a wide audience, even if they never meet their viewers in person. Communication that once required handwritten letters can now be done instantly through texts or video calls, eliminating the need for physical presence. In online games, players from different continents can talk and cooperate in real time, demonstrating how technology can bridge geographic gaps.

Nevertheless, the reduction of direct human contact can have drawbacks. In the workplace, face‑to‑face interaction helps build strong relationships among colleagues. Romantic partners also benefit from personal conversations rather than relying solely on texting. In educational settings, while digital resources are valuable, discussing ideas with classmates in person can deepen understanding. Ultimately, both human interaction and technological communication have their strengths and weaknesses. Many people prefer the convenience of a quick online search over reading a book, but the internet does not always provide accurate answers.

In conclusion, technology offers many advantages, yet it also imposes limits on personal contact that can be detrimental in certain situations. While we should embrace the benefits of digital tools, we must also remember the importance of genuine, face‑to‑face communication. Balancing both will help us make the most of what technology has to offer without losing the human connections that enrich our lives.

I believe that honesty should be practiced at all times. When I am truthful, I am not deceiving anyone, and this builds trust. If people know that I always tell the truth, they will feel confident asking me for advice or relying on me for help, even if they themselves are not completely honest in their own affairs. For me, honesty is the most important trait because it creates a foundation of trust that helps relationships grow and mature.

Another reason I value honesty is that it gives me confidence in my own abilities. When I tell myself that I will study hard and do my best on an exam, I am more likely to succeed, and I am less likely to become a target of bullying. Of course, being honest does not guarantee that everyone will be pleased. Sometimes my truth may upset someone who expected me to lie, and that person might decide never to trust me again. It would be disappointing if I had to admit something uncomfortable just to keep a friend or family member happy, especially when the potential negative outcome is unlikely.

If a breach of trust occurs, the relationship may suffer. A friend or relative might doubt my honesty and turn to someone else they consider more reliable. This could lead to arguments and prolonged conflict. The best way to avoid such disputes is to address concerns directly, meeting with the other person and discussing the issue calmly. By doing so, feelings are less likely to be hurt, and the friendship can be preserved.

When people feel trusted, they are less prone to negative thoughts such as anxiety, depression, or self‑destructive behavior. Even if someone tells me they no longer trust me, I will not let that lead to despair. I will stand by my commitment to honesty, even if I have let them down before. My personal honesty will not be a failure; it remains the core of who I am.

If I anticipate failure on a test, I will honestly admit my doubts but also commit to working hard and improving. If I perform poorly, it is not honesty that caused the result but my own lack of preparation. Honesty can motivate me to study better and avoid repeating mistakes.

I would like everyone to make honesty their primary characteristic because it helps resolve conflicts that are otherwise hard to settle. Some people argue that honesty should not be absolute, claiming that others must first understand its true meaning. They also think that intelligent people are naturally more honest, but this is a mistaken belief. Both intelligent and less‑educated individuals can be honest, and both can improve over time. A person’s honesty may wane if they are not taught to value truth, which is why families and teachers play a crucial role in reinforcing it.

Friends may sometimes tempt me to abandon honesty, but I know that staying truthful will ultimately earn their respect. When others see my growth, they will be surprised and may wonder how I changed so much. Their curiosity will spread, and eventually everyone will recognize the importance of honesty.

In conclusion, honesty should be the number‑one quality in every person's life because it builds trust, reduces conflict, and supports personal growth. It is the best policy for a successful and harmonious future.

Dear Council,

I am in favour of introducing a curfew for teenagers because it would keep them out of trouble. Some young people loiter on the streets after dark and cause problems for others. Requiring them to be home by 10 p.m. would reduce the amount of time they spend idle and potentially disruptive. There are also many teenagers who attend school early in the morning and need to sleep; a curfew would help them get enough rest. If a curfew were implemented, a law could be passed stating that any teenager found on the streets after 10 p.m. would be breaking that regulation.

A considerable number of adolescents end up in jail for activities they should not be involved in. While some possess illegal items such as weapons, many are caught simply because they are in the wrong place at the wrong time and become associated with those who have such items. The presence of weapons and other contraband often originates from the streets, where they are hidden or passed around, making it easier for the police to locate them. A curfew would help the city council protect teenagers by keeping them away from these dangerous situations.

Some argue that a curfew intrudes on young people's freedom. Yet, when we consider the other side of the story, it is clear that many teenagers are engaging in behaviour they should avoid. The curfew is intended to safeguard them, not to restrict them without reason.

In conclusion, I believe it is a sensible measure to prevent teenagers from being on the streets after 10 p.m., as it will help keep them safe and out of trouble.

Ralph Waldo Emerson once claimed that “unless you try to do something beyond what you have mastered you will never grow,” and his words ring true. To grasp his meaning fully, we must recognise that claiming mastery means being able to perform a task flawlessly. Personal growth, therefore, requires us to set new challenges for ourselves. Even modest steps move us forward on the road to larger achievements. Success does not always come easily; it may take years of practice to acquire or perfect a skill, but with sufficient confidence and self‑belief we can eventually achieve mastery.

If you can ride a bicycle, try learning to ride a motorcycle; if you can bake cupcakes, attempt a full‑size cake; if you can float, teach yourself to swim. These small undertakings build on existing abilities and sharpen them. By enhancing what we already know, we open the door to greater opportunities and more ambitious projects. Without pushing ourselves beyond our current limits, our goals will remain out of reach, yet dedication and perseverance can carry us to those objectives and beyond what we thought possible. A single failure at a minor task does not mean we cannot master it; we must keep trying until we succeed, because only then do we truly develop. Ultimately, the choice lies with you—to strive for personal growth or to remain unchanged and forfeit the chance to achieve your aspirations.

I believe that allowing students to take lessons from home would be advantageous because it lets them start classes feeling more prepared and can help them concentrate better.

One reason for this view is that, in a traditional school setting, many pupils feel embarrassed about showing their abilities. For instance, a bright student might be told, “You can’t do this” or “Your English isn’t good enough,” which can damage confidence. Yet if the goal is to succeed, students can work toward it without having to be physically present at school.

Consider a learner who is alone at home and receives no direct instructions on how to complete the tasks assigned in an online class. Faced with numerous questions, he will have to search for solutions on his own. If, during a long day of study, he becomes hungry, he can simply pause, prepare a quick snack in the kitchen, and then return to his work. When a doubt arises, he can message a teacher for clarification. This kind of low‑pressure environment can be especially useful for shy students or those who would benefit from one‑on‑one explanations.

Flexible timing is another benefit. Students who dislike early mornings can choose to study later in the evening, without the need to be ready for a school bell. This flexibility is crucial for pregnant teenagers or young mothers, who might find it hard to attend school daily. I have heard from a friend who continued her education throughout her pregnancy and even after giving birth, attending classes from home while caring for her baby. Her experience shows how much easier learning becomes when the location can be chosen.

Nevertheless, there are challenges. Some families cannot afford the technology required for online learning, and not all students have a quiet place to study. Many young people also need to work to support themselves, which can lead to missed school days or lack of focus in class. In such cases, a blended schedule—working a few hours and studying online afterward, or alternating work days with study days—can make it possible to keep up with coursework and pass important exams.

Online education also offers practical advantages. Video lessons can clearly demonstrate how to solve math problems or explain other subjects. Students who study from home can:

In conclusion, providing the option to attend classes from home can support students’ health, motivation, and academic success, especially for those who face social anxiety, early‑morning schedules, or family responsibilities. One topic that people debate a lot is whether students are expected to identify a career by the time they enter high school. The courses of study in high school are selected to guide them toward a specific career. I think it is not a good idea for a student to commit to a career at a young age because students are not old enough; they can be careless and may not make the best decision when they are young.

One reason why this would not be a good idea is that students are not old enough to know which specific career they want. They are not prepared for the world, and high‑school students often have no experience in any career.

I think it is a little too early. I will explore all types of careers when my junior year starts; then I will make sure to select the right courses that will prepare me or give me experience for my chosen career.

Another reason this is unwise is that teenagers can be careless, and something may go wrong in their lives, or they may simply want to try something new. The classes I selected from freshman year will not be worth it if I have to take new classes later. For example, my friend chose a technology class in freshman year, looked up how much people in that field earn, and found it was not what he expected. He then switched to a materials and processes class to learn how to cut and build houses.

A further reason is that when you are young, you can make the wrong decision. In my case, the best decision during high school was to wait, study better classes, and consider a more suitable career. To do that, you have to care about your classes and be responsible with school and career planning.

As you can see from these reasons, I think the best approach for students is to focus on high school and get good grades. By senior year or college, you will know more about life and careers, and that will be the best time to select the classes that will guide you toward a specific career.

The question of whether students should decide on a career before they even start high school is a source of much discussion. In many schools, the subjects chosen in the freshman year are meant to steer pupils toward a particular profession. I believe this approach is unwise; teenagers are simply not mature enough to make such an important decision at such a young age.

First, most high‑schoolers have little knowledge about any specific occupation. They have not yet entered the workforce, so they lack real‑world experience that would help them understand what a job actually entails. Because of this, choosing a career path so early often leads to a mismatch between expectations and reality.

Second, adolescents tend to act impulsively. A decision made in ninth grade can easily turn out to be wrong, and the student may end up taking courses that no longer serve any purpose. For instance, a friend of mine enrolled in a technology class during his freshman year, only to discover later that the salaries in that field were far lower than he had imagined. He switched to a materials‑and‑process course to learn practical skills like cutting and building, which better suited his interests.

Finally, postponing the choice allows students to explore a wider range of subjects and to develop a clearer sense of their strengths and preferences. By the time they reach their senior year—or even college—they will have a stronger grasp of the world and can pick classes that genuinely support their chosen career.

In short, the most sensible strategy for high‑school students is to concentrate on achieving good grades and gaining a broad education, leaving the final career decision until they are older and better informed.

This lesson is very important because many people now don’t do this and just take things, and many parents don’t really care anymore, so schools have to step in and teach young kids what’s wrong and what’s right. When somebody drops something, always hand it back. Why? Because if you drop something you think you’ve lost—say, your favorite toy that you bought with your own money—you would be mad, sad, and upset if someone saw it and took it. You would feel terrible because your favorite toy is gone, and the person who took it didn’t need it; they just wanted it or saw no one around.  

Now imagine you drop your favorite toy and someone sees it, runs up, and gives it back to you. You would feel happy, proud, and delighted because that person returned it without any selfish intention. The owner of the item could have just walked away and never realized they had dropped it until they needed it.  

I lost my iPad years ago because the person who saw it took it and didn’t care. I don’t know who it was because I never paid attention; I was just happy and didn’t think anything would happen. When it did happen, I was very upset and had to use my mom’s phone until my dad bought me a new one. That’s why this lesson is crucial: taking something that isn’t yours is not smart or needed. Many people don’t care, but when it happens to them they wonder why it happened. The reason is that they didn’t leave what they took where it was found, so the person who saw the item did the same thing—they took it, and you will probably never see it again.

If someone loses their phone, they would be furious—today’s phones cost over $1,000 and can be even more expensive. Losing a phone and discovering it was taken would make them very unhappy; they would search everywhere and do anything to get it back because phones are essential for calling someone to pick you up, for staying in contact, or for calling for help.  

If somebody stole my phone, I would be very angry and sad because the item I just lost is expensive and not easy to replace; new phones cost as much as a used car you can buy online.

Have you ever found something on the ground, picked it up, and pretended it was yours?  
That is a lie, and it is wrong because you never know whose money or belongings you are taking. When the rightful owner returns looking for the item, it may already be gone, taken by someone who walked away with something that belonged to someone else.

As a child I often saw people drop objects. My habit was to pick them up and either return them or tell the owner that they had dropped something. Most people’s first thought when they see something lying around is to keep it, but that is not a good idea. You have no idea who it belongs to or how it got there, and taking something that isn’t yours is stealing. Many advise leaving things where they are because the owner will likely come back searching for them; no one intentionally leaves their possessions for strangers to walk away with.

Schools usually teach this lesson. In my elementary school there were signs everywhere reminding us not to take what isn’t ours and to leave items where we found them. Most children followed the rule, but some simply ignored it, which is unacceptable. If someone truly needs something, they can usually buy a replacement; wanting something for the sake of bragging or fun does not justify taking it from someone else.

The basic rules are simple:

- Do not keep something you find.
- If you see someone drop an item, give it back.
- Think about the consequences of your actions.
- Resist peer pressure.
- Be helpful and kind.

These values are crucial because many people today ignore them and parents often do not enforce them, leaving schools to teach youngsters what is right and what is wrong. Imagine losing a favorite toy that you bought with your own money. If a stranger took it, you would feel angry, sad, and upset. Now picture someone noticing you drop the toy and immediately returning it to you. You would feel happy, grateful, and relieved. That is the difference that honesty makes.

I once lost my iPad because someone who saw it simply took it. I never knew who it was, and I was left frustrated, having to use my mother’s phone until my father bought me a new one. This experience shows why it is important to teach children that taking what does not belong to them is unnecessary and harmful. When people experience loss, they quickly realize how badly they feel, even if they previously thought it was no big deal.

Expensive items, especially smartphones, illustrate the point well. Phones can cost over a thousand dollars, and many people rely on them for daily tasks and emergencies. If someone loses a phone and discovers it was stolen, they will be furious and will search everywhere to retrieve it. The loss is not just financial; it can affect safety and communication.

In summary, returning lost items and respecting other people’s belongings is a simple yet vital lesson. It teaches honesty, responsibility, and empathy—qualities that benefit both individuals and the community.

In conclusion, President Thomas Jefferson gave us this quote to make us think about what we do—or should do—in our lives. It is good to take a break, but don’t forget you have goals and dreams that you must turn into reality.

Thomas Jefferson once said, “It is wonderful how much may be done if we are doing.” In other words, constant activity—whether for society or for oneself—leads to achievement. But does perpetual effort always trump inactivity, or can rest also play a valuable role? Some argue that periods of inactivity are essential because they provide a chance to recover, regain strength, and continue working effectively. Others maintain that constantly staying busy is superior, since hard work brings personal goals within reach and makes one productive for the community.

Every morning millions of people rise and head to their jobs, striving to give their best. However, what about those who are not employed? Even without a formal job, a person can contribute to society and personal development through volunteering, helping neighbors, or simply staying active. Rest is certainly important, but excessive downtime can prevent us from achieving our dreams and ambitions.

Being continually engaged is beneficial when the activities are meaningful. Working hard with passion helps individuals reach their objectives—whether those goals involve earning money, supporting a family, or simply finding personal satisfaction in labor. My mother often tells me that if you desire something, you must pursue it and make it happen. We all want a brighter future, and that desire drives us to keep moving rather than remaining idle.

From a societal perspective, it is necessary to be active, even if one’s ultimate dream is still unclear. People need income to cover food, housing, taxes, and other necessities, which typically means holding a job. Beyond that, one can also engage in unpaid activities like community service, which foster personal growth and benefit others. Whether the work is paid or not, being productive contributes positively to society.

Activity is the engine that keeps humanity progressing. Dreams and goals motivate people to act; inactivity can dull that motivation. In summary, Jefferson’s quotation invites us to reflect on how we spend our time. While taking breaks is healthy, we should not lose sight of the aspirations that drive us to turn our dreams into reality.
