Four‑day School  

Debate between benefits and disadvantages. Resume any school activities on the regular five‑day schedule and change that to only four days.  

To have a four‑day school week is an option that should be adopted not only by some business workers but also by each high school and higher‑education institution after considering these reasons.  

The schedule would consist of losing ten hours per week, but those missing hours can be recouped by extending the school day by two hours and increasing the time for each class. This extension would give more attention to each class, allow completion of any project or assignment set by teachers, and provide extra time for students to receive support from friends and teachers when someone is failing.  

We could also use the extra two hours on the fourth day for library time, which would be amazing for students who love reading, as well as for those who want additional time for sports or any after‑school activity.  

The fifth day of the week could be used for doctor appointments or other health situations; the usual excuse for missing classes is a parent’s note explaining an absence. Handling these situations outside regular school time would decrease student absences during class periods.  

We must not forget teachers, many of whom are also parents and need an extra day for family time and regular activities with their children.  

Seniors face the most difficult decisions about the future and need time to evaluate university and college options, as well as possible weekend jobs. Freshmen—students transitioning from middle school—also need understanding and extra activities as high school changes from their previous routine.  

Another option is to use a free Friday or Monday for community service, with parental permission and adult supervision. Students who want to participate can help clean streets, rivers, or engage in other community projects. Schools could also create programs that involve large companies looking to help students find part‑time jobs on this new free day.  

Considering only a four‑day school means abandoning the fifth day (no partial attendance; all time is used during the four days). This creates three free days per week, which can be spent with family or friends, or on anything students and parents wish. There would be no need to wake up on Friday mornings—or on Monday mornings, depending on which day the school designates as the third free day—allowing time for rest and personal responsibilities.  

The idea may be inconvenient for students with part‑time jobs, because extending the school day by two hours would reduce their work hours. However, if the free fifth day is available for a full‑time job, students could still earn three full‑time jobs.  

Balancing two different activities per day can be hard and exhausting; going from school to work leaves little time for rest. Yet, with only four school days—even with a two‑hour extension—students would have time after school for rest, projects, or homework, and could use the other three days for any job they find suitable.  

Knowing the disadvantages also reveals solutions and benefits for each disagreement on this project, because there are more benefits than disadvantages for over 90 % of students.  

After mentioning all points concerning benefits, disadvantages, and solutions for a four‑day school week, I conclude willingly with: “Everyone needs three days free from school and only four days of school.” Even if a student’s situation differs—staying at home, handling family routines, helping at home, working, or studying—the consensus on this document gives us the power to fight for this new right for high‑school and college students. On the same power, together for a new right.

A four‑day school week has become a topic of much discussion, with supporters pointing to several clear advantages. The proposal is that high schools and colleges replace the traditional five‑day schedule with four longer days, allowing students and teachers to enjoy an extra day off each week.

The most obvious benefit is the reduction of total instructional time by ten hours per week. Those missing hours can be recovered by extending each school day by about two hours. Longer classes give students more time to focus on each subject, complete projects, and receive help from teachers. The additional two hours also provide opportunities for social interaction and peer tutoring, which can be especially useful for learners who are struggling.

The extra day could be devoted to activities that enrich the school experience. Students who love reading could spend more time in the library, athletes could use the additional hours for practice, and clubs could schedule meetings without cutting into academic time. Moreover, the free day would make it easier for families to arrange doctor appointments or handle other health matters, reducing the need for students to miss class during regular hours.

Teachers, many of whom are also parents, would gain a valuable day to attend to family responsibilities or simply recharge. Senior students, who are busy researching university options, applying for jobs, or completing internships, would also benefit from the flexibility that an additional day off provides. Younger students transitioning from middle school would find the change less disruptive if they have more time for extracurricular pursuits.

Community service is another promising use of the free day. With parental permission and adult supervision, students could participate in street clean‑ups, river restorations, or other local projects, gaining real‑world experience while helping their neighborhoods. Schools could even partner with businesses to create part‑time job opportunities for students on the non‑school day.

Critics argue that extending the school day might cut into part‑time work hours for students who rely on employment. However, the extra day off still leaves three full days for work, and the longer school days could reduce fatigue by consolidating academic tasks into fewer, more focused periods. This balance allows students to rest, complete homework, and still have sufficient time for employment.

In summary, the advantages of a four‑day week—more concentrated learning, additional time for personal development, easier scheduling of appointments, and opportunities for community involvement—outweigh the drawbacks for the vast majority of students. Everyone deserves a three‑day weekend and only four days of school, and with collective support we can make this new right a reality for high‑school and college students alike.

It is essential that students be able to choose the electives that interest them. If a pupil is forced to attend a class they dislike, they are likely to become disengaged and attend less regularly. Frequent absences lead to lower grades, which in turn cause frustration and a loss of motivation. When motivation drops, students may quit altogether, missing the credits they need to graduate. Without a high‑school diploma, they cannot enter university, which limits their chances of finding a good job. Unemployment can lead to serious financial hardship, even homelessness. Therefore, allowing students to select electives that appeal to them is crucial for their academic success and future stability.

Supporters also claim that everyone has unique talents, and electives give students a chance to discover and develop them. When a learner is good at a subject, they are more likely to enjoy class, achieve higher marks and want to learn more. This not only earns them the necessary credits but also creates valuable experience that employers appreciate. For instance, a student who excels in drama may be hired by a theatre company, become a recognised actor and possibly earn a substantial income. Moreover, individuals usually possess multiple abilities, not just one, and mastering several skills can further enhance their career prospects. That is why finding one’s strengths through electives is so important.

Looking ahead, the skills gained from preferred electives can shape a smoother transition from school to higher education and eventually to adult life. Students who follow their passions are better prepared for the challenges that await after graduation, and they are more likely to achieve their long‑term goals. By building competence in areas they love, they reduce the difficulty of future tasks, know what steps to take, and move toward a fulfilling destiny.

Nevertheless, some people argue that making electives mandatory might backfire, as some students may lack the motivation to participate seriously and could treat the classes as a joke. Even with this concern, the benefits of allowing students to pursue electives that match their interests outweigh the potential drawbacks.

Some schools and companies worldwide have introduced a four‑day work week in an effort to save resources and cut energy consumption. Although some people argue that our school should keep the traditional five‑day schedule and not add two extra hours to each day because we already use resources responsibly, I believe that switching to a four‑day school week and lengthening the school day by two hours would actually help the environment and allow us to manage energy more efficiently.

Opponents of this idea claim that our school does not waste resources or energy; they say we need the current schedule to support learning and that a shorter week would not make a difference. These arguments are understandable, but they overlook the growing strain our school places on the environment.

First, a reduced week would improve our ecological footprint. A recent article from my county reported that resource consumption at our school has risen by 70 % in recent years. This increase has led to a surge in the number of trees cut down in the surrounding area, harming the local environment and giving our school a poor reputation for sustainability. By moving to a four‑day week and extending each day, we could concentrate activities into fewer days, giving us more time to implement recycling programmes and reduce overall waste.

Second, a shorter week would help us control energy use. The number of computers, smart boards and other electronic devices on campus has grown dramatically because we have the largest student population in the county. According to an energy‑saving website, about 80 % of a school’s electricity is consumed by these technologies. If we operate the school for four days instead of five, the total time these devices are powered on would decline, resulting in significant energy savings.

Many people still maintain that we do not waste resources and therefore do not need to change the schedule. However, the evidence shows that a four‑day school week with two additional hours each day would benefit both our school and the wider community. Imagine how you would react if your own household faced rising energy bills—wouldn’t you also look for ways to limit consumption? The same applies to our school.

Schools often ask pupils to finish summer projects so that learning does not stop during the holidays. I believe that these projects should be created by the students themselves. Learners already know what topics interest them, where they struggle, and what they need to practice. By working on self‑designed projects, they can develop additional skills, keep their knowledge fresh, and return to class better prepared.

One reason for supporting student‑chosen projects is that pupils feel more comfortable when they control the subject matter. Because they have selected the topic, they already understand its basics and can approach it with confidence, which makes the work easier and more enjoyable. 

A second benefit is that continuing personal projects over the break helps prevent forgetting. When students keep practising what they have studied, the material stays alive in their minds. This is especially important for language learners; if an ESL student does not engage in independent tasks, the vocabulary and grammar learned during the school year may quickly fade. Ongoing work also discourages laziness, as students remain active rather than stopping completely during the vacation.

In short, allowing learners to design and carry out their own summer projects is advantageous. It keeps previously acquired knowledge from slipping away, encourages active engagement, and showcases each student’s abilities. Therefore, schools should give pupils the freedom to choose and manage their summer work rather than imposing teacher‑directed assignments.

Ralph Wallace Emerson once said, “To be yourself in a world that is constantly trying to make you something else is the greatest accomplishment.” I agree with this idea because when we stay true to ourselves we stand out, we encourage others, and our achievements can influence the way people think.  

First, being authentic inspires those around us. When we go beyond what is expected—such as helping a classmate solve a math problem even though it is not our duty—we show a willingness to help that others notice. This extra effort makes people admire us and want to act the same way.  

Second, living honestly can turn us into role models in many settings: at home, in the neighbourhood, at school or university, even in a place of worship. Imagine a neighbour who always keeps the garden tidy or assists others with chores; this behaviour can motivate nearby residents to do the same. By consistently showing kindness, we become a source of inspiration for many.  

Third, our personal successes can change others’ attitudes. When people see how we have progressed—whether we have built a small business or improved our family’s situation—they begin to wonder how we did it. Sharing our story and the steps we took lets them believe that they, too, can achieve similar results. In families where some members earn modest wages while others run their own companies, the example of a self‑driven relative spreads optimism and hope.  

In conclusion, as Emerson suggests, constantly striving to be ourselves while helping others leads to real achievement. More than half of people recognize the value of such behaviour, and the positive message it sends spreads far beyond the individual. By acting authentically, we not only reach our own goals but also become an example and a source of inspiration for countless others.

Creating a homework club is an excellent way to boost student achievement. Such a club would allow pupils to raise their grades, enjoy more free time, feel less exhausted after school, and have a supportive environment where teachers and classmates can help one another.

First, a homework club can directly improve academic results. When students work together and receive guidance from teachers, they are able to complete assignments more efficiently and understand the material better. For example, if a learner struggles with a particular problem, staying after school in the club gives them a chance to receive immediate assistance, reducing the risk of poor test scores.

Second, the club frees up evenings for other activities. With homework taken care of during the club’s meeting time, students can spend their remaining hours with family, friends, or pursuing hobbies. Knowing that they are not alone in facing difficult tasks makes the experience less stressful and more enjoyable.

Third, the extra support reduces fatigue. When pupils know they have help available, they worry less about failing and can get enough rest before the next day’s lessons. Considering how many pressures modern students face, having a reliable place to finish schoolwork can make a big difference to their overall well‑being.

Finally, a homework club also encourages personal growth. Many teenagers feel discouraged when they think they cannot succeed, but a collaborative environment shows them that perseverance and teamwork lead to improvement. By offering a space where students can share knowledge and motivate each other, the club nurtures confidence and a more positive attitude toward learning.

In summary, establishing a homework club would benefit students by raising their grades, giving them more leisure time, decreasing tiredness, and providing a grateful sense of support.

Success is not simply a chain of failures, even though Winston Churchill claimed that “success consists of going from failure to failure without loss of enthusiasm.” I disagree with this view. While everyone experiences setbacks at some point, achieving a goal does not require moving from one failure to another. Determination, hard work, and maintaining enthusiasm are far more important than repeatedly failing.

First, it is impossible to find a person who has never failed. Everybody makes mistakes, whether in studies, work, or personal relationships. Some people may seem to have an almost flawless record, but even they have faced challenges or disappointments that are not always visible. My own cousin, for example, has never let her parents down, earned excellent grades, received a scholarship, and is now studying at Virginia Tech. Her story shows that success can be built on consistent effort rather than a series of defeats.

Second, reaching a dream demands persistent effort. When a setback occurs, we should not become despondent; instead, we must recognize that life constantly offers new chances. Hard work and resilience enable us to bounce back and keep moving toward our objectives. If one path fails, we can adjust our plans and explore alternative opportunities rather than staying stuck. The willingness to try again, while learning from past mistakes, is what ultimately drives success.

Finally, enthusiasm is essential. A genuine passion for what we do fuels perseverance and prevents us from giving up. Those who lack enthusiasm tend to drift without clear direction, accepting whatever results come their way. In my own experience, I excelled academically in my home country, but after moving to the United States I had to start over because I did not know English. My enthusiasm for learning the language motivated me to study hard and eventually succeed.

In conclusion, I do not share Churchill’s belief that success is built on a sequence of failures. While setbacks are inevitable, they are not the foundation of achievement. By staying determined, working diligently, and keeping our enthusiasm alive, we can reach our goals without needing to fail repeatedly. Success stems from perseverance and passion, not from a continual march through failure.

Technology can affect our lives and the way we interact with others, and I believe this influence is often negative. Many people argue that technology harms families and reduces face‑to‑face contact, and I think they are right because they see how it changes daily habits. Below are some of the main ways technology can interfere with personal relationships.

First, people become addicted to their phones or video games. When someone is constantly glued to a screen, they start thinking only about themselves. For instance, if a person needs help, they might ignore the request because they are preoccupied with a game or social media. This can happen to both adults and children, and it makes us forget the importance of kindness and empathy.

Second, online shopping can turn into a compulsive habit, especially among women. Buying clothes on the internet can be useful and empowering, but for some it becomes an excessive craving. Those who shop too much may spend money they do not have and develop a dependence that distracts them from more meaningful activities.

Third, when individuals stop communicating with people around them, they lose motivation and inspiration for their own future. A person who never engages in real conversation or shared experiences may feel isolated and purposeless, which can negatively affect their personal growth.

In conclusion, we need to shine a light on the growing addiction to smartphones and other digital devices because it harms both our present lives and our future prospects. I agree with the view that technology, while useful, is not the greatest invention humanity has created, and its drawbacks must be carefully managed.

Reading aloud is a skill I rely on because it deepens my comprehension of any text. When I vocalise the words, the material sinks into my mind more firmly, allowing me to articulate the ideas later with greater clarity. This habit also proves useful when I have to compose an essay about what I have read.

Speaking the passage out loud helps me gauge how well I am understanding it. I can notice if I am stumbling over certain words or pausing too often, which signals that I need to focus on those parts. By hearing the words, I can also identify any unfamiliar terms and look up their meanings right away.

Moreover, reading aloud enables me to summarise the story more effectively. The vocal rehearsal stores extra details in my memory, so after I finish, the main points remain fresh. In contrast, silent reading often leaves me forgetting many facts. Others also benefit from hearing a text spoken, as it can make the content clearer for them as well.

When it comes to writing an essay, this practice gives me a solid foundation. Because I have already spoken the material, I can generate many ideas and explanations without feeling anxious about the task. The act of reading aloud keeps the whole narrative clear in my head, ensuring that my essay stays focused on the author’s intended message.

In conclusion, reading aloud improves my understanding, aids memory, and makes essay writing easier, so I always choose to read out loud whenever I study a book.

Small acts of kindness can make a real difference in other people’s lives. As the ancient Greek storyteller Aesop once said, “No act of kindness, no matter how small, is ever wasted.” A simple gesture—perhaps a smile, a brief helping hand, or a kind word—can lift someone’s spirits and improve their day.

These tiny deeds matter because they can bring a smile to a face that might otherwise stay down. A smile not only brightens the mood but also benefits health, reducing stress and encouraging a more positive outlook. We never truly know what difficulties others are facing, which is why a modest act of kindness can be especially valuable. When someone receives such a gesture, they are often compelled to pass it on to others.

People who experience kindness usually feel loved and appreciated. The warmth of another’s consideration can make them feel happy both inside and out. This feeling is one of the most rewarding sensations we can have. Kindness does not require expensive gifts; a simple, sincere act can make someone’s day much better.

When we receive kindness, we should try to return it in our own way. Showing love and care doesn’t have to be grand; just being present for someone can demonstrate that we value them. Helping a neighbour clean their house, offering a listening ear, or simply sharing a smile are all ways to give kindness back. These small actions signal that we are willing to support one another.

In our families, these modest gestures are especially meaningful. When a family member offers a kind act, the whole household feels a sense of warmth and togetherness. Experiencing kindness at home encourages us to extend the same courtesy to others outside the family circle.

In everyday life, we all encounter moments that make us feel cared for—a friendly greeting, a door held open, or a brief word of encouragement. To be kind to others, we can start with these simple practices: smile, listen, help without being asked, and show genuine interest in people’s well‑being. Kindness, at its core, is any action that aims to make another person’s life a little easier or brighter. By embracing these small acts, we create a ripple effect that spreads goodwill throughout our communities.

There’s a problem with your sink and you don’t know how to fix it. So what do you do? You call a plumber to fix your sink pipes. The plumber goes away to do another job, and your sink starts to spit out water again. You try to fix it because you were watching the plumber. The first time you try to fix it, the water leak gets worse and starts to flood your house, so now you have to call the plumber again and pay again. You could have called him before it started leaking again; he could have walked you through it.

Some kids have pets, and when those pets pass away, the parents try to replace the pet with another one. It will be hard for the kid; he might not eat, sleep, or even talk for a long time. When my dog Lucky died, it was hard for me and my brother—we barely ate or talked. My dad tried to get another dog, but my brother and I both knew it wasn’t going to be the same.

When you’re in school and you see a kid who is sad, you ask him, “What’s wrong?” and he doesn’t say anything back. You start talking about coming over after school because you have to do a project with this student, and you say, “Ask your dad if I can come over.” Then the kid starts to cry because his dad died in a car accident last night. You made him feel worse than he was 20 minutes ago just by saying one simple thing.

So, American jazz legend Duke Ellington, I disagree with that because you can make a lot of things way worse than they were by doing one thing—like trying to fix the sink, trying to replace a passed‑away pet, or trying to make someone feel happy when you meant to help them.

American jazz legend Duke Ellington once said, “A problem is a chance for you to do your best.” He meant that when difficulties arise we have an opportunity to solve them before they get worse. I do not share this view. In many cases trying to fix a problem can actually make the situation more damaging, and there are times when a problem simply cannot be resolved.

Consider a clogged sink. You do not know how to repair it, so you call a plumber. After he leaves to attend another job, the sink starts leaking again. Because you watched the plumber, you feel confident enough to try fixing it yourself. Your first attempt makes the leak larger, flooding the house and forcing you to call the plumber once more, paying for the extra work. If you had simply waited for the professional the second time, the damage could have been avoided.

The same idea applies to emotional loss. When a family’s pet dies, some parents think that bringing home a new animal will help the children cope. In reality, the children may become withdrawn, losing appetite and sleep, because no new pet can replace the one they have lost. I experienced this when my dog Lucky died; both my brother and I were so upset that we barely ate or spoke, and our father’s suggestion of getting another dog only emphasized how different the new pet would be.

A similar situation can happen at school. Imagine you notice a classmate looking sad and you ask what’s wrong. He does not answer, so you try to lighten the mood by inviting him to work together on a project after school, saying, “Ask your dad if I can come over.” The boy then breaks down and tells you that his father died in a car accident the night before. Your well‑meaning comment has unintentionally added to his distress in those few minutes.

These examples show that attempting to solve a problem without the right knowledge or sensitivity can worsen the original issue. Therefore, I disagree with Duke Ellington’s statement. Trying to fix a leaky sink, replacing a beloved pet, or trying to cheer up someone grieving can all end up making things worse rather than better.

In short, because our first reactions are strong, often unrepeatable, and continue to shape later perceptions, changing first impressions is a very difficult task.

Many people don’t try new things because they are quick to judge the presentation of a new item or person, but if they actually gave the new experience a chance, it could be life‑changing—for better or worse.

So, going back to “trying something beyond what I have mastered,” I won’t grow—or something like that. It’s all a matter of perspective. If I wish to try something new and become a better person in society, I will. But if I choose to stick to the same boring routine day after day, sooner or later I will get bored of everything. Some may argue, “that’s how I succeeded in the first place—by doing the same routine over and over.” In some cases that works; for example, an athlete must repeat the same drills until they improve, and a dancer practices the same routine until it’s ready to be shared with the world. For others, trying a new routine can lead to success (though not everyone is naturally talented).

In conclusion, trying something new changes who you are, either helping or harming you. Some people grow wise with age; others remain young and reckless. Ralph Waldo Emerson was right to say, “Unless you try something beyond what you already have mastered you will never grow.”

Have you ever found that you learn best through hands‑on help rather than by looking at examples? As Albert Schweitzer once remarked, “Example is not the main thing to influence others.” In other words, there are several ways to affect people that do not rely on providing examples.

Another problem with examples is that they can sometimes cause confusion. Imagine a drawing assignment where the teacher asks you to create something from your imagination. If she then supplies specific pictures of what she expects you to draw, you may start to doubt whether you should follow your own ideas or try to copy the examples she gave. In such cases, the examples distract rather than clarify, especially in subjects that rely on personal creativity.

Some people argue that examples are powerful because they demonstrate experience and teach a method step by step. Indeed, many learners benefit from seeing a model before trying a task themselves. Nevertheless, I believe that other techniques—such as direct support and encouragement—can be stronger and make examples less decisive in influencing others.

For these reasons, I maintain that there are more effective ways to influence people than simply providing examples.

First, every failure teaches us something. Second, how we react to failure reveals the kind of people who really matter to us. Third, and most importantly, we must avoid repeating the same mistakes.

Because mistakes are inevitable, we should always try to extract a lesson from each one. Moreover, a failure exposes genuine relationships. Sometimes a friend you thought could be counted on disappears when you stumble, while someone you regarded as a rival may be the one who offers support. For instance, a true partner will stay by your side during your first disappointment instead of abandoning you. Finally, it is crucial not to repeat the same error over and over. The first thing we lose when we keep encountering the same failure is our enthusiasm, and it becomes increasingly difficult to stay motivated. Although setbacks will continue to appear, learning from at least one of them makes handling multiple challenges much easier.

In conclusion, everyone experiences failure, but the most successful outcome is to turn each setback into a lesson and resolve never to repeat the same mistake. Changing one’s life is possible for anyone, provided the person truly wants it and is prepared to make the necessary changes.

In recent years students have begun to rely on cell phones far more than they did in the previous fifteen years, when these devices first became a regular part of everyday life. Back then, phones were banned from classrooms, but the rules have now changed and pupils are permitted to bring and use them during lessons. This essay will examine the effects of allowing mobile phones in the classroom.

At first glance, the change brings several advantages. It makes it easier for both teachers and learners to complete tasks. Students can quickly look up information on a topic with their phones, which is often more convenient than waiting for a computer when there are not enough workstations for everyone. Teachers, too, can benefit: by allowing phones they can incorporate apps and digital tools that would be difficult or impossible to use on a standard PC, thereby enriching the classroom activity. 

However, the benefits are not without drawbacks. Many pupils begin to use their phones irresponsibly once they are allowed in class. Some check messages or browse social media while the teacher is speaking, and others distract their classmates by playing games or making noise. These behaviours can disrupt the learning environment and undermine the advantages that mobile technology might otherwise provide.

In summary, permitting students to use cell phones in school offers clear positives, such as easier access to information and new teaching resources, but it also introduces problems related to misuse and distraction. The overall impact therefore depends on how well schools manage and regulate phone usage.

Do curfews keep teenagers out of trouble, or do they unfairly interfere with young people's lives?

In my opinion, yes, curfews have to take care of them; it does matter if they are young, **especially** if they are out at night. This is a good intention from curfews, **namely** to protect them, **and** in the end the only beneficiaries are the teenagers.

For example, if they are out in the middle of the night they can get into trouble, because they might do whatever they want when nobody is watching them. **On the other hand**, if curfews say they must respect the rules, **then** they are more likely to stay safe.

Otherwise, nobody is in the street playing or doing something good at night; all people are at home resting or with their family doing other things. **Therefore**, the same rule should apply to teenagers.

In conclusion, curfews have to take care of teenagers; this is good for them.

Do curfews keep teenagers out of trouble, or do they unfairly interfere with young people’s lives?

In my opinion, yes—curfews are needed to protect young people, especially at night. This good intention ultimately benefits the teenagers themselves.

For example, if they are out in the middle of the night they can get into trouble because they may do whatever they want when nobody is watching. On the other hand, if curfews require them to respect the rules, they are less likely to encounter danger.

Otherwise, nobody would be out on the streets playing or doing anything positive at night; everyone would be at home resting or with their families. The same principle should apply to teenagers.

At night someone might steal your property or harm you or another person. You might intervene because you notice something wrong and try to help.

Some people think having fun at night is a good idea, but I disagree. Going to clubs, for instance, is risky. In Las Vegas, almost three years ago a club was shot in the middle of the night, and many people died. In conclusion, curfews help protect teenagers, and that is beneficial for them.

In my view curfews are necessary to look after young people, especially during the night. Their main purpose is to keep teenagers safe, and ultimately the ones who benefit most are the adolescents themselves.

If teenagers are out late, they are more likely to get into trouble because there is less supervision and they may act without anyone watching. A curfew forces them to follow a set rule, which can prevent risky behaviour.

When most adults are at home resting or spending time with family, the streets are empty. The same expectation should apply to teenagers, keeping them off the streets after dark.

Nighttime also brings a higher chance of crime, such as theft or assault. A teenager who is out late might become a victim or even an unwitting participant in a harmful situation, simply because they are in the wrong place at the wrong time.

Some argue that staying out at night is harmless fun, but I disagree. Going to clubs, for instance, can be dangerous. A few years ago in Las Vegas a shooting at a nightclub resulted in many fatalities; incidents like that illustrate the risks involved.

In short, curfews serve to protect teenagers, and that protection is a positive and necessary measure.

Online classes from home have become a hot topic, and while some people claim they are convenient, I believe they are far less effective than attending school in person. Supporters argue that studying online saves time for homework and is easier than commuting, but the lack of direct teacher guidance means students often learn very little. In my view, learning from a teacher in the classroom is essential, and many students also enjoy the social atmosphere of school.

There are learners who can work independently, yet many others need the assistance that teachers provide. My sister, for instance, regularly stays after school to get help with subjects she finds difficult. She tells me that the explanations she receives from teachers make a huge difference. When she fails a test, she meets with the teacher, reviews the mistakes, and improves her understanding. Teachers are willing to invest extra time—even though they have many other responsibilities—because they want their pupils to succeed.

Social interaction is another reason why going to school matters. My brother, for example, loves playing sports during recess. He says that the fun of chatting and competing with classmates makes school enjoyable. Being in a school environment helps students develop interpersonal skills and stay informed about what is happening around them. Regular attendance also builds a routine that prepares young people for future success; when they graduate, they are more likely to feel proud of their diploma.

Some argue that online learning suits those who prefer to study alone, claiming that the home setting eliminates distractions. However, many students actually need the structure and peer interaction that a school provides. My friend, for instance, finds that participating in sports or group activities at school keeps her motivated and focused. Interacting with teachers and older adults also offers valuable life advice that cannot be replicated through a screen.

In conclusion, teachers play a vital role in explaining concepts that students do not yet understand, and they do so far more effectively in person than through an online platform. Attending school offers not only academic instruction but also social experiences, extracurricular activities, and a supportive community. For these reasons, students should continue to go to school rather than rely solely on online classes, as a solid education is the foundation for a successful future.

The British writer John Lubbock once said, “Your character will be what you yourself choose to make it.” This statement raises an important question: to what extent are we really in charge of the traits we develop, and how much are we shaped by forces beyond our control?  

First, it is clear that many young people alter their personalities simply because they feel insecure or dissatisfied with themselves. Although personal traits have a strong influence on behaviour, external pressures often dominate. Society, the internet and popular culture flood us with images and ideas that we cannot fully regulate. We constantly receive messages about how we should look, speak and act, and these messages can push us to change in order to fit the expectations of others. The challenge, then, is to discover the influences that genuinely reflect our own values and to remain committed to them, even as the world around us shifts.

Second, moving to a new environment can illustrate how powerful these outside forces are. After relocating to Virginia, I noticed that my sense of “normal” was reshaped by the media I consumed—whether it was music, rap lyrics or celebrity gossip. Artists and influencers deliberately craft their images to attract attention and profit, and many of us, especially teenagers, tend to imitate them without questioning why. This demonstrates that, while we may feel we are making independent choices, much of what we decide is guided by the cultural currents that surround us.

Finally, the modern world presents new threats—pandemics, pollution, wars—that amplify our anxieties. The constant flow of alarming news can make us fear for our safety, reinforcing the idea that we are being steered by forces beyond our control. Nevertheless, recognizing these pressures allows us to reflect on our own decisions and to strive for a character that truly reflects our personal choices.

People ought to look to specialists and governing bodies for advice on the important choices in life, because relying solely on one’s own instincts often leads to mistaken judgments that conflict with established rules.

Consider the regulations that govern everyday activities. The use of illegal drugs is prohibited in most states, and even when a substance is permitted, a license or prescription is required. Alcohol may be legal, but only individuals aged twenty‑one or older may purchase it. Firearms can be owned legally, yet buyers must obtain the appropriate permits and meet age requirements. Driving is another example: a licence is necessary, and while teenagers may apply at sixteen, they must be accompanied by an older, responsible passenger until they have proven sufficient experience. These controls exist to ensure that people act safely and within the law rather than following unchecked personal whims.

In the workplace, employees must adhere to schedules and assigned duties. A fixed timetable tells a worker when to arrive and when to leave, helping the employer organise operations. If an accountant chose to show up in the afternoon instead of the morning when the company needs morning reports, the firm’s finances could suffer and the employee would be blamed for the disruption. Likewise, tasks are allocated according to each person’s skills; ignoring these assignments can lead to dismissal. Thus, following established guidelines is essential for the smooth functioning of an organisation.

Society at large also limits personal freedom for the common good. One cannot decide to set fire to a library simply because the idea seems exciting, nor is it acceptable to assault strangers for the sake of a joke. Entering private property to pick a flower you like is likewise prohibited. These restrictions prevent individuals from acting on impulsive desires that would harm others or break the law.

In summary, while people retain personal rights, they should not be allowed to act on every impulse they have. Guidance from knowledgeable experts and authoritative institutions is necessary, especially for young individuals who have not yet developed the full capacity to discern right from wrong.

This essay discusses how some schools offer distance learning as an option for students to attend classes from home via online platforms or video conferencing. I believe certain students would benefit from taking classes at their residences, because some students work at night. This creates a problem for those night workers, as school begins at 7:30 a.m., which is too early for students who are employed and cannot sleep well.

One example concerns my friend, who works after school, sometimes between 5 p.m. and midnight, and then must wake up at 5 a.m. to go to school. I think this schedule is burdensome for him because he is always tired in the first class due to insufficient sleep at night. Nevertheless, he needs to graduate from high school, as it is the only path to a better life. Many high‑school students work after school; I think this program could help them because they could continue working while getting more rest. More sleep could improve their grades, since poor performance often results from a lack of time for homework and test preparation.

A second example involves the many high‑school girls who become pregnant. This program could assist those girls, as I have observed many do not want to return to school while pregnant. They often face negative judgments because they are perceived as too young to have a baby. With distance learning, they can take classes from home, enabling them to graduate despite their circumstances. Some girls attempt to stay in traditional schools, but when they have a baby they cannot continue because they must care for the child. This program allows them to complete their coursework.

In conclusion, this is a worthwhile idea because it can help many students who face various challenges. It enables them to finish high school even when they lack time due to work or other responsibilities. Thus, distance learning offers a valuable solution for these students.

This is a problem for night‑working students because school starts at 7:30, which is too early for them; consequently, they do not sleep well.

Example one is about my friend, who works after school. Sometimes he works between 5 p.m. and midnight, and after this he has to wake up at 5 a.m. to go to school. I think this is heavy for him; as a result, he is always tired in the first class because he cannot sleep well at night. Yet he needs to graduate from high school because that is the only way he can have a better life. Many high‑school students work after school, and I believe this program can help them because they can continue working while also getting more sleep. In turn, this can lead to better grades, since sleep deprivation often causes poor performance when students lack time for homework and test preparation.

Example two concerns the many girls in high school who become pregnant. This program can help these girls because I see many do not want to return to school when they are pregnant; people often say bad things about them, claiming they are too young to have a baby. However, with distance learning they can take classes from home. This enables them to graduate from high school, which is a better way to complete their studies. In fact, many girls who try to continue in regular schools drop out after having a baby because they must care for the child, whereas online classes allow them to finish their coursework.

In conclusion, this is a good idea because it can help many students who face various problems. It allows them to finish high school even when they have to work, and it supports those who need flexible schedules. Therefore, distance‑learning programs are beneficial for these students, as they enable them to study from home and improve their overall outcomes.

Ralph Waldo Emerson claimed, “To be yourself in a world that is constantly trying to make you something else is the greatest accomplishment.” I disagree with this statement. To achieve something truly great, we should not let the world dictate our lives; instead, we must take charge of the world around us and decide who we want to become. Being authentic does not mean surrendering our freedom to external pressures; it means making our own choices and following our own path.

First, we must refuse to give the world the authority to decide for us. When we let others or society choose our direction, we risk losing our sense of purpose and becoming exhausted by a life that feels imposed. By taking responsibility for our decisions, we stay aware of why we act the way we do, and this awareness creates a solid foundation for a promising future. Those who hand over their choices to outside forces often end up feeling weary and unfulfilled.

Second, genuine accomplishment comes from pursuing what we truly enjoy, not from conforming to what the world expects. If we engage in activities that match our interests, the effort never feels like a burden. Passion fuels perseverance, and when we love what we do, the pursuit of greatness feels natural rather than forced. Allowing the world to steer us away from our passions only hampers the realization of our dreams.

Finally, authentic self‑direction helps us discern right from wrong, select suitable careers, and set meaningful goals. Only we truly understand our strengths, values, and aspirations; therefore, we should be the ones to shape our lives. Many people surrender their decisions to societal expectations and later regret the lack of personal direction, finding themselves stuck or dissatisfied.

In summary, do not permit the world to change you or dictate your path. Allowing others to choose for you leads to dissatisfaction and a bleak outlook. Embrace who you are by actively choosing what you love—whether it is a sport, a profession, or any pursuit that excites you. When you follow your own preferences, work never feels like a chore, and true accomplishment becomes attainable. The greatest achievement is not merely “being yourself” while the world pushes against you, but taking control of your own destiny.

I agree with Albert Einstein when he said that imagination is more important than knowledge. For example, when you are stuck on a math problem during a test, recalling the relevant formulas and methods usually leads to a solution faster than simply dreaming up an answer. Even reading a book can expand your vocabulary and provide concrete knowledge that imagination alone cannot supply.

Often, however, the two work best together. When we try to create something, imagination first supplies the ideas and possibilities, while knowledge supplies the practical steps needed to turn those ideas into reality. Imagine wanting to build a piece of furniture but having no clear plan; imagination suggests many designs, and then knowledge of materials and construction techniques guides you in making the final product.

Both imagination and knowledge can also have negative sides. If you feel down, your imagination may convince you that nothing can make you happy, leading to a hopeless outlook. Likewise, an overly vivid imagination can cause misunderstandings with friends, especially in childhood games where exaggerated ideas may seem unfair. In school, extensive knowledge can bring success on tests, but boasting about high scores can damage friendships, just as bragging about a low‑performing friend can.

Consider a 16‑year‑old who wants a job but has poor grades. Without sufficient knowledge from studying, he may struggle to find employment, while peers with better academic records obtain the positions they desire. If he cannot earn money, he might rely on friends for food, eventually falling into debt and even homelessness.

Children naturally possess great imagination because they have few expectations. At night they may imagine monsters in the closet and call for their parents, who reassure them there is nothing there. Later, they might hear strange noises and think the monster has returned, only to discover the sounds were simply their parents playing a prank. This illustrates how imagination can create vivid scenarios, even when knowledge tells us otherwise.

Technology enables us to accomplish many tasks without having to interact with other people. We can borrow books, shop and play games without speaking to anyone. While this convenience is undeniable, the reduction of human contact caused by technology has harmful effects on our lives. In many ways we have become dependent on gadgets every second of the day, and this reliance is damaging.

One of the most obvious negative impacts is seen in education. Today many teachers present lessons online, which often fails to show students how to complete their assignments. The personal connection between teacher and pupil is lost. When I was a child in my country, we had no such devices. Teachers explained the work on the blackboard, repeated the explanations until everyone understood, and we built a real relationship with them. I also remember spending lunch breaks in the school cafeteria chatting with friends about our day. Now, during lunch, most of my classmates stare at their phones and hardly talk to each other. The lack of face‑to‑face interaction harms our social skills.

Technology also contributes to a broader disengagement from the world. Because we can watch movies, read books and play games at home, many people rarely leave the house. This isolation makes us indifferent to events happening outside, even tragedies. The ease of ordering a book online, for example, has turned us lazy: instead of walking to the library, we stay on the couch and click a button. Meals that used to be shared at restaurants, where conversation flowed naturally, are now often delivered to our door while we stare at our screens. The result is a weakening of human connection.

In the workplace, technology can be a source of distraction. Employees may abandon their tasks to follow a sports game or play a game on their phone, which can lead to poor performance, dismissal, and the need to find a new job. Such problems would be far less common without the constant presence of digital devices.

Safety is another area where technology has introduced new risks. Drivers who text while behind the wheel miss signals, make wrong turns and cause accidents that can result in death or serious injury. One careless moment can ruin many lives and leave families grieving.

In summary, while technology offers many conveniences, it also brings significant drawbacks. It makes people more isolated, lazy and vulnerable, and it erodes genuine human interaction. Overreliance on gadgets turns us into passive observers, far removed from the connections that make life meaningful.

Another important reason why students won’t benefit from online classes is that they may have big problems in their lives and need someone to talk to. One reason is that they can ask a brother to do the work, so they are not really learning anything. Another example: a student may request extra help but won’t get it because there is no teacher with them, so they don’t understand and then fail the test. Family problems can also keep them from participating in online classes, leading to a lack of focus. Having online classes won’t help students in their lives; for example, they won’t make friends and may have trouble talking to people in the real world because they don’t know how.

Most counselors guide students in the right direction and teach them about the careers they want, but in online classes they don’t have the opportunity to chat with a counselor.

When lessons are delivered remotely, many learners lose concentration and treat the time as free time, which prevents them from acquiring the knowledge they would obtain in a classroom with a teacher present. Moreover, online classes cannot provide the immediate, personalized assistance that a student may need.

Students often have off‑days when they are less attentive and fail to complete the assignments given to them. In a virtual setting, they can simply look up answers without really learning the material, assuming that nobody is watching. Consequently, they may pass a course without truly understanding the subject. Another serious drawback is the lack of emotional support. Some pupils are dealing with personal problems and need someone to talk to; in a school environment they can approach a teacher, coach, counselor, or any trusted adult. At home, they may feel isolated and discouraged, which further hampers their learning.

Remote education also makes it easier for students to cheat or delegate work to others. A youngster might pay someone else to do the assignments or ask a sibling for help, so they are not actually mastering the content. Even when they request extra help, there is no teacher physically present to explain the concepts, leading to confusion and poor performance on tests. Family issues or other distractions can also reduce a student's focus during online lessons.

Social development suffers as well. Without daily interaction with peers, students miss out on building friendships and practising communication skills, which are essential for life after school. Access to counsellors, who guide students in career choices and personal growth, is also limited when learning is entirely virtual. Teachers, don’t think the summer is too long; it is a short period for students to have a vacation, and teachers also enjoy the vacation!!

Most students look forward to the summer break because it is one of the most enjoyable times of the year. During these months we can spend quality time with our families and friends, something that is hard to do during the regular school term. Some teachers argue that the vacation is too long and that students forget what they have learned, but I believe the benefits of a summer holiday far outweigh any possible loss of information.

Summer is a special period because it allows us to be closer to the people who matter most. Many parents work ten to twelve hours a day, six or seven days a week, leaving little time for family activities. When school is out, they can finally relax and share moments with their children. In my own experience, the holidays are the best time to be with my mother, who has always supported me through good and bad times. She gives me advice, helps me stay focused at school, and encourages me in my church activities. Those weeks together make me feel stronger and more confident in every area of my life.

My mother is the most important person in my life, and the summer months give us the chance to create lasting memories. I also use this time to grow spiritually, reading and reflecting on what matters most. The two‑month break is perfect after nine months of classes; it prevents us from feeling burned out and gives us a chance to recharge. While some people propose a year‑round school with only short breaks, I do not agree. A single month of vacation would not be enough to relax or to enjoy time with family, and the constant pressure of schoolwork would remain in our minds.

Having about two months off, plus a couple of short breaks during the year, clears the mind and reduces the stress of homework and projects. I remember a time when I stayed at home to finish school assignments while my family went on a trip. I felt I was missing out on valuable moments with them, and later realized that balancing study and family time is essential. When we prioritize family, we avoid regretting lost opportunities later.

Education is certainly important; it teaches us about humanity, nature, science, and many other subjects that will help us in the future. However, family should not be neglected. We need to schedule our lives so that school occupies weekdays, while weekends are reserved for faith, friends, and relatives. By keeping this balance, I have learned to concentrate on my studies from Monday to Friday and to enjoy my mother, father, and extended family on Saturdays and Sundays.

For many students, especially those whose parents live far away, the summer break is the only chance to be together. It is crucial to make time for everything that matters—education, family, and personal growth. While teachers may worry about forgetting lessons, most knowledge remains in our brains and can be refreshed when school resumes.

In conclusion, a two‑month summer vacation is valuable. It gives students the opportunity to reconnect with loved ones, relax, and return to school refreshed. Teachers, too, benefit from the break, and when the new term starts, a quick review is all that is needed to regain any forgotten details. So let’s enjoy the summer, cherish our families, and return to class ready to learn.

People who have never tried basketball might wonder where to start, so here are some basic tips that can help you get into the sport. The first thing to consider is the setting. While many play indoors, playing outdoors is a great option, especially on warm summer days when the temperature is comfortable. It’s best to avoid extreme heat or cold, because very hot or very cold weather can affect your performance. Finally, choose daylight hours for your games; playing at night limits visibility and can make it harder to follow the action.

The court should be spacious enough for the game and have a flat surface so the ball doesn’t bounce away unpredictably. A sturdy hoop with a pole tall enough to meet official height standards is necessary, and the rim should be wide enough to catch the ball while the net is short enough to allow the ball to pass through cleanly. Marking the boundaries of the court clearly helps players line up shots and stay in bounds.

Teamwork can turn a losing situation into a win simply by passing the ball effectively to teammates. Regular practice improves shooting accuracy and helps you create scoring opportunities. Thoughtful strategies with your teammates can give you an edge over the opposition, and planning ahead provides backup options when things don’t go as expected. Influence is a huge concept that can be understood in many different ways. Although it can be used for good, I think it is mostly harmful because it often leads people down the wrong path. Influence is essentially the power to persuade others to act in a certain manner, and that persuasion is not always positive.

For instance, imagine someone offering you a beer, wine, or even drugs—those are classic examples of a bad influence. If a friend urges you, “Come on, let’s steal that bicycle,” that is another form of negative influence. I also know people who simply imitate the lifestyle of others, copying habits that are unhealthy or reckless, which is certainly not right. Moreover, influence can appear in everyday choices, such as encouraging the purchase of junk food, energy drinks, or fast‑food meals; these habits are detrimental to health.

In conclusion, I believe that influencing others is largely detrimental because it pushes many individuals, especially children, toward harmful behaviors. While the word “influence” can occasionally describe positive effects in work or personal development, the negative aspects far outweigh the benefits.

I agree with Ralph Waldo Emerson’s claim that individuality is essential. Being true to yourself can make some people feel at ease, while others may feel uncomfortable, but nothing matters more than staying authentic. When you challenge yourself, you discover abilities you never imagined. The world will try to push you down, presenting temptations or pressures that might lead you to act wrongly or imitate someone else. nevertheless, you must resist giving others the power to diminish you. Even if people begin to resent your achievements, you do not have to heed their criticism or abandon your convictions.

Often, others attempt to make decisions on your behalf. For instance, when you choose a career, friends or family may suggest a path you dislike. You are not obliged to follow their advice; you can make your own choice. As an adult, you should pursue what you truly enjoy, which is why staying true to yourself is vital, regardless of circumstances.

My own life illustrates this point. My father left, leaving my mother to work tirelessly so I could have a future. Her dedication inspires me to be myself and to strive hard every day. In my country, gangs roam the streets and could have drawn me into their world, but I was raised by my grandmother and received a good education, which kept me on a different path. I never pretended to be someone I was not, echoing Emerson’s words: “The reward of being yourself in a world that constantly tries to make you something else.”

Life is difficult, and no one promises it will be easy. Success requires hard work and a firm belief in yourself, not in the opinions of a world that may not want to see you flourish. Trust in God and in your own strengths, and you will witness remarkable achievements. In short, ignore those who oppose your decisions, because their intent is often to hurt you, not help you.

If they can identify a career, they can focus on school and study more quickly, allowing them to finish high school faster. Students can also be prepared for the career they want to pursue.

However, they can also see what requirements they need to meet in order not to take too long to graduate. Many students do not like staying in school longer than necessary and want to finish quickly, especially those who plan to work right after high school.

Second, students should commit to a career because identifying one lets them focus on school. Many students will concentrate on their future. By choosing a career early, they have the opportunity to study what they really want at school. Knowing their career path also helps them prepare for college.

Third, if students have a specific career in mind, they can use high school to prepare for what they want to be or study in the future. This benefits them when they go to college, because they will not have to spend extra time deciding on a career. Students won’t need to spend as much time in college or university if they have already made progress toward their career in high school.

Finally, students should be expected to identify a career by the time they enter high school. Knowing this helps them understand how long they will be in high school and when they will graduate. These are the reasons why students are expected to commit to a career at a young age.

Students ought to decide on a career path before they begin high school. Knowing their future direction helps them understand how long they will stay in school and when they can graduate. When pupils have a clear idea of their intended occupation, they can concentrate their studies, work more efficiently, and finish high school more quickly. This early planning also allows them to prepare for the field they want to pursue.

First, having a career goal lets students estimate the time they need to complete their education. They can identify the requirements for graduation and avoid unnecessary delays. Many young people are eager to leave school as soon as possible because they prefer to start working, so a defined aim can streamline the process.

Second, committing to a specific career helps students focus their efforts while at school. When they know what they want to do, they can choose subjects and activities that are relevant, which keeps them motivated about their future. Early exposure to a chosen field also gives them a head start, making the transition to college smoother and more purposeful.

Third, a clear career plan enables high‑school students to acquire the skills and knowledge they will need later. By concentrating on the subjects and experiences that relate to their intended profession, they arrive at college already well prepared, reducing the time spent figuring out their direction. Although some professions require long periods of training, beginning that preparation in high school shortens the overall time needed later on.

In conclusion, students should be expected to identify a career before entering high school. This foresight allows them to plan their education, stay focused, and accelerate their progress toward graduation. By knowing what they want to study early, they can make the most of their high‑school years and enter higher education with a clear purpose.

Thomas Jefferson once wrote that we should never be idle, a thought that remains incredibly important today. It is wonderful when a community comes together and supports each other, just as Jefferson valued helping people in any way he could. When someone is idle, we should not give them unnecessary attention or let them distract us from our own goals. Everyone has different talents, and sometimes jealousy causes a person to try to hold others back. This is unfair, because each person has their own dreams and must work hard to achieve them.

In my opinion, we should act as a group to prevent people from making others idle. If we ignore those who waste others’ time, the problem will continue and repeat itself. Some individuals simply do not like to help, which fuels the issue, but a united community can address it and strive to eliminate such behavior.

The first impression occurs when you currently meet someone or something. It is the initial opinion your mind creates, but this impression or idea can change as you get to know the subject better. When we first meet a person, our mind forms an idea that may be false or true; we can only determine its accuracy over time.  

The change can be either detrimental or beneficial. Sometimes we think something is good when it is bad, and vice versa. An example of a negative effect is buying a car that looks beautiful on the outside, only to discover during a mechanical inspection that it has many damages. An example of a benefit is hearing someone say something unflattering about another person, then discovering through conversation that the claim was false.  

First impressions can change for many reasons that our mind creates, such as false opinions, disappointment, anger, or self‑correction. All of these can influence how you revise your impression of someone or something. For instance, when we are angry, everything seems bad or annoying. Another example is when we correct a belief we previously thought was bad or incorrect.  

In conclusion, first impressions are very important, but they are not always good or bad; your opinion will change. I think that when you do not know someone or something, it is better to wait a little before forming a positive or negative idea about it. For that reason, I believe that first impressions can change as time passes.

First impressions are formed the moment we encounter a person or a situation. They are the initial judgments our mind creates, but these opinions are not fixed; they can shift as we learn more. When we meet someone for the first time, we may form an idea that turns out to be either accurate or mistaken, and only with time can we discover the truth.

These changes can have both positive and negative effects. Sometimes we think something is good and later find it is bad, or the opposite. For instance, a car may look attractive on the outside, yet a thorough mechanical inspection might reveal serious damage. Likewise, we might hear a negative rumor about a person, only to discover through direct conversation that the gossip was unfounded.

Various factors cause first impressions to evolve, such as mistaken assumptions, disappointment, anger, or a willingness to revise our views. All of these influence how we reassess our initial judgment. When we are angry, everything can seem unpleasant or irritating. Another example is when we correct a previously held belief that turned out to be wrong.

In conclusion, first impressions are important but they are not always reliable. Our opinions are likely to change as we gain more information. It is often wiser to wait a little before forming a strong positive or negative judgment, because, as time passes, those initial impressions can indeed be altered.

Imagine a teacher asking you to stay after class to finish your assignments. I believe that offering after‑school clubs is beneficial because they can actually improve students’ performance at school. Such programs encourage pupils to complete their work more quickly and help them grasp the material better. Many children are reluctant to do homework at home, but if they have engaging activities waiting for them after school, they are more likely to want to finish their tasks so they can join in.

First, students often become bored simply sitting and doing homework. When they participate in enjoyable activities, the monotony disappears and they become more motivated to tackle their assignments. Active, fun environments help them work faster and more efficiently. For example, a child who wants to play sports may be told that he must finish his homework first; his desire to play will push him to complete the work. Today, many learners prefer to practice skills through math games, card games, and similar interactive tasks. Teachers can use these methods to explain concepts more clearly, leading to deeper understanding.

Secondly, emphasizing the importance of the work makes students take it seriously, which can raise their grades. Young people often lack a serious attitude toward school, so adults need to demonstrate how homework affects academic results. Constant encouragement and gentle pressure can help them succeed later in life. Many students give up on schoolwork, but when learning is combined with enjoyable activities, they are less likely to abandon their efforts. Moreover, a quiet room where they sit still can become tedious; most children thrive when they are active and engaged.

Finally, putting effort into assignments is essential for comprehension and completion; otherwise, the tasks become overwhelming. Remember to persevere and keep striving toward your goals, because the same determination will serve you beyond school. In summary, these points illustrate why after‑school activities are a good idea for schools—they motivate students, improve understanding, and support better academic outcomes.

Teachers and some adults think that students are expected to have the capacity to identify a career by the time they enter high school. Students are the only ones who can decide whether they are able to take on that responsibility.  

In my opinion, I think differently; I do not believe that young students are able to choose a career, and I will support my reasons. First, consider the students who are already independent. They probably have a job and need to pay their own bills, rent, and phone, leaving them little time to handle both their education and a career. They must work hard to study, which is not easy. At the same time, they likely have a lot of homework and must be responsible at their job.  

Another reason is that some students have no help or support from others to determine whether they are capable of caring about a career in high school. Many students can do it, but some cannot afford the help or the materials needed for the classes. Some are lucky to find people who want to help them and give them opportunities to make decisions about a career, but teachers or others often refuse to assist because they think the students are not ready, are still learning, and lack the capacity to work on it. Consequently, the students are not given the chance to explain or demonstrate that they can handle the responsibility.  

A lot of students are fighting hard with their education and are giving up; they become tired of the many classes and responsibilities they carry. That is why it is hard for them to keep studying in high school. Yet many students remain strong and continue preparing, even if they face problems at home or with their families; they just want to move on.  

Even though some students are very young in high school and are still learning about life and how hard it is to take on adult responsibilities, they may think it will be difficult to identify a career when they enter high school because they must take more than the normal courses. For some reason, students do not even think about a career when they first enter high school; they are probably focused on the responsibilities they already have or will have in their education, and they must take care of those.  

Many students make mistakes, such as ignoring their education and focusing on being popular, how many friends they have, or how good they look. They need to mature in their attitude and start thinking about their education—how they can improve their grades, make their families proud, and how far they can go if they keep working hard and take pride in themselves.  

People may think it would be easy for them, or some may think it would not. I believe it is not a good idea to push students toward a specific career; therefore, I have explained my reasons so they can see that it will be difficult, hard, and stressful. They are too young to take on such a big responsibility.

Some teachers and adults claim that students should already know which career they want to pursue by the time they start high school. I disagree with this view because I believe that most young people are not ready to take on such a responsibility.

First, many teenagers are already trying to be independent. They may have part‑time jobs to pay for rent, phone bills and other expenses. Balancing work with schoolwork is already difficult, and adding the pressure of choosing a future profession makes the situation even harder. These students have a lot of homework and must also fulfil the duties of their jobs, which leaves little time or energy for long‑term career planning.

Second, not all students have the support they need to explore career options. Some can afford tutors or career‑counselling, while others cannot afford these services and receive little guidance from teachers who may simply assume they are too young to decide. When teachers dismiss their abilities, the pupils lose the chance to demonstrate that they are capable of making thoughtful choices.

Third, many young people are already struggling with the demands of school itself. They feel overwhelmed by the workload and the responsibilities they carry at home, which can lead to burnout and a loss of motivation. Even those who persevere often have to deal with family problems or personal issues that make it hard to think about a future job.

Finally, high‑school students are still learning about life and the many responsibilities that adults manage. Expecting them to pick a career at such an early stage adds unnecessary stress, especially when their schedules are already filled with regular classes. Some teenagers focus more on social life or personal image than on their studies, and they need time to mature before they can set realistic professional goals.

In short, pushing students to decide on a career before they have the experience, support, and emotional maturity needed is unrealistic. It creates pressure, anxiety and can hinder their overall development. Young people should be allowed to concentrate on their education and personal growth before being forced to make such an important decision.
