A few years ago, before my uncle started his medical career, I witnessed him suffer from anxiety attacks caused by the endless hours of studying in medical school. He eventually realized that taking part in different activities helped distract him and eased his stress. Encouraging every student to join at least one extracurricular activity is a sensible idea, whether it is sports, a book club, or community service. If all learners engaged in such pursuits, their lives would become richer, less stressful, and more varied.

Physical activity is especially beneficial for a student’s health. Most pupils spend countless hours sitting in classrooms, and many continue to lounge on the couch at home. The body, however, needs movement to stay healthy. Regular sport promotes better fitness and supports the physical changes that teenagers experience as they grow. Even a modest routine—just twenty minutes of exercise each day—can make a noticeable difference.

Book clubs offer another enjoyable way to unwind. Sometimes the mind simply needs a break, and reading provides exactly that. Books can transport us to far‑away lands, imagined realms, or historical periods without us leaving our seat. They deliver adventure, drama, romance, and ideas we might never encounter otherwise. Discussing a book with fellow club members lets us share impressions, debate interpretations, and sometimes discover someone who thinks exactly like us.

Volunteering in the community benefits both others and the volunteer. How does it help the student? By working with others, young people learn the value of cooperation, experience the satisfaction that comes from helping, and develop a stronger sense of responsibility. In addition, community service often earns valuable credits for advanced diplomas or even scholarships for higher education. If you think service work is dull, consider it an extracurricular option that can be both rewarding and practical.

In short, every pupil should take part in an extracurricular activity after school so that both body and mind receive a constructive rest. Any form of involvement can relax and rejuvenate. Choose something you enjoy, and make the most of the time after classes to pursue it.

**Moreover**, it depends on the knowledge of the student if he/she can take everything on his/her head because some students have the capacity to learn a lot without forgetting, **whereas** others do not, possibly due to apathy in some classes or because they are more interested in other things. **Since** some school districts offer programs that can contain classes that students don't want to learn, **this** can be very helpful for the students who want to graduate quickly from high school **because** maybe they want to work without an interruption from high‑school activities or they want to go to college without spending a lot of time in high school. Also, some students think that they have the capacity to graduate from high school in a short time, **while** others prefer to graduate in the normal number of years because some students want to obtain an advanced diploma that can give them good opportunities.

**In addition**, more time may lead the students to know what they want to do after high school because some students graduate so fast that they didn’t think correctly about what they want to be or do after graduation. **Consequently**, you have to do something in your life that can help you to live economically in the world. For example, you graduate today but in a week or a month you are doing nothing because you don't know what you want to do, yet you need something for your life. **Furthermore**, if you want to graduate quickly from high school you need a plan such as: “I’ll work after high school because I need money,” or “I want to study more because I think I need to know more for my future.” For example, the people who work after high school are those who know what they want regardless of the time they took in high school, **whereas** the people who are still studying are because they are not ready to know what they want or they are still studying for a career.

**Additionally**, having elective classes can help the students to be good workers in the future because they become more creative, and elective classes lead the students to learn new things that can help them in the future and in their daily life. For example, if they take an art class they will be more creative; if they take a music class they can produce their own record. **Also**, elective classes give more opportunities than a program that contains only the usual, boring classes. Finally, summer is a good time to take a break from high school and you have the opportunity to be in a class online if it’s difficult for you to remember something during that time.

In conclusion, some programs that allow high school students to graduate in three years are good for the students who know what they want to do after high school, **whether** they want to work or continue studying. **Moreover**, taking a little bit less time to graduate is not too bad because you will still have the opportunity to learn new things during the elapsed time and to think more about what to do in the future. **Finally**, if you have the capacity to remember things for a long time, the idea of graduating in three years is not too bad. The only thing a student needs to know is to make a plan for the future with clear ideas and to be sure of what he/she wants.

It is a good idea for students to finish high school in three years? Many students graduated from high school in a very short period, but do they know what they need to know? In some cases students didn’t remember something from high school. Many students forget everything they learned during the summer or when they stop going to school, and this happens in a very short time. It depends on a student’s knowledge whether he or she can retain everything. More time might help students decide what they want to do after high school, and elective classes can help them become good workers in the future because they become more creative.

Whether a student can retain everything depends on his or her capacity to learn without forgetting. Some students have the ability to learn a lot and retain it, while others may be apathetic in certain classes or more interested in other things. Some school districts offer programs that contain classes students don’t want to take. However, a fast‑track graduation can be very helpful for students who want to enter the workforce without interruption or who want to go to college without spending many years in high school. Some students believe they can graduate quickly, while others prefer the normal four years because they want an advanced diploma that can provide good opportunities.

More time may allow students to figure out what they want to do after high school. Some students graduate so fast that they don’t think clearly about their future plans, leaving them unemployed a week or a month after graduation because they don’t know what they want. If you aim to graduate quickly, you need a plan, such as “I’ll work after high school because I need money,” or “I want to study more because I need more knowledge for my future.” For example, people who work after high school are often those who know what they want, regardless of how long they spent in high school, whereas those who continue studying may not yet be ready to decide on a career.

Elective classes can help students become better workers in the future because they foster creativity. Elective courses expose students to new skills that are useful in both their future careers and everyday life. For instance, an art class can make a student more creative, and a music class might lead to creating a personal record. Electives also provide more opportunities than a program that only contains the usual, sometimes boring, classes. Finally, summer is a good time to take a break from high school and to attend a class online if it is difficult to remember material during the regular school year.

In conclusion, programs that allow high school students to graduate in three years can be beneficial for those who know what they want to do after high school, whether that is working or continuing their education. Graduating a little faster is not bad, because it gives students the chance to learn new things and to think more about their future. If a student can retain information for a long time, graduating in three years is a viable option. The only thing a student needs to do is make a clear plan for the future and be sure of what he or she wants.

Finishing high school in three years can be appealing, but it raises the question of whether students truly master the material they need. Some pupils manage to absorb the curriculum quickly, yet many forget much of what they learned during the summer break or after leaving school for a short period. The amount of knowledge a student can retain depends on the individual’s capacity and motivation. With a longer high‑school experience, students have more time to consider their future plans and to choose elective courses that may nurture creativity and better prepare them for the workplace.

Students differ in how much information they can keep in mind. Certain learners can study intensively without losing much, while others become disengaged or prefer to focus on subjects that interest them. Some districts even offer programs that include classes many students find irrelevant. For those who wish to finish quickly, an accelerated path can be useful—perhaps because they want to start working without a gap or because they aim to enter college as soon as possible. Conversely, many students prefer the traditional four‑year schedule to obtain an advanced diploma, which often opens better opportunities.

Having more time in high school can help young people clarify their goals. Those who rush through their studies sometimes realize later that they have not thought carefully about what they want to do after graduation, leaving them idle for weeks or months. A clear plan—whether to earn money immediately or to continue studying—makes the difference. People who enter the workforce right after high school usually know what they want, regardless of how long they spent in school, while those who stay in education often do so because they are still deciding on a career path.

Elective courses can also play a vital role in shaping future workers. By exposing students to subjects like art or music, schools foster creativity and provide skills that may become useful later on. Electives broaden horizons beyond the standard, sometimes monotonous, curriculum and can lead to new opportunities. Summer breaks, for instance, can be a good chance to take an extra class or catch up on material, especially if online resources help reinforce learning.

In summary, programs that allow students to graduate in three years can be beneficial for those who already have a clear idea of their next steps, whether that means entering the job market or continuing with higher education. A shorter timetable is not inherently negative, provided the student can retain knowledge and has a solid plan for the future. Ultimately, success depends on careful planning, self‑awareness, and confidence in one’s goals.

Success in life often depends on how we respond to setbacks. I agree with Winston Churchill’s idea that maintaining enthusiasm even when we fall can lead to future success. Although life can be difficult and obstacles may seem overwhelming, a positive and energetic attitude helps us overcome challenges and makes our journey smoother.

When we stumble, we are confronted with many negative experiences. The world may feel harsher than we expected, and it is easy to become discouraged. Yet, if we summon strength and enthusiasm, we can turn these setbacks into opportunities. Without motivation, reaching our dreams becomes almost impossible. For instance, imagine a student who wants to attend university. If he is lazy, neglects his studies, and avoids work, he will not earn the money needed for tuition. The same applies to someone who wishes to own a car, a house, a pet, and travel the world. Without effort and a willing attitude, he risks losing his job and cannot finance those aspirations. Negative thoughts, therefore, block the path to a brighter future.

Enthusiasm, on the other hand, brings optimism and eases the pursuit of goals. A hopeful mindset reduces stress, increases energy, and encourages patience. Consider a pupil who wishes to pass a difficult school exam. By studying regularly, listening to the teacher, completing assignments on time and staying calm, he can succeed without overwhelming anxiety. Even if he fails a math test, he can keep trying, seek extra help after school, or prepare more thoroughly for the next attempt. The willingness to keep trying makes the obstacle manageable.

Failing without losing enthusiasm can actually pave the way for later achievement. When we stay positive after a setback, we learn valuable lessons and discover new chances to move forward. Suppose a student does not graduate because he failed a required class. He may repeat the year, enroll in a different school that offers extra support, or seek tutoring to master the material. Similarly, if someone loses a job after accidentally breaking a delicate item, the disappointment can be a signal to look for other employment where his experience is appreciated. By maintaining energy and a constructive attitude, he can impress future employers with his dedication.

Negative thoughts, however, only lead to further problems. When we focus on what we cannot achieve, we become stuck and fail to reach our objectives. In contrast, enthusiasm drives us to work hard and enjoy the process, creating the attitude many admire. Although life is full of hardships, some people demonstrate that perseverance and a positive outlook can turn adversity into progress. By refusing to give up and consistently moving forward, we can transform failure into future success.

In summary, embracing enthusiasm after a fall prevents the spiral of negativity and opens the door to new opportunities. Churchill’s message reminds us that staying upbeat, even in difficult times, is essential for building a happier, less stressful, and more successful life.

Moreover, technology has altered our lifestyle; people once visited parks to converse with one another. Families no longer spend quality time together. Students are distracted by their cell phones at school. Children no longer read books or play as they once did. Now everything has shifted because of this issue.

One reason that technology has negative effects on people's lives is that some stores have closed because consumers no longer shop in them. Another reason that technology has negative effects on people's lives is that certain public spaces—parks, lakes, and malls—are becoming deserted. People choose to remain at home playing video games and shopping online.

Some individuals argue that technology is a superior medium for self‑expression. However, there are countless alternatives such as painting, drawing, playing music, or dancing.

When I encountered difficult words, I used Google Translate, so technology was occasionally helpful. Yet I have observed students using their cell phones during class. On the other hand, some people will argue that technology has positive effects on our lifestyles. Technology enables us to communicate with family and friends. Nevertheless, it also confines the way we express ideas without a cell phone. It has eroded our culture. It hinders children’s development because they refuse to go outside to play with peers. Dear Mr. Principal, today I would like to discuss why most employers look for certain qualities in candidates even when the applicants have no prior experience in the specific role. I agree with this view because a person does not always know how to perform a job at first, but they can acquire the necessary skills over time.

When someone starts a new job, they often do not know exactly what to do and must be trained by an experienced colleague, usually a manager. Employers may hire a manager who lacks direct experience in the position, yet they expect that person to learn while working. For instance, when I first arrived in this country I helped my step‑father with roofing. I knew nothing about the trade, but by working alongside him I gradually mastered the techniques. Last summer I worked as a cashier in a restaurant and struggled with the local coinage, which is different from that in my homeland. The manager patiently taught me, and my determination to learn helped me become successful in the role.

People who already understand a job tend to work hard because they want to deepen their knowledge, and even seasoned workers can pick up new insights from coworkers or supervisors. In the United States many employees put in great effort not only for personal advancement but also for the benefit of their families. They realise that hard work sets an example for their children, who can learn from their parents’ experience and become better individuals. Some workers are driven by personal goals or the desire for a brighter future.

Responsibility is another key trait that employers value. A responsible employee is more likely to be hired and retained, because managers appreciate reliability. Companies grow when their staff consistently meet the tasks assigned to them. In my home country I saw several shops fail because the hired staff frequently arrived late and ignored their duties, forcing the businesses to close. Demonstrating punctuality and accountability, especially when you are new, signals to employers that you can be depended upon—a quality most workplaces seek.

Patience is also essential, particularly for managers who must train newcomers. Some managers are impatient and refuse to invest time in teaching, assuming the trainee will never learn. However, many restaurants and stores have managers with a positive attitude who willingly help beginners develop their skills.

In conclusion, a candidate does not need to possess all the technical knowledge at the outset if they are responsible, eager, and willing to learn. Experience is acquired through facing challenges and learning from mistakes, and with the right attitude any employee can become successful.

Many students and teachers think that taking online classes is bad for both students and schools. They argue that students might not take notes on what the teacher is saying and that they often become distracted from the lecture. Because of these issues, students cannot benefit from online classes.  

Students might not take notes while attending an online class. For example, at school students take notes because the teacher can see them; they are less likely to do so when they are not being watched. If the teacher is on the screen but cannot see whether a student is writing, most students will not worry about being checked. Taking notes helps a topic stay in the mind and aids understanding, but online teachers cannot see whether students are doing this, and many students may not be paying attention.  

Students might also fail to pay attention to the lecture. When a student looks around the classroom instead of at the teacher, they miss valuable information; the same happens in online classes. Missing information is problematic because students may overlook what is happening in class, forget assignments, or not know how to complete their work. Students should focus on the teacher to gather the necessary information for assignments. When they do not take notes, they miss key details and may panic when trying to solve a problem on an assignment.  

Overall, students cannot benefit from online classes because they might not write valuable information in their notes and may not pay attention to the teacher’s lecture. They are unlikely to take notes when no one watches them, and they may miss crucial information needed for assignments. This lack of note‑taking and attention explains why online classes can be ineffective for students.

Many pupils and teachers claim that online lessons are disadvantageous for both students and schools. They argue that learners often fail to take notes and become easily distracted during virtual lectures. Consequently, they believe that online teaching offers little benefit because students neither record important information nor focus on the teacher’s explanations.  

One major problem is the lack of note‑taking in a digital setting. In a traditional classroom, teachers can see whether students are writing down key points, which encourages them to keep up with the material. When the lesson is delivered through a screen, however, the teacher cannot monitor each learner’s actions, and many students simply stop taking notes. Without the habit of writing things down, the information is less likely to stay in their memory, and they miss the chance to review and clarify concepts later.  

A second issue is the tendency to lose concentration during online sessions. In a physical classroom, looking around the room usually means glancing at the board or the teacher, but in a virtual environment a student can easily divert their gaze to other tabs, notifications, or even the surrounding room. This distraction leads to missed explanations and important details, which can later cause confusion when completing assignments. Missing even small pieces of information can make it difficult to understand tasks, solve problems, or follow instructions.  

Because of these two factors—insufficient note‑taking and poor attention—students gain little from online classes. Teachers cannot verify whether learners are engaged or recording the lesson, and many students do not feel compelled to do so when they are not being observed. As a result, essential knowledge may be overlooked, and students may struggle to complete their work correctly. In short, the inability to ensure active participation and focus is why many argue that online education is ineffective for students.

Do we choose our own character traits?

As the British naturalist and politician John Lubbock wrote, “Your character will be what you yourself choose to make it.” I certainly agree that everyone is capable of choosing their own character traits; they are independent enough to have control over themselves, they’re capable of choosing what type of environment they want to be in, or how to react to bad or good circumstances. At the end of the day we all have the freedom to choose who, and what we want to be.

John Lubbock wrote, “Your character will be what you yourself choose to make it.” Everyone has the complete control over themselves. No matter how bad the circumstances may be or how tough a problem is, everyone will always be allowed to choose either to smile or cry, to be positive or negative, for example:

Failure is something most of us try to avoid in everyday life. Many people steer clear of any situation where they might fall short, while a smaller group embraces failure as a chance to learn and eventually achieve great things.

Fear dominates many of our choices. We ask ourselves how we look, whether we have made the right decision, and what the outcome of our actions will be. In most cases the anxiety about failing stems from uncertainty about success and the possible consequences. This fear splits people into two camps: the cautious, safety‑oriented individuals and the bold, risk‑taking ones. Both approaches have advantages and disadvantages.

Those who prefer the safe route rely heavily on the knowledge they have accumulated over the years. The label “shy” does not fully capture them; it only applies when they encounter something completely new. They avoid risks because they do not want to fail, and, paradoxically, they often never fail because they never try. Whether it is answering a question in class, trying a new sport, going to the gym, or wearing a different style of clothing, fear acts as a barrier. If they do try and lose, they view it simply as a loss. The only upside is that they believe they will not lose anything at all, but this mindset also limits the amount of success they can experience. This does not mean they live in constant terror; they just choose a more secure path. Their past mishaps—saying something foolish in class, embarrassing themselves in a sport, feeling weak among more fit peers—make them hesitant to repeat the experience.

Conversely, the people who constantly test new things and learn from their mistakes are the ones who create lasting achievements. Winston Churchill is a classic example. His career shows how essential trial and error are to success. Becoming Prime Minister of the United Kingdom was far from easy; his biography records numerous setbacks before he finally attained power. Figures like Churchill treat failure as a teacher, refining ideas, perfecting actions, making better decisions, and answering questions correctly. When a mistake occurs, they confront it and, more importantly, feel proud of the lesson learned and of the knowledge that will help them avoid similar errors in the future. They may stumble again, but ultimately they emerge as winners, driven by genuine enthusiasm.

Enthusiasm fuels goal‑pursuit. Churchill’s determination during World War II stemmed from his desire not to let his country, humanity, or his own legacy fail. Enthusiasm can appear as duty, as the joy of a musician, or as a parent’s wish to make children happy. Its persistence depends on the individual, not on the size of the goal. Anyone can aspire to be president if they are willing, yet the same person may skip the gym if they lack the willpower. Whether a goal is short‑term or long‑term, enthusiasm can survive setbacks or even grow stronger after them.

My own experience with martial arts illustrates this point. I set out to learn how to wield a nunchaku with both hands, despite being right‑handed. Practising with my left hand caused my forearm to bleed and turn red after countless spins. Friends asked why I kept trying. The answer was simple: my enthusiasm for mastering the nunchaku kept me going. After months of painful practice I can now perform the moves without hurting myself, even though I am far from a master.

Sometimes failure can be extreme, even life‑threatening. A boy who loved performing bicycle tricks was hit by a car and lost a leg. After months in a wheelchair, doctors fitted him with a prosthetic limb. Although he was angry and broken for a long time, he never gave up. He kept trying, falling repeatedly, until he could ride again—now with the same skill he had before the accident. His story inspires me and shows that perseverance can turn tragedy into triumph.

In agreement with Churchill, I believe that we must experience failure to learn and to enjoy what we eventually achieve. We can stay within our comfort zones and avoid risk, or we can confront failure, gain experience, and grow. The choice is ours.

Having students take summer courses in order to finish high school in three years is not a wise choice. I believe this approach creates several problems: many pupils would need extra credits, many work during the summer and would become overwhelmed, and many simply want a break between school years.

If they lack the required credits, they must double‑up on courses, which can lead to high stress and pressure. A typical four‑year high‑school experience allows youngsters to join clubs, play sports and attend regular lessons without feeling swamped. This balanced schedule also looks attractive on college applications. Trying to fit all those activities into a compressed three‑year plan would likely leave students exhausted and overextended.

Second, a lot of teenagers hold summer jobs to earn money. They rely on this time to save for a car, a future college tuition or simply to have some spending cash. Combining a job with summer classes would leave little room for work, reducing their earnings and limiting the time they can devote to hobbies or relaxation. The summer break is often the only period when students can focus entirely on making money without academic distractions.

Finally, many graduates prefer to take a gap after high school. This pause gives them the chance to work full‑time, save for future needs, and reflect on what they really want to study. A break can provide financial stability for expenses such as a vehicle, a house, or college fees, and it helps them enter higher education feeling rested rather than rushed and fatigued.

In short, compressing high school into three years is problematic. Students may need additional credits, they often have summer jobs they would have to sacrifice, and many value a break to earn money and consider their future plans.

Dear members of the city council,

I appreciate that you are taking the time to consider a new curfew policy, but I must express my reservations about the proposal. While I understand the concern for safety after dark, many teenagers have commitments that keep them out past the suggested 10 p.m. curfew. Some of us have part‑time jobs, sports practice, music lessons, or other after‑school activities that cannot be shifted to earlier hours. In many cases we are simply stuck in traffic rather than choosing to be out late. I also believe that, contrary to popular belief, young people are often able to stay alert longer than adults; fatigue is not the only factor that determines how well we can drive.

Nevertheless, I recognize that night time does pose genuine hazards. Alcohol‑impaired drivers, wildlife crossing the road, and the general decrease in visibility all increase the risk of accidents after dark. Moreover, the longer a driver stays on the road, the higher the chance of fatigue leading to a crash. Because of these dangers, I do think it would be reasonable to require teenagers to be off the streets by midnight rather than a stricter 10 p.m. limit.

In summary, I understand why the council wants to limit teenage driving during the late‑night hours, given the increased risks. At the same time, I hope you will consider that many of us are out late for important responsibilities such as work and extracurricular activities, and that we are capable of driving safely when we are aware of the dangers. A compromise that allows us to be on the road until midnight would balance safety concerns with the realities of teenage life.

Do you think confidence comes from achievement or from praise? Many people argue that students must already be self‑confident in order to learn, while others claim that self‑esteem grows only after you have succeeded. In my view, confidence must precede achievement. Without a belief in yourself, it is impossible to reach any goal.

First, self‑esteem is essential for hard work and continuous learning. Consider a doctor who must keep updating his knowledge because new diseases and medicines appear constantly. Or a person trying to master a foreign language. English words often have several meanings, and many do not resemble their Spanish equivalents. You will never know a language perfectly, not even a native speaker, but the confidence that you will keep improving keeps you motivated to study a little each day.

Second, confidence and a positive attitude are needed to accomplish tasks. Anger or doubt can destroy concentration and lead to chaos. When the end of the school year approaches and exams loom, the confidence built by attending classes every day—even when you feel unwell—helps you retain the material and perform better on those important tests. Regular study creates a feeling of preparedness that reduces anxiety when the exam finally arrives.

Third, confidence means feeling sure about what you are about to do. Imagine looking for a new job without believing in yourself. Fear will paralyse you, and the interviewer will notice your insecurity. Only by letting confidence replace fear can you present yourself as the right candidate and increase your chances of being hired.

Some people maintain that self‑esteem results from achievement. They argue that succeeding gives you proof of your abilities, which in turn boosts confidence. For example, after months of preparation for a national exam, finishing it and knowing that summer is near gives a great sense of relief and accomplishment. Even if you fail the first time, the effort you have already invested can eventually lead to success, and each victory strengthens your belief in yourself. Positive individuals tend to think that hard work will pay off, and they keep telling themselves they will master a new skill or job. This optimism is rooted in the confidence that they are capable of overcoming obstacles.

Nevertheless, I still contend that confidence must come first. It is the courage that allows a person to face fear and take the first step toward any achievement. Without that inner belief, nothing can be accomplished.

In summary, confidence is the foundation of achievement. It drives people to work hard, stay positive, and tackle new challenges. By cultivating self‑esteem before setting out to achieve, we can turn fear into motivation and ensure that our successes are lasting.

Attending lessons from home is not a good idea. From my own experience I believe that going to school is far more beneficial for students. When you study online you do not have a teacher physically present to explain the parts you do not understand, and you are left to figure things out on your own. This lack of immediate help makes it easy to fall behind, and many students end up wandering on the internet instead of concentrating on the work they should be doing. I firmly disagree with the view that studying at home is advantageous for learners.

Having a teacher in the classroom is extremely valuable. There are moments when you have numerous questions about the topic being discussed, and the teacher can provide clear examples and explanations on the spot. In a physical class you can also turn to a classmate for assistance, and most friends are willing to help. With an online course, you lose that close‑by support; you must rely on yourself and take extensive notes to grasp the main ideas. I have personally struggled with this format: I had to study three to five lessons each day, write notes for every one, complete at least five quizzes, and reread the material several times to capture the essential points. Although it does teach organization and independence, the workload is overwhelming, and I think students are better off attending school in person.

Teachers also keep students focused by enforcing rules about electronic devices during lessons. At home it is tempting to browse the phone or laptop while the class is ongoing, which reduces concentration and leads to missed information. Without the presence of a teacher, many pupils feel they can do whatever they like, which often results in poor performance and even failure, requiring them to retake the course.

Some students might prefer online classes because they can sleep in, have a relaxed morning, and avoid the rush to catch the bus. I understand the appeal of extra sleep, but responsibility remains essential. If you want to succeed, you must manage your time, complete assignments before the deadline, and prioritize the coursework over leisure. Studying at home does not excuse neglecting your duties.

In summary, I believe that students do not gain much from attending classes at home. It requires a great deal of self‑discipline to keep up with lessons, finish assignments, and submit work on time without a teacher’s direct guidance. For these reasons, I consider home‑based learning an unsuitable option for most students.

Saying “thank you” and “you’re welcome” is a simple way to show respect and kindness to others. When we speak politely and express gratitude for the things people do for us, we encourage them to behave in the same courteous manner. Good manners create a cycle of friendliness: if we are kind, others are more likely to respond kindly, which makes everyone feel happier.

Treating people with courtesy—using phrases like “please,” “thank you,” and “you’re welcome”—helps us build good relationships. When we thank someone for a favor or acknowledge a small act of help, we make their day a little brighter, and they are more inclined to treat us with the same consideration. In this way, polite behaviour becomes a social exchange: we receive the respect we give.

Being polite also makes it easier to make new friends. If we consistently use good manners, we appear approachable and trustworthy, which attracts others who value the same behaviour. A simple “thank you” after someone assists us or a friendly comment can leave a lasting positive impression and strengthen bonds.

Even if we sometimes forget to say thank you or apologize, it is never too late to correct the mistake. Apologising sincerely and offering a kind word can repair a strained interaction. People appreciate when we acknowledge their feelings, and they are more likely to respond with kindness in return. Small gestures—like picking up something someone dropped and saying “you’re welcome”—demonstrate that we care about others.

Manners and kindness reveal a lot about our character. When we interact with service workers, for example, asking how their day is going or thanking them for their help shows that we value them as individuals, not just for the service they provide. A brief, polite conversation can lift their spirits and encourages them to treat us with the same respect. Even a simple “have a nice day” followed by a reciprocal wish can spread positivity.

In everyday situations, such as dining out, saying “thank you” and leaving a tip are practical ways to express gratitude. If we notice a worker having a tough day, inviting them to share a meal or offering a small token of appreciation can make a big difference. Consistently expressing kindness and good manners not only benefits others but also brings us the same treatment in return.

In short, courteous language and kind actions create a mutually reinforcing cycle of respect. The more we practice good manners, the more likely we are to receive kindness from those around us. By staying polite and considerate, we help build a friendlier, more supportive community for everyone.

The question of whether schools should dictate how students spend their free time is often discussed. Some argue that schools ought to manage extracurricular activities, believing that more structured learning will enhance students’ knowledge. I disagree; I think pupils should decide for themselves how to use the hours after classes, because many have responsibilities such as working to support their families, looking after younger siblings, or simply pursuing interests like sports, art, or additional study.

Firstly, a number of students have to work part‑time to help their parents or to save money for future education. Juggling a job with schoolwork can be exhausting, leaving little energy for extra lessons or hobbies. While a study hall might give them a chance to finish assignments, these students rarely have the time to join clubs or teams. Still, their employment can be a sensible investment in their future, so they must sacrifice some leisure activities in order to meet both work and school demands.

Secondly, some learners must return home early to care for siblings while their parents are at work. Because many families cannot afford a babysitter, these children often take on household chores—cooking, cleaning, laundry—while also trying to keep up with homework. Their ability to participate in clubs is limited to occasional free days when a parent is off duty, making it hard to balance school responsibilities with family duties.

Thirdly, there are students whose after‑school hours are devoted to personal interests. Many enjoy regular exercise and join sports such as basketball, baseball, tennis or gymnastics. Others are drawn to the arts, environmental projects, or learning a new language, and they sign up for clubs that match their passions. These pupils clearly engage in extracurricular activities, but the choice comes from them, not from school mandates.

In short, schools should not control what students do after the final bell. Understanding each youngster’s individual goals and challenges helps us appreciate the diverse ways people work toward success and happiness.

To commit to a career at a young age is a good idea for students who are interested in studying a long career, for example: doctors, pediatrics, lawyers, teachers, etc. If students start to study these careers at a young age, they will be a great future for this country.

To start a career at a young age also has some disadvantages. Here are some examples why it is not a good idea to start a career at a young age: they may get tired of school, they may regret studying a career that years later they realize they do not like.

In conclusion, to commit to a career at a young age is an excellent idea for the students. That is why we have to motivate and support them with their careers. It would be a good idea if teachers and counselors start to help them find the correct career for their life.

Starting to study for these fields while still young gives them a better chance of becoming skilled professionals who will contribute positively to society.

In addition, beginning a career path early provides more time and flexibility to develop the necessary qualifications. For instance, a young person who decides to become a teacher can still explore other interests later, because their age allows them to acquire additional training without too much difficulty.

Nevertheless, there are drawbacks to committing to a career too soon. Young people may become bored with their studies or later realize that the chosen profession does not suit them, leading to regret and a possible need to change direction.

Overall, encouraging students to think about their future occupations can be worthwhile, provided they receive proper guidance from teachers and counselors. With appropriate support, young learners can make informed decisions that match their abilities and interests.

Creativity thrives when the mind is free to choose!

Summer projects could be enjoyable, but only if students are allowed to select them. When learners pick assignments that match their interests, they become more engaged, are more likely to complete the work, and actually have fun doing it.

Often teachers spend weeks—or even an entire summer—designing a topic for students to tackle during the break. Yet many pupils put little thought or effort into these assignments. This wastes the teachers’ time and energy. If students were given the chance to devise their own project ideas, the motivation to work on them would be far greater.

When learners choose a project, they are usually driven by curiosity about a subject they want to explore. Curious students tend to dig deeper, become absorbed in the material, and want to learn more. Allowing them to create their own projects can lead to innovative ideas that they might never have considered otherwise. Working on a topic that genuinely interests them stimulates the mind and opens up new possibilities.

Summer projects can also boost academic performance. For instance, a student who struggles to keep up with the regular class pace can use a self‑chosen project to study at a rate that suits them. Those who find it difficult to work in a crowded classroom gain an opportunity for independent study. By setting their own deadlines, students can manage the workload throughout the whole summer without the pressure of a fixed due date. If they still fail to finish, it is simply a result of laziness, which will affect their grade.

The subject of an assignment can have a huge impact on a student’s willingness to work. Being given a task in a field they dislike may lead to procrastination or abandonment altogether. For example, if I received a history project and a science project, and my science teacher asked me to write a paper on gene mutations, I might ignore it because science does not captivate me the way history does.

Allowing students to select their own summer projects makes the work more enjoyable and gives them something to look forward to. Students should design their own assignments; this reduces the teachers’ workload and encourages learners to think outside the box. In doing so, they can make their teachers proud and start the next school year with enthusiasm.

The world’s negative influence shows up in the rising abuse of drugs, ongoing wars, and popular music that glorifies violence, substance use, and sex. These messages can steer young people toward harmful paths, and if we do not reclaim our individuality and make healthier choices, the consequences could be dire.

It is easy to blame society for our mistakes, but ultimately we decide whether to engage with destructive behaviours. I hope that the world will evolve for the better, because there is still time to make a difference. I wish the next generation the courage to reshape society into a kinder, more supportive place where being yourself is not only accepted but celebrated.

Kindness and a simple smile can brighten others’ days and make the world a more pleasant place. People naturally seek connection and want a better environment for everyone. Therefore, fostering a positive attitude at work and in everyday life is crucial—not only for personal health but also for creating a more supportive community. Although many display negativity, those who choose optimism contribute greatly to a healthier, happier society.

People often think that altering their mindset or the impressions they hold is a difficult task, but I believe it is entirely possible. Making changes in our lives can help us reach future goals, even if it seems complicated at first. Every individual has unique ambitions, and no goal is truly unattainable; new opportunities constantly appear, like a window that invites us to step through. When we decide to take on a change, we open ourselves to chances that can lead to personal growth.

In my view, beginning a different way of living with the aim of improving my objectives creates fresh opportunities that boost my ability to achieve the dreams I cherish. Such a shift can reshape my future, giving me new targets to pursue and the determination to keep trying until success arrives. The notion that impressions are unchangeable is false; they can evolve into new chances that help us refine our goals and plans.

New possibilities emerge throughout our lives, often resembling a door that leads to job offers, further education, or projects that expand our knowledge. By embracing these chances, we can apply what we learn, generate innovative ideas, and contribute positively to society—especially as technology advances each day. This continuous learning enables us to undertake diverse projects that benefit the community.

Improving our aspirations for the future is the most effective way to refine the ideas and strategies we hold. Discovering fresh concepts, practicing what we have learned, and staying enthusiastic about our objectives drive personal development. We must also acknowledge our mistakes, learn from them, and make necessary adjustments. Although some people may falter because they ignore their errors, the crucial step is to turn those mistakes into lessons and keep moving forward.

Creating plans that enhance our capacity to realize our ideas involves thoughtful consideration and listing the goals we want to reach. By organizing our thoughts, we can improve our knowledge, develop projects, and ultimately raise our standard of living. A well‑structured plan can also strengthen our financial situation, as consistent effort in any job leads to personal and societal improvement.

In conclusion, making deliberate changes is essential for turning our ideas into reality. While it may sometimes feel challenging, embracing change is the best path to develop our abilities, execute our plans, and seize the opportunities that life presents. By committing to improvement, we can achieve the goals we set for ourselves and enjoy a better, more fulfilling life.

The school’s option for attending classes online can lead to either positive or negative results, depending on how it is used. Schools differ in how they handle this kind of program: some offer it, others do not, and people have varied opinions about it. While some think that online lessons are a great idea, others consider them a poor choice. One advantage of studying online is that you do not have to wait for classmates; you can work at the speed that suits you. However, there are several drawbacks. A slow or unreliable internet connection can make it difficult to complete assignments, and the lack of a shared physical environment with peers of the same age can limit interaction and motivation.

When a student takes lessons online, it can become hard to finish the tasks that have been assigned. It is often impossible to ask a teacher a question immediately, so the learner must figure out the solution on his or her own. Some websites give incorrect information, leading to completely wrong answers. Though instructional videos exist, they do not always cover the specific topic a student needs. In a traditional classroom, a teacher can demonstrate a problem‑solving method directly, which usually helps students understand better. Online courses frequently lack real‑time teacher support, and students may postpone their work, thinking they will finish it later—only to never complete it. Meeting deadlines becomes a challenge.

Being surrounded by peers of the same age creates a supportive study environment where students can share notes and help each other. In an online setting, you are usually alone in front of a computer. You may have friends, but they are often not taking the same class, making collaboration difficult. Socialising with new classmates is also limited, and many online learners end up working or interacting with people of different ages, which can feel isolating. Having a physical classroom provides a sense of community that the home setting lacks.

Online courses sometimes pile a large amount of work into a single day, requiring immediate submission. This can be overwhelming, especially when the material is unclear. Completing assignments is essential for understanding the subject, yet some students resort to copying solutions they find online without truly learning. Procrastination becomes common, leading to rushed work, lower grades, or even having to retake the class. Distractions from other aspects of life make it easy to fall behind, and failing to keep up means the course will not be finished on time.

Schools usually give students a choice between attending in person or studying online. While the flexibility can free up time, it can also be abused; some students might simply stay at home and avoid responsibility. Life’s unexpected difficulties can make online learning especially tough when there is no teacher readily available to help. Ultimately, students must decide what works best for them, but online classes often prove difficult to manage, limit interaction with age‑matched peers, and increase the risk of unfinished work. Online attendance does not always lead to successful outcomes for learners.

Overall, great results are produced when people collaborate, exchange ideas, and create entertaining performances. This not only brings happiness to the audience but also fills teammates, families, and teachers with pride. Working in a group is therefore a more rewarding and enjoyable experience.

I believe schools should set up an after‑school homework club because many pupils find homework confusing and are unsure how to complete it correctly. If such a club existed, imagine how many assignments would actually be finished. Some people think homework isn’t important, but it usually counts for about ten percent of a student’s grade. That may seem small, yet it can make a real difference, especially when preparing for tests. A single piece of homework can contain the material needed to pass an exam or a quiz that might otherwise be failed. Moreover, when students do not understand the work assigned in class, how can teachers expect them to finish the homework on their own?

Middle‑schoolers already have a lot on their plates. They must keep up with homework from seven different subjects, and teachers often assign more than one task per class—sometimes two or three pieces of work each night. This workload can be overwhelming. An after‑school club would give students a chance to ask questions about anything they didn’t grasp during lessons. Teachers could clarify the confusing points, and students who lack time after the regular school day would finally have a slot to complete their assignments. The focus would not be on simply giving answers, but on helping learners understand the material, which in turn could raise grades—from a B to an A, for example.

The benefits would extend beyond individual students. When more assignments are completed correctly, the school’s overall performance improves, enhancing its reputation. Teachers would also have clearer insight into which students truly understand the material, rather than seeing only copied answers. Even those who can do the work independently sometimes struggle to turn it in on time; a dedicated after‑school session would reduce lateness and missing work.

In summary, an after‑school homework club would be a valuable addition because homework is a significant issue in many schools. Some students underestimate its importance, thinking “it doesn’t matter,” yet it directly affects test results and overall learning. By providing a structured time and support for homework, the club would lower stress, improve comprehension, and free up afternoons for other activities once the assignments are finished. Implementing such a program would help students succeed academically and make the school community stronger.

Ralph Waldo Emerson once said that being true to yourself in a world that constantly tries to shape you otherwise is the greatest achievement. I fully support this idea.

First, let us clarify what “accomplish” means. To accomplish something is to fulfill a goal or realize a desire. When a person abandons authenticity and pretends to be someone else, they are unlikely to achieve genuine fulfillment. 

Consider a recent example I witnessed. A woman pretended to be wealthy and famous in order to obtain a high‑paying director position at a large company. Everyone assumed she was rich and influential, and she faced a rival candidate who was modest, talented, and experienced but not deceptive. After months of evaluation, the board had to choose a leader. During the announcement, the spokesperson explained that the two women had been closely observed. The deceptive candidate had borrowed half a million dollars, bought two houses and three new cars to maintain her false image, yet she still failed to secure the role. In contrast, the honest applicant, who stayed true to herself, was appointed and went on to succeed in the position. 

This story illustrates that trying to live a fabricated life may bring temporary advantages, but it ultimately leads to failure and disgrace when the truth emerges. Staying authentic, on the other hand, enables real accomplishment and lasting satisfaction.

In conclusion, living genuinely in a society that constantly pressures us to become someone else is indeed the greatest achievement. Those who cling to falsehoods may enjoy short‑term gains, but they will never truly accomplish anything meaningful.

One question has been asked for a long time: is it better to work alone or to work in a group?  

Most people and analysts have concluded that working in groups can be more beneficial.  

One factor that supports this idea is that you get to hear different thoughts, ideas, and ways of seeing life, which can help you in difficult situations. For example, if you are planning something as big as a school event or as simple as a classroom presentation, there are occasions when you run out of ideas. In a group, members will provide diverse solutions to the problem; by yourself, you might feel like you are on a road with no exit.  

Working in a group can also help you relax, laugh, and stay positive, even in challenging moments or when you are stressed. When you work this way, you do not experience boring moments; there is always something to talk about, and you and your team will create memories that will later become sources of laughter.  

Another fact about working in a group is that you finish work faster. More people tackling a series of tasks quickly makes a big difference. This creates space for creativity, allowing you to practice more, add detail to the work, or even produce new creations.  

Because you are working in a team, you do not focus only on “I”; you open your mind and start thinking “we.” This will be useful in the future, when you enter the real world. Working with other people requires you to deal with different personalities and thoughts, and the ability to work as a team will become ingrained in your mind.  

When a team completes all its tasks, a great euphoria follows the results. It makes everyone proud and serves as a method to keep pushing forward and never give up.  

Sometimes working in a group may seem difficult, but you gain new experiences and abilities. It becomes a valuable tool for developing character and growing as a person. You learn how to speak with others and how to present your ideas clearly. That is why many people agree that working in teams brings more benefits than working alone.

The question of whether it is better to work alone or in a group has been debated for a long time. Most people and researchers now agree that collaborating with others is usually more advantageous.

One reason for this view is that a group brings together a variety of thoughts, ideas and perspectives, which can be especially helpful in difficult situations. Imagine you are organizing a school event or preparing a simple classroom presentation and you suddenly run out of ideas. In a team, members can offer different solutions, whereas working alone might feel like being stuck on a road with no exit.

Being part of a group can also make the experience more enjoyable and less stressful. When you collaborate, there are always conversations, laughter and a positive atmosphere, even during challenging moments. This prevents boredom and creates shared memories that may later become funny stories.

Another benefit is speed. More people working on a task can complete it much faster than a single individual. This efficiency leaves room for creativity, allowing team members to add details, experiment, or develop new ideas.

Teamwork also shifts the focus from “I” to “we.” This mindset is valuable later in life, when you enter the workplace and must interact with different personalities and viewpoints. The ability to cooperate and understand others becomes ingrained in your thinking.

When a group successfully finishes a project, the sense of accomplishment is powerful. It makes everyone feel proud and motivates them to keep striving and not give up.

Although collaborating may sometimes seem daunting, it offers the chance to acquire new skills and experiences. You learn how to communicate clearly, express your ideas, and listen to others. For these reasons, many people conclude that working in a team provides more benefits than working alone.

When kids want to go to school, their parents often say, “the education here is not going to guide you anywhere.” This attitude contributes to the rise of terrorism in many countries, as parents discard their children’s dreams. Many parents should give teenagers the opportunity to study, explain how important a good education is, and let them think about the career they want at a young age.  

The importance of knowing and thinking about the future at a young age has an impact today because, in many parts of the world, teenagers do not consider their future; they do not care about school, jobs, education, or their families. In the U.S., however, teenagers have many chances to obtain a good job, a healthy life, and a great education.  

Teenagers will have their lives set after high school.  
They will be an inspiration for others and will have a good job.  
Ensuring that students have a career in mind by the time they enter high school helps them learn more, prepares them for college, and allows them to inspire many other teenagers and others to recognize the importance of a good education and career.

During the eighth‑grade year, middle‑school students begin to encounter a variety of occupations and start forming ideas about which path they might follow. They should be allowed to decide what they want to study, yet many are forced to pursue the careers their parents prefer, often because they see no other option. In today’s world, teenagers have the right to choose the field they wish to pursue. By the time they reach high school, learners are acquiring different subjects and skills; acquiring a broad range of abilities prepares them for future work and helps them cope with unexpected problems. Guiding young people toward their interests early on is sensible, because it encourages continuous learning and mental development. For instance, students often research their preferred professions, ask experienced people for advice, and gradually clarify their goals. After completing high school, they are ready to enter college and should be able to make informed decisions about what suits them best.

In several regions, however, adolescents do not even have the chance to attend school. Countries with limited resources—such as Honduras, El Salvador, Guatemala, and many African nations—see many young people abandoning education to work instead, resulting in poor schooling. This scarcity of opportunities drives many to immigrate to the United States, where they believe an American education can secure a better future. Children as young as twelve arrive with big dreams, hoping to make their families proud and become the primary providers through a respectable career. As populations in those countries grow, finding a job becomes increasingly difficult, even for those with diplomas, because the local job market is saturated. Some parents even discourage schooling, claiming it “won’t lead anywhere,” a mindset that can contribute to social unrest and even terrorism when youths’ aspirations are crushed. Parents should therefore encourage their children to pursue education and discuss the importance of choosing a career early in life.

Recognising and planning for the future at a young age has become crucial. In many parts of the world, teenagers show little concern for schooling, employment, or family expectations, whereas in the United States young people have many opportunities to obtain good jobs, a healthy lifestyle and a solid education. By the time they finish high school, students have largely set the direction of their lives, becoming role models for their peers and securing respectable employment.

Consequently, it is essential that pupils think about their future careers before entering high school, so they can continue to build knowledge, prepare for college, and inspire others to understand the value of education and a clear career path.

Choosing a profession is a personal matter that depends on one’s own development and the opportunities that arise later, not something that has to be settled once and for all in adolescence.

First, I disagree with the idea that young people should be told what career to follow. Adolescents tend to obey adults, and this often leads them into jobs they neither enjoy nor feel suited for, wasting their dreams, money and time. They need inspiration and role models—doctors, architects, teachers, and other professionals—who can show them what is possible. Support from parents or other family members is also crucial; without it, many youngsters ignore advice or lack the confidence to pursue a path that truly interests them.

Second, young adults need a broader view of the working world. Watching videos, attending workshops, or meeting people who are already employed can reveal how different jobs actually function. It would be helpful to compare two contrasting stories: one of a graduate who holds a stable, well‑paid job, and another of someone who dropped out and now struggles to make ends meet. Such examples illustrate that life after school can be tough, especially when one has not prepared adequately.

Ultimately, every person imagines a positive future for themselves and their families. If you love drawing, studying architecture makes sense; if you enjoy building, engineering might be your calling. Many people lack a clear vision, but what matters most is staying in education and gaining experience. For those who consider leaving school early because of limited opportunities, programs that combine study with apprenticeships could provide the guidance and support they need to make informed career choices.

In this essay I will discuss how failure and success relate to one another in life. Many people become upset when they do not achieve what they wanted, while others try to keep their confidence alive; some even become angry with themselves.

First, people often feel sad after a failure because they have given their best effort and expected everything to go smoothly. They may never have imagined that they could fail, and the disappointment can even bring them to tears.

Second, there are those who deliberately try not to lose their enthusiasm after an initial setback. They maintain a positive outlook, telling themselves that the next attempt will be successful, which prevents their spirit from collapsing the first time they encounter failure.

Third, some individuals become angry with themselves when they make a mistake and fall short of their goals. This anger, however, can be a learning tool: the errors they notice become the basis for future improvement.

While some claim that failure is a hindrance to success, others who refuse to let their enthusiasm drop keep moving forward until they finally succeed. Their repeated falls turn into lessons that help them avoid the same mistakes later on.

In conclusion, for many people failure is seen as something undesirable.

Skateboarding has become a daily activity for me because it takes all my stress and problems away, and I enjoy it so much. I skate everywhere—to the store, a friend's house, and even to school. Although I get lots of injuries like scrapes, bruises, and more, I still love this sport because skateboarding has taught me a lot, such as confidence when I try new things, getting right back up when I fall, and learning from my mistakes. Skateboarding isn’t just a sport, skill, activity, or hobby; it’s a way of life. Even though it may not be the safest sport, it’s still one of my favorite skills, and I don’t think I’ll get bored of it any time soon.  

When I was nine, I had lots of friends who skateboarded, and I didn’t know anything about it at the time, so it was really cool to observe such a unique sport. I would always see them practicing and skating everywhere, and that encouraged me to try it one day. A couple of days later I went to my parents and told them I wanted to try something new—skateboarding. My mom said she would think about it because she didn’t want me to hurt myself, but my dad told me to just go for it, and that’s exactly what I did.  

The next day after school I asked my mom if we could go to the nearest skate shop, and she said yes. When we got to the shop I was looking around, confused by decks, wheels, and so much more that I didn’t even know about. The guy working there asked, “Is there something specific you are looking for?” I told him I was new to skateboarding and had never been on a board, so he taught me about the deck, grip tape, trucks, wheels, and hardware. After that we assembled my first ever skateboard. Once I was done picking out all the parts, we paid, and he started assembling it. When he finished we left the shop; it was too dark, so I didn’t get to skate that day, sadly.  

The next day I got home from school, put down my backpack, and immediately went outside to try my new skateboard. The only thing I knew was how to ride, but I immediately fell in love with skating. Since that day I’ve been skating every day, and if it’s not every day, it’s every other day.

Skateboarding is the talent I cherish most among the many abilities I have. Mastering a trick can demand countless hours, days, even years of practice, which is why the sport feels so special and demanding. It has become part of my everyday routine, wiping away stress and worries, so I love spending time on a board. I ride to the store, a friend’s house, and sometimes even to school. Although I often end up with scrapes, bruises and other minor injuries, I remain passionate about skateboarding because it has taught me valuable lessons: confidence when trying something new, the resilience to get up after a fall, and the habit of learning from mistakes. 

For me, skateboarding is more than a hobby or a sport; it is a lifestyle. Even if it isn’t the safest activity, it remains one of my favorite skills and I doubt I will ever tire of it. When I was nine, many of my friends already skateboarded, and I was fascinated watching them glide around. Their constant practice and the way they moved sparked my curiosity, and eventually I decided to give it a try. I approached my parents and said I wanted to try skateboarding. My mother hesitated, worried about possible injuries, but my father encouraged me to go for it, so I did. 

The following afternoon I asked my mom to take me to the nearest skate shop, and she agreed. Inside, I was overwhelmed by decks, wheels, trucks and all the parts I had never heard of. An employee noticed my confusion and asked what I was looking for. I explained I was a complete beginner, and he patiently described each component—deck, grip tape, trucks, wheels, and hardware—and helped me assemble my first board. After we finished, we paid and left, but it was already dark, so I couldn’t ride that night. 

The next day, as soon as I got home from school, I dropped my backpack and rushed outside to test my new skateboard. All I knew was how to ride, yet I instantly fell in love with the feeling of skating. Since that moment I have been on my board almost every day, or at least every other day, and the passion has only grown stronger.

When failure appears on the path to achievement it can provide three crucial benefits: motivation, insight for improvement, and valuable experience. None of these has to be negative.

First, failure often sparks the drive that people need to keep moving forward. A student who fails an exam learns that she must rise, study again and try once more. Would she simply quit after a single disappointment? Most successful individuals understand that aiming high inevitably brings occasional defeats, and they use those moments as fuel for further effort. Consider a pupil who spends the night preparing for a test, feels confident, but receives a poor grade. The chance to retake the exam gives her a new reason to work harder, showing that a setback does not mean the goal is unattainable—it merely signals that more effort is required.

Second, failure forces us to reflect on what went wrong and how we can do better. The old adage “you learn from your mistakes” is especially true in this context. If a mistake repeats itself, it signals that we have not yet understood the underlying problem. By analysing the failure we discover where adjustments are needed, and those adjustments bring us closer to success. Many people who have reached their goals recount that at least one failure was essential for their eventual triumph.

Finally, experiencing failure gives us practical knowledge that we could not obtain otherwise. Each setback adds to a personal repertoire of coping strategies and problem‑solving skills. When success finally arrives, the story includes the obstacles that were overcome, and sharing that narrative can inspire others who are tempted to give up. Knowing that failure was part of the journey reassures both the storyteller and the listeners that setbacks do not preclude future success.

In summary, failure can be a powerful ally on the road to achievement if we treat it correctly. Rather than surrendering, we should harness it as a source of motivation, a catalyst for improvement, and a source of experience. In this light, failure is not something to fear but a useful step toward the goals we pursue.

I believe that switching to a year‑round school calendar would be beneficial. One of the main reasons is that many students forget a great deal of what they learned during the long summer break. If students can keep earlier lessons fresh in their minds, teachers would not have to spend as much time reteaching old content. This would free up class time for new topics in subjects such as mathematics, history or English. The extra contact hours mean that concepts can be practiced repeatedly, making them stick. When students receive regular help and practice during class, they become more confident when it comes time for tests or assignments.

Students who work in hot areas find simple tasks more difficult than those who work in milder climates, because heat makes it hard to focus.

Students look forward to this season for their holidays because it is perfect for going to the beach with family and friends or traveling abroad; we do not miss any school days. A trip can take a long time, and students think summer is the ideal period for it. Some students also use this time to find a job; without school, they can focus more on earning money. Summer is known for its scorching weather, and schools traditionally use this period to give pupils a long break—almost two months of holiday. Some teachers argue that the break is excessively long and suggest moving to a year‑round school model, where the summer vacation would be reduced to one month and the winter break extended. I disagree with this idea because the extreme heat of summer makes attending school uncomfortable, and the holiday gives students valuable time to travel with family and friends.

The temperature during summer can reach 96 °C or higher in some places, which is far too hot for effective learning. Such heat often leaves students irritable, causes headaches, and can lower concentration in class. When the streets are sweltering, many pupils perform worse academically and become more prone to frustration. Likewise, children who have to work in very hot environments find even simple tasks harder than those in milder conditions. In short, the heat makes it difficult to focus on schoolwork.

The long summer break also provides an important opportunity for families to plan trips and enjoy leisure activities together. Many families reserve this time for major vacations, especially trips to the beach or abroad, because there are no school days to miss. The two‑month interval gives students ample time to travel, explore new places, and relax. Additionally, some students use the break to find summer jobs; without school commitments, they can concentrate on earning money. Thus, the holiday is essential both for recreation and for gaining work experience.

In conclusion, the extreme heat of summer makes attending school undesirable, while the extended break offers students a chance to travel, spend time with family, and earn money. For these reasons, the government should keep the traditional summer holiday rather than cutting it short. This period is a well‑deserved pause after a year of hard work, allowing students to relax and recharge before the next academic year begins.

Today in English class my friends argued that first impressions are almost impossible to change. I disagreed, believing that a person's behaviour at any moment can be influenced by many factors, and that people are not always treated the same way. When someone explained this to me, I thanked them for the insight.

First, a person may be going through a difficult period and therefore behave in a way that leaves a poor first impression. Imagine someone who has just moved far away from friends and family, or who has suffered a loss in the family. I have experienced this repeatedly because my parents’ jobs force us to relocate almost every year. Each move made me feel upset and reluctant to attend school; I only wanted to have fun and felt insecure about leaving the friends I had made. This year we might have to move again in January, and the thought worries me because at my current school the teachers are supportive, the staff help with any problem, and the classmates treat me well. Losing that environment would be a huge blow, showing how temporary circumstances can shape how we appear to others.

Second, people are not always treated equally, and this can affect the impression they give. Once I went to a party expecting to meet a group of friends, but when I arrived they ignored me. A girl later told me they had heard a rumor about me that I hadn’t done anything to cause. I clarified the misunderstanding, even mentioning that I have a twin sister whose personality is the opposite of mine, and the tension disappeared. We spent the rest of the night together, proving that a single moment of miscommunication can create a false first impression.

Finally, a classmate pointed out that some children behave differently because of personal challenges. A boy he knew could be friendly one moment and suddenly angry the next, not because he wanted to be rude but because he struggled to control his emotions due to a condition. Teachers who understood his situation explained it to others, which helped the class treat him more fairly.

All these examples show that first impressions are far from fixed. People make mistakes, circumstances change, and misunderstandings happen. Because of this, we should give others a chance to show who they really are. Thank you for listening.
