It is a pleasure to share my thoughts on this topic, and I am grateful for the chance to do so. Although I recognize that life is short and unpredictable, the question of whether first impressions are almost impossible to change is one I can answer confidently: I disagree. Based on my own experiences, I believe that an initial judgment can indeed be altered, although it does not happen instantly.

First, many people claim that the first impression you make is crucial. There may be some truth to this idea, especially for individuals who care a great deal about how others see them. However, the significance of that early judgment depends largely on who is involved. For example, if you meet a boy you like, you may want him to have a positive view of you at first. Yet, if the situation changes—if you spend more time together—both of you have the opportunity to revise those early opinions. The first impression may last only a few seconds, but it can evolve as more information becomes available.

Second, we often judge others by their appearance or facial expression. This can lead to mistaken conclusions. A year ago I spoke with a woman who seemed angry at the start of our conversation; her facial expression suggested irritation. In reality, she was not angry at all, and as we continued talking, my initial perception vanished and was replaced by a completely different understanding of her character.

Time and communication play a vital role in shaping our views. While some impressions may fade quickly, others linger and can be reshaped as we learn more about a person. The first impression does not have to be permanent; it can be updated or even forgotten as we gain new experiences.

In summary, I think the possibility of changing a first impression is real. Although the initial perception may stay in memory, it does not prevent us from forming a new, more accurate opinion later on. We always have the chance to adjust our judgments, and that flexibility is essential in human relationships. Thank you for reading.

Many people assume that to influence someone you must set an example, but I believe influence can arise from many sources—online media, spoken words, friends, or family. I disagree with Albert Schweitzer’s claim that “example is not the main thing in influencing others; it is the only thing.”

First, an example is not the sole means of influence. Imagine attending a party where several under‑21 guests are drinking alcohol. I do not need to know them personally for their behavior to affect me; the mere fact that others are drinking creates pressure to join in, even without any role‑modeling intention.

Second, mass media can sway opinions and actions without any personal example. Television commercials, for instance, persuade viewers to purchase products they rarely use. People often do not consider the cost or necessity of these items, and after buying them they quickly forget about the purchase.

Nevertheless, some argue that only exemplary behavior can influence. In my own life, my mother serves as a role model. When she makes a mistake, I do not automatically repeat it; I recognize that being a good example is valuable, provided the negative actions are not imitated.

In sum, influence operates through a variety of channels, not just through personal example. Whether we influence others or are influenced ourselves, many factors beyond simple role‑modeling are at work.

I think I understand why Thomas Jefferson wrote his famous words for the American people. He wanted to test whether citizens could take responsibility for their own actions instead of wasting time on trivial matters, and he hoped his ideas would help them achieve their dreams. At the time the nation was still haunted by the legacy of slavery, which made many people fearful.

Abraham Lincoln later became president of the United States, and his leadership illustrates three reasons behind Jefferson’s message.

First, Jefferson devoted his effort to examining how closely his citizens followed his advice. Too often people ignore what they are capable of, preferring to spend time with others instead of pursuing their own ambitions. Many feel shy or frightened to follow their dreams because they worry about criticism or doubt from others. Some never succeed simply because they never try. If they made the effort, they could turn their aspirations into reality.

Second, a careful reading of Jefferson’s writing reveals a deeper lesson about commitment. Without personal dedication, we cannot improve our futures. Some students attend school only because their parents send them, yet they fail to see the opportunities education provides for future success. By reflecting on Jefferson’s words, we can learn the value of hard work and understand that studying well and aiming for good grades are essential steps toward fulfilling our goals.

Third, today we enjoy more freedom and leisure time than ever before, but many choose to spend it partying with friends rather than focusing on their ambitions. If we keep repeating this pattern, we will never make meaningful progress in our own lives. Greater resolve is needed to identify what we truly want and to act on it.

In sum, youth gives us an advantage: we have the energy and potential to achieve great things. Colleagues might think, “He really messed up right away.” If they are willing to give you another chance, you can demonstrate a different, more competent side and change their opinion: “Wow, he’s completely different now.” Providing the chance to reshape first impressions benefits everyone.

In summary, giving people the chance to amend their first impressions allows them to reveal who they really are and helps others see beyond an initial mistake.

If students were given the chance to visit a restaurant like this, they could see firsthand what happens to people who have little education or who do not take their studies seriously. That is why I would choose a job that does not pay much as a field trip destination – to show students the consequences of neglecting school.

Seeing a workplace where employees work quickly and hard every day for only a small salary might change students’ attitudes toward “goofing off” in class. They would realise that they do not want to end up in a job that pays so little, which could motivate them to concentrate more on their studies and aim for a better future.

Many parents cannot afford to keep their children in school, and as a result their children may have to take low‑paid, demanding jobs. Students who have the opportunity to receive an education should recognise this advantage and use it to secure a well‑paid, stable career. Conversely, teenagers who abandon their education are more likely to end up in positions that offer only minimal pay.

If learners treat their education casually, the money their parents have spent on schooling is wasted. Lack of effort means they gain no knowledge, and they will struggle to find a good job later on. By visiting a place like McDonald’s, students can see the stark difference between a life of hard work for little pay and the possibilities that come from taking school seriously. A solid education can lead to a well‑paid, successful career, while neglecting school leads nowhere.

Therefore, I would write to McDonald’s asking them to allow a school visit. I want students to observe what happens when people work hard for little money, and to understand that by valuing their education they can avoid ending up in such a job. Hopefully, this experience will encourage them to pay attention in class and pursue better opportunities in the future.

People often debate whether technology has a positive or negative impact on our lives. Some argue that it allows us to finish many tasks without interacting with others, while others claim it reduces face‑to‑face contact. I believe that the advantages of technology far outweigh its drawbacks and that it is a great help in everyday life.

In today’s busy world we have many responsibilities. Teenagers, for example, face a heavy load of homework and many also have part‑time jobs after school, leaving little free time in the evenings. Technology makes these demands easier to manage. Without digital tools, a simple assignment might require a trip to the library to find pictures, historical data or coloured materials, which would cost both time and money. With the internet and various apps, we can obtain the same resources instantly, saving both effort and expense.

Critics point out that technology can harm personal relationships. They note that families often sit together at the dinner table while each member scrolls on a cellphone, weakening their bond. Nevertheless, technology also provides essential ways to stay connected. It enables us to keep in touch with friends and relatives who live far away, and it helps us navigate unfamiliar places using services like Google Maps. These benefits show that technology can support, rather than replace, human interaction when used wisely.

I have experienced these benefits personally. My family lives in another country and my friends are scattered across different states. When I miss them, I can call or video‑chat, and we share birthdays and special moments as if we were together. On my birthday, my relatives FaceTime me in the morning, and I do the same for my grandmother’s birthday. The same tools also help my mother find my father’s workplace each day, making the daily commute much smoother.

Overall, technology is a valuable aid when applied correctly. In fields such as medicine, science and engineering, sophisticated equipment has led to cures for many illnesses and advancements in knowledge. These examples further illustrate how technology improves our quality of life.

In conclusion, technology brings mostly positive effects to our lives. It helps us stay close to loved ones who are far away, simplifies everyday tasks, and supports progress in many areas. How we choose to use it determines its impact, and when we use it responsibly, it becomes an indispensable ally.

Statements like “If you don’t do this, I’m not your friend anymore,” “You don’t love me if you don’t,” or “If you don’t drink with me, I’ll tell everyone your secrets,” make students fear losing friends or partners and compel them to act against their own best interests. High‑school teachers are tough on students; however, some students do not care about their education and attend school only to chat with friends or distract others, affecting overall learning. Energetic students who constantly get into trouble, distract peers, and act as a bad influence could be referred or suspended, but recommending homeschooling might avoid many problems.

Saving money for college or the future while holding a job is a good idea. Yet studying or doing homework while working is difficult; students become stressed and frustrated trying to attend both school and a job. Schools waste time on lunch or other activities that could be used for work; at home, students can finish assignments within a few hours and attend to other responsibilities. At home, they can take their time and avoid rushing through assignments or tests, reducing stress over school work. Waking up early is hard for most students; lack of sleep can affect grades, concentration, cause falling asleep in class, lead to inattention, constant fatigue, or skipping classes, all of which impact graduation.

In conclusion, the opportunity to homeschool can make a significant, positive difference for schools and student education. It offers an easy way to learn the same material as other students, but more conveniently. The Internet provides many apps that make learning fun, unlike sitting in a classroom for two hours. Students can avoid disruptive peers who do not care about their own lives or others’ education. Attending school is no longer considered essential by some teenagers; any student can now take a class online.

Distance learning can be a useful option for many students. With the internet, learners can attend classes online and stay in touch with teachers without having to be physically present in a school building. They can acquire the same knowledge from home, often with greater convenience. One of the biggest advantages is that online schooling can help avoid the bullying that is common in traditional classrooms. Teenagers sometimes pressure each other to drink, smoke, or even use drugs, and eliminating face‑to‑face contact can reduce these negative influences. Many pupils also have responsibilities after school, such as caring for younger siblings, working a part‑time job, or taking extra courses, and distance learning makes it easier to balance these duties.

Even though teachers try to prevent bullying, it is difficult to guarantee that every student behaves appropriately; some ignore rules, some are lazy, and some simply do not listen. Many young people face hard lives for various reasons—parents who do not pay attention, overwhelming school workload, or the pressure of a job in addition to bullying. Such stress can lead to severe outcomes, including suicide, when students feel ignored and unsupported. Occasionally teachers recognize bullying but fail to act, thinking that dealing with the problem at school is easier than involving parents or taking stronger measures. Some teenagers do not understand that their actions—mocking, hitting, or pressuring peers—can have serious legal consequences, even leading to imprisonment, and can ruin lives.

Peer pressure can also push students toward harmful habits that affect their future health and freedom. Nowadays it is often seen as “cool” to drink, smoke, or use drugs, and friends may threaten to end the relationship or reveal secrets if a pupil refuses. This fear of losing friendships can force young people into behaviors that offer no benefit and may cause lasting damage. While high‑school teachers are generally strict, many students are indifferent to their education, using school time to chat with friends or distract others, which harms the learning environment. Energetic students who constantly cause trouble can be a bad influence; rather than only giving them referrals or suspensions, allowing them to study from home could prevent further issues.

Saving money for college and holding a job are important goals, yet juggling work and school creates stress and frustration. Some school activities, such as long lunches, take up time that could be used for homework, while at home students can complete assignments quickly and attend to other responsibilities. Working from home reduces the rush to finish tasks or prepare for tests, lowering anxiety about schoolwork. Waking up early is a challenge for most teenagers; insufficient sleep negatively impacts grades, concentration, and attendance, and can hinder graduation.

In summary, offering the possibility of homeschooling or online classes can significantly improve education for many students. It provides an easy way to learn the same material as classmates, often more comfortably. The internet gives access to many educational apps that make learning enjoyable without spending hours in a traditional classroom. Distance learning also helps avoid the influence of disengaged or disruptive peers, allowing students who do not value school to pursue their studies online instead.

Most students enjoy summer vacation, but some educators feel that the summer break is too long; when students return in the fall, they become lazier and have more difficulty retaining information.

Summer break is the only long break that schools give students to do things they couldn’t accomplish during the school year, and it allows them to rest for an extended period. I don't agree for these reasons:

First, many students want to work or pursue other activities that require more time, but they cannot because they have too much homework or need to study for tests that week. In summer break they have three months to work and do the things they couldn’t during the school year. This extra time lets students gain experience that can help them when they apply for better jobs and learn new skills.

Next, students need a break after the school year. Most students feel stressed from the workload and tests teachers assign; their brains need to relax because constant work leads to fatigue. Summer break is the best time to rest and unwind. Students can go to the beach, enjoy more time with their families, hang out with friends, visit new places, and take advantage of the pleasant weather.

Finally, during summer break students do not have to worry about assignments or tests that might be due when the break ends. When they have fall, winter, or spring breaks, schools give only one week, and teachers often assign work and tests to be completed after the break. Consequently, those short breaks feel more like study periods rather than true rests. In summer, students can truly relax and enjoy the time they have.

Some people may disagree, thinking that more breaks during the school year are better for students. However, they need to recognize that students receive assignments and must study for tests during those breaks, so they do not get the restorative time their brains need.

In conclusion, summer break is the only long period that students have to relax, and it allows them to do many things they cannot accomplish during the school year because of heavy workloads and test preparation. Therefore, summer break should remain as it is; it is the best season for students to enjoy and have fun during a long break.

Most students look forward to the long summer vacation, and I believe it should remain unchanged. Critics claim that the break is too lengthy and that pupils become lazy or forgetful when school resumes, but the advantages of a three‑month holiday outweigh those concerns.

First, many teenagers want to earn money or gain experience during the year, yet they are often trapped by heavy homework loads and upcoming exams. A three‑month pause gives them the time they need to take a job, volunteer, or learn new skills that would be impossible during the regular school term. Such experiences improve their résumés and broaden their horizons, helping them when they later apply for better positions.

Second, a continuous school year is exhausting. Constant assignments and tests place a great deal of stress on young minds, and without a substantial rest period they risk burnout. Summer provides the perfect opportunity for relaxation: students can visit the beach, travel with family, meet friends, or simply unwind in pleasant weather. This mental break restores energy and prepares them for the challenges of the new academic year.

Finally, unlike the short autumn, winter or spring breaks, which last only a week, summer offers a true pause from schoolwork. During those brief holidays teachers usually assign projects and prepare exams that must be completed after the break, leaving students with little genuine downtime. In contrast, the long summer holiday allows pupils to forget about assignments and tests completely, giving their brains a chance to recover fully.

Some people argue that more frequent, shorter breaks during the school year would be better. However, those interruptions still come with homework and test preparation, so students never get a real period of rest. Only a lengthy summer vacation can provide the uninterrupted relaxation they need.

In summary, the summer break is the sole extended interval that lets students recover from the pressures of the school year and engage in activities they otherwise could not. Keeping the long summer holiday is essential for their well‑being and personal development.

If the school cafeteria were to change its menu, many children would probably be disappointed because they are used to eating the tasty foods they love. However, just because something tastes good does not mean it is good for their health.

The United States is known for its high consumption of fast food, and this diet contributes to a large number of deaths linked to high cholesterol. Nowadays, modern technology encourages a sedentary lifestyle: we drive everywhere instead of walking, we send text messages instead of speaking face‑to‑face, we check the weather on our phones rather than looking out the window, and we can watch movies at home on Netflix, Hulu, Disney+ or other apps. All of these conveniences make people lazier and, consequently, heavier, leading to health problems such as heart attacks and high cholesterol.

If nothing changes, the situation will only get worse for future generations. One way to help schoolchildren develop better habits is to teach them that there are alternatives to fast food—healthy options that can be just as tasty, even better. Foods like avocado, fresh fruit juice, Caesar salad, fish and other nutritious choices can provide the balance their bodies need while satisfying their cravings.

The school menu itself can be a practical tool for this education. By offering dishes that students have never tried before and that contain less fat than pizza, the cafeteria can introduce them to a wider variety of flavors. When these children grow up, they will be less likely to seek only hamburgers, Chinese takeout, or chicken wings; they will know there are many other foods that support their health.

Learning these habits now is essential, because establishing them later becomes much more difficult. As a member of the school community, I care about my own future and that of my classmates. Failure is an inevitable part of life. Although we often label it as something negative, it is actually a vital ingredient of success because it prepares us for tougher challenges. If we never make mistakes, how can we improve? Errors teach us valuable lessons, build resilience, and remind us that nothing worthwhile comes easily. The more effort we invest in our goals, the more we will encounter setbacks, but those setbacks are simply stepping stones toward progress.

Often we need to try different approaches to solve a problem, and failure shows us which paths are not worth pursuing. When we fall short, we learn what to avoid and discover new possibilities. For example, when I first started playing soccer I could only kick the ball in one way, so I missed many chances. Instead of quitting, I experimented with various foot positions, adjusting my strike for power or precision. Those repeated failures revealed that there are many techniques, not just a single “right” way, and helped me become a better player.

Failure also hardens us emotionally. Each time we are knocked down and manage to get back up, we emerge as a more determined person—someone who does not surrender because of a simple error, someone who, when everything seems lost, returns with greater confidence and a commitment not to repeat the same mistake. The adversity reshapes us into a tougher version of ourselves.

Thomas Edison was once asked how it felt to fail a hundred times while inventing the light bulb. He replied that he had not failed; he had simply taken a hundred steps toward his goal. His attitude shows that persistence turns apparent failures into progress.

In sum, mistakes and setbacks teach us important lessons, provide alternative routes to our objectives, and strengthen us beyond our former selves. People should not fear failure; they should embrace it, because when they finally achieve their goals, the satisfaction will be all the more intense.

The first impressions are almost impossible to change because when people meet a new person, their only information is what he or she looks like; therefore, it is hard to alter those initial judgments, and people do not often change them.  

Firstly, people form first impressions and guess who the other person is because that is what humans do every time they meet someone new. For example, a student meets a new person who does not have a healthy-looking body and assumes the boy cannot play any sports, yet the boy turns out to be the best player on the team. However, some people can change a first impression by building a good relationship with the person they meet. For example, a man who is large and has an angry face scares everyone away, but a student who approaches him discovers that he is pleasant to talk to. Sometimes people can modify their first impression, which makes the other person feel better and allows easier conversation.  

In addition, a first impression can be altered by showing a clear change from past behavior. For example, a student who has been mean to friends realizes that this is wrong and begins to act kindly, helping others instead of being mean. The friends then revise their first impression of him, which makes both parties happier and fosters a stronger friendship.  

In spite of these issues, it is still almost impossible to change first impressions, so everyone should not focus on them too much.

First impressions are extremely hard to alter because when we meet someone for the first time we only have limited information – mainly their appearance – and that initial judgment tends to stick.

People automatically form an opinion based on what they see. For instance, a student meets a boy who looks thin and unfit and immediately assumes he cannot play sports. Later the boy proves himself to be the best player on the team, yet the student still finds it difficult to discard the original image of someone who looks unhealthy and unathletic.

Another reason first impressions persist is that they become a personal belief that individuals are reluctant to give up. Imagine a man who is very shy and avoids conversation; people conclude that he does not want to talk and therefore keep their distance. Even if he later opens up with friends and shows he enjoys chatting, the initial perception of shyness remains, making it hard for others to approach him.

Nevertheless, occasional changes are possible when a person builds a genuine relationship with someone who gives them a chance. A large man with an angry expression might frighten everyone, but a student who decides to talk to him discovers a friendly and pleasant personality. In such cases the new interaction can soften the original impression and make future communication easier.

Similarly, showing a clear change in behavior can modify how we are viewed. A student who used to be mean to classmates may realize the harm of that attitude and start acting kindly and helpfully. As friends notice this transformation, their first impression of him shifts, leading to happier and stronger friendships.

Even with these exceptions, altering first impressions remains largely unattainable. Therefore, we should not place too much importance on them.

Ralph Waldo Emerson once said, “To be yourself in a world that is constantly trying to make you something else is the greatest accomplishment.” I share his view: staying true to who you are, and refusing to let others reshape you, is indeed a remarkable achievement. Nobody should allow outside pressure to dictate their identity.

Being authentic is the key to real success because many people will try to persuade you to follow a path that does not suit you. You must take the time to discover what you truly want to achieve in life and ignore the opinions of those who do not understand your goals. Often, well‑meaning advice can be misguided, so trusting your own judgment is essential. When you believe in yourself, you are more likely to accomplish great things by pursuing what you love.

Make decisions that feel right for you, whether that means working alone or seeking guidance from others. Frequently, people are skeptical of others’ choices, but a strong conviction that staying true to yourself is the best route shows that you are comfortable with your own company. If you are confident that you will succeed, that confidence itself becomes a powerful motivator. Follow the path you consider correct and do not let anyone force you into actions you deem wrong.

Of course, there are situations where allowing some change can be beneficial, especially when it leads to improvement. For instance, if someone repeatedly breaks the law or behaves irresponsibly, offering constructive criticism can help them make better choices. Similarly, helping a friend who is struggling by giving sound advice can steer them toward success.

In the end, being yourself paves the way for genuine accomplishment. I stand by Emerson’s statement: many try to alter us because they doubt our ability to succeed, but staying true to our own vision remains the most reliable route to achieving our goals.

Some schools are thinking about offering distance learning so that pupils can take lessons from home, either through live streams or recorded videos. While a number of learners might see advantages in this approach, I believe that teaching students remotely is not a good idea.

First, studying at home creates many opportunities for distraction. Young people are easily drawn to the kitchen, where food can take their attention away from the lesson. The television is another lure; a sudden program can pull them out of the learning flow. Perhaps the most constant source of interruption is the mobile phone, and when there is no adult present to enforce limits, students are likely to spend a lot of time checking messages or browsing the internet instead of focusing on the class.

Second, the home environment makes it harder for learners to take the work seriously. In a familiar setting they tend to feel more relaxed and may skip lessons or not put in full effort because nobody is there to remind them of their responsibilities. In a classroom, teachers set clear rules, provide examples, give immediate feedback and keep the pace steady. These structures help pupils stay motivated and understand the material better.

Third, remote instruction reduces the chances for interaction. When students cannot raise their hand and ask questions face‑to‑face, they miss out on prompt explanations and the personal guidance that teachers normally provide. Consequently, the amount of learning they achieve is usually lower than what they would obtain in a traditional classroom.

Supporters of distance learning point out that it saves commuting time and can continue even when weather conditions make travel unsafe. It also helps those who do not have reliable transport, allowing them to attend lessons without paying for a ride or walking long distances. These benefits are certainly worth noting.

Nevertheless, the drawbacks outweigh the positives. At home a learner can be surrounded by noise, family members, or the temptation to fall asleep while watching a video lecture without anyone to keep them engaged. Without the presence of a teacher, the level of instruction, attention and support is greatly diminished.

In conclusion, while online classes may appear convenient, I remain opposed to replacing classroom teaching with distance learning. The distractions, lack of discipline, and reduced interaction make home‑based study less effective. Students learn best when they are physically present in school, where teachers can guide them, maintain order and provide the support necessary for future success.

Technology enables us to accomplish countless tasks without ever meeting another person. We can borrow books, shop for groceries, or play video games without speaking to anyone in person. But this reduction in face‑to‑face interaction has brought more harm than good to our lives.

The decline of direct communication threatens the fabric of society. As smartphones become ever more advanced, the risk that they will dominate human relationships grows. Imagine a boy and a girl who only know each other through social‑media messages. When they finally decide to meet, the encounter is initially uncomfortable, yet it soon leads to a genuine friendship that blossoms into a deeper relationship. They start going to the cinema, the mall, restaurants, and eventually become a couple. This story is touching because it shows that real connections are possible, but it also highlights how awkward and difficult it is to move from a screen‑based interaction to a genuine personal bond.

Confessing love through a screen may feel easier, but it raises the question of sincerity. Saying “I love you” repeatedly can be comforting, yet delivering such feelings in person carries far more weight. Likewise, ending a relationship through a text message suggests a lack of courage to face someone directly. People who rely solely on their devices miss out on the richness of direct human contact and should at least try to engage face‑to‑face to discover what life truly offers beyond a screen.

Eventually, people may become so fed up with the intrusion of technology that they destroy their phones to avoid becoming “robotic” victims. By uniting against the obsession with electronic gadgets, we can reclaim meaningful interaction. Opening up to another person is like a flower ready to bloom; seeing someone you care about in real life is a delight that no digital message can replace.

In short, the growing reliance on technology to avoid personal contact is a negative development for humanity. We must recognize this danger and work together to restore genuine, face‑to‑face communication before our society is lost to the screens.

Some people believe students will benefit from being able to attend classes from home; however, homeschooling is a great way for students to study because they can focus, it is safer, and they can avoid bad influences from others.

Attending classes through online or video conferencing has many benefits, as mentioned in the first paragraph: homeschooling can help students concentrate on their studies. For some reasons, students who go to a traditional school can’t focus because they are distracted by a naughty classmate. For instance, some people are so disruptive that, even if you confront them, they won’t listen, and sometimes other students become proud and walk out of class rather than accept any objection to their behavior. Another reason for homeschooling is that it is safer. In today’s society many bad things happen, such as school shootings that cause innocent students to die—as in the recent incident in Florida. A further reason for homeschooling is that students can avoid negative influences. Some schools are ethnically diverse, and student behavior varies widely: some like to go to malls, stroll around, bully others, fight, or stay after school at houses they barely know, among many other traits.

Although students enjoy benefits from attending classes at school, homeschooling offers even more advantages. Attending classes from home via online or video conferencing benefits students because they are safer, can focus better on their studies, and can avoid negative influences from others.

Many people think that studying from home can be advantageous, and indeed homeschooling—whether through online platforms or video‑conferencing—offers several important benefits. Learners can concentrate better on their lessons, enjoy a safer environment, and stay away from negative influences that may arise in a traditional classroom.

One major advantage of remote learning is the ability to focus without the usual distractions found in a physical school. In many classrooms, noisy or mischievous classmates can break a student’s concentration and make it difficult to keep up with the work. When lessons are delivered at home, learners can create a quiet, personalized study space that helps them stay on task and absorb the material more effectively.

Safety is another compelling reason to choose homeschooling. Recent events, such as the tragic school shootings that have occurred in places like Florida, have highlighted the vulnerability of students in large public schools. Studying at home eliminates the risk of being caught in such dangerous situations, giving both pupils and their families greater peace of mind.

Finally, learning from home reduces exposure to harmful peer pressure and undesirable behavior. In a diverse school setting, some students may be tempted to skip class, shop, bully, or engage in fights, and they might even spend time with strangers after school. By staying at home, learners are less likely to encounter these negative influences and can focus on their education in a controlled, supportive environment.

Overall, while traditional schools have their merits, the advantages of online or video‑based homeschooling—greater safety, improved concentration, and protection from detrimental peer influence—make it a compelling option for many students.

Technology enables people to carry out many activities without having to meet anyone in person. We can borrow books online, shop from home, and play video games without speaking to another person. Yet this development has both advantages and disadvantages. While some argue that technology is beneficial, especially in emergencies, many others feel that it can alter people’s attitudes and make virtual interactions more important than real‑world relationships.

Supporters of technology point out that it is essential in urgent situations. Imagine a family living in a remote area with no neighbours nearby; in such a case, the ability to call for help or obtain information can be a matter of life and death. In my own country, many families lived far from towns and lacked any means of communication. When someone fell ill, the absence of a phone or internet often meant that no one could reach them in time, and some people died simply because they could not get assistance. This illustrates how vital technology can be when immediate help is required.

On the other hand, many people believe that technology can negatively affect attitudes. In the past, for example in the late 1970s, people were generally more respectful toward one another, even if they did not have formal education. Today, some argue that media such as movies, music, novels and cartoons shape behaviour, but the constant use of electronic devices can also lead to mental health problems and even physical issues like eye strain. I know a family with a fifteen‑year‑old girl who watches countless TV shows. She behaves as if she were older than her peers, disregarding her parents’ rules and acting poorly. Her parents blame her on their own willingness to buy endless gadgets without supervising how she uses them. Allowing children to spend too much time with technology at a young age can make it difficult for parents to guide them later, as the bad habits are already formed. Instead, parents could spend more time interacting with their children rather than relying on screens.

Furthermore, many argue that technology puts virtual contacts ahead of real people. A large number of individuals stare at screens for most of the day, which can reduce face‑to‑face communication. As the psychologist Dr. Generic_Name notes, “It is better to have conversations in person because people can understand situations more clearly.” When we communicate through devices, it is easier to hide behind anonymity and lie. For instance, I recently read a novel called *Behind the Web* in which a teacher converses with someone she believes to be a man, only to discover later that the person was a woman pretending to be a man. This deception happened through messages, highlighting how online interactions can be misleading. Such examples are common in everyday life.

In conclusion, technology can be either helpful or harmful, depending on how it is used. It continues to develop rapidly, so people must learn to employ it at the right times and in the right way. When used wisely, technology can improve lives; when misused, it can damage relationships and attitudes.

I agree with Ralph Waldo Emerson that many people are content with the situation they find themselves in, but it is always worthwhile to step out of that comfort zone and try new things. Without exploration we can never discover what we are capable of, and we miss the chance to grow. It is fine to be satisfied for a while, yet when a real challenge appears we must push forward to see who we truly are. Emerson is right, especially in my own community where many people settle for the status they have reached.

The more we explore, the more we develop. Take Bill Gates, for instance: had he been satisfied with what he already knew and never ventured beyond his early ideas, he would never have built Microsoft or become a billionaire. Likewise, if Barack Obama had been happy with the education he already possessed, he might never have become a senator, let alone the first African‑American president of the United States, and his vision would not have reached the nation. These examples show that staying within the limits of what we have mastered prevents us from learning who we really are and what we can achieve. When we push beyond familiar ground, we often uncover hidden talents and new opportunities. Without trying, we never discover our true worth.

Some people believe that venturing out will only lead to failure, but the opposite is true: the more we explore, the farther we advance. We should always pray to move to a higher level rather than remain at the one we have already mastered. My mother always told me, “Never be satisfied where you are; step out of your comfort zone and explore.” Only then can we truly understand ourselves.

Consider a workplace scenario: a manager leaves and a vacancy opens, and you have the knowledge and ideas needed for the role. If you stay where you are out of fear of rejection, you miss the chance to grow. In academia, many students are comfortable with a master’s degree and are afraid to pursue a doctorate, thinking the master’s is the end of learning and doubting their own ability. Certain environments can make people content with the status quo.

Being happy with your current situation is not inherently bad, but increased exploration leads to greater personal development. We should never settle completely; we must keep striving for a better future and a richer life. As Neil Armstrong famously said, “one small step for man, one giant leap for mankind.” Some of us need to take that giant leap in our own lives. The more we explore, the more we learn about ourselves and the paths that lie ahead.

It would also help students who had a bad experience at school. Students who were bullied can lose the will to study and be successful in life. Bullying even nowadays still has a huge impact on why some schools do not meet high standards, and it shows that students are highly affected by it. For some students it is a nightmare, but online classes would pull them away from that environment and allow them to focus on their studies.

Furthermore, students who are in their comfort zone will likely be able to focus and not have any distraction. Being in a comfortable learning zone will highly benefit them and allow them to show their potential. Being in the right environment also helps students focus. Students who are really serious about being successful and have high standards are more likely to succeed. Family can also motivate them to keep pushing, even though it might be hard; having family by their side can really encourage perseverance.

Therefore, I really believe that students should have the option to take online classes or video conferencing. By just having that option, it would benefit many students who have problems socializing with other students or teachers, help those who had a bad experience in school, and benefit students who are in their comfort zone. Giving them this chance would increase the likelihood that more students will be successful.

Offering distance learning—through online platforms or video‑conferencing—can be a valuable alternative for many pupils. It especially helps those who find it difficult to interact with classmates and teachers, or who have had negative experiences in a traditional school setting. When students can study from a place where they feel comfortable, they are more likely to concentrate and avoid unnecessary distractions.

Critics often claim that learning from home leads to more interruptions and a lack of discipline, suggesting that students will not complete their tasks or will miss out on the social aspects of school life. While these concerns are understandable, they overlook the fact that many learners actually thrive when they are not forced into a noisy, crowded classroom. For students who struggle with social anxiety or who have been bullied, the pressure of being in a physical school can be overwhelming and can diminish their motivation to succeed. By removing the need to face such stressful environments, online classes give these pupils a chance to focus on their education without fear of harassment.

Every child grows up with a unique background, and some have endured difficult childhoods that affect their behaviour and confidence at school. Providing an option to study remotely allows them to work in a familiar, supportive setting—often their own home—where they can demonstrate their true abilities. This flexibility can unlock potential that might otherwise remain hidden in a conventional classroom, where forced social interaction can become a distraction rather than a benefit.

Furthermore, when students are in their “comfort zone,” they tend to be more attentive and productive. A stable home environment, possibly reinforced by family encouragement, can boost perseverance and drive. Those who are serious about achieving high standards may find that the combination of personal comfort and familial support propels them toward greater academic success.

In conclusion, I strongly believe that schools should make distance learning an available choice. It can greatly assist students who struggle with social interaction, those who have suffered from bullying or other negative school experiences, and learners who simply perform better in a comfortable, familiar setting. By offering online or video‑based classes, we give many pupils the opportunity to reach their full potential and increase their chances of success.

How we act and behave defines our character, and I believe that each person can shape his or her own traits without being dictated by anyone else. Some people argue that character is molded by the people we interact with—especially parents—or that our personality is simply a reflection of others’ traits. I disagree.

The choice of who we become rests with us. When we fail to decide for ourselves, we may feel insecure and struggle to understand our identity or direction in life. Developing a personal character is therefore essential. Many individuals simply imitate the habits or attitudes of their parents or famous figures, but possessing a distinct character means being truly unique. Research conducted at the University of Virginia found that individuals who actively define their own behavior tend to report higher levels of happiness than those who merely copy someone else’s personality.

From the moment we are born we begin to build our character, and we retain control over the kind of person we want to become. Critics may claim that parents determine our personality by selecting certain traits for us, but this is inaccurate. Our character is forged through the experiences we encounter. As John Lubbock once observed, “Your character will be what you choose to make of it.”

In short, we have the power to become who we wish. Our character emerges from the choices we make and the lessons we learn, not from external forces. Although others may judge us, we should follow our own convictions, cherish our individuality, and refuse to let anyone—parents included—dictate how we act. By doing so, we create a character that truly reflects who we are.

Imagine a world washed in black and gray, where people drift through life weighed down by depression. Such a bleak picture could arise from the belief that tiny gestures of kindness are meaningless. In truth, even the smallest acts can ripple outward, transforming societies and even the entire planet.

One of the most straightforward ways to build a good reputation is simply by being kind to those around us. Kindness strengthens existing relationships and can spark new ones. Often, a brief compliment or a friendly word brightens someone’s day, and when we’re feeling low, the goodwill we have shown earlier tends to return to us. I have experienced this myself: a short, sincere compliment can lift someone’s spirits, and later, when I was visibly upset, others offered me kindness in return. Over time, people begin to notice you as the friendly person in the group, and they may seek you out for encouragement or simply enjoy being near a positive presence.

Kindness also has the power to improve communities and, by extension, the world. Though corruption and negativity are widespread, a single act of generosity can set off a chain reaction. When you treat someone kindly, they feel happier and are more likely to pass that feeling on to others. This creates a loop: more kindness leads to more kindness, spreading goodwill throughout the community. I saw this at my school when I made a conscious effort to be nicer to my classmates. Suddenly, I became more visible, and my peers started behaving more kindly as well, each hoping to be noticed themselves. In this way, everyone benefits.

Finally, a simple act of kindness can boost a person’s self‑esteem. As Aesop wrote, “No act of kindness, no matter how small, is ever wasted.” A genuine compliment can change someone’s entire day, and the positive effect spreads to the people around them because they witness that small moment of care. My own life bears witness to this truth: around eleven years old, I faced difficulties at school and at home, but friends who offered constant support turned that year around for me. Their kindness gave me hope that some relationships would last a lifetime. Extending such support to those struggling at home or school can redirect their lives toward greater happiness.

These examples demonstrate that, no matter how minor they seem, acts of kindness have the power to alter lives and even reshape the world.

In summary, while technology can reduce direct social contact, it also offers considerable benefits for our generation and for future societies.

Some schools now allow pupils to attend lessons from home by using online platforms or video‑conferencing. The idea is that this option helps students who cannot or do not want to be physically present at school, for example because of illness. While home learning shares some advantages with traditional schooling, it does not provide an overall benefit.

I believe that studying from home can be useful in certain situations, particularly for students with health problems, but it is not a complete solution because the quality of learning often suffers compared with face‑to‑face classes.

First, remote lessons are advantageous for pupils who have medical conditions that make commuting difficult. A child with arthritis, for instance, may be unable to walk to school, so taking classes online or via video calls allows them to continue their education and eventually obtain a diploma. The same applies to students whose parents keep them at home for personal reasons. In addition, pupils who experience bullying or frequent fights at school might feel safer learning from home, where they can still receive instruction with the support of a tutor or a digital classroom.

However, this arrangement is not beneficial for students who simply do not like school. Without the structure and supervision of a teacher, many learners may become undisciplined and fail to grasp the material. Language learners illustrate this problem well. As a non‑native English speaker, I find that being surrounded by classmates and teachers who constantly speak English speeds up my progress. At home I would only hear the language a few times a day, making it harder to improve. Interacting with peers also provides opportunities for practice and encouragement that are hard to replicate online. Personally, I notice that attending school, despite its challenges, helps me develop my language skills more effectively than studying alone at home.

In conclusion, studying from home is not an unqualified advantage. It can be helpful for students with particular health issues or difficult school situations, but for most learners it limits the amount and quality of instruction they receive. Whether a student learns at home or in a classroom, the important thing is that they keep learning, but traditional schools still offer the best environment for most people to grow academically and socially.

Many people believe that a positive attitude is the essential ingredient for success. It is often claimed that the right mindset is the best way to achieve one’s objectives, and I completely agree that maintaining optimism is crucial for a successful life.

A constructive outlook can greatly improve one’s chances of getting a job. Imagine two candidates facing an interview: the first answers questions with enthusiasm and confidence, while the second responds with a sour tone and negativity. The applicant who displays a positive attitude is far more likely to be hired, because a pleasant demeanor reveals the person’s true character.

Moreover, a positive attitude reflects one’s upbringing and the values taught by parents. When someone behaves rudely or disrespectfully, it suggests that they were not raised with proper manners. In contrast, courteous behavior indicates that the family emphasized respect and good conduct.

The same principle applies to education. A good attitude is perhaps the most important factor in learning, since nobody wants to teach a student who is hostile or indifferent. Showing eagerness and a willingness to engage during a lesson signals to the teacher that the student is putting in effort and is serious about succeeding.

Some people argue that attitude does not matter for success, pointing out that everyone has off‑days when a bad mood is hard to control. While it is true that emotions can fluctuate, the ability to choose a constructive approach remains within our control.

In conclusion, adopting a positive attitude helps individuals reach their goals because it demonstrates good character, proper upbringing, and a genuine commitment to learning. A hopeful mindset not only reflects the values instilled by one’s family but also shows a sincere desire to achieve higher education and personal growth.

Longer classes could give teachers more time to cover material in depth, and a shorter week might lower the school’s energy consumption and other operating costs. I would like to point out the advantages of collaborating in a group. In my view, teamwork makes tasks easier and more enjoyable because it allows students to share ideas and learn from one another, while also exposing them to different perspectives.

First of all, working together simplifies the work for students. Each member can take on a specific part of the assignment: one person conducts the research, another writes the text, and a third looks for graphs or other useful data. This division of labour not only speeds up the process but also creates a pleasant atmosphere, as classmates can chat, joke, and laugh at their mistakes while they cooperate.

Moreover, group work helps learners acquire knowledge beyond the subject itself. By exchanging thoughts and viewpoints, they gain insight into various angles of the problem. If one student is stuck on a question, another may know the answer, so the group can collectively solve difficulties that would be harder to tackle alone.

Finally, many students feel more comfortable in a supportive group setting. They can encourage one another and respect each other’s ideas, which leads to higher‑quality outcomes. Through discussion and the sharing of diverse opinions, the whole team benefits and gains a deeper understanding of the material.

In summary, collaborative learning offers several benefits: it makes tasks simpler, fosters richer learning, and promotes respectful dialogue, all of which lead to better results for the students involved.

The purpose of this essay is to examine the pros and cons of a four‑day school week in which each day lasts ten hours, a schedule some claim would save energy and resources.

As a pupil, I can see the appeal of a shorter week, but I do not support extending the school day by two extra hours. Most students already spend about eight hours at school, and many become fatigued after sitting in a classroom all day. In almost every class there is someone who nods off because they have a heavy homework load, a part‑time job, or sports commitments after school. Adding two more hours to an already long day simply makes it harder for these students to stay awake and concentrate, even if a three‑day weekend sounds attractive.

The argument that a four‑day week saves energy is also questionable. The additional two hours each day from Monday to Thursday total eight extra hours, which replace the five‑day schedule’s eighth hour. In other words, the total amount of time the building is heated, lit and ventilated remains the same, so any claimed energy savings are minimal.

Consider two personal examples. My friend Alex likes the idea because it gives him an extra day for homework and to spend time with his girlfriend, so it works well for him. My boyfriend Ben, however, disagrees. He plays basketball after school for two hours, then works four hours to help his mother with car insurance payments, and finally has to finish his assignments. The longer school day would leave him exhausted and short on sleep, a situation shared by many students who juggle work and family responsibilities.

Teachers’ opinions matter as well. They would also have to teach for ten straight hours, which is unrealistic; educators are not machines programmed by the government. Their fatigue would affect the quality of instruction, so they are unlikely to welcome this change.

For these reasons, my school should not adopt the ten‑hour, four‑day model. Any decision must consider the well‑being of students, teachers, and all staff members. What works for some businesses does not necessarily translate to a high‑school environment, where extracurricular activities and varied schedules create a different context. Until we have clear evidence that such a system would benefit the whole school community, it should be rejected.

While some people say this is a good thing, some people think it's bad for our lives because people stop interacting face‑to‑face in public, they don't want to get out of the place where technology is at, and some might have an aggressive behavior when they are told technology is bad for them.  

In the past people always met in the street; there was no technology that allowed us with a single ring to see our friends on a little screen and talk to them. Now this problem has become a bad thing in our society: people don't go outside to meet friends or just enjoy how the city looks, they prefer to stay at home and talk to people whose identities they do not know. Some of these people might say that there is no difference when they talk to a stranger online because we used to talk to strangers in the street; however, there is a risk when you talk to people online, since some use fake accounts to hack personal information and other things. When we used to meet strangers in the street, we saw how they behaved and what they were doing, and that is how people made friends in the past—by observing how they acted and behaved. Now the Internet is the key to making a friend, and we don't know if that friendship is real.  

When we were kids it was all fun to play outside: in the streets, going to a friend's house, or even going to the park with them. But now things have changed a lot since we were those kids who played in the streets. With new technology people have created video games, and they are now the popular thing among kids and teenagers. All we have to do is connect the device to the TV and play, but some people play the whole day and they don't want to go outside to play any sport or to a friend's house. When they go to school, the most common topic among every kid is video games, and that can affect their lives because playing all the time won't help anyone study for an important test or do their homework. In the past, when the first console was created, it was a wonderful thing, but some kids didn't have enough money to buy it; instead of saving for a tiny console they saved money to buy an ice cream, a burger, and to go to amusement parks. Now we can see how the kids and teenagers of today don't want to leave the places where technology is.  

Due to the amount of technology we have now, a new behavior has developed: if we prohibit them from using technology, they become aggressive. Families have issues when their kids become aggressive just because the parents prohibited the use of technology, and this reaction is trendy right now in different parts of the world. Some doctors say the reason they react that way is because they are in an imaginary world where they can do whatever they want until the parent tries to take apart their “world” to make them a normal kid; but now that technology is in every single corner, it's hard to make a kid stop using it. Even teenagers have reached a point where, when they are playing video games, they break everything they see, including the video‑game device that their parents bought for them.  

Some people might say that technology is something positive in our lives because we create artifacts that make our lives simpler; however, technology is bad for our lives because we stop acting like normal people, we want to make our lives easier, and that can affect how our society will be in the future if we don't control the use of technology.

Technology plays a huge role in our everyday lives today, and its influence will only grow. Humans constantly search for ways to improve their existence and make tasks easier. Although some claim this progress is beneficial, many argue that it harms our lives: people avoid face‑to‑face contact, they become unwilling to leave the environments where technology is present, and they can react aggressively when told that technology is damaging them.

In earlier times people met on the streets; there were no devices that let us see friends through a tiny screen. Today that habit has turned into a serious social problem. Instead of going out to meet friends or simply enjoy the surroundings of a city, many prefer to stay at home and converse with strangers they have never seen. Some might say that chatting with unknown people online is no different from striking up a conversation with a passer‑by, but the internet carries a much higher risk. Fake accounts, identity theft and other scams are common, whereas in the past we could judge a person’s character by observing their behavior in person before forming a friendship.

When we were children, playing outside—running up and down the street, visiting a neighbor’s house, or going to the park—was the norm. Nowadays, video games dominate the leisure time of kids and teenagers. All it takes is plugging a console into a TV, and many youngsters spend entire days indoors, neglecting sports or visits to friends’ homes. At school, the main subject of conversation among pupils is often the latest game, which can distract them from studying for exams or completing homework. The first consoles were once marvels, but they were expensive; families often saved money for simple pleasures such as ice cream or a trip to an amusement park. Today, many young people would rather stay glued to their screens than step outside.

The widespread availability of technology has also created a new kind of behavior: when children are denied access to their devices, they can become angry and even violent. Families worldwide report that children lash out when parents try to limit screen time. Some physicians explain that these kids have built an imaginary world where they are free to do anything, and when adults try to pull them out of that world, they react defensively. Because technology permeates every corner of modern life, it is increasingly difficult to make a child put it aside. In extreme cases, teenagers have smashed the very consoles they were given after becoming frustrated with a game.

Critics may argue that technology brings many conveniences and makes life easier, but the negative side outweighs the benefits. It isolates us, discourages normal social interaction and creates a dependency that, if left unchecked, could shape a future society that lacks real human connection. Controlling our use of technology is essential if we want to preserve healthy social habits for generations to come.

Participating in at least one extracurricular activity should be compulsory for every student. The school principal’s suggestion makes sense because these activities bring useful benefits that help both now and later in life.

First of all, joining a club or a sport is good for mental and physical health. Numerous studies show that people who take part in regular physical activity have lower chances of heart disease, breathing problems and other health issues. Playing sports such as basketball, baseball, track or even cheerleading helps students stay fit, lose excess weight and develop a habit of staying active. The research is clear: the more active you are, the more health advantages you enjoy.

Extracurriculars also have a positive effect on emotions. When you are involved in something enjoyable, you get a break from academic pressure and everyday worries. Activities that involve teamwork—like helping a counselor, working on the yearbook, or volunteering around the school—provide a distraction from stress and give a sense of purpose. Putting students into different groups each day would encourage them to meet new people, build friendships and have fun together, rather than remaining isolated.

In addition, these experiences are valuable for university applications. Colleges look beyond grades; they want to see well‑rounded individuals who can manage responsibilities, work with others and show commitment. Being a member of a sports team or a school club makes a résumé stand out and can even increase the chances of receiving a scholarship. Admissions officers interpret such involvement as a sign that a student is independent, reliable and capable of handling the challenges of higher education.

Overall, requiring every student to take part in at least one extracurricular activity brings many advantages—healthier bodies, less stress, stronger social skills and better university prospects. Since trying an activity cannot cause harm, I fully support the principal’s proposal and encourage all students to give it a chance.

Music, drama and art are usually offered as elective subjects in schools. They are not essential for everyday life and they are not required for graduation, so students should not be forced to take them. Everybody has different interests and career goals, and making these subjects compulsory would limit personal choice.

The knowledge we gain at school that we really need in daily life is basic mathematics – it helps us calculate taxes, manage bills and handle other practical matters. Music, drama or visual art, on the other hand, are more like hobbies than necessities for a stable livelihood. Employers rarely look for the ability to write a song, perform theatrically or paint a masterpiece when they hire new staff. Only those who are exceptionally talented and dedicated can turn such skills into a viable profession.

Electives exist precisely because they allow students to explore possible future paths. If every school made art, music or drama a mandatory subject, the curriculum would become overly rigid and would not serve the diverse aspirations of students. Moreover, colleges and universities do not consider these subjects when evaluating applications; they focus on core subjects and the major a student intends to study. Changing a career aim – for example, moving from medicine to scientific research – does not require any background in the arts, which remain unrelated to most other fields of study.

It is true that some people can earn a living from creating music, acting or producing visual art, but such success is limited to a small, highly skilled minority. For the vast majority, these areas do not provide a reliable income, and therefore should not be imposed as compulsory schoolwork.

Students who study online or at home are often more intelligent and learn more because they concentrate on what they are doing. In schools, students may be distracted by playing or talking with friends. If a competition were held between an online student and a regular‑school student, the online student might win because they are often better prepared. Regular‑school students sometimes go just to play with friends, are not focused, or even fall asleep while the teacher explains, leading to poor performance on exams or quizzes. When students are in their own environment they can give their full attention to the lesson, which often leads to improved understanding. Although classroom settings give the chance to make friends, those social benefits do not outweigh the academic advantages of remote learning.  

People who study from home are less likely to be interrupted by noisy classmates or group discussions, so they can work more efficiently. This concentration can make them better prepared for any situation that arises, since they spend their time actually processing the material. In contrast, students in a traditional school may spend part of the day chatting, playing, or even falling asleep, which harms their learning and can result in poor performance on exams.  

When the end‑of‑year assessments arrive, those who have studied online often know more of the content because they have been consistently focused. They tend to perform better on standardized tests, while some pupils in a regular school may fail simply because they did not engage with the material.

However, each person can decide how much interaction they need and choose the learning method that best fits their goals. While teachers may have good intentions, they often overlook how the students themselves feel. For this reason, schools should not adopt a year‑round calendar; instead, there should remain a three‑ to four‑week summer vacation together with a short week off in spring and autumn.

First, a lengthy break gives children the chance to spend quality time with their families. When school occupies most of the year, young people come home each day only to finish homework and prepare for the next lesson, sometimes juggling projects as well. This constant focus on schoolwork can limit the time they actually share with their parents, and it may even lead to a lack of honest communication about what is happening in their lives. A reasonable summer vacation helps restore that family connection, which teachers sometimes forget when they claim that breaks are too short.

Second, students often have responsibilities outside of school. During the longer holidays they can help their parents, run errands, or pursue other activities without the pressure of daily assignments. Free from the incessant cycle of homework and projects, they can relax and develop skills that are not taught in the classroom. Moreover, many pupils feel that much of the material taught in school is quickly forgotten after the break, so a shorter, more frequent holiday schedule would not improve learning but would instead reduce the time they have to fulfill personal duties.

In summary, although some educators worry that a long summer holiday harms retention, the evidence shows that keeping a traditional break schedule is more beneficial. A three‑ to four‑week summer vacation, plus brief intervals in spring and fall, allows students to maintain family ties and attend to their own responsibilities, which are both essential for their overall development. Therefore, schools should not replace the current system with a year‑round calendar.

Students may find it harder to comprehend explanations delivered online, and many already have trouble following teachers in a traditional classroom.

Some schools continue to offer classes from home, believing it benefits students. At home, students can relax, have more time to do homework, feel comfortable, and feel safe with their families. They also tend to sleep more and have more energy for online classes. However, being near family can increase distractions, and students may not want to pay attention.

In conclusion, when students take classes online from home, they are more prone to distraction and less inclined to focus. They often prefer to play or use their phones, which is not conducive to learning. This results in frustration and reduced understanding, making home‑based classes a less effective option for many students.

Many schools in the United States now offer distance learning, allowing students to attend classes from home through online platforms or video calls. The idea is presented as a helpful alternative, especially for those who have experienced bullying in middle or high school. However, studying from home often leads to a decline in learning.

One of the main problems is the easy access to distractions, such as smartphones. When students are at home they tend to feel bored and may spend a lot of time doing nothing productive. The comfort of the home environment can make it tempting to sleep in, listen to music, or play games instead of focusing on lessons. Many students also have part‑time jobs, which leaves them exhausted and unwilling to concentrate on schoolwork.

Attention spans are usually shorter at home than in a classroom. When a teacher explains a concept face‑to‑face, students can ask questions and receive immediate feedback. Through a screen, comprehension becomes more difficult, and many pupils struggle to follow the lesson. Consequently, learning outcomes suffer, and students often feel frustrated because they do not understand the material as well as they would in a traditional setting.

Supporters of home‑based classes argue that students can relax more, have extra time for homework, and feel safer with their families. They claim that a good night’s sleep at home gives learners more energy for online lessons. Yet the proximity to family members can also create additional interruptions, making it hard for students to stay focused.

In conclusion, while distance learning may seem convenient, it typically results in greater distraction and reduced engagement. Students are less likely to pay attention, find the material harder to grasp, and often prefer to spend their time on phones or games. Therefore, offering classes from home does not appear to be a beneficial option for most learners.

A city council is debating the adoption of a curfew for teenagers—10 p.m. on weekdays and midnight on weekends. Some people regard this as a sound proposal, but others, especially young people, oppose it. There are divergent opinions on this issue. In my view, imposing a limit on teenagers who stay out late is advisable. I believe this measure can improve adolescents’ sleeping patterns, deter unhealthy eating habits, and enable teens to spend more time with their families.

Curfews that prevent teenagers from remaining out late help them obtain better sleep. When they are at home, they retire at a more appropriate hour than if they stay out until midnight. Young people should obtain at least seven to eight hours of sleep because of their developing bodies. Proper rest makes them more energetic. Staying out late disrupts bedtime for teens, rendering them sluggish, fatigued, and disengaged from surrounding activities. Insufficient sleep can also increase the risk of operating a vehicle. Drowsiness while driving is hazardous. Many adolescents perish in road accidents because of inattention caused by inadequate sleep, and such inattention is often compounded by drinking and driving after a night out. To protect teens from premature death, curfews should be implemented. When I cannot sleep well, I am unable to concentrate in class, which frequently harms my grades. Moreover, staying awake late isolates me from real‑world events, because while others around me are awake, I am unfocused and drowsy.

This policy also influences teens’ dietary habits. Staying out often entails consuming unhealthy, junk food, which is detrimental to young people’s health. Along with sufficient sleep, maintaining good nutrition is essential for staying fresh and active. It is crucial for adolescents to eat wholesome food because they have their whole lives ahead, and poor nutrition can precipitate early‑onset diseases. In addition, when teens go out with friends they may drink alcohol or beer, which is unsuitable at that age. Unhealthy eating weakens the immune system and promotes early disease. Moreover, excess fat accumulation affects teens socially, mentally, and physically. If teens remain at home, they eat meals prepared by their parents, which are typically healthier and less greasy. Whenever I consume junk food I feel ill, and in unfamiliar settings people tend to keep their distance, making me uncomfortable. I have observed a relative who gained considerable weight from excessive junk food; he now requires assistance to rise from a chair, is frequently teased for his size, and tires quickly when walking. To avoid such negative comments and an unfit physique, teens should favor nutritious, home‑cooked meals.

Beyond diet and sleep, a curfew keeps teenagers at home with their families, fostering interaction rather than constant outings with peers. Often, generational gaps emerge because of limited engagement within families. Sharing dinner together encourages discussion of various matters affecting us. For example, when our family gathers we talk about new experiences—my sister and I made new friends after relocating here this year—and we exchange information about recent health concerns.
