A city council is debating whether to adopt a curfew for teenagers—10 p.m. on weekdays and midnight on weekends. Some people think this is a good idea, but others, especially young people, do not. There are conflicting opinions on the topic. In my view, setting a limit for teenagers who stay out late is beneficial. This adoption can improve teens’ sleeping habits, prevent unhealthy food habits, and allow them to spend more time with their families.

Curfews that stop teenagers from going out late at night help them improve their sleep. When they are home, they go to bed earlier than they would if they stayed out until midnight. Young people should get at least 7–8 hours of sleep because their bodies are still growing. Well‑rested teens are more energetic. Staying out late disrupts bedtime, which makes teens lazy, tired, and inactive in everyday activities. Inadequate sleep also increases the risk of accidents while driving; drowsiness can cause dizziness and dangerous inattentiveness. Many teens die in road crashes because of sleep‑related inattentiveness, often compounded by drinking and driving after staying out late. To protect teens from such early‑age deaths, curfews should be adopted. When I cannot sleep well, I am unable to concentrate in class, which often hurts my grades. Staying awake late also isolates me from what is happening around me, because when others are awake I am still trying to stay focused while sleepy.

The curfew also affects teens’ eating habits. Going out often leads to consuming unhealthy junk food, which is detrimental to young people’s health. Adequate sleep and proper nutrition are both necessary to stay fresh and active. It is essential for teens to eat healthily, because unhealthy diets can cause diseases at an early age. When teens go out with friends they may also drink alcohol or beer, which is unsuitable for their age. Unhealthy food weakens the immune system, leading to early illnesses, and it adds excess fat that impacts teens socially, mentally, and physically. If teens stay home, they eat food provided by their parents, which is generally healthier and less oily. Whenever I eat unhealthy food I feel sick, and in places where I am unknown people tend to keep their distance, making me uncomfortable. I have seen a relative who gained a lot of weight from junk food; he now needs help to get up, is teased for his size, and tires quickly when walking. To avoid such negative comments and an unfit body, teens should eat healthy, home‑cooked meals.

Often, generational gaps arise from a lack of interaction within families. Having dinner together allows discussion of current events, new experiences—like my sister and I making new friends after moving here this year—and health concerns. We share our happiness and problems, strengthening our family bonds.

Many more examples show how this policy can steer teens toward positive outcomes. Proper sleep, healthy food, and family interaction become possible if curfews are adopted. To raise a future generation that is healthy and focused on the development of our country, such laws are needed. Healthy teens will become fresh, present‑minded citizens who work hard to achieve their dreams. When they interact with their families, they contribute to a more satisfied society. Teens should view this as a positive step rather than a restriction on freedom. It is not a limitation but a key to a healthy, fresh, and active lifestyle. Give teens life by guiding their habits instead of allowing an unchecked, improper lifestyle.

The city council is debating whether to impose a curfew on teenagers—10 p.m. on weekdays and midnight on weekends. Some people support the idea, while many young people oppose it. I believe that such a curfew would be beneficial, because it would improve teens’ sleep patterns, encourage healthier eating habits, and give them more time with their families.

First, a curfew would help teenagers get enough rest. When they are required to be home earlier, they are more likely to go to bed at a reasonable hour instead of staying out until the early morning. Adolescents need at least seven to eight hours of sleep each night for their bodies to develop properly. Adequate sleep makes them more energetic and better able to take part in daily activities. Lack of sleep, on the other hand, can leave them feeling sluggish, inattentive, and even unsafe behind the wheel. Drowsy driving is a major cause of accidents among young drivers, and many of those crashes involve teenagers who have been out late, sometimes after drinking. By keeping teens home earlier, we reduce the risk of sleep‑related accidents and help them concentrate better in school, which in turn can improve their grades.

Second, the curfew would have a positive effect on teenagers’ eating habits. When they stay out late they often turn to fast food, junk snacks, and sugary drinks, or even alcoholic beverages, all of which are harmful to a growing body. Poor nutrition weakens the immune system and can lead to obesity and related health problems at a young age. If teens are home, they are more likely to eat meals prepared by their parents—food that is usually more balanced and less greasy. I have seen a relative gain a great deal of weight from constant junk‑food consumption, which caused him physical discomfort and social embarrassment. Eating healthier meals at home can help prevent such issues and keep teenagers fit and confident.

Finally, a curfew encourages more family interaction. When teens are home earlier they can share dinner with their parents and siblings, discuss the events of the day, and receive advice about school, health, or personal problems. These conversations help bridge the generation gap that often grows when young people spend most of their free time with friends outside the home. My own family talks about new experiences, health concerns, and personal challenges during evening meals, which strengthens our bonds and gives us mutual support.

In summary, enforcing a reasonable curfew for teenagers can lead to better sleep, healthier eating, and stronger family connections. These benefits will help young people grow into well‑adjusted, productive members of society. Rather than viewing the curfew as a restriction on freedom, it should be seen as a protective measure that guides teens toward a healthier, more balanced lifestyle. By limiting late‑night outings, we give them the chance to develop good habits that will serve them—and the community—well into the future.

In my view, students both should and should not be allowed to use their phones at school. On the one hand, smartphones are convenient and fast, and today’s pupils rely on them for almost everything. On the other hand, they can easily become a source of distraction that interferes with learning.

One major drawback of permitting phones in class is that they tend to pull students’ attention away from the lesson. Instead of concentrating on the teacher or doing the assigned work, many youngsters would rather scroll through social media or send messages to friends. Schools already provide computers and libraries for researching information, so a phone is rarely needed for that purpose. Allowing unrestricted use would likely encourage laziness and reduce the quality of students’ work.

Even when teachers ask students to hand over their devices, many pupils become upset because they are accustomed to using them constantly during lessons. Learning is more effective when students read, think, and engage with the material themselves rather than simply looking up answers online. One possible compromise is to have students give their phones to the teacher at the beginning of a class and retrieve them when the period ends, which would minimise the temptation to cheat during tests.

Nevertheless, there are some advantages to mobile phones. They are portable, quicker to operate than a full‑size computer, and can help students find explanations for concepts they do not understand. A phone can also be a useful tool for exploring alternative perspectives and gathering information on the spot, and many students are more comfortable typing on a phone than on a keyboard.

In summary, the use of smartphones at school has both positive and negative aspects. While they offer speed and accessibility, they also pose a serious risk of distraction and cheating. Should a student's work be praised regardless of its quality? The idea sounds appealing at first glance, but in education it would be disastrous. Everyone likes to receive praise; encouragement can boost confidence and make practice more enjoyable, which in turn helps learning. However, if praise is given for every effort without pointing out areas for improvement, the incentive to grow disappears. Imagine receiving an A+ on every assignment without any constructive feedback—what would motivate you to keep learning? Students would become accustomed to constant flattery, develop an intolerance for criticism, and begin to expect endless attention.

Consider artists as an illustration. Creators often despise many of their own pieces, even as they improve. They may receive compliments, but it is the dissatisfaction with their work that drives them to refine their craft. Criticism, taken thoughtfully, becomes a tool for advancement rather than a source of discouragement. If we applied the same “praise‑only” policy to students, we would strip away a crucial element of learning: the ability to handle negative feedback. In the real world, professionals face critiques regularly; those unable to accept them risk stagnation or even losing their jobs.

In short, praising students indiscriminately is not the solution, nor is making them loathe their studies. The goal should be a balanced approach—pair each compliment with constructive criticism. This teaches learners that success comes with both strengths and weaknesses and prepares them for a world where praise is not constant but earned.

The idea of adopting a four‑day school week, with each day lasting ten hours, has been suggested as a way to save energy and resources, mirroring the shift some companies have made to a four‑day work schedule. Many people, however, argue that schools should not follow this model and that extending the school day by two hours would be unwise.

First of all, a ten‑hour school day would be exhausting for students, teachers and all staff. Longer days mean more fatigue, and the four‑day week would actually feel longer than the usual five‑day schedule. Moreover, the extra time might lead schools to increase the amount of material needed for graduation, which would further lengthen the workload for everyone. Critics also point out that there are simpler ways to conserve energy without altering the school calendar, such as switching off lights when they are not needed and opening windows for natural ventilation.

A large number of pupils have part‑time jobs or other responsibilities after school, and some even work full‑time. Extending the school day would make it difficult for them to balance work and study, and it would not lead to a significant reduction in energy consumption. Involving people outside the school could generate better ideas for saving energy than changing the school schedule.

In conclusion, the best approach is to discuss the issue openly and consider the diverse needs of students. Many learners need more time to grasp new concepts, and a four‑day week would make it harder for them. Simple energy‑saving measures—like turning off unnecessary lights and improving natural ventilation—are easy to implement and do not require sacrificing instructional time. Therefore, schools should keep the traditional five‑day schedule and focus on these straightforward ways to conserve energy.

Technology has undeniably improved our lives, even if some worry that it reduces face‑to‑face contact. I think the overall effect is positive. Just as buildings, cars and airplanes have reshaped everyday life, modern tech is changing the way we shop, dine and travel. For example, many restaurants now use digital ordering systems, which means customers no longer need to worry about tipping or waiting for a server to take their order.

Critics often point out that technology can eliminate jobs, but it also creates remarkable efficiencies. The automotive industry illustrates this well: Ford uses advanced robotics to assemble a vehicle in roughly ten minutes. Cars and trucks can be purchased entirely online, without ever speaking to a sales representative, and parts can be ordered and delivered the next day. Even the Ford dealership near me includes a restaurant that relies heavily on technology to run smoothly.

In restaurants, tablets allow diners to order meals with a few taps, making the experience faster and more reliable. Although this reduces the number of staff needed and limits personal interaction, it also eliminates the need for tips and minimizes human error. While employees may be free to attend to other tasks until called upon, the overall service becomes more efficient.

Long checkout lines have also become a thing of the past. I have watched cashiers take an excessive amount of time scanning items, and errors in change are all too common. Self‑checkout kiosks solve these problems: customers simply scan, pay, and leave. Although machines occasionally malfunction, they are generally dependable, and soon most American stores will feature them.

Having technology at our side has made life easier and less stressful. Imagine if Ford had to hire thousands of workers to assemble a single car over several hours, or if every restaurant needed a large, often inattentive staff, or if Walmart relied solely on cashiers who took ages to scan items. Without the innovations we enjoy today, everyday tasks would be far more cumbersome. Technology, despite its flaws, brings significant benefits that enhance our daily existence.

Of course, there are situations where first impressions seem harder to overturn. Employers, for example, often look for candidates who appear confident, diligent, and responsible during an interview. If an applicant fails to make a positive impression at that moment, the chances of getting the job drop dramatically.

Nevertheless, even in such cases the initial judgment can be revised over time. A candidate who did not shine in an interview might later prove their abilities through a trial period or a follow‑up meeting, allowing the employer to reassess their earlier impression. In my view, first impressions are not set in stone; they can be changed as we learn more about the person behind them.

Many people think that a person’s character can be judged from the way they dress or present themselves, assuming that appearance reveals personality. I disagree with this view. A first impression is often misleading, and there are three main reasons why it can change: clothing does not reflect one’s true nature, a deeper understanding of the individual is necessary, and our opinion of someone can evolve as we get to know them.

First, what we wear or how we look says very little about who we really are. You can’t tell whether someone is kind, generous or reliable simply by observing their outfit or hairstyle. Appearances are superficial and can be chosen for many reasons that have nothing to do with inner traits.

Second, getting to know a person takes time. My own experience shows that initial judgments are frequently wrong, especially in close friendships or romantic relationships. Only by spending time together, sharing experiences and listening to each other can we discover the real qualities of a person.

Finally, many strong bonds begin with a poor first impression. Some of my closest friends were once strangers I didn’t think much of, or even people I regarded as rivals. As we spent more time together, their true character emerged, and we built lasting, positive relationships.

In conclusion, while first impressions are useful for introducing ourselves, they are not a reliable guide to a person’s real nature. By getting to know someone better, we often find that our initial judgments change, revealing the true individual beneath the surface.

I disagree with students attending classes from home or via video conferencing. The reason I oppose this online approach is that many students will not engage; they will fall asleep and fail to do their work, and consequently a lot of kids could fail. I say this because I am a student myself, so I can explain why I feel this way.

The first reason is that students often procrastinate, saying “I’ll join next time,” and continue to do so until they think the class is useless. Then they skip the session entirely and go outside to play with friends, or their parents have to keep reminding them to log on, and they may ignore them or switch to their PS4 or phone instead.

The second reason is that they can fall asleep while logged in, and the teacher cannot do anything about it. In a real classroom, a teacher can ask students to stand up and make sure they are doing what they’re supposed to, which makes the teacher’s job much easier.

The last reason, but not least, is that they will not do their work. Even if they log on, there’s no way to know if they are the ones actually completing assignments; they could have someone else do it for them or even pay someone to finish it. Some might argue that attending classes from home is the best option because students don’t have to go through the morning routine—they can simply open their laptops, join the teacher via webcam, and learn. However, many students cannot learn effectively that way; they need someone right next to them to understand the material better. That is why I disagree with students attending school from home.

I am against the idea of students attending lessons from home via video‑conferencing. From my own experience as a pupil, I have seen several problems that make online classes ineffective.

First, many learners simply do not log on. They keep postponing until they convince themselves that the session is useless, then they go outside to play or distract themselves with video games or phones. Even when parents remind them to join, the temptation to ignore the lesson is strong.

Second, it is easy for students to fall asleep during a virtual class. A teacher cannot intervene the way she could in a physical classroom, where she can ask a drowsy pupil to sit up or move around. In a real classroom the teacher can keep an eye on everyone and ensure that attention is maintained, which makes the whole teaching process smoother.

Third, there is no reliable way to know whether the work submitted online is the student’s own. Some may ask friends to complete assignments or even pay others to do them. While some argue that learning from home saves time—no need to get up early, just turn on a laptop and join the lesson—many teenagers actually need the immediate presence of a teacher to understand the material fully.

Because of these reasons—lack of participation, the risk of sleeping in class, and the difficulty of monitoring genuine work—I disagree with the notion that schooling should be done from home.

Do you realize how many people are miserable because they live as someone else? Today, millions of individuals around the world do not experience life the way they truly want. It is often hard to stay true to yourself in a society that tells you being different is wrong, yet the greatest achievement for any person is to embrace individuality. Being authentic is the key to happiness, and fighting the prejudices of others is no small task; it can feel like a battle when the whole world seems determined to reshape you.

Many believe that a successful, wonderful life means having lots of money, a prestigious position, or material possessions. In reality, these things do not help you be yourself. A person may own all of those, but they do not define who he or she is, nor do they guarantee happiness. If you lack happiness, everything else is meaningless. Studies show that around sixty percent of people are dissatisfied with their lives, yet this can change when they become honest with themselves and eliminate what they do not truly want. The first step toward contentment is to be yourself. No one can thrive while living a lie, because that only leads to a miserable existence. One must accept one’s personality and interests based on genuine thoughts. Ignoring this honesty can cause serious problems such as depression, a common consequence of not accepting who you are and how you live. For this and many other reasons, being yourself is difficult, but it brings the greatest reward.

Throughout life you will constantly make choices, and it is vital that you listen to your inner voice. You must not allow others to decide for you, especially when those decisions affect your identity.

First, know exactly what you want, because that knowledge is the foundation of true self‑satisfaction. Prioritise your own opinion; this is the secret to real happiness. It is far too easy to follow the advice of others or to be swayed by a world that constantly tries to turn you into someone else. In the end, what matters most is what you truly desire.

Everyone is searching for the right path in life, and being honest about one’s feelings is essential to reaching that goal and feeling fulfilled. The world can feel like a perpetual war, with many people fighting for their rights and for authenticity. It is not an easy task, but the only opinion that truly matters is your own. You do not need to worry about what others think; you only need to care about your own perspective. Unfortunately, not everyone understands this, and many demand that society accept them simply for being themselves. It is extremely hard to stay true to yourself when countless others try to change your mind and refuse to accept diversity. Diversity is part of a natural balance; we should respect one another regardless of race, colour, language, traditions or customs. This respect, not equality in every detail, is what is needed. Today many people are working to create a world free of prejudice, where everyone can be who they wish and enjoy the rights they deserve. The struggle is tough, but the result is the greatest accomplishment. When people are happy with who they are, accepting both strengths and flaws, nothing can bring them down. Research repeatedly shows that external opinions lose their power when you are secure in your own identity.

Philosophers and scholars argue that societies that reject difference do so because, since the beginning of time, people have hidden their true feelings and interests for fear of rejection. Part of the blame lies with us, for staying silent when something is wrong, yet it is never too late to change. Most people now seek to reshape the world’s standards of what is acceptable. Accepting yourself can feel like a war when the whole world pushes against you, but you must stay strong and not let anyone undermine your choices. Moreover, being your own harshest critic makes it even harder to be authentic; we often demand more from ourselves than anyone else. If everyone were honest with themselves, this would become normal, but today uniqueness is still viewed as a flaw. We need to change that mindset and make self‑acceptance ordinary.

Clearly, we still have much to learn, but I believe we are moving in the right direction. People must overcome many obstacles to claim their individuality, always remembering where they are and where they want to go.

Life is a series of stages that we all pass through: birth, childhood, adolescence, adulthood and old age. Each phase brings its own challenges and responsibilities, and understanding this progression is essential if we want to make the most of the time we have. I completely agree that a straightforward, raw approach to life is the most effective way to handle these stages.

A direct attitude forces us to treat life like a game in which we must take responsibility for our own outcomes. Instead of waiting for money or support from our parents, we learn to earn our own income and plan for the future. This mindset teaches us how life really works.

I can illustrate this with my own experience. When I was a little boy I already began to understand what it meant to be responsible. At eight years old I took care of my own breakfast, kept myself clean and dressed for school. By the time I turned fifteen I started working a small job, earning my own money and learning the value of hard work. Those early experiences gave me a clear picture of what I wanted for the future and helped me set realistic goals and dreams.

If we avoid taking action, our quality of life can deteriorate quickly. Therefore, it is crucial to comprehend what we truly want, to define our personal vision, and to plan accordingly. When we create our own roadmap and rely on nothing but our own effort, we become free to shape our destiny for ourselves and for the families we care about.

Deciding whether teenagers should choose a career path early is a question that invites both support and criticism. While some argue that young people already have many responsibilities—such as part‑time jobs, household chores, and other commitments—there are compelling reasons to encourage them to start thinking about a profession while still in school.

First, committing to a career early gives students a head start. When they know which field they prefer, they can concentrate on relevant subjects, practice the necessary skills, and become familiar with the work environment long before they graduate. This focused preparation means they are less likely to encounter difficulties when they finally enter the labour market, because they will already have a solid foundation of knowledge and experience.

In many societies, high schools expect pupils to identify a future occupation. This requirement helps both the students and the community: teachers can see which areas a youngster excels in, and the student can discover his or her own strengths. Knowing early what you want to become can be especially valuable for those who are uncertain about their dreams. As I have learned from my own life, I once refused every extra‑curricular offer—English classes, computer lessons, guitar, dance—preferring to play instead. Only later did I understand how important it is to acquire diverse skills and to demonstrate to the world what you are capable of. Nothing is impossible when you invest time in learning.

Moreover, schools that provide career‑oriented programs allow students to gain practical experience during the summer or after school. In my country, most schools lack such options, leaving students without hands‑on training and forcing them to rely solely on their parents for income. Without elective courses that link directly to professions, many young people finish their studies with little idea of how to work in a real job. Offering career choices in school helps bridge that gap.

In conclusion, it is beneficial for students to begin exploring a profession while they are still in high school. This early exposure not only equips them with useful knowledge and skills but also prepares them for the workforce, reducing doubt and uncertainty about their future jobs. The aim of these programmes is not merely to showcase a chosen field to others; they are intended to serve the student’s long‑term development. Taking advantage of such opportunities can give young people a clear advantage in their lives and help them build a successful future.

First, volunteering offers a chance for students to develop useful skills and a sense of responsibility. By working with local organisations, they learn teamwork, communication and problem‑solving, which are valuable for future careers.

Second, community service helps improve the neighbourhood. When young people contribute their time, they can assist charities, clean public spaces or support the elderly, making the area a better place to live. This creates a positive feedback loop: the community gains help, and the volunteers feel proud of their contribution.

However, I think community service should not be imposed as a punishment or a compulsory requirement. Making it mandatory can turn a helpful activity into a chore, reducing motivation and enjoyment. It is better to encourage participation through incentives and positive examples rather than forcing everyone to do it.

In summary, community service is a great idea because it benefits both participants and society, but it works best when it remains optional and driven by genuine willingness rather than obligation. This approach ensures that those who choose to help do so with enthusiasm, making the experience more rewarding for everyone involved.

It is often argued that pupils should decide on a future profession before they finish secondary school. In my view this expectation is reasonable, because it gives young people a solid foundation for their studies and allows them enough time to explore different possibilities.

Firstly, when students choose a career path during high school they can start building the knowledge and skills required for that field early on. Early commitment encourages them to take responsibility for their future and to set clear goals. For instance, a teenager who knows he wants to become an engineer can focus on mathematics and physics, which will improve his chances of entering a suitable university program later.

Secondly, deciding on a career while still in secondary school provides ample time to investigate various options and to change direction if necessary. This flexibility prevents wasted effort and expenses at the university level. A pupil who discovers, after a year of study, that medicine is not what he expects can switch to a different discipline without having invested years in an unsuitable course. Consequently, the student saves both time and money and enters higher education with a more confident sense of purpose.

In conclusion, expecting students to identify a career before they leave high school is beneficial. It helps them acquire relevant experience early, gives them the opportunity to research and, if needed, revise their choices, and ultimately avoids the pitfalls of studying a subject they do not enjoy.

People who prize self‑reliance often see it as the belief that each person should trust his or her own judgment and follow personal instincts rather than depending on experts or authorities for every decision. This attitude can be illustrated through the way people treat material possessions, money, and work.

First, many individuals place great importance on the things they own—clothes, phones, shoes, and other gadgets. For example, a young woman who spends $100 on a pair of shoes will likely become very upset if those shoes get dirty or are damaged. She may feel that the value of the shoes reflects her personal taste and that anyone who harms them is disrespecting her choice. In the same way, a man who buys an expensive pair of sneakers from brands such as Nike, Adidas or Jordan may become angry if the shoes are ruined, especially if they cost several hundred dollars. He will avoid activities like walking in mud or doing manual labour, because such work could threaten the condition of his prized footwear.

If a person knows that he will be doing outdoor or physical work, it would be wiser to purchase cheaper shoes—perhaps $20‑$50—rather than spending hundreds on a pair he cannot protect. This practical approach teaches an important lesson: buying less‑expensive items allows one to focus on the task at hand instead of constantly worrying about preserving a costly object. Young people, especially teenagers, often want the latest high‑priced items. When they start earning their own money, they learn the real cost of such goods and understand that they must work for what they want. By earning their own cash, they are more likely to appreciate the purchase and take better care of it.

Working for oneself also builds a sense of responsibility. When teenagers take a part‑time job, they discover how much effort is needed to earn money for the things they value. This prevents a habit of constantly asking parents for expensive gifts. Instead, they develop a realistic view of the price of items and the effort required to obtain them. In my own experience, I save part of my earnings to buy things I truly need. When I bought a pair of AirPods for a friend as a Christmas present, I felt that the gift was more meaningful because I had paid for it myself. My friend was delighted, and the gesture strengthened our friendship.

In summary, valuing self‑reliance means learning to make independent choices, working to afford the things we cherish, and taking responsibility for our possessions. By earning our own money and buying items within our means, we gain a deeper appreciation for them and avoid the frustration of losing or damaging expensive goods we cannot protect. This approach fosters confidence, personal responsibility, and genuine satisfaction in the objects and relationships we value.

Some schools allow students to use cell phones in the classroom for educational purposes. While many people claim that phones are useful tools for looking up information, I believe that they should not be permitted in class. My reasons are threefold: students spend most of the day on their phones and therefore do not pay attention, phones can be used for many non‑educational activities, and they are a constant source of distraction.

First, when pupils have a phone in their hands they tend to focus on it rather than on the lesson. School is a place for learning, not for browsing the internet. A phone can indeed help a student find a fact quickly, but if the entire class is occupied with their devices, they will miss the teacher’s explanations and perform poorly on tests and quizzes because they have not absorbed the material.

Second, phones are easily turned into tools for chatting, gaming, watching videos, listening to music, or taking pictures and videos for personal amusement. Some students even record or photograph classmates to post online or to use for bullying. These activities have nothing to do with the curriculum and only waste valuable classroom time.

Finally, even when a phone is used for a legitimate purpose such as researching a homework assignment, it is tempting to drift into other apps, send texts, or make video calls. This multitasking leads to unfinished work and lower grades, as the student’s attention is constantly pulled away from the task at hand.

In summary, although a few schools try to incorporate cell phones into learning, I think they should be prohibited in the classroom. The presence of phones prevents students from concentrating on lessons, encourages off‑task behavior, and ultimately hinders academic achievement.

First impressions matter a great deal, and they are often difficult to alter. I agree with this view, as we can see in everyday situations such as choosing food, meeting new people, or deciding where to shop.  

When we enter a restaurant, we expect a satisfying meal. If we wait fifteen minutes and the dish arrives looking unappetizing, we instantly feel disappointment and may even refuse to eat it, regardless of how good it might actually taste. Conversely, a beautifully presented plate can make us willing to try the food, even before we know its flavor.  

The same principle applies to personal interactions. Imagine a friend introducing you to someone who talks incessantly, like a buzzing fly. If you prefer calm conversation, that constant chatter will create a negative impression, causing you to feel uneasy and perhaps avoid further contact with that person. The initial perception shapes your attitude toward them.  

Shopping offers another example. While exploring a new area with a close friend, you might find a store that looks attractive at first glance. However, after checking online reviews and seeing that most of them are negative, you are likely to change your mind and choose a different shop, assuming the quality will be poor.  

In short, the first impression we form tends to stay with us. Even when we try to revise it later, the original feeling often resurfaces, proving that first impressions are indeed hard to change.

Ralph Waldo Emerson once wrote that “to be yourself in a world that is constantly trying to make you something else is the greatest accomplishment.” I do not agree with this statement. In reality, many people do not succeed in being true to themselves; they spend their lives trying to become someone they are not and consequently fail to reach their own goals.

When society pressures individuals to follow a particular path, they often abandon the objectives that truly matter to them. A person should be free to decide whether a goal fits their own aspirations, not be forced to pursue what others deem appropriate. Frequently, people are dissatisfied with their ambitions because the expectations of the outside world push them toward a different identity. As a result, they become confused about what they genuinely want and end up imitating others instead of following their own path.

Most individuals attempt to adopt a façade rather than reveal their authentic selves. Though some try to be themselves, they frequently feel lost and unable to define who they are. The sheer size and complexity of the world make it tempting to hide one’s true nature in order to fit in. Those who choose to masquerade as someone else usually do so at the expense of their happiness, because they are suppressing their real personality.

In short, many people are unhappy precisely because they do not express who they really are. They conceal their true identity and present a false version of themselves to the world. This avoidance often stems from a failure to discover their own self‑image. Consequently, they are more inclined to become something else rather than follow the goals that belong to them.

Therefore, the claim that being oneself is the greatest achievement does not hold up. People commonly sacrifice their own aspirations and authenticity in order to become what others expect, which shows that the quote does not reflect the way most individuals actually live.

A further reason involves online classes. Many people take this route because they are older, need to work, or have other commitments. Some think it is better for graduation because they can balance work and study. Others believe it is worthwhile to do both. People can help each other; for example, a student may take this journey to graduate because a class meets only four days or fewer per week, making it difficult to attend school regularly. Many students choose this path because going to work seems more practical, while some simply do not care about school at all.

Offering night learning is also a good option. Some people think it is a better choice, yet not many have the opportunity to attend classes at home in the morning or evening. Many students take advantage of online schooling to finish their education. They do so because they have other responsibilities, such as work, or they prefer to stay at home.

In summary, it is great for some students to have the option of taking classes at home. For example, some people work to help their families. In the place where I was born, people walk long distances to learn and graduate; sometimes teachers come to the house to teach. People can help each other, which is one reason for taking this journey to graduate. Some people see this as a better option, though not many have the chance to attend classes at home in the morning or evening. My choice is to continue learning or finish high school online because it allows me to share my experience with others about completing school online. Opportunities lead to major actions and great outcomes for individuals.

In this essay I would like to discuss why allowing students to attend classes from home can be beneficial. First of all, the possibility of studying at home offers great flexibility for many learners. Some young people have to help their families by working, and travelling to school every day would take away precious time they need for those responsibilities. Others live in remote areas where reaching a school is difficult, or they cannot afford the cost of public transport. In these situations online lessons provide an equal opportunity to continue learning without having to abandon family or financial duties.

Responsibility is another important factor. In many regions students must walk several kilometres just to get to the nearest school, sometimes even before sunrise. When teachers are willing to give lessons at home or through the internet, pupils can save the time and energy spent on commuting and instead focus on their studies. This also helps those who cannot pay for transport to keep up with the curriculum and work towards graduation. Moreover, students who demonstrate commitment and good results often qualify for scholarships, which can further support their families.

Online education is already popular among many groups, including older learners who balance work and study. For younger students, the same advantage applies: they can attend school while also contributing to household income or caring for relatives. When school attendance is limited to only a few days a week, many learners find it more practical to study at home and use the remaining time for employment or other duties. Even if a student does not feel very motivated about school, the convenience of remote learning can encourage them to stay engaged.

Offering courses in the evenings or at flexible times is another plus. Not everyone can attend morning classes because of work, childcare, or other commitments. By providing online options, schools enable a larger number of students to complete their education at a pace that suits their personal circumstances. This flexibility helps people who might otherwise drop out or never start secondary education.

In conclusion, studying from home presents many advantages: it alleviates travel difficulties, supports family responsibilities, reduces financial strain, and accommodates different schedules. For these reasons I strongly support the use of online classes as a viable way for students to finish high school and achieve their future goals.

For children living far from school, especially in rural areas, the problem is even greater. Consequently, many students would be less likely to participate in after‑school activities.

Extending the day by ninety minutes would considerably raise that figure, diverting funds from other important needs such as facility upgrades, new learning resources, or technology improvements. The higher operating costs would strain the budget and limit the board’s ability to invest in other areas.

In summary, extending the school day would increase student stress, interfere with extracurricular schedules, and exacerbate electricity expenses. For these reasons, the school board should keep the current length of the school day.

People who value self‑reliance often describe it as the belief that each person should act according to his or her own instincts and ideas. When it comes to important life choices, however, I think individuals are better off following the advice of experts and authorities rather than relying solely on personal judgment.

First, guidance from experienced professionals is usually far more reliable than decisions made in isolation. Those who have spent years in a particular field possess knowledge and insight that most of us simply do not have. By listening to their counsel, we can acquire new perspectives and learn valuable lessons that would otherwise be difficult to discover on our own.

Second, while some people prefer to decide everything by themselves, others are comfortable sharing their choices with trusted advisers. In either case, presenting one’s situation to knowledgeable mentors allows them to benefit from the mentors’ experience. This interaction not only broadens their understanding but also provides useful information that can improve the outcome of their decisions.

Third, individuals who insist on making every decision alone often underestimate the challenges they will face. Life is rarely easy when we rely only on our own limited experience. Encountering people who have already navigated similar problems offers a realistic view of what to expect and how to act more effectively.

In conclusion, before making major choices, it is essential to seek out information and learn from those who have proven expertise. By consulting experienced authorities, we can make better‑informed decisions and benefit from the wisdom that comes with real‑world experience.

I believe technology is largely beneficial because it makes everyday tasks much easier. These examples show how technology has improved people’s lives in many ways.

Communication has also become easier. My grandmother lives in a different city, yet we can see and talk to her through video calls, which would have been impossible a few decades ago. When I travel, my older sister checks us in online, so we avoid long lines at the airport and already have our seats assigned. Mobile payment systems like Apple Pay let us pay for purchases without a wallet, adding another layer of convenience.

It is often claimed that first impressions are almost impossible to alter, but I disagree. In my experience, a person’s initial image can shift dramatically once you get to know them better.  

At first you might think someone is indifferent or uncaring, yet as you spend time together your perception can change and you begin to see a different side of them. I have personally encountered a situation that illustrates this point. I once believed I had met the woman I could spend my whole life with. My initial impression was that she was kind and good‑natured. However, after getting to know her, I discovered a very different reality: she turned out to be spiteful, full of hatred, and constantly looking for reasons to blame me. Her manipulative behavior gradually eroded the affection I once felt.

These examples show that first impressions are not set in stone. People, even family members and loved ones, can reveal new facets over time, proving that our initial judgments can indeed be changed.

Why is it a bad idea to save energy and resources at school?

Some students argue that it is a good idea because it would reduce energy consumption and protect resources. I disagree. When we have homework that requires a computer and many of us do not have computers at home, we must finish the work at school – in the library, a study room, or the classroom. If the school cuts electricity, those computers will not work, and we will be unable to complete our assignments on time. This can lead to lower grades and even penalties for late work.

Imagine a school day that runs for only two hours a day, four days a week, with the lights and computers turned off. Many students would struggle to finish their tasks because they lack the necessary tools. They would feel frustrated, and the situation could also cause tension at home.

Some pupils come from families that can afford internet access and devices, which is why they may support energy‑saving measures at school. However, many other students cannot afford such luxuries. Their parents may be unemployed, single, or have many children to support, making it difficult to pay for internet service. For these youngsters, a reduction in school electricity would directly affect their ability to do homework.

While I believe that schools should not completely eliminate energy and resources, providing reliable electricity is essential for students to complete their work confidently. If the school were without power for several days, the large number of students would have to share a few working computers, leading to long waiting times and unequal access to assignments. This would make learning much harder for everyone.

Some classmates claim that saving energy is unnecessary because a few students waste the internet on social media or video games. Yet, many use the connection responsibly for research, reading, and completing projects. It is unfair to punish all students because of a minority’s misuse.

Another problem with cutting energy is the loss of climate control. If electricity is unavailable, air‑conditioning or heating will not work, and extreme weather – whether cold snow or hot heat – can make the classroom uncomfortable and even cause illness. Without power, phones cannot be charged, making it difficult to contact parents or call for emergency services. Reliable electricity is therefore vital for safety and communication.

On the other hand, using less energy does have some benefits: the school’s electricity bill would be lower, and the saved money could be redirected to other resources or outdoor activities. Nevertheless, these savings do not outweigh the difficulties students would face without consistent power.

In conclusion, turning off electricity for several days would create many obstacles for students. While businesses might be able to adjust their energy use according to their circumstances, schools need a stable supply of power to support learning and ensure the well‑being of their pupils.

My friend and I took IB Mathematics together last year, and it was very difficult for both of us. One day she said to me, “You won’t pass this class; your grades are too low. You need to change that, or you’ll have to retake it next year.” I went home feeling stressed for about an hour, worrying about what she had said. Then I convinced myself that she was right, and I stopped studying for the exam because I didn’t want to put in the effort.

On the day of the exam I didn’t stress myself; I felt okay. I asked my friend whether she had studied, and she admitted she hadn’t. I felt a little relieved because it was Friday. We both took the test and failed, and I felt terrible afterward. When I got home, my dad asked about my grade. I told him I had failed because the subject was hard for me. He became angry, and I didn’t say anything. He told me that my biggest mistake was not trying or studying for the exam, adding that nothing is impossible if you give your best effort. His words made me feel even worse about my result. I expected my friend to feel the same way, but she seemed happy and didn’t care about her grade.

That moment made me decide that I wanted to become an A‑plus student in that class and in all my subjects. I committed myself to pursuing success and pushing myself hard, no matter what. I spent the entire weekend studying for my IB math class, doing my utmost.

On Monday I asked my teacher if I could retake the exam. I prepared very well, and the retake turned out to be easy because I had studied thoroughly. My friend, however, did not improve; she received another low grade and continued to move from failure to failure without losing her enthusiasm. That is why she is still taking the class this year—she never changed her approach. If she had let her failures affect her more seriously, she might have succeeded in the class and in life. In my view, failure should have a negative impact; otherwise people may ignore their mistakes and never grow.

The statement “Unless you try to do something beyond what you have already mastered, you will never grow” is, in my view, inaccurate. Even when we make mistakes, we always have the chance to learn from them and develop further.

First, let me illustrate this with a school project. In a group assignment, each student brings a different viewpoint, but one person usually takes the lead. The group discusses the problem and begins working, yet the result is incomplete and unsatisfactory. The leader rejects the draft, saying it cannot be accepted because it is unfinished. The team then returns to the problem and re‑works it. Nobody in the group says, “I don’t want to do this,” because everyone wants to prove themselves. Instead, they understand that a poor result does not mean they are unable to improve; they simply try again. This shows that growth does not require a brand‑new skill every time—revisiting and refining what we have already attempted is also a form of development.

Second, consider situations in which we realize that the work we have done is wrong. Everyone, regardless of their background, receives multiple chances to improve. Making a mistake once does not condemn us to repeat it forever; we must use those opportunities to become better individuals, better classmates, and better members of society. For example, a person who has committed a crime can still be given the chance to study and rehabilitate. Even though they have broken the law, they deserve a second, perhaps third, chance to grow into a more responsible citizen. If we deny them this chance, we ignore the fact that every human being is capable of improvement. No one wants to end up in prison without learning anything for the future; offering education and support to offenders benefits both the individual and society.

This text aims to encourage a world where everyone can become better. While many enjoy abundant opportunities, I come from a place where they are scarce. Nevertheless, my goal remains the same: to become a better person today, tomorrow, and in the future.

I agree with Emerson’s claim that our actions should be guided by our personal experiences. The more we try new things, the more positions we occupy, and the richer our experience becomes. As we accumulate experience, we become less likely to retreat; instead, we move upward, taking on greater challenges because we have already learned how to deal with difficulties.

Without experience, we lack a solid foundation and are unprepared for the tasks ahead. Support alone cannot replace the value of lived experience: it is only through actually doing something that we grow. When we have practiced a skill, we gain confidence and the chance to seize new opportunities. This readiness stems directly from the knowledge we have gathered over time.

Conversely, those who have never truly engaged with a task remain passive and cannot progress. They may lack the necessary practice, and without it they cannot advance. Experience acts as a catalyst that makes further learning easier; the more we have done, the simpler it becomes to take the next step. Therefore, before attempting something difficult, we should first ensure we have a solid base of experience.

In many cases, when we are uncertain, we turn to a teacher, a mentor, or a supervisor for guidance. Their questions and advice help us fill the gaps in our understanding, allowing us to complete tasks more efficiently. By asking for help and reflecting on our experiences, we deepen our knowledge and become better prepared for future challenges.

Overall, experience is the cornerstone of personal development. It not only equips us with practical skills but also builds the confidence needed to face new situations. Accordingly, I support Emerson’s view that our actions should be based on what we have learned through our own experiences.

Phones are dangerous, yet everyone uses them because everything is electronic. Computers and phones help a lot; they have everything: Facebook, maps, dictionaries, calculators, documents, everything in one place. So, all students use phones, but they lose eyesight and focus. I know a cell phone helps communication, but it is also dangerous.

Finally, I don’t think learning at school alone guarantees a good life because teachers only give some ideas on how to learn. Students know little about the world outside because they spend all their time at school. If students had more time, they would learn from friends, mom, dad, sisters, and brothers, gaining more knowledge. Businesses have adopted a four‑day work week, and students have a four‑day week, which is different. Students wear uniforms, have a lot of homework, and learn some things, but businesses already know what they need.

Considering the advantages and disadvantages of a four‑day school week, I believe it would be a poor idea for our school to adopt this model. The main reasons are that it would reduce family time, increase the amount of homework, and create a long, tiring day for students.

First, a shorter week would mean that school days become much longer. When classes last from early morning until late afternoon, pupils spend most of their waking hours at school and have little chance to be with their parents after lessons. Children would return home exhausted, and the few hours left for family activities would be quickly spent on chores or relaxing, rather than meaningful interaction. If students are not allowed to meet their friends after school because they are still in class, many would feel frustrated and unhappy.

Second, longer school days would inevitably lead to more homework. Teachers would have to cover the same curriculum in fewer days, so they would assign extra assignments to make up for the lost time. After a full day of lessons, students would come home still hungry and tired, only to find a pile of tasks waiting for them. The constant pressure of studying, completing assignments, and trying to find moments for leisure would make the day feel endless and stressful. While some pupils might use their phones to listen to music or watch videos during brief breaks, this does not replace the need for rest and proper meals.

Third, many families rely on parents being at home when their children return from school. Younger students, especially those under eighteen, need adult supervision after the school bus drops them off. If school finishes later, parents might have to adjust their work schedules or worry about their children’s safety. Some teenagers also have part‑time jobs; a longer school day could clash with these responsibilities, making it difficult for them to earn money and gain work experience. In such cases, students might prefer the income over staying in class, which could diminish their motivation to learn.

Finally, extending the time spent in school does not automatically improve learning. When pupils are in the classroom for many continuous hours, they can become bored and lose concentration. Modern classrooms already use computers, smartphones and other electronic tools, which are helpful but also pose risks to eyesight and attention spans. If students are forced to sit for extended periods, the negative effects of screen fatigue and mental overload could outweigh any educational benefits.

In conclusion, I do not think a four‑day school week would lead to a better education or a healthier life for students. While some businesses have successfully tried a reduced work week, schools are different environments where long days and excessive homework would harm family life, increase stress, and limit the time young people need for rest, personal development, and real‑world experiences. Maintaining the traditional five‑day schedule is therefore the wiser choice.

"Technology can be Positive or Negative"

Positive: Everyone knows that technology can be like a friend for people who like to use it all day—for example, communicating with friends or family who live far away. The technology also lets people use it as a tool to find books or shop for items that you would normally find in a mall or other places you like to go. In other words, technology has an impact on society: it helps people find jobs without needing to walk the streets, allows students to get information from a college without going there, and enables shoppers to buy things without traveling far. Technology also has an advantage when you have problems at home; many people turn to games that help clear the mind, or use it to address issues with their building.

Negative: In other words, technology often shows its good side, but no one talks about the other side, which can become a weapon for yourself or for people around you. You may find a page that looks safe, yet you never know who created it or why. On many occasions people use technology for bad purposes—for example, terrorist groups use it to reach adolescents and recruit them, especially when those adolescents have fathers who do not care about what their children do. In other cases, technology is a tool that people spend a lot of time on, such as Facebook or online shopping, but some use it as a weapon to sell fake items and take money from people who think they are being deceived.

We now know technology has two faces—positive or negative—and which one you encounter depends on how you use technology.

Technology can be either beneficial or harmful.

On the positive side, many people treat technology like a faithful companion that they use all day. It makes it easy to keep in touch with friends and family who live far away, and it serves as a handy tool for finding books, buying items online, or locating places you want to visit. In other words, technology has a noticeable impact on society. It can help job seekers find work without having to wander the streets, allow students to obtain information without physically going to a college, and enable shoppers to purchase goods without traveling long distances. Moreover, when daily life becomes stressful, many turn to video games or other digital entertainment to clear their minds, and technology can also assist with problems related to home repairs or building maintenance.

However, technology also has a dark side that is less often discussed. While it often presents a friendly face, it can become a weapon for both the user and those around them. For instance, a website may look safe and trustworthy, yet you never know who created it or what their real intentions are. In many cases, people misuse technology for harmful purposes. Terrorist groups, for example, exploit the internet to reach young people and try to recruit them, especially when those youths lack parental guidance. Additionally, social media platforms like Facebook can be abused for fraud; some individuals sell counterfeit goods and deceive unsuspecting buyers who think they are making a smart purchase.

In conclusion, technology has two faces—positive and negative—and which side you encounter depends largely on how you choose to use it.

I disagree with the claim that first impressions are impossible to change. While we often form quick judgments about people, objects or animals, a portion of us cling to those initial views because we feel certain about them. Yet, when we pause and examine the basis of our perceptions, we can see that they are not set in stone.

For instance, one afternoon I was at home exercising when a sudden thought crossed my mind: I imagined that my girlfriend was cheating on me with my best friend. The idea was shocking and made me angry, but I also realized that acting on such a vague impression could cause serious trouble. I knew I had to verify whether my suspicion was justified, so I called my girlfriend and we talked at length. I struggled to express the vague feeling I had, and my mind was a mess of doubts and fear. In the end, the conversation cleared up the misunderstanding, and I learned that my original impression was unfounded.

This experience shows that first impressions can indeed be altered. Sometimes we hold onto a negative view because we are unsure or because we have been hurt before, but by confronting the situation and giving it time, we can discover whether the initial judgment was accurate. In my case, keeping the impression to myself until I could discuss it helped me reassess and ultimately change my viewpoint. Therefore, first impressions are not immutable; they can be revised as we gather more information and reflect on our initial feelings.

My reference is the option “class from home by way of online.” It is the best option and more beneficial for learning at home, easier for time constraints or other problems, and I cannot wait for everything to stay good for my classes.

Online learning is, in my view, the most suitable way to attend classes.  

I believe that the advantages of studying from home outweigh those of going to school in person. When you study online you can fit lessons around a job or other commitments, and schools often provide extra support such as after‑school sessions that can be accessed from home. For many people, especially those who work, it is impossible to spare even an hour each day to travel to a campus; studying online saves that time and makes learning far more practical.  

If you are not employed, you have plenty of free time, which you can devote to online lessons without the need to commute. Even for those who do have a job, the flexibility of the internet allows you to decide when to watch a lecture, take notes, and complete assignments, thereby improving both work performance and academic results.  

Young adults, for example eighteen‑year‑olds, often face many responsibilities that make daily attendance difficult. When a teacher says a particular class is essential, the online format lets you meet that requirement without sacrificing other duties. Video‑conferencing tools further enhance interaction, making it almost as effective as face‑to‑face teaching.  

Studying at home also offers a comfortable environment: you can relax, have meals whenever you need, and avoid noisy classrooms. This calm setting helps you concentrate, think more clearly, and produce better work. Moreover, many students lack reliable transportation, so attending classes online eliminates the need for a car or public transit.  

In conclusion, taking courses online from home is the best option for most students. It provides flexibility, saves time, and adapts to personal circumstances, making education more accessible and manageable despite the occasional lack of immediate teacher assistance.

The question of whether students should begin thinking about a career while they are still in high school is often discussed. I am convinced that it is advantageous for young people to consider their future professions early, because it allows them to explore different fields, discover whether a particular job suits them, and keep their options open.

First, starting the career‑planning process at a young age gives students the chance to learn about various occupations. By visiting workplaces, attending career fairs, or taking specialised courses, they can gain a realistic picture of what a job actually involves. This early exposure helps them decide if a certain path is appropriate before they invest many years in a specific direction.

Second, early planning encourages students to perform well academically. Those who understand the relevance of their subjects to future work are more likely to study diligently and earn good grades. Strong academic results not only improve university applications but also make it easier to enter competitive programmes that are closely linked to particular careers.

Third, the skills and knowledge acquired in high school become a solid foundation for later life. When students have already identified their interests, they can choose electives and extracurricular activities that develop the necessary competencies. This preparation reduces the learning curve later on and increases the likelihood of success in both higher education and the job market.

In conclusion, students who start thinking about their careers while still in high school are better equipped to make informed choices, achieve higher academic standards, and build the skills needed for future employment. By using the resources and opportunities available during these formative years, they set themselves up for a smoother transition to university and, ultimately, to a satisfying professional life.

I agree with Winston Churchill’s observation that “success consists of going from failure to failure without loss of enthusiasm.”  To achieve success, we must accept that setbacks are inevitable and keep our determination alive.

First of all, everyone who follows a clear plan and works together can avoid losing hope.  When people understand the importance of persisting through difficulties, they are more likely to reach their goals.  Churchill’s idea reminds us that it is not the absence of failure that leads to triumph, but the willingness to keep trying despite obstacles.

Moreover, confronting failure builds inner strength.  Each defeat teaches us something new and prepares us for the next attempt.  In this way, failure becomes a stepping‑stone rather than a dead end.  If we maintain confidence in ourselves and in a higher purpose, we can turn every loss into motivation for future success.

Finally, success is impossible without first experiencing failure.  Those who never encounter setbacks often lack the resilience needed to grow.  By embracing challenges and refusing to give up, we create the conditions for genuine achievement.

In short, Churchill’s statement is a powerful reminder that perseverance amid failure is the key to lasting success.  By staying enthusiastic and learning from each mistake, we can continuously move forward toward our goals.

I believe that students should not be forced to enroll in elective courses because these subjects are not essential for graduation and often waste valuable time. Since electives do not count toward the required credits, many learners treat them lightly, receive poor grades, and see their GPA drop. Some students even avoid these classes altogether, finding them dull and unnecessary, which can lead to further difficulties.

Electives are not mandatory for earning a diploma, so students frequently prioritize the core subjects that are needed for graduation. When they are allowed to choose, those who wish to finish their studies quickly can focus on required courses and avoid spending hours on classes that do not contribute to their degree. Schools should therefore give pupils the option to either take electives or concentrate solely on credit‑bearing subjects.

Because elective courses are irrelevant to graduation requirements, many students do not take them seriously. They recognize that their performance in these classes will not affect their ability to graduate, so they devote their energy to more important coursework. This lack of motivation often results in failing grades, which can lower the overall GPA and create problems when applying to universities or seeking competitive jobs later on.

Furthermore, some students simply find electives boring. Not everyone enjoys subjects such as music, drama, or visual arts; many would rather spend time on sports or other interests, or they just want to complete the necessary credit courses as quickly as possible. When students skip or disregard electives, they risk disciplinary issues and may jeopardize future academic or career opportunities, especially in fields where a strong GPA is required. Making electives optional would eliminate this source of trouble.

In conclusion, compulsory elective classes are unnecessary and can harm students’ academic records. Since they are not required for graduation, learners often neglect them, receive low marks, and may even skip them, which can affect future prospects. Schools should prioritize student choice by offering electives as an optional component rather than a mandatory one.

Some businesses have adopted a ten‑hour workday for a week, arguing that it benefits employees because it generates more money. For example, workers who put in ten hours a day are consistently at work. The school, however, does not follow this model, since students do not attend every day.

The school does not adopt the business model because students are not present every day and need to come to learn, while businesses take up all their time. When students attend school only two days a week, they miss the instruction provided during the other days. Moreover, students need to attend school to learn, become responsible citizens, and be prepared for work after graduation.

The school does not want students to attend just two days. One disadvantage is that they will not achieve good grades. Another problem is that absent students do not know what teachers are covering in class, leading to lower grades because they miss the work.

One benefit of working is earning money. Some students work four days a week, putting in ten hours a day, which gives them time to work but prevents them from attending school. Another option is to work after school; this allows them to attend classes, earn good grades, and complete all coursework. In doing so, they will respect teachers, complete homework, and pay attention in class.

In conclusion, schools and teachers want all students to graduate, become good people, and obtain good jobs. They aim to help every student achieve a bright future, and students need to attend school every day in order to learn and be able to work after school.

Some companies have started to require their employees to work ten hours a day for a week, claiming that longer hours increase profits. This approach might be beneficial for the business, but it is not suitable for schools. Students cannot be expected to follow the same schedule, because regular attendance is essential for their education.

First of all, pupils need to be in class every day to learn the material and develop the skills they will need later on. If they were only present for two days a week, they would miss a large amount of instruction and fall behind. Unlike factories, schools are not places where work can be compressed into a few long shifts; learning is a continuous process that requires daily practice and interaction with teachers and classmates.

Moreover, irregular attendance would have a negative impact on students’ grades. When students skip most of the lessons, they are unable to follow the teacher’s explanations, participate in class activities, or complete assignments on time. This would inevitably lead to lower marks and a weaker understanding of the subjects being taught.

Working longer hours can indeed help employees earn more money, but for students the priority should be education. If a student wants to earn an income, the best solution is to take a part‑time job after school hours. This way they can still attend all their lessons, keep up with their studies, and achieve good grades. By balancing work with school responsibilities, they also learn time‑management skills and show respect for teachers by completing homework and paying attention in class.

In conclusion, schools aim to help every pupil graduate, become responsible citizens, and find good jobs in the future. To achieve these goals, students must attend school every day, while any employment should be scheduled outside of school hours. This combination ensures that they receive a proper education and are prepared for a successful career.

Although signing differs from speaking, both require remembering symbols—whether they are spoken words or hand movements—to convey meaning. Learning sign language is a personal choice, but it offers a fresh, valuable skill for anyone willing to try.

For example, blind individuals use Braille, a tactile code that functions much like reading but through touch. Thomas Jefferson once said, “Determine never to be idle… it is wonderful how much may be done if we are always doing.” In other words, he urges us to resolve never to be idle and to keep ourselves occupied, because by doing so we can achieve far more than we might expect.  

People react to this idea in different ways. Some argue that it is not always necessary to be constantly busy; they believe that work should be done only when it is truly needed or when we feel motivated. Others think that we can wait for the “right moment” to pursue our goals, assuming that effort is only required in critical situations. While I do not accept Jefferson’s statement as an absolute truth, I do think there is value in staying active and avoiding laziness.  

In many societies, negative attitudes discourage people from striving for their dreams, leading them to become passive and make excuses for inactivity. This mindset often results in missed opportunities and unfulfilled potential. By contrast, those who keep moving forward, even when the task feels small or routine, tend to see tangible results and develop a sense of accomplishment.  

Therefore, I cannot say I agree with Jefferson completely, but I do believe that maintaining a habit of continual effort brings us closer to the successes we desire. By persisting and working toward our goals, we eventually witness the fruits of our labour and build a stronger foundation for a prosperous future.

Although some people argue that attending school in person is beneficial, I believe that taking classes online is a much better option.  

First of all, studying from home eliminates the need to travel to a school building, wake up early, or sit on a crowded bus. You can stay in the comfort of your own room and eat whatever you like, whenever you want, instead of being forced to eat the school lunch. Online learning also gives you more freedom from strict school rules; you can set your own schedule and create a study routine that suits you.  

When it comes to exams, the internet can be a handy tool. While taking a test online you can quickly look up information, which makes it easier to pass than when you are stuck in a traditional classroom. In a physical school you must arrive on time, sit in a small desk, and follow numerous regulations. If you are late repeatedly, you may be sent to an in‑school suspension room where you cannot use your phone or talk to anyone. The school will also contact your parents, which can lead to arguments at home.  

Disrespecting a teacher or getting into a fight can have serious consequences as well. Security staff may be called, the principal and even the police might become involved, and the incident could be recorded on your disciplinary record. Such a record can hurt your chances of getting into a good college later on, because admissions officers do not want students with a history of trouble.  

The same applies to drug‑related problems. Possessing or selling illegal substances can lead to severe punishment from the school, legal action, and even expulsion. Being forced to change schools would mean leaving friends behind, which is a painful experience for anyone.  

Considering all these drawbacks of traditional schooling—strict schedules, punishments, and the risk of damaging your future—I think online classes are a much smarter choice. They allow you to eat what you want, avoid many of the hassles that come with being on campus, and give you a safer environment to focus on learning. Trying online education could be a valuable experiment for anyone who wants to escape the many problems associated with conventional schools.
