In a group, the workload is divided, so each member only handles a portion of the material; consequently, no single student becomes familiar with the whole project. When a learner tackles the assignment by himself, he must gather every piece of information, solve all the examples and explain the results, which forces him to understand the subject completely.

Group work does have its merits. It can be quicker and easier, since the responsibilities are shared and the total time needed is reduced. Moreover, if one member is confused, another can clarify the concept, helping the whole team reach a common understanding. Many students favor collaborative projects for this reason, and sometimes a single individual may not contribute, leaving the rest of the group to pick up the slack.

Nevertheless, I still believe that individual work is the better choice. By doing everything on his own, a student not only learns more but also gains a deeper comprehension of the material. In the future, people will encounter both situations—some tasks will require teamwork, others will demand solitary effort—so it is useful to be comfortable with both. Yet starting with independent work is particularly beneficial, because it lets teachers observe each pupil’s personal abilities and thinking style without the influence of peers. This insight helps educators assess students more accurately.

In summary, both collaborative and solitary approaches have advantages, but working alone is preferable for personal learning and for allowing teachers to gauge each student’s true capacity.

When teenagers grow up, they begin to form opinions about the issues that surround them. It is not true to claim that first impressions are almost impossible to alter. In fact, people can change the way others see them, even if the initial impression was negative.

A person’s appearance or behavior might lead others to think badly of them at first, but this perception can be modified. By showing friendliness, respect, and a positive attitude, anyone can improve the image they project. For example, if someone is known for being rude, demonstrating kindness and a willingness to help can gradually replace that bad reputation with a more favorable one.

It also helps to be expressive in a pleasant manner. Smiling, speaking politely, and acting cooperatively make a lasting impact and allow others to view you as approachable and trustworthy. Even when you have felt sad or angry, making an effort to convey a calm and positive demeanor can change how people judge you.

In many situations, especially at work, the first impression matters a great deal. Employers often look for candidates who appear friendly and capable of good teamwork. If you initially seem unfriendly, you can still win them over by consistently showing a professional and courteous attitude. Over time, this will replace the early negative impression with a more positive one.

In conclusion, first impressions are not set in stone. By behaving kindly, demonstrating respect, and maintaining a constructive attitude, you can reshape how others see you and create a more favorable impression.

I agree with Ralph Waldo Emerson’s view that trying new things is essential for personal growth. He argues that if we never take risks, we remain stagnant and unable to achieve anything meaningful. Although some people may feel frightened by the prospect of change, Emerson suggests that by confronting these fears we can expand our horizons and develop a deeper understanding of ourselves and others.

When we are willing to listen to different opinions, we open the door to mutual comprehension. Emerson believes that agreement does not mean blind conformity; rather, it involves recognizing the value in other viewpoints while still holding onto our own convictions. By engaging in this exchange, we can learn from the experiences of others and become more confident in our choices.

Emerson also stresses that personal growth depends on experience. Individuals who are open to new ideas and willing to act on them inevitably become richer in knowledge and insight. If we remain passive, we miss the opportunity to build the skills and confidence needed to succeed. Therefore, embracing Emerson’s advice leads not only to personal improvement but also to a more vibrant community where people support one another’s endeavors.

In practice, this means encouraging others to try something new, offering help when needed, and sharing the lessons we have learned. When people see that taking risks can lead to positive results, they become more inclined to participate and to respect differing perspectives. In this way, Emerson’s philosophy becomes a catalyst for collective advancement, showing that agreement, informed by experience, is the foundation of true growth.

Currently, most pupils spend around seven hours at school each day. Even that already feels tiring, especially since many have to get up as early as 5:30 or 6:00 a.m. to prepare for the day. Adding two more hours to each of the four days would make the school day almost nine hours long. This would take away valuable time that could be used for rest, extra learning, or simply enjoying life outside of school.

In short, a four‑day week would not give us more free time; it would merely concentrate the same amount of school work into fewer, much longer days. I would rather keep the five‑day schedule, which allows a better balance between study and personal life.

In many rural areas a school has been set up that provides distance‑learning opportunities for the local population. The community held a meeting, everyone agreed to the idea and, after a few weeks, the classes began. Teachers from outside travel to the village, give lessons and support the residents, who are eager to learn new things.  

I believe that allowing students to attend lessons from home is highly beneficial.  

First, some villages have never had a school, so children usually help with hard labour instead of studying. When outsiders visited one of these villages, they decided to offer teaching there, and the first classes started. At first many people thought the idea was odd, but once everyone began to learn they saw the advantages. Through online or video lessons they learn how to grow a garden, how to manage crops and how to improve their daily work.  

Second, people who never receive any education are likely to encounter many problems later in life. Some think that studying is unnecessary, but education can help solve several issues:  

1. Girls under eighteen are discouraged from early marriage.  
2. Families learn how to plan their families responsibly.  
3. Children gain a chance for a better future.  
4. Both boys and girls acquire basic skills that are essential for life.  

Third, education is crucial for the whole world’s future generations. Without schooling, people cannot communicate effectively or take part in modern society. In this village, children now attend school, and the teachers help them with everyday tasks and knowledge.  

In conclusion, whether it is a second, a minute, a day, a month or a year, education is necessary for everyone. Those who do not study are more likely to remain poor. I support the school’s decision to bring learning to the village, because education never ends – we keep learning new things every day until the end of our lives.

Some school districts offer programs that allow high‑school students to graduate in three years instead of the traditional four.

Students who come from different countries face challenges because they speak different languages and come from different cultures. Their future depends on adapting to a new environment, and many young people find it hard to graduate from high school when they do not speak English. Without understanding the language, they cannot follow the lessons, fail their classes, and end up taking the usual four‑year path. The difficulty is compounded when they do not put enough effort into their studies, which threatens their future prospects.

I arrived in this country three years ago without speaking any English, but I worked hard to pass my classes because I wanted a better future for my mother and younger brother. I graduated because the country offers more opportunities. In high school I passed Algebra 1, which made me very happy, even though I still face problems and my family continues to struggle.

Some students do not return to school after working for one or more years because they plan to attend college later. These students hope to improve their future and support their families.

Some school districts now offer programs that let high‑school students finish their studies in three years instead of the usual four.  

For many students, especially those who have come from other countries, this option is especially appealing. They often face the difficulty of learning in a language that is not their mother tongue and trying to adjust to a new culture. Because they have to work hard to understand the lessons and pass their classes, completing high school quickly can feel like a lifeline for their future.

In my own experience, finishing high school in three years has been a great relief. When I first arrived in this country I barely spoke English, which made school very hard. Yet I was determined to succeed for the sake of my mother and my younger brother. After passing Algebra 1 and other courses, I finally graduated, and I felt a huge sense of accomplishment. The extra year would have meant more problems for my family, so I was glad I could finish early and open up better opportunities.

Many students do not stay in school for the full four years because they need to start working to support their families. For them, going straight to college after an accelerated program can improve their prospects and help their relatives. The three‑year pathway therefore offers a practical way for immigrant and low‑income students to achieve their goals and build a better future.

Curfews are intended to protect teenagers, but many people feel that they intrude on young people’s freedom. The idea behind a curfew is to keep youths safe by limiting the hours they can be out on their own, especially late at night. Some argue that such restrictions are unnecessary interference in their lives, while others believe they are a useful way to prevent trouble.

Supporters of curfews claim that setting a specific time—often 10 p.m. on weekdays and midnight on weekends—helps deter illegal activities and keeps teenagers away from dangerous situations. They see the rule as a preventative measure rather than a punishment, hoping it will reduce the likelihood of crimes or accidents involving minors.

Critics, however, feel that curfews impose an unfair control over personal choices. They argue that if the policy truly protected young people, it would eliminate the need for such rules altogether. Moreover, many teenagers and their families dislike being told when they may or may not be out, seeing it as a violation of their independence.

In my view, curfews aim to safeguard teens, not to dominate their lives. While the intention is good, the enforcement often feels restrictive, especially when it applies to all youths regardless of individual circumstances. A balanced approach—perhaps flexible hours based on age, location, or parental consent—might achieve the protective goal without appearing overly intrusive.

A second advantage concerns the cost of higher education. Many high‑schoolers work part‑time to save for college. If they can graduate a year sooner, they gain an additional year to earn money, which can help reduce the amount they need to borrow or spend on tuition and fees.

Finally, students who use these accelerated programs may have a better chance of securing admission to a reputable college, finding suitable housing near family, and entering the workforce more quickly. An earlier graduation can open doors to opportunities that might otherwise be delayed.

In conclusion, these three‑year high school programs provide valuable options for students who are eager to move on to college and begin their adult lives.

Some locals assume that newcomers are only after money, ignore the hardships endured to reach the new country, and judge them by skin colour or nationality. When you are treated badly because of these stereotypes, it is unreasonable to expect you to remain upbeat.

However, even when these positives exist, they do not erase financial problems, broken friendships, or lies from people who claim they will help but cannot. When you are constantly reminded of these setbacks, staying positive becomes extremely difficult.

In short, a cheerful attitude can be valuable, but it cannot solve every problem, especially for immigrants who are separated from their families, face legal hurdles, or confront prejudice. Negative experiences will still arise despite one's best efforts to stay optimistic.

Many people think that everyone simply repeats what has already been done, but I disagree with that view. In my opinion, trying new things is essential for personal growth and a better future. There are three main reasons for this belief: exploring different activities can improve one’s prospects, we should not be afraid to step outside our comfort zone, and constantly staying the same limits both self‑knowledge and understanding of the world.

First, experimenting with various experiences helps shape a brighter future. For instance, my sister once spent a lot of time doing the same routine tasks without any real direction. After our mother urged her to think about her goals, she began to study harder and eventually became a doctor. By abandoning the habit of doing only what she already knew, she opened up a completely new career path.

Second, we must not let shyness prevent us from trying something different. My father used to be scared of changing his business because he believed the work would become too unfamiliar. I encouraged him to take the risk, reminding him that without trying new approaches we cannot develop. He eventually embraced new methods, and the company flourished, showing how courage to change can lead to success.

Third, staying exactly the same prevents us from truly knowing ourselves and the world around us. My mother often told me to “be yourself,” but I pointed out that if we never challenge our habits, we miss out on opportunities for growth and wealth. By trying activities that push us beyond our comfort zone, we discover hidden talents and achieve goals we never thought possible.

In conclusion, I do not believe that people are stuck repeating what has already been done. On the contrary, we need to think about our futures and start doing different things rather than remaining unchanged. Only then can we grow, learn, and reach our full potential.

When people ask you for advice, they sometimes talk to more than one person. They ask for good advice because, if they do not have good advice, they cannot think about a good decision. Sometimes a person who has trouble in his or her life—whether depression or any happiness—cannot control themselves. Consequently, they get panic; sometimes they cannot think what to do, and they don’t know how to act. That is why they ask many people. However, when they seek multiple opinions, they become confused and cannot select the opinion that is best for them. They want to think about it, but they can’t, so they ask many people for different opinions. This is both good and not good; therefore, they need to figure out what they should do.

What I think is that it’s ok to ask people their opinions, but we should also use our own mind. Without our mind we cannot do anything. The opinions given by other people should be thought about: what are they saying, what is the point, is it good for us or not, and will following this opinion cause trouble? Then you can ask a friend or a person who is very close to you; if that person says yes, you will be like, “Ok, let’s do it!”

So you go through a whole long process to get one good opinion. What you need to do is ask opinions from two or three people, and then, if you think it is not a good opinion, think for yourself and then make a good decision. Everyone makes their own decision. I think that if you want to ask for an opinion, you should find a trustworthy adult who really wants to help you and who will give you a better choice; then think about it, and if you think that he or she is right, just follow the directions.

For example, I have a birthday party and I need to select the dresses for everyone, arrange the party, and I don’t have enough time. I am so worried and confused; I don’t know what to do. I needed help, so I asked my friends, cousins, family, and teachers. Then I realized I had a lot of opinions, so I couldn’t choose.

What I did was ask my older cousin, and we discussed it. She told me in detail what to do, and then I managed my time, chose the dresses, and arranged the birthday party in one week. Everything was so good—that’s how we make better choices for ourselves. If you can’t do that, at least think on your own or ask for help from a good person, not anyone you don’t know well, because people can take advantage of you. Therefore, I think asking an adult is better than asking a lot of people, because an adult will help you more. The first time I needed help, I asked many people and was so confused; I was like, “What is going on with me?” It was my first experience, I didn’t use my mind, and it was a waste of time—everything was ruined. That’s why I learned never to do anything that your parents or an adult doesn’t like.

Here is another way to make a better choice: always listen to your parents and other adults. Sometimes the decisions you think are good turn out to be bad after some time, leading to trouble. So do what your parents tell you, not just what you want. It’s ok to listen to your heart, but sometimes it is not. The best way to make a better choice is to listen to your parents and adults.

The second way is to use your mind to decide whether something is good or bad. The third way is to ask an adult who is nice and truthful. Believe in yourself and in your God; these are the best ways to make a better choice. We should always believe in ourselves and our parents, because they will always tell us what is good for us. Just think that your parents tell you to do something, and again believe in yourself. If you do everything, it will be good; if you feel good, believe in your God, because He will help you everywhere—He is with you. So these are the best ways to make good choices.

When people ask you for advice, they often talk to more than one person. They want good advice because, without it, they cannot make a good decision. Sometimes a person who is having trouble in life—whether dealing with depression or happiness—cannot control their emotions and panics. In those moments they do not know what to do, so they seek many opinions. When they receive multiple viewpoints, they become confused and cannot select the one that is best for them. They want to think about it, but they cannot, so they keep asking different people for opinions. This can be both helpful and unhelpful; therefore they need to figure out what to do.

I think it is okay to ask people for their opinions, but we also need to use our own minds. Without thought we cannot do anything. The opinions we receive should be considered: what are they saying, is it good for us, and will following it cause trouble? Then we can ask a close friend or someone we trust; if that person says “yes,” we can decide to go ahead.

Instead of a long process to get one good opinion, ask two or three people. If their advice does not seem useful, rely on your own judgment and make a decision. Everyone makes their own choices. When you want an opinion, find a trustworthy adult who truly wants to help and who can give you a better choice. Think about their suggestion; if you think it is right, follow it.

For example, I had a birthday party to plan, needed to choose dresses for everyone, and was short on time. I was worried and confused, not knowing what to do. I asked friends, cousins, family, and teachers, but ended up with too many opinions and couldn’t choose. So I asked my older cousin. We discussed the details, I managed my time, chose the dresses, and arranged the party in one week. Everything turned out well. That is how we make better choices for ourselves. If you cannot do that, at least think on your own or ask for help from a good person—not just anyone you don’t know well, because some people might take advantage of you. Asking an adult is often better than asking many people, because an adult can guide you more effectively.

My first time asking many people left me confused and wasted; I didn’t use my mind, and everything was ruined. From that experience I learned never to do something your parents or an adult disapproves of. Another way to make better choices is to always listen to your parents and other adults. Sometimes a decision seems good at the moment, but later you realize it was not. You may get into trouble, so do what your parents tell you, not just what you want. It is okay to listen to your heart, but not always.

The best ways to make a good choice are:  

1. Use your mind to evaluate whether something is good or bad.  
2. Ask an adult who is kind and truthful.  
3. Believe in yourself and in God.  

We should always trust ourselves and our parents, because they will tell us what is best. If you believe in yourself and feel good, everything will be fine; believe in God, who is with you everywhere. These are the best ways to make good choices.

People often turn to several others when they need advice, hoping to receive good guidance that will help them make a sound decision. When someone is facing a problem, feeling depressed, or simply dealing with everyday stress, they may become panicky and unsure of what to do. In such moments they tend to ask many people for their opinions, but this can lead to confusion because they receive too many differing views and cannot decide which one is the most useful.  

In my view it is fine to seek other people’s opinions, but it is equally important to think for yourself. Any advice you receive should be examined critically: What is the person actually saying? Does the suggestion suit your situation? Could following it cause new problems? After you have considered these questions, you can decide whether to accept the advice or rely on your own judgment.  

To avoid being overwhelmed, ask only a few trusted people—perhaps two or three—and then reflect on their input. If none of the suggestions seem right, use your own reasoning to reach a decision. It is essential to choose someone reliable, an adult who genuinely wants to help and can offer a sensible option. If you agree that their advice is sound, you can follow it confidently.  

For example, I once had to organise a birthday party, choose dresses for the guests, and manage everything within a very tight deadline. I felt anxious and confused, so I asked friends, cousins, family members, and teachers for help. The sheer number of opinions made it impossible to choose. I finally turned to my older cousin, discussed the details with her, and she gave me a clear plan. By following her guidance, I managed my time, selected the dresses, and arranged the whole party within a week, and everything turned out well.  

This experience taught me that asking many strangers can waste time and lead to poor choices, while seeking advice from a trustworthy adult is far more effective. It is also wise to listen to your parents or other responsible adults, because they often have a broader perspective on what is best for you. Sometimes a decision may seem attractive at first, but later you may realise it was harmful; that is why you should respect the counsel of those who care for you.  

In summary, the best way to make a good choice is to: (1) think carefully about whether a suggestion is good or bad, (2) ask a reliable adult for help, and (3) trust in yourself and, if you are religious, in a higher power. By combining sound advice with personal reflection, you will be able to make decisions that are both sensible and satisfying.

Some schools have programs in which older kids can help younger kids, whether the younger students are confused about something in school or outside of school, or simply need assistance. For older students, this can involve teaching a concept they themselves struggled with or sharing knowledge they have mastered. Younger students benefit because they are challenged a little more than they would be at home or in a regular classroom, and they can finish their homework during the after‑school program. When they return to school, their assignments are already done, so they are less likely to be late and can relax, play games, or go outside.  

These programs also prepare students for good jobs later in life, giving more kids the chance to study and improve through better school offerings. If most schools adopted such programs, older students could help younger ones with homework, and younger students who finish early could assist even younger peers. This helps those who are strong in subjects like math but face harder assignments; they can spend extra time reviewing past work and, if needed, receive help from an older student.  

The collaboration allows students to finish projects faster, though they can also choose to work independently. After completing homework, many kids will either go on their computers or play outside; roughly half will go out, while the others stay inside, keeping the program fun and not just focused on schoolwork. This balance lets them regain energy, so when they return indoors they are refreshed and not constantly fatigued during the after‑school program.

Schools that run programs in which older students help younger ones can be very beneficial. When younger pupils struggle with a subject, either inside or outside the classroom, they can receive assistance from peers who have already mastered the material. This not only helps the younger child understand the topic better, but it also gives the older student a chance to review concepts they once found difficult and to strengthen their own knowledge.

For younger learners, having an older buddy to turn to means they can tackle challenging assignments more confidently. They are often able to finish their homework faster and with fewer mistakes, which leaves them free to relax after school—whether that means playing games, going outside, or simply enjoying some downtime. When homework is completed promptly, students are also less likely to fall behind, which can improve their overall academic performance and, in the long run, increase their chances of obtaining good jobs.

The advantages extend to the older students as well. By teaching their younger classmates, they reinforce their own understanding and develop leadership and communication skills that will be useful later in life. If most schools adopted such peer‑assistance programmes, the whole school community would benefit: younger children would receive the help they need, and older children would gain valuable experience while contributing positively to their environment.

In summary, after‑school tutoring schemes that pair older and younger pupils create a win‑win situation. They help younger students keep up with their studies, give older students a chance to practice and improve their knowledge, and make the school day more engaging for everyone involved. More schools should therefore implement these programmes to give all students the support and opportunities they deserve.

Some people agree with the statement “success consists of going from failure to failure without loss of enthusiasm” because failure helps them learn how to be prepared and gain a better understanding. Many people, however, disagree with Churchill’s view, arguing that they do not believe failure is necessary; they think that if they fail at something, they will simply do better the next time. Since no one is perfect, everyone has both bad and good experiences, and this does not change how others perceive them.

Although many people are concerned that failure prevents them from becoming better individuals, they also recognize that it can be a catalyst for improvement. Some people think that failure is important for their lives because it allows them to learn new things and motivates them to become better people. In other words, these people attribute everything to the avoidance of failure.

Additionally, many people do not view failure as something that hinders personal growth; they see it as an event that can lead to becoming a better person. If they fail a class or do not pass an exam, they keep trying and never give up. Surely, through failure they learn from the experience and do not lose enthusiasm.

As you can see, failure is not always a direct path to major success. To succeed, one must pay attention to failure, use it to become a better person, and work hard. When people try, the things they do will improve. Although many people achieve success despite failure, they often do so by learning from it.

Truly, failure is part of life, and we need to understand our failures so that we can succeed. By understanding our failures, we learn how to do better and stop worrying about them. When we are less worried about failures, we can have more enthusiasm for success.

The saying that “success consists of going from failure to failure without losing enthusiasm” is something I agree with. When we fail we gain valuable lessons that help us prepare for future challenges and develop a deeper understanding of what we need to improve. Although some people doubt this idea because they think failure should be avoided at all costs, I believe that experiencing setbacks is essential for growth. Nobody is perfect; everyone encounters both good and bad moments, and these experiences do not separate us from one another.

Many argue that failure is necessary for becoming a better person, even if it seems difficult to accept at first. Those who view failure as a learning opportunity often dedicate themselves to improving and strive to become more capable individuals. In other words, they see every setback as a chance to work harder and avoid repeating the same mistakes.

Furthermore, there are those who dismiss failure altogether, claiming that it merely happens in life and does not contribute to personal development. Yet, when someone fails a test or does not achieve a goal, the important response is to keep trying and never give up. By reflecting on what went wrong, people maintain their enthusiasm and use the experience as motivation to move forward.

In short, failure is not the opposite of success; it is a component of it. To achieve success, we must pay attention to our failures, learn from them, and continue to put in effort. Consistent dedication to your own path will eventually bring visible results, making you feel proud of what you have accomplished.

In conclusion, embracing who you truly are, working hard, and making careful choices are the best ways to secure a satisfying future. By staying authentic, you not only fulfill Emerson’s idea of the greatest accomplishment but also build a life that reflects your own aspirations.

In my experience I don't disagree that Emerson's idea—that mastery will never make a person grow—holds true.  

First, people become mastered, and that stops them from growing in the areas they try to improve. For example, if you are a manager and you see the product you sell declining, your job is not going well. Of course, you may be forced to try selling another product, and if that fails you will feel terrible and think you are not valuable enough to continue in your job because you can see your performance dropping instead of rising.  

Second, mastery can make you resistant to feedback. Imagine a friend pointing out that you are stuck in a circle with what you are trying to do. After your friend tells you that you are going nowhere, you realize you are indeed stuck. You try to do the right thing, but mastery prevents you from having another chance to try again. Everyone is reluctant to attempt something they have already mastered. For instance, a teenager who does poorly on a test may feel so bad that she does not try to retake the test, even though the test represents an opportunity to overcome mastery.  

Third, fear of trying again at something you love can keep you from improving. You might think that trying again will produce the same result as the first attempt, but each new try gives you more experience. You will try to avoid the mistakes you made the first time and will be more careful because you have learned from those experiences. We can all repeat an activity; the key is to believe in ourselves.  

You will see that you can grow no matter how hard it is or how many times you get upset. You must stay positive and avoid becoming trapped by mastery.  

Conclusion: Never give up on what you try, no matter how many times or changes you face. Even if you feel mastered, you always have another chance to start again and trust that you can do it, because that belief is all you need to begin anew.

I do not disagree with Emerson’s claim that mastering a skill can actually hinder personal growth.  

First, when people become too comfortable with what they already know, they often stop improving. Imagine a manager who watches his sales decline but refuses to try new products because he relies on the methods that once worked. He will feel discouraged and begin to doubt his value, simply because he cannot accept that his current approach is no longer effective.  

Second, being stuck in a mastered routine can make us ignore useful criticism. A friend might point out that we are stuck in a circle, repeating the same mistakes. When we finally acknowledge this, we may attempt to correct our behavior, yet we often remain trapped in the same patterns. For instance, a teenager who fails a test may feel ashamed and avoid retaking it, believing the result proves he is incapable, rather than seeing the failure as an opportunity to learn.  

Third, fear of repeating past failures can prevent us from trying again at something we love. However, each attempt gives us new experience, allowing us to avoid previous errors and to act more carefully. By believing in ourselves and staying positive, we can keep improving despite setbacks and the lingering feeling of having “mastered” something.  

In conclusion, we must never give up simply because we think we have mastered a task. No matter how many times we stumble, there is always a chance to start anew, trusting that we can succeed if we keep trying.

I agree with Emerson’s claim that “to be yourself in a world that is constantly trying to make you something else is the greatest accomplishment,” because it highlights the importance of personal success, authenticity, and taking charge of one’s own life.  

First, personal success matters not only for the individual but also for society. We need people who can give back, such as philanthropists who help reduce poverty, and innovators whose inventions—cars, the internet, computers—have become essential to modern living. Second, being true to yourself is a real triumph. When you act in line with your own values, you present an honest image to those around you and avoid pretending to be someone you are not. This honesty leads to a more meaningful existence, because you are living according to your own convictions rather than trying to fit a mold imposed by others.  

Third, owning the direction of your life is crucial. You have the power to decide what kind of future you want, and making those choices independently brings a sense of gratitude and wellbeing. This self‑determination helps you build a fulfilling and healthy life.  

Some may argue that it is easier to follow others’ instructions or that individuality is unnecessary. Yet the ability to create your own success, stay authentic, and steer your own path is essential for human development and for each person to determine what they want to become and how they plan their future.  

In this way, embracing one’s own story—recognizing that each individual writes a different script—leads to genuine accomplishment. Living authentically in a world that constantly pushes conformity is, indeed, a remarkable achievement.

Cell phones in the classroom have become a controversial issue, and opinions differ widely depending on the school, the teacher, and even the country. Some teachers want their pupils to concentrate on the lesson and therefore forbid any use of mobile devices, while other instructors allow phones as a learning tool or simply because they do not see them as a major distraction.  

In many schools, students who are not interested in their studies simply ignore the teacher’s instructions and spend the lesson scrolling through social media or chatting with friends. These pupils often feel that the school does not care about their personal needs, and they use their phones to fill the idle time. In contrast, some teachers believe that a carefully managed use of cell phones can enhance the learning experience. They may permit a phone for quick research, for checking facts, or for accessing educational apps, and they argue that this practice can make lessons more interactive.  

The policies differ even more from one region to another. In some states, phones are completely banned during class; if a student is caught using one, the teacher may call the parents or even send the pupil home. The underlying idea is that students must listen to the teacher and focus on the material in order to understand the subject better. Other schools adopt a more relaxed approach, allowing phones only after the lesson ends, so that students can still communicate with friends but do not let the devices interfere with their learning.  

Internationally, the rules can be even stricter. In certain countries, using a mobile phone inside the classroom can lead to serious consequences, such as being expelled or having the parents notified immediately. The expectation in these places is that students respect the teacher’s authority and use the time in class solely for study.  

Despite these differences, a common theme emerges: students who lack engagement with the lesson are more likely to turn to their phones for entertainment. When teachers provide stimulating and relevant content, the urge to check a device diminishes. Therefore, schools should aim to create an environment where the curriculum is interesting enough to keep students’ attention, while also establishing clear guidelines about when phone use is acceptable.  

In summary, the use of cell phones in classrooms varies widely, but the goal should always be to promote effective learning. Allowing phones only when they serve an educational purpose, and enforcing strict limits otherwise, can help students stay focused and gain the experience they need to succeed in school.

There are three reasons I disagree with what Emerson wrote: looking for new things and learning them can make people grow; small, vital experiences can make people grow; and other vital matters can make people grow. I disagree with Emerson’s statement.

People can look for new things and learn them to grow. New things are not always under human control, but students who learn new things increase their knowledge and can grow in this way. This is illustrated by my mother. When she first came to America she didn’t know any English. She learned English for three years, and now she can speak a little English to others. Nobody can say she has not grown; she learned a language she never knew before. Her story shows that not only the things you have already mastered make you grow—new things can make you grow, too.

People can have many small things they overlook that still help them grow. In a science experiment, a tiny mistake can ruin the whole experiment. Students of science who make such small errors may see their mastery challenged; no one knows whether the experiment will lead to change. I think these small issues are significant for scientific learners’ growth. They can influence whether something happens or not. In my experience, little things can expand into big problems that affect your life.

People can have many experiences in life that make them grow. When you enter society you will notice how different it is from school. In the workplace you realize that effort is not the only path to advancement; there are many ways to reach a higher level. Understanding this marks true adulthood. A wedding can be a wonderful moment when you grow again. Then, when you have a baby, you truly understand responsibility, and responsibility brings the word “grow up.” Work, a spouse, children, and other aspects all contribute to real growth.

Ralph Waldo Emerson wrote, “Unless you try to do something beyond what you have already mastered, you will never grow.” That may work for Emerson or for some people, but I disagree with his claim. People are different; they have many ways to grow, not just the one Emerson describes. People can study new subjects to expand their knowledge, learn from small mistakes they make, and grow through societal experiences. In China there are many reasons that foster growth.

In China we do not share the view expressed by Ralph Wallace Emerson. He claimed that unless we attempt something beyond what we already master we will never mature. I disagree with this statement. People differ, and growth can come from several sources besides tackling entirely new challenges. I will discuss three reasons why Emerson’s idea is too narrow: learning new things, learning from small details, and the influence of life experiences.

First, acquiring new knowledge can certainly help a person develop, but it is not the only route to maturity. My mother’s experience illustrates this. When she first arrived in the United States she spoke no English. After three years of study she could converse a little with others. Everyone can acknowledge that she has grown, yet her progress was not the result of abandoning what she already knew; it was simply the addition of a new skill. This shows that growth does not require abandoning previous mastery, only expanding one’s repertoire.

Second, minor details—often overlooked—can also foster development. In a scientific experiment a tiny error can ruin the whole procedure. A student who makes such a mistake learns the importance of precision and may become more careful in future work. That small slip, although seemingly insignificant, can lead to a deeper understanding and personal improvement. Thus, attention to what appears trivial can be just as important for growth as any major undertaking.

Third, everyday life events shape us in profound ways. The transition from school to the workplace reveals a world far different from the classroom, where effort is only one of many paths to success. Getting married, starting a family, and assuming responsibility for a child each bring new challenges that force us to adapt and mature. These social and personal milestones teach lessons that no textbook can provide, proving that growth is also a product of lived experience.

Emerson’s maxim may inspire some, but it does not capture the full picture. Individuals can develop by adding new knowledge, by learning from small mistakes, and by navigating the various stages of adult life. In China, as elsewhere, many different factors contribute to personal growth, and none of them must involve stepping completely beyond what one already knows.

People should rely on their own judgment rather than constantly following the advice of experts or authorities. When you are on your own, without any prior experience to lean on, you have the chance to learn through your own actions and mistakes. Making decisions independently means you set your own rules and are not disturbed by others trying to direct your life.

If someone more experienced is always behind you, they will constantly correct you and interfere with your plans. Some argue that it is safer to follow someone else’s choices, but many believe that true growth comes from creating your own decisions and establishing personal guidelines. Just as a family shapes its own way of life, you should not let others dictate what you do; you are better off building your own “family” of choices and principles.

First, being alone lets you learn from your errors. When a decision leads to a mistake, you gain valuable experience and understand how to become more responsible. Each failure strengthens you, makes you feel more capable, and shows others that you can succeed on your own. People who see you handling difficulties independently will develop confidence in your future potential.

Second, you should set and follow your own rules. When you create the rules, nobody can tell you otherwise; anyone who wants to be with you will simply respect them. In contrast, if you depend on someone who has more experience, you must accept their rules, which can feel restrictive. By establishing your own guidelines, you can anticipate the outcomes and act with confidence, whereas following another’s rules leaves you uncertain about what will happen.

Finally, staying independent means no one will constantly bother or hinder you. You control every aspect of your life, becoming an expert in your chosen field, whether it is work, school, or a business. Relying on someone else’s judgment means they will try to steer you in a direction you may not want, limiting your freedom. By walking your own path, you gather unique experiences and develop personal rules that suit you best.

In conclusion, individuals should make their own decisions and avoid depending on more experienced people or institutions. Starting from scratch and learning from your own mistakes makes you stronger, more knowledgeable, and more resilient. Create and follow personal rules, stay organized, and you will know what to expect from your actions. When you are alone, you are the boss of your life, free from interference, and you can guide others by example. Ultimately, independence leads to personal growth and expertise, proving that the best approach is to rely on yourself rather than others.

Listening to other people's opinions gives me a clearer picture of how a project or assignment should be approached. When students have the opportunity to share their ideas, they become more confident and are less afraid to speak up.

Group work, however, offers the advantage of dividing the task into separate sections. For example, one person might handle the introduction, another could design the visuals, and a third could conduct the research. By splitting the project, each student can choose the part that suits their strengths or interests, making the whole job easier.

Tasks are usually completed more quickly in a group. When each member concentrates on their assigned portion, the overall progress speeds up. If you finish your part early, you can volunteer to help a teammate who is lagging behind, perhaps because they are working alone and need extra support.

In conclusion, group work teaches students to listen to different viewpoints and to cooperate effectively, making it the best learning approach. While some argue that solo work promotes independent decision‑making and personal writing skills, the benefits of collaboration outweigh those advantages.

The benefits to working in a group or working alone.  

The benefits of working in a group are that we can share information with others to help answer the problems we are working on. When I work alone I have to rely only on my own ideas. My three reasons for preferring group work are: we will work together, we receive more support from the other people in the group, and I feel more relaxed.  

The three reasons I think working alone is less beneficial are: I have to support my ideas by myself, and if I become confused nobody can help me; I feel more frustration trying to finish the work; and the ideas I propose may not be good. I believe group work cannot help the student as much because we cannot support each other.  

My first reason for working in a group is that we work together, which makes it easier to finish the work on time. By learning how to work in a group we share information with one another, and everyone in the group contributes information. This increases my motivation.  

My second reason is that we get more support. In a group we can help each other; if someone does not know the answer, we can assist them. This is why I like working in a group.  

My last reason is that we feel more relaxed because we are less likely to become frustrated. The other people in the group can help us when we are confused about problems and give us support in finding answers.  

These are my three reasons for preferring group work and for not liking to work alone. Working alone can be more frustrating, and we cannot share homework, give, or receive support. In a group, it is easier because we can check each other’s ideas, see which are good, and divide the work so that one person does one part and another person does another; this collaborative approach works better than working alone.

Working in a group has many advantages compared with completing a task alone. When we collaborate, we can exchange information, help each other solve problems, and share responsibilities. If I were to work by myself, I would have to rely only on my own ideas and resources, which can be limiting.

First, teamwork allows us to finish assignments more quickly. By pooling our knowledge, every member contributes useful facts or strategies, which speeds up the whole process. Knowing that others are also working toward the same goal keeps me motivated and makes the work feel less burdensome.

Second, a group provides emotional and academic support. If someone does not understand a question, another member can explain it in a different way, offering assistance that would be unavailable when studying alone. This mutual help creates a supportive environment where each person can improve their understanding.

Finally, collaborating reduces stress and frustration. When a problem confuses me, I can ask a teammate for clarification instead of feeling stuck. The shared effort also means that no single person bears the entire burden, making the experience more relaxed and enjoyable.

In contrast, working alone requires me to defend my ideas without any feedback, and if I become confused there is nobody to turn to. This often leads to frustration, especially when my solutions turn out to be ineffective. For these reasons, I strongly prefer group work, because it combines different strengths, offers continuous support, and makes the learning process smoother and more satisfying.

First impressions are extremely difficult to alter because they create the initial image we present to others. People tend to judge us based on that first encounter and will usually treat us in the same way we treated them at the beginning; changing their opinion is not easy.

The importance of a first impression lies in the fact that it becomes the mental picture people carry of us. If that picture is negative, it will colour every later interaction, even if we are actually cheerful. For example, if I happen to be in a bad mood and appear grumpy, others may label me as a sour person, regardless of my usual disposition.

What others think about me largely depends on that initial impression. When I make a poor first impression and later try to act friendly, they are likely to doubt my sincerity because the earlier negative image still dominates their perception.

In general, we receive the same treatment we gave at the outset, which makes it even harder for others to revise their early judgment. Nonetheless, it is not impossible. If someone makes a genuine effort, shows good intentions, and consistently behaves differently, the initial impression can gradually be replaced. Actions can shift a bad first impression to a positive one, or even the reverse, but change does require time and effort.

In summary, first impressions are hard to modify because they form the primary picture people hold and influence how they respond to us. Yet, with persistent, sincere behavior, it is possible to reshape that initial view.

Looking at several different points of view can lead to better decisions.

Likewise, when we are worried or afraid because someone important is absent, the reassurance of varied opinions can calm our anxiety.

In conclusion, consulting many opinions benefits us by preventing bad decisions, helping us determine which advice is credible, and giving us confidence in our choices. If you imagine a world where students stay home and take online classes, it would be great for those who cannot go to school. Online classes are a big help for people in the hospital, for those who have cancer, or for anyone whose health makes attending school difficult. Some students say there is no problem with not coming to school, whether they want to or not, but they are hesitant because they do not dislike school; their bodies are simply not strong enough to attend every day. Schools do allow online classes, but they often require payment, and students cannot play sports while paying for every class. 

When I was five years old, I choked on a cold and my parents took me to the doctor. I did not want to go to school; I started to cry, and my grandfather told me to stop crying, eat my food, and go to school. He shared a story from his youth, when there were no online classes and many people could not attend school because of hardship. Despite the difficulty, he kept trying, and in the end I went to school, thinking about my grandfather’s perseverance.

Now, at eighteen, I am grateful to my grandfather for teaching me that education is hard but worthwhile. I realize that staying home does not replace a good education. Whether you take an online class or a regular one, you need to consider how you spend your time—whether with friends, family, or work—and think about the long‑term results. In the end, the choices you make will shape your future, help you support your family, and allow you to live a happy life.

Imagine a world where students can stay at home and attend classes online. This would be a great solution for those who cannot go to school because of illness or hospitalization. It would especially help people who are battling serious conditions such as cancer or other severe health problems; they would not be forced to leave the safety of their beds to sit in a classroom. Some students argue that there is no real need to attend school in person, whether they are healthy or not, and that education can continue without a physical presence. Others, however, miss the social aspect of school and feel that being at home all the time can be isolating. Online learning offers a flexible alternative, but it often comes with a cost, and not every student can afford the fees or the required technology. Moreover, staying at home means missing out on sports and other extracurricular activities that are an important part of school life.

My own experience illustrates why the option is valuable. When I was five years old I fell seriously ill with a cold and my parents kept me at home. I did not want to go to school and began to cry, but my grandfather encouraged me to keep trying. He told me stories about his own school days, when online classes did not exist and children had to endure many hardships just to attend lessons. His tales made me realize that education is a privilege, and that staying home because of health reasons should not mean giving up learning.

Now, at eighteen, I feel grateful to my grandfather for his wisdom. I understand that education can be difficult, especially when one is forced to stay at home, but it is still better than missing out entirely. Whether a student chooses an online class or a traditional one, the goal remains the same: to gain knowledge and grow. In the end, the decision should consider the student’s health, family support, and personal circumstances, allowing them to pursue a happy and productive life while staying connected to their loved ones.

I believe that introducing an after‑school homework club at our school would significantly boost students’ achievement. Many pupils struggle with their assignments and would benefit from teachers staying after class to guide them through the material. When students receive that extra support, they understand the lessons better, feel less confused during exams, and are more likely to achieve higher marks.

Unfortunately, some learners refuse to attend such sessions, even when invited, which frustrates teachers who have set aside personal time to help them. Teachers sacrifice part of their social life to ensure that homework is completed on time, but when students simply do not show up, the effort is wasted. Some teachers have even stopped offering extended deadlines because students repeatedly ignore them, warning that they will receive low grades if they do not finish their work.

A dedicated homework club would solve many of these problems. Students who finish their assignments quickly could stay after school to assist classmates who need help. In practice, however, when teachers allow students to work together, many end up chatting or playing instead of focusing on the tasks. Moreover, some pupils dislike receiving help from peers because they cannot explain the solution as thoroughly as a teacher would, and they fear being accused of copying.

If a structured club were established, both teachers and students could volunteer to support those who are beginning to fall behind. Many pupils forget or neglect their homework simply because they do not understand it. Having a set time after school to complete assignments would reduce this difficulty. Even in subjects where homework is not regularly assigned, students often claim they have none, yet teachers know otherwise. When teachers try to intervene, some students still refuse to try, preferring to accept a poor grade.

Some students prefer to finish their work during class so they do not have to stay after school. They ask the teacher or a classmate for help and then use the remaining time for rest or leisure. Others would rather stay after school to finish together with peers or a teacher, especially when they enjoy collaborative learning. Teachers who encourage peer assistance believe it deepens understanding, as students can ask each other questions and clarify doubts.

Parental involvement could also improve results. If teachers inform parents that their child needs to attend the homework club, families are more likely to support the extra study time, preventing the habit of forgetting assignments at home. When students consistently attend the club and complete their work, they feel motivated by the progress they see in their grades. Recognising their effort with small rewards would further encourage participation.

Overall, an after‑school homework club would help many students prepare for tests, as regular homework practice is essential for mastering the material. Schools that lack such clubs often assume that everyone understands the work, leading to missed help and lower performance. By offering a dedicated space for homework, we can ensure that struggling students receive the assistance they need, while those who are willing to help their peers can do so in an organized environment. This collective effort would raise overall achievement and create a more supportive learning community.

I agree with the idea of a half‑day schedule because it gives teachers the chance to plan enjoyable activities for their pupils, making the school day more engaging. By ending classes earlier, students can return home in time to finish any homework or unfinished classwork, which helps them keep up with their studies.

Many teachers support this arrangement, believing that an early dismissal allows children to rest and then concentrate better when they return to study. Some people, however, argue that students should stay at school longer, but I think it would be unwise to keep the same timetable every day. A shorter day once in a while can give both staff and students a useful break.

Opponents claim that sending kids home early might hinder their learning, but I see it as an opportunity for schools to use the extra time for preparation and planning for the following day. This extra preparation can improve the quality of education and ultimately make students more productive in life. While some people still prefer the traditional full‑day schedule, I remain convinced that occasional half‑days are beneficial.

In conclusion, many educators and parents agree that a half‑day schedule can be advantageous, offering rest, extra study time at home, and better preparation for teachers, which together enhance the overall learning experience.

Did technology have a negative or positive effect on people’s lives? I think people are experiencing negative effects, because they can’t control it. Nowadays everyone seems to forget how beautiful life can be without technology. We can still do many things without it: play outside with friends, go to libraries, and spend time in nature.

Some people say that kids need limits on what they do on computers or cell phones. Others argue that teenagers should have no limits, because they can learn more. I believe teenagers need limits on their phone use, and parents should check what their children are doing on the internet.

However, some people think it is good for teenagers not to have limits, because they will learn more for their future. On the other hand, others claim that teenagers can’t complete tasks without contact with other people. I think having a conversation with others is valuable; it helps you get to know someone and strengthens relationships. Meeting a stranger on the internet is dangerous, because not everyone is a good person. Some parents assume their kids are just playing online, but they may be doing more. I think conversations or games without speaking should have limits until you know the person well.

In addition, people sometimes buy a lot of things from the internet without knowing the seller, which is risky. Websites may offer what they claim to have, or they may just want your money. If you are going to buy anything online, make sure the site is safe. Buying stuff on the internet can be problematic because people may avoid going out and spending time with family. Since sites like Amazon, eBay, and others appeared, people started getting everything from the web. Bad actors exploit this by creating many fake sites to scam people.

To reduce kids’ reliance on technology, take them outside to have fun with friends. Spending time with friends in a video game or on social media is not healthy for children. You have to get to know a person before playing or talking with them, because some people trick kids into doing bad things.

That is why technology should not be allowed for kids at all, or, if parents decide to give a cell phone or a computer, there must always be limits.

Technology does not allow people to complete tasks without contact with others. I think this has a negative effect on people’s lives; people are being scammed because they use many unsafe websites. Websites are not safe, so there must be limits and careful monitoring. Kids who become absorbed in technology are losing their childhood. Furthermore, parents must set limits for their children.

Technology has a largely negative impact on our lives, mainly because many people cannot control its influence. Nowadays, we seem to forget how wonderful life can be without gadgets. There are still many activities we can enjoy without screens, such as playing outside with friends, visiting libraries, and spending time in nature.

Some argue that teenagers should have unrestricted access to computers and cell phones because it helps them learn. I disagree; young people need clear limits on how they use these devices, and parents should regularly monitor their children’s online activities. While unrestricted use might broaden knowledge for the future, it also prevents teens from developing the ability to complete tasks without interacting with real people. Face‑to‑face conversation builds relationships and helps us understand others better. Meeting strangers on the internet can be dangerous, as not everyone has good intentions. Some parents believe their children are only playing online, but the reality is often different. Interactions that do not involve spoken communication should be limited until the child knows the person well.

Another risk involves online shopping. People frequently purchase items from sites they do not trust, exposing themselves to fraud. Some sellers operate on dubious websites that may be scams or simply aim to make money. Before buying anything online, it is essential to verify that the website is secure. The convenience of platforms like Amazon or eBay has led many to order everything from home, reducing family time and outdoor activity. Scammers exploit this trend by creating fake sites to trick consumers.

A practical solution is to encourage children to spend more time outdoors, playing with friends rather than staying glued to a screen. Social media and video games are not healthy for kids if they dominate their free time. Children should get to know people in person before interacting with them online, as predators often try to manipulate youngsters into harmful actions.

In summary, technology should not be freely accessible to children; if parents allow a phone or computer, strict limits must be set. Unrestricted use hinders personal interaction, exposes users to unsafe websites, and erodes the joys of childhood. Parents need to enforce boundaries to protect their kids from the negative effects of excessive technology.

To conserve energy and resources.

In my opinion, resources such as land, minerals, or natural energy that exist are valuable. Businesses have a great idea: adding a short workday and making eighty hours a week across four days is a big benefit, especially when the businesses or corporations are large. They will have more profit in the future—not just money, but in other ways they will receive help. For example, food for people might be seen as a disadvantage for the businesses, because some will understand this and some will not.

In this case, at my school I think we should follow the model, but a little differently, because a school is not a business. We could extend the day by two hours, though not everyone will want that. If people understand it, the extension is good because conserving energy and resources—such as land, minerals, or natural energy—benefits the environment, which will conserve more energy.

The most important thing is how to adopt the hours to conserve energy; we will do it to provide good results and achieve extraordinary success.

Conserving energy and natural resources is essential for our future. In my view, resources such as land, minerals and renewable energy are finite, and businesses can play a key role in protecting them. One practical idea is to adopt a shorter work schedule—eighty hours spread over four days instead of five. Large corporations that implement this system could benefit in many ways. Although the profit margin might not increase directly, the advantages appear in other areas, such as lower food consumption and reduced waste. Some companies may see these changes as a drawback, but others will recognise the long‑term value.

The same principle could be applied in schools, although with some adjustments because educational institutions are not profit‑driven. Rather than imposing a uniform reduction, schools might extend the day by two hours for those who wish to stay, while still allowing a shorter timetable for others. If students and teachers understand the purpose, a flexible schedule could lead to significant savings of energy and resources. For example, less heating, lighting and electronic use would lessen the strain on land, minerals and other natural supplies, helping the environment to conserve energy.

Ultimately, the success of any reduced‑hour scheme depends on how well we adapt our routines to protect the planet. By carefully planning work and study hours, we can lower consumption, preserve vital resources and move toward a more sustainable future.

Technology influences our daily lives more and more, and I believe it can be very helpful. It makes many tasks easier and can improve our personal routines. For example, it allows us to stay in touch with other people, to play games, and to chat with friends, all of which are positive aspects. Moreover, we can shop online when we do not want to go to a physical store, and we can manage work tasks without leaving home. Knowing how to use technology is increasingly essential in today’s world; many jobs require internet skills, and tools such as digital maps let us find locations that would once have been impossible to locate.

The main reason technology is beneficial is that it gives us the freedom to do what we want, provided we have the necessary skills. If someone does not understand how to use a computer or a smartphone, they may feel frustrated and unable to accomplish simple tasks. Therefore, practicing and learning how to handle these devices is important, whether for employment, school, or everyday activities like buying an iPhone. People often ask for advice about technology, so being able to explain its proper use is valuable. It is important to use technology for good purposes rather than harmful ones, and to think before we accept every request that comes our way.

There are some downsides, especially for children who become overly dependent on gadgets. When they know how to do everything on their own, they may become impatient and expect instant results, which can affect their development. Still, technology also offers opportunities to create and innovate, which can shape a better future if we consult knowledgeable people and avoid harmful habits. Listening to our own judgment about what is right or wrong is essential.

Overall, technology gives us countless possibilities, but we must set limits and use it responsibly. Without careful thinking, people may focus only on negative actions and ignore the consequences. Modern devices—phones, computers, and the internet—allow us to communicate, play games, conduct banking, and even deposit checks online. Because of these capabilities, it is crucial to understand how to use technology wisely and to recognize when it is helpful and when it might be harmful.

Although some say that students’ self‑esteem should come from praise—because they receive it when they take a test or need to pass a class—students should not rely on praise alone; their self‑esteem should stem from achievement, effort, energy, and persistent work.

Students make an effort to do their work. When they are absent, they stay after school with their teachers to complete missed assignments. Some students seek praise after they have studied and earned a good grade. They sometimes do not like doing homework during breaks.

This focus on achievement builds genuine self‑esteem and encourages students to do their best.

Although some people argue that students should base their self‑esteem on praise—especially when they are about to take an exam or need to pass a class—I believe that self‑esteem should not depend on external compliments but on personal effort, motivation, and consistent work.

First, students demonstrate their commitment by putting effort into their studies. When they miss a lesson, they stay after school to catch up with the teacher and complete the work they missed. Instead of waiting for praise, many pupils focus on studying first and only later receive good grades as a result of their hard work. Even when homework seems boring during a break, dedicated learners keep at it because they understand that effort, not applause, is what truly matters.

Second, students try to boost the energy they need to study. They start the day with a healthy breakfast and often bring a snack to keep their concentration up. They recognize that confidence comes from within and that it is essential for learning. When they struggle, they ask teachers for help, and teachers respond with guidance. Organising their assignments as soon as they receive them also helps them stay motivated and sustain their energy throughout the day.

Third, students work continuously to achieve high‑quality results. They review material at home after school, complete homework, and practice exercises during any free moments. Many visit the library to read additional books related to their subjects, knowing that extra reading can improve their understanding and increase their chances of passing. This persistent effort shows that their self‑esteem is rooted in what they accomplish through dedication rather than in fleeting compliments.

In summary, while praise can be encouraging, true self‑esteem for students should stem from their own effort, the energy they invest, and the steady work they put into their studies. It is this inner drive, not external validation, that leads to genuine confidence and academic success.

I agree with the idea that our emotions can be expressed through three simple concepts: anxiety, feeling, and a lack of belief in ourselves.

First, anxiety dominates the lives of most people. Almost everyone worries about how to accomplish tasks, solve problems, or simply get through the day. This constant pressure creates a lingering impression that stays with us long after the stressful event has passed. Many people hide their anxiety because they feel embarrassed to admit it, and this secrecy prevents them from making any real changes in their lives.

Second, genuine feeling is often concealed as well. Some individuals never show what they truly experience; they keep their emotions inside and become confused about what they want or need. When they doubt their decisions, they fear that any mistake is permanent and that they will never be able to correct it. This internal turmoil only deepens their uncertainty.

Third, a lack of self‑belief compounds the problem. When people do not respect or trust themselves, they tend to rely on others to complete tasks for them. They may even assign someone else to do something they consider shameful, rather than facing it directly. This avoidance reinforces the feeling that they are incapable of handling their own responsibilities.

In life, nothing is impossible if we are willing to try. Over time, circumstances, relationships, and emotions will change, but we must not be ashamed of our needs or mistakes. Perfection is unattainable, and learning from errors is essential for growth. By choosing the right path and embracing our imperfections, we can lead a fulfilling life without being weighed down by fear or doubt.

Some school districts have programs that let students graduate in three years because they don’t have time to stay an extra year. Reasons include being older, not wanting to spend too much time in high school, or simply disliking school. Some families also oppose a fourth year because they want the student to start paying taxes or working to support themselves. Consequently, many students aim to graduate in three years, especially when their families provide little assistance, and because they want to attend college. Most of these students take summer classes, seeing them as a good way to finish high school in three years.

Other school districts offer programs that require four years of study, allowing students to take the classes they prefer. When a class is difficult to pass, the additional time lets students retake it without pressure. They can also use the extra time for other high‑school activities, such as pursuing more education, playing games, and studying for exams. Some students prefer staying longer because they have friends, enjoy working together, or have favorite teachers, which is why they choose a four‑year high‑school experience.

Some school districts offer programs that allow students to finish high school in three years. The main reasons for this accelerated path are that many students do not want—or cannot afford—to spend an extra year in school. Some are older and feel they have no time left, while others simply dislike school and want to leave as soon as possible. Families often share this view, urging their children to start working and contributing to taxes rather than remaining in school longer. Consequently, many students choose the three‑year route because they receive little support at home for staying in school and because they wish to move on to college quickly. Taking summer classes is a common strategy for those who want to complete their high‑school requirements within three years.

On the other hand, other districts encourage a four‑year high‑school experience. This longer schedule gives students the flexibility to choose the subjects they prefer and provides a safety net for those who find certain courses difficult. If a class is failed, there is time to retake it without jeopardising graduation. The extra year also reduces pressure, allowing students to pursue a wider range of activities—such as additional coursework, extracurricular games, and thorough exam preparation. Many students prefer staying the full four years because they value friendships, enjoy working together with peers, and have favorite teachers they do not want to leave behind. These social and academic benefits make the traditional four‑year high‑school path appealing to many.

Disadvantages in a group: there will always be a person who wants to be just playing around and doesn't like to do any type of work, just have fun.
