You will finish your work faster and the way you want the work to be done, but some disadvantages are you will not have fun because you have no one to be with and it will be difficult to have a lot of ideas. I think working with a group is more beneficial because, if you think, there will be more people at the presentation helping you and you will feel more secure with your work.

Working with a group can help you increase your skill level of talking, self‑confidence, and being social (meet new friends). Working alone can sometimes get boring and you don’t finish the work because you don't have someone to share ideas with.

Working alone can cause damage to your personality and your appearance. People will think, “He doesn’t like working with another person around, so he should work by himself,” and then there will be a lot of chaos; that person may fall into depression because no one accepts him, and it was because you made them feel that way.

While you are working with a group you learn skills like having respect for others and different ways of doing things and work as a team. For example, you love playing sport; you cannot do it by yourself because there will be a team, and how will you work as a team without learning how to work as a group? You need to learn how to work as a team if you want to be successful in the community, in your future, working with a group of people you trust. You learn that friendship is always good for you; having that confidence that people you like being with help you increase your life. That is a feeling that no one can easily afford.

When you are working with a group, friendship will always be there. Why? Because it is the key to being successful in your life, your future, and your career, in your job.

For example, let's say that you were driving on the highway, driving normally, but you forgot to stop by the gas station. You are in the middle of the street and you don't have gas. Well, if you don't like to work with a group, then you will push your car and probably you will end up getting a disease or crashing another car.

When you work as a group you gain respect and great friendship because if you help with everything then everyone will love working with you and you will now feel that you are important and useful, something that working alone will be difficult to achieve.

Let's make everyone happy, having a good time helping others, and always be respectful.

Well hello, today I will discuss the difference between working with a group and working alone. First, let me ask you a question: how do you like to work— with a group or alone? I chose working with a group; let’s see why.

Working in a group and working alone each have advantages and disadvantages. I like working in a group because your team can help you with ideas and ways to do your work, and you can have fun while you are doing it. A disadvantage of a group is that there will always be a person who just wants to play around, doesn’t like to do any work, and only wants to have fun. You may finish your work faster and exactly the way you want it done, but a disadvantage is that you will have no fun because you have no one to be with, and it will be difficult to generate many ideas. I think working with a group is more beneficial because, during a presentation, there will be more people helping you and you will feel more secure about your work.

Working with a group can help you increase your speaking skills, self‑confidence, and social abilities (you meet new friends). Working alone can sometimes become boring, and you might not finish the work because you have no one to share ideas with.

Working alone can damage your personality and appearance; people may think you don’t like working with others and that you should work by yourself. This can lead to chaos, depression, and feelings of rejection, which may be caused by the way you treat others.

When you work with a group you learn skills such as respecting others, understanding different ways of doing things, and teamwork. For example, if you love playing sports, you cannot do it by yourself because a team is required. You need to learn how to work as a team if you want to be successful in the community and in your future. Working with people you trust teaches you that friendship is always good for you; it gives you confidence that the people you like being with help you improve your life, a feeling that is hard to afford alone.

When you are working with a group, friendship will always be there because it is the key to success in life, in your future, and in your career.

For example, imagine you are driving on the highway and you forget to stop at a gas station. You run out of gas in the middle of the road. Hello everyone, today I would like to discuss the differences between working in a group and working alone. First, think about your personal preference: do you enjoy collaborating with others or tackling tasks by yourself? I prefer group work, and here’s why.

Both approaches have their merits and drawbacks. In a team, you benefit from a variety of ideas and perspectives, and the process can be more enjoyable because you share the experience with others. The downside is that sometimes a member may shirk responsibilities and treat the project as a pastime rather than a serious effort. When you work alone, you have complete control over how you complete the task and you don’t have to worry about anyone else’s opinions. You may finish faster, but you also miss the social interaction and the burst of creativity that comes from brainstorming with peers.

I believe that collaborating in a group is more advantageous. Having several people involved in a presentation, for example, can boost your confidence and make you feel more secure about the outcome. Group work also improves communication skills, self‑esteem, and the ability to make new friends. In contrast, solitary work can become monotonous, and without someone to exchange ideas with, progress may stall.

Moreover, constantly working alone can affect one’s personality. Others may think you dislike teamwork, which can lead to isolation and even depression. Being part of a team teaches respect for different viewpoints and the importance of cooperation—skills that are essential in sports, professional life, and everyday community interactions. Success in the future often depends on the friendships and trust built through teamwork, giving you confidence that cannot be easily replaced.

Consider this analogy: imagine you are driving on a highway and run out of fuel. If you try to push the car by yourself, you might injure yourself or cause an accident. However, if a group of people assists you—some pushing, some directing traffic, others calling for help—you are far more likely to resolve the problem safely.

In summary, while working alone may suit certain personalities, everyone will eventually face situations that require collaboration. By learning to work together, you gain respect, strong friendships, and a sense of usefulness that is hard to achieve on your own. Let us encourage more social interaction, help each other, and create a happier, more cooperative future.

**Two reasons**

**Bad reason**

**Example**  
Imagine a 17‑year‑old in the 10th grade whose mother is a single parent. If her job does not pay enough to cover basic needs, the student might stop pursuing a career and say, “I can’t do this anymore,” because she sees the harsh reality. Yet, when she is younger, she might think, “I can help my mother and still finish my career,” believing that anything is possible if she wants it.

**Ideas**  

- Young students can imagine more possibilities.  
- They can believe that everything is possible.  
- They may have more opportunities for the future.  

These are real reasons, as the examples illustrate. Young students represent the future.

Do you see the conclusion that people can seize opportunities, even if older people feel they are not ready for what they want? I saw a video that highlighted how young students, once dismissed as inexperienced, now have money, power, and influence in society. The reason is that they never gave up; they pursued what they wanted and needed for their futures.

Deciding on a career while still young is a question that generates both support and criticism. In my view, it can be beneficial for some students, but it also carries significant risks.

One advantage of committing early is that young people often see the world in fresh, unconventional ways. Their perspective is not yet limited by the routines and habits that can develop later in life. Because they are still forming their ideas, they may be more willing to pursue passions that older individuals might dismiss as unrealistic. This openness can lead to innovative career choices and a stronger sense of purpose.

On the other hand, there are clear drawbacks. Youthful optimism can sometimes prevent a realistic assessment of the job market and the effort required to succeed. When a teenager chooses a path without fully understanding the challenges, they may become discouraged and abandon their goals when obstacles arise. Moreover, external pressures—such as a need to support a family—can force a young person to take a job that is far from their chosen field, causing them to give up their original ambition.

Consider a typical scenario: a 17‑year‑old high‑school student whose single mother struggles to make ends meet. To help, the teenager takes a low‑skill job that pays little, leaving little time for studies. Over time, the pressure of earning money outweighs the desire to continue the planned career, and the student abandons the original plan. Yet, if the same young person had been encouraged to balance work with education, they might have seen that it was possible to support their family while still moving toward their professional goal.

Young students often possess a vivid imagination and a belief that anything is achievable. This mindset can open doors to opportunities that older individuals might overlook. Their capacity to think beyond conventional limits can be a powerful asset for future success. However, confidence alone does not guarantee success; it must be paired with realistic planning and support.

In conclusion, while early career commitment can nurture ambition and creativity, it also requires careful guidance to avoid disillusionment. Young people are indeed the future, but they need both encouragement and a realistic outlook to turn their dreams into lasting achievements.

I do not agree with Ralph Waldo Emerson’s claim that “to be yourself in a world that is constantly trying to make you something else is the greatest accomplishment.”  

First, a person cannot achieve such a feat alone. Even someone who wants to be extraordinary needs the support of schools, teachers, and mentors; without guidance it is impossible to develop fully. Learning from others is essential, and trying to succeed in isolation prevents us from gaining the insight and experience necessary to reach our goals.  

Second, collaboration is crucial for personal growth. Working with groups allows us to test our ideas, receive feedback, and refine our ambitions. Individual effort alone limits our understanding and makes it difficult to explore and realize our dreams. By engaging with others we discover more about life and increase our chances of becoming truly accomplished.  

Finally, becoming the greatest version of ourselves requires extensive knowledge of the world. We must study, research, and acquire many skills before we can claim to be the best. This process cannot happen in a vacuum; it relies on education and interaction with the wider community.  

In conclusion, I disagree with Emerson’s statement because being oneself in a constantly changing world is not, by itself, the highest achievement. True accomplishment comes from learning, working together, and constantly expanding our understanding of the world around us.

The question of whether pupils should be allowed to use their cell phones in class is often debated, but I believe that, when used properly, mobile phones can be a valuable educational tool. Students need to understand that the privilege of having a device in the classroom comes with the responsibility to focus on schoolwork rather than on unrelated activities.

In many classes teachers invite us to look up information online or to use apps that can help us solve problems. Unfortunately, some students take advantage of this permission to play games, browse Facebook or Instagram, or chat with friends, which distracts them and wastes valuable time. Such misuse defeats the purpose of the teacher’s instructions and can lower the overall quality of learning.

From personal experience, I have seen both sides. In a language lesson, the teacher asked us to research a particular story on the internet, and the information we gathered enriched the discussion. In a mathematics class, a student used a calculator app to check his work, which was perfectly acceptable. However, another student ignored the task, opened social media, and spent the entire period sending messages. This not only harmed his own progress but also disrupted the class atmosphere.

For many learners, especially those who do not have much time outside school, a smartphone can be the quickest way to clarify a doubt. When I encounter an unfamiliar word in English or a confusing symbol in math, I can instantly look it up and continue with the lesson. This immediate access to information helps me stay on track and improves my understanding.

Ultimately, the benefit of allowing phones in the classroom depends on the students’ choices. If we treat the device as a learning aid and remain grateful for the opportunity, it can enhance both our own education and the teacher’s instruction. Misusing it, on the other hand, risks lowering grades and wasting the chance to learn.

In my science class we often watch the teacher perform experiments that show chemical changes, such as a flame changing colour. Seeing those reactions makes me love the subject even more, because it helps us understand how things on Earth work. Many people who become scientists do not simply decide one day to work in a laboratory; they spend years studying and training in school and college. Only through long‑term effort and disciplined learning can they acquire the knowledge needed to carry out experiments, whether they are testing the properties of a metal blade or studying the biology of a cow.

Science is not limited to the laboratory. It also appears in stories we read, such as science‑fiction novels that imagine new discoveries, drastic environmental shifts, or journeys into space. These tales inspire us to think about how scientific ideas can change the world. In everyday life, we also use scientific methods, for example when we write numbers in scientific notation—expressing a value as a number between 1 and 10 multiplied by a power of ten. This system makes it easier to handle very large or very small quantities, such as the distances in the solar system.

To become a scientist, or any professional who works with science, you must follow a clear educational path. A person who wants to be a nurse, for instance, must complete four years of university studies and then attend nursing school for another four years. The same principle applies to anyone who wishes to pursue a career in science: you need to study hard, gain experience, and keep improving your skills.

Experts in any scientific field have usually spent many years mastering their subject. Whether they are investigating nuclear reactions, where the splitting of one atom releases neutrons that cause other atoms to split, or studying the chain reactions that power a reactor, they rely on careful observation and experimentation. The first scientists who discovered atoms opened the door to modern chemistry and physics, showing us how matter can be broken down and recombined.

My own dream is to become a teacher, because I enjoy sharing the excitement of experiments with younger students. To achieve that goal I will have to go to university and complete a teaching qualification, just as my mother and sister advised me: stay focused, work hard, and do not brag about your achievements. When my sister’s boyfriend wanted to study science, she encouraged him to follow his heart, even though the relationship eventually ended. That taught me that pursuing a genuine passion is more important than trying to please others.

My advice to anyone who wants to work in science is simple: follow your dreams, no matter what obstacles appear. Listen to your inner voice, stay dedicated to your studies, and do not let anyone discourage you. Life will not do your homework for you; you must put in the effort yourself. If you love a subject, let that love drive you forward, whether you picture yourself researching cows, designing new tools, or exploring the stars.

In conclusion, science is a part of everyday life and runs through our blood like a vital current. If you have a passion for it, do not let anything stop you. Keep learning, keep experimenting, and keep dreaming. By doing so, you will not only achieve personal fulfillment but also contribute to the progress of the world. Let your heart guide you, work hard, and never give up on the science you love.

I disagree with the policy that requires students to decide on a career before they even start high school. In my view, asking young people to commit to a specific profession at such an early stage is not a good idea.

In many societies today, students are expected to pick a career path as soon as they enter high school, and their course selections are arranged to steer them toward that chosen field. I believe this approach is misguided because it forces adolescents to make a lifelong decision before they have had enough time to explore their interests and develop a clear understanding of the options available to them.

Choosing a career is a serious commitment that should be based on experience, personal growth, and thorough preparation. Most people need to finish high school, then attend college or receive vocational training before they are ready to enter the workforce. Expecting teenagers to decide beforehand puts unnecessary pressure on them and ignores the fact that many individuals discover their true passions only after several years of study and practical experience.

Therefore, I think students should be given the freedom to explore a variety of subjects and postpone career decisions until they have acquired the knowledge and maturity needed to make an informed choice.

Thank you for considering my opinion. If you have any questions, please feel free to contact me.

High‑school students should not enroll in accelerated programs that let them graduate in three years instead of the usual four. These schemes usually require taking extra classes after school hours, during the summer, or eliminating elective subjects altogether. As a result, pupils have less time for homework, family, friends, and leisure activities, and they miss out on valuable electives such as foreign languages, nutrition, music, computer skills, or health‑physical education.

In some cases, students may be forced to study two courses from the same discipline—for example, English 9 and English 10—in a single year. While supporters argue that an accelerated path enables college‑bound youths to finish higher education sooner, and non‑college‑goers to enter the workforce earlier, the rapid pace also raises the risk of burnout, failure, or dropping out—problems far less common in the standard four‑year track. For these reasons, high‑school students are better off staying in the traditional program rather than rushing through an early‑graduation plan.

I believe that high‑school pupils ought not to be required to complete their schoolwork online from home.  

First, studying at home makes it difficult for students to receive the assistance they need. In a classroom the teacher is present and can answer questions immediately, while at home a learner may be left to struggle on their own. If a pupil cannot understand an assignment, there is no one nearby to explain it, which often leads to frustration and poorer results. Therefore, doing classwork at school is far more effective than trying to manage it alone in a private setting.  

Second, the most capable students should be allowed to finish their courses early and move on to higher education or work, rather than being forced to attend regular classes. Those who have already passed the required exams and maintain a high GPA do not need the same daily schedule as their peers. By letting them leave school sooner, they can concentrate on preparing for college, starting a business, or entering the workforce, which better matches their abilities and ambitions.  

Third, online lessons could be reserved mainly for younger children. For younger pupils, learning from home can be simpler because the material is often less complex and parents can supervise more easily. However, many parents still prefer that their children attend school in person, where teachers can provide structured guidance. Limiting virtual classes to elementary ages would make the system easier for both teachers and younger students, while keeping high‑school education primarily face‑to‑face.  

In conclusion, while some remote learning options might be useful for certain groups, high‑school students should mainly attend school in person. This arrangement ensures they receive direct teacher support, allows advanced learners to progress more quickly, and keeps the educational environment suited to the age and needs of the students.

Technology, in my view, is a positive force because it lets us shop, read, and socialize without ever leaving our homes. With just a few clicks we can order groceries, browse millions of books online, and join multiplayer games that connect us with new friends across the globe.

For many people, especially those who cannot drive or have mobility issues, meeting friends in person is difficult. They can simply call family members overseas or chat with acquaintances through video calls and messaging apps. Online platforms also make it easy to find people who share similar interests and to play games together, turning solitary evenings into social experiences.

Students benefit greatly from digital tools as well. The internet provides access to tutorials, educational videos, and social media sites where learners can see what others are doing. Schools increasingly incorporate technology into lessons, allowing pupils to complete assignments, collaborate on projects, and develop the skills they will need later in life. When used responsibly, technology becomes a safe environment for learning and for practicing digital literacy.

Critics argue that technology reduces face‑to‑face interaction and limits outdoor activities. However, the advantages are clear for those who prefer staying at home or working remotely. Remote work eliminates the need for daily commutes and unnecessary small talk, which can improve productivity and personal comfort.

Older adults also gain a lot from digital resources. E‑books on topics ranging from history to sports are just a tap away, and video‑calling apps let seniors keep in touch with distant relatives. Learning to navigate the internet empowers seniors to handle everyday tasks such as paying taxes or ordering meals, services that can be delivered straight to their doors.

The gaming industry illustrates another benefit: many people enjoy online games, download them for offline play, and even earn money through professional gaming or streaming. Teenagers can finish homework faster with online research tools, while some turn their hobby into an income source.

In short, technology touches every aspect of modern life. It helps us make new friends, finish schoolwork efficiently, and manage daily chores with ease. As we continue to integrate digital tools into our routines, life becomes more convenient and connected. For these reasons, I firmly believe that technology is a valuable asset that should remain a central part of our everyday lives.

Thomas Jefferson once said that we must always strive to do more, because by engaging in many activities students can discover the information they need, share ideas with their peers, and inspire other schools. If pupils only sit idle, they miss the chance to think differently about education and to develop fresh perspectives.

Introducing new sports or enjoyable activities can also relieve stress. When students constantly focus on work, they may achieve great things, but they risk losing the joy of youth. A balanced schedule that includes fun pursuits allows young people to grow while still appreciating the moments of play and relaxation.

Inactivity, on the other hand, can be just as harmful. When time is spent solely on one task, students may neglect family life and miss valuable moments with loved ones. Sharing experiences with family helps build a well‑rounded character.

Dreams become reality when we keep doing what we love. The more we practice, the better we become, and the results are rewarding. Pursuing a sport, for example, requires daily effort if one wants to become a top player or to meet a personal challenge. Success comes from focus, hard work, and a clear sense of purpose, which ultimately leads to happiness.

Jefferson’s message encourages creativity and enthusiasm in life. He wants us to be open to many possibilities, to try our best, and never give up, even when difficulties arise. By staying strong and keeping our heads up, we can turn setbacks into stepping stones toward our goals.

In short, I agree with Jefferson: we should constantly seek new experiences, take responsibility for our actions, and remain persistent. His ideas serve as a reminder that perseverance and a willingness to explore bring both personal growth and satisfaction.

Knowledge works like a group effort: you must search for information to know what you will do. If you rely only on imagination, you may not be prepared, just as you need knowledge at work to know what tasks to tackle each day.

First of all, without a solid base of facts and information, imaginative ideas are likely to remain vague or unrealistic. When we try to create something—whether it is a story, a scientific theory, or a practical solution—we must first understand the relevant details of the situation. Only then can we use our imagination to develop something useful. For example, a writer cannot produce a convincing narrative simply by dreaming up characters and plots; they must also know the historical context, the social setting, and the logical consequences of the events they describe. Otherwise the story will lack credibility.

The same principle applies in everyday tasks. If you go to work without knowing the procedures required for the day, imagination alone will not help you complete your duties. A student studying biology must first learn the structure and function of a plant before they can imagine how it might react to different conditions. In law enforcement, police officers must gather factual evidence and understand the circumstances of a crime before they can envision how the investigation should proceed. In each case, knowledge guides and shapes imagination, turning it into something practical.

Some people argue that imagination comes first and drives all progress. While it is true that creative thinking can inspire new ideas, those ideas need to be grounded in reality to become valuable. A vivid picture in one’s mind is easier to develop when the underlying facts are already known. Knowledge provides the coordinates that give imagination direction and purpose.

In conclusion, imagination without knowledge is like a ship without a map—it may sail, but it is unlikely to reach a meaningful destination. Therefore, I believe that knowledge is more important than imagination, as it equips us with the tools necessary to turn creative thoughts into real achievements.

Allowing cell phones in the classroom is a contentious issue. While a phone can be a handy tool for finding information or checking an answer, it can also become a major distraction. Nowadays many schools permit students to bring their devices, but the benefit depends entirely on how they are used.

When a student employs a phone for educational purposes—such as looking up a definition, researching a topic, or accessing a learning app—it can enhance understanding and make lessons more interactive. In those cases the device is a useful resource. However, if the same phone is used to scroll through social media, chat with friends, or play games, the result is usually a loss of concentration. The constant notifications and the temptation to check messages make it difficult for learners to stay focused on the teacher’s explanations.

Some teachers allow phone use in specific situations, while others ban them altogether. To keep attention on the lesson, it is better to restrict phones to times outside of class, using them only when they directly support the subject matter. In summary, I believe that phones should not be allowed during lessons; students need to ignore apps and concentrate on their studies.

Winston Churchill once remarked that “success consists of going from failure to failure without loss of enthusiasm.” I disagree with the idea that this statement encourages people to keep trying after every setback.  

First, when someone experiences repeated failures, it is natural to wonder whether persisting will ever bring a positive result. There is no guarantee that continuing down the same path will eventually lead to success, and endless repetition can become exhausting rather than motivating.  

Second, failure does play a role in everyone’s life, but it does not automatically compel a person to keep trying. If a person repeatedly attempts the same thing without changing their approach, they are likely to encounter the same disappointment over and over again. The decision to try again must be a personal one, based on realistic assessment rather than blind optimism.  

When an opportunity arises, it is important not to label oneself a failure prematurely, especially while enthusiasm is still present. No one has the right to tell you that you cannot achieve something, yet it is equally important to recognize when a particular goal is unattainable and to redirect your efforts elsewhere. The question of whether constant activity or occasional inactivity is more beneficial invites discussion. I argue that students should remain active throughout the school year and, indeed, throughout their entire lives. Staying active improves our abilities; repeated practice turns a novice into an expert. Some people claim that periods of rest prevent exhaustion and slow aging, but the evidence shows that continuous involvement yields greater achievement.

Students who take part in sports, for example, develop stronger endurance and better health. Regular exercise not only keeps the body fit but also cultivates habits that are useful in any job. Being active helps us become more professional and reliable, qualities that employers value highly. Moreover, involvement in school activities provides experience, builds confidence and often earns recognition such as extra credits or awards.

Opponents of this view suggest that inactivity is more productive because it avoids boredom and allows more time for study. They argue that students who do not join sports or extracurricular programmes can concentrate on their lessons and rest their minds, which may improve exam scores. While rest is certainly important, it does not replace the benefits of active participation. A balanced routine that includes both study and activity leads to the best results.

Practising what the teacher asks us to do, whether in class or on the playing field, sharpens our skills and speeds up learning. This habit also makes us more attractive to future employers, since a strong work ethic and a record of involvement—such as community service or school projects—serve as excellent references. Sports, in particular, teach perseverance and physical resilience, qualities that translate into a hard‑working attitude later in life. Schools often reward athletic achievement with points, trophies, or scholarships, which add to a student’s motivation and provide new experiences and friendships with like‑minded peers.

Adequate sleep and proper nutrition are essential to sustain this level of activity. A good night’s rest ensures that students wake up refreshed and ready to give their best at school. Eating a healthy breakfast supplies the energy needed to stay alert and engaged throughout the day, especially when early mornings are required.

In the long run, the ability to stay active helps us reach our goals. Whether it is participating in class discussions, collaborating on projects, joining a sports team, acting in drama productions, or contributing to school announcements, active involvement builds the skills and confidence needed for higher education. Many universities offer scholarships to students who have demonstrated consistent effort and achievement during high school.

Overall, maintaining an active lifestyle brings greater accomplishments and prepares us for future success. It not only enhances personal development but also positively influences those around us, showing that we are not content with remaining stagnant. Students ought to give their best by taking part in school life, but activity should stem from personal motivation rather than compulsion.

Educational programs already require students to take courses during the summer if they do not finish important subjects. Making a rule that students must finish high school faster—by taking courses in the summers or evenings, or by forgoing elective courses—is not a good idea.

Of course, some schools can offer a three‑year education program, but only a few can do so. Educational programs must provide extra time and be interesting to all students.

Most high schools enroll more than a hundred pupils, yet many of them choose relatively easy subjects such as art and music rather than more demanding courses. The current curriculum already requires students who fall behind to attend summer classes in order to complete essential subjects. Introducing a rule that forces every pupil to finish high school more quickly—by mandating summer or evening classes and limiting the choice of electives—would be a poor decision.

Life is already full of commitments: hobbies, travel, personal development, and regular schoolwork all demand time. For students who need extra time, the situation would become even harder. Immigrant learners, for example, often need additional hours to finish homework and adapt to a new language. How could they succeed if the schedule becomes tighter? They already struggle to meet the demands of a four‑year program, and cutting down their free time would only hinder their progress.

Teachers would face similar problems. Would students be motivated to study material that is rushed through? Teachers need preparation time to plan lessons, explain concepts clearly, and offer extra help when pupils do not understand the material during class. If the timetable is compressed, teachers will have less opportunity to support their students adequately.

In reality, nobody has an unlimited amount of extra time. While a few schools might be able to offer a three‑year track, this could not be applied universally. The curriculum should remain flexible enough to give all students enough time to learn and stay interested, rather than forcing everyone into a hurried schedule.

There needs to be a curfew for teenagers because they should be home by midnight on weekends and go to sleep. A study says that teenagers who have a curfew work hard at school, but those who don’t have a curfew break the law more and have trouble doing well academically. Why should teenagers be out on the street at midnight? They might be doing something wrong, coming back from a party, or involved in gang activities. Going out at midnight is exhausting; nobody wants to be outside that late.

If the curfew is adopted, teenagers will no longer be on the street at that hour.

The new law from Generic City Council sets the curfew for teenagers at 10 p.m.

It means that a teenager walking on the street after 10 p.m. breaks the law.

If a police officer sees this, the teenager can be taken to jail. The city made the law for the safety of teenagers, recognizing how unsafe it can be to be out at midnight. We think teenagers should be inside at home, not on the street.

The community asks why a curfew for teenagers is necessary.

Everyone wonders why such a law is made and whether it is good for teenagers’ lives.

Does a curfew keep teenagers out of trouble?

A curfew alone cannot solve the problem; everyone needs to work together as a team to keep teenagers out of trouble.

First, we need to know what time teenagers are going outside and where they are going. Talk to the police; they can see a teenager walking at midnight, ask where his home is, and possibly take him to jail.

One thing is child safety: we can prevent teenagers from doing wrong things at midnight. For a police officer, it is hard to call a mother and say her son or daughter is dead. This is why a curfew is needed—to prevent anyone from facing such hard times.

We are interested in teenagers’ lives because they may not know what is bad or good. Seeing a large problem, they need help, which is why we say safety comes first.

A city council is adopting a curfew. The curfew starts at 10 p.m. Does it keep teenagers out of trouble? The teenagers need a curfew.

Yes!

The city council has decided to introduce a curfew for teenagers.  

There are good reasons for such a rule. Young people should be home by midnight, especially on weekends, so they can get enough sleep. Research shows that teenagers who have a curfew tend to perform better at school, while those who are allowed to stay out late are more likely to break the law and see a decline in their academic achievements.  

If teenagers are allowed to roam the streets after midnight, they may become involved in risky activities – attending late‑night parties, joining gangs, or simply being in unsafe situations. Most of us would not want to be out that late, and a curfew helps keep everyone safer.  

In Generic City the new regulation sets the curfew at 10 p.m. After that hour, anyone under the age of eighteen found walking on the streets is breaking the law. Police officers are authorised to detain them and, if necessary, take them to a station. The purpose of the law is to protect young people from the dangers of being out late at night.  

Some community members question why the council chose to impose a curfew, arguing that it interferes with teenagers’ freedom. However, the main goal is to reduce trouble and keep youths out of harmful situations. A curfew is not a solution that can be handled by one person; it requires cooperation between families, schools, police and local authorities.  

First, we need to know where teenagers are going and at what time. If a police officer sees a minor on the streets after ten at night, they should ask for his or her address and, if necessary, escort the young person home or to the police station. This not only protects the teenager but also eases the burden on parents, who might otherwise discover that their child has been involved in a dangerous incident.  

By establishing clear limits on nighttime activities, we give teenagers a safer environment in which to grow. They can recognise the difference between risky and responsible behaviour, and they will have the chance to seek help before problems become serious.  

In summary, the city council’s adoption of a 10 p.m. curfew for teenagers aims to keep young people out of trouble and to ensure their safety. The evidence suggests that such a rule is beneficial, and therefore, a curfew for teenagers is indeed necessary.

Curfew actually helps teens avoid doing wrong things. Teens just need to sleep or play on their gaming systems. They can hang out with friends during the day or have a sleepover. Whatever you do, avoid sneaking out to get food or be with your girlfriend. Just stay at home, call your friends or even your girlfriend, so you won’t put yourself at higher risk of getting in trouble.

A city council is currently considering a rule that would set a 10 p.m. curfew on weekdays and midnight on weekends for teenagers. If such a curfew were enacted, any teen found on the streets after those times would be breaking the law. The question is whether curfews actually keep young people out of trouble or whether they unjustly intrude on their lives.

A curfew can protect adolescents because night time can be hazardous. When youngsters wander around after dark they are far more vulnerable to crimes such as kidnapping or being in the wrong place at the wrong time. They may think staying out late is “cool,” but the reality is far more risky. If a police officer stops them, the teen will be asked whether a parent knows where they are. A negative answer usually leads to the officer calling the parents, who then have to retrieve their child. This not only creates trouble for the teenager but also causes unnecessary worry for the family.

Parents often lose sleep when their kids are not home at an appropriate hour. While teenagers want to meet friends and hang out, the danger of being abandoned by peers who are not willing to take responsibility is real. A curfew reduces the chance that a teen will be left to face trouble alone. It also sends a message that parents can trust their children, yet it recognises that the night brings hidden dangers: poor visibility, strangers, and even drunk drivers.

Because a curfew is a legal restriction, breaking it is a punishable offense. Police officers are strict about enforcing it, not to punish youths, but to keep them safe and encourage them to obey their parents. Teens may view late‑night meet‑ups as exciting, but families want their children to behave responsibly to avoid serious consequences. Losing parental trust for the sake of a brief night out is rarely worth it.

Respect for one’s parents is another important aspect. When a teenager disregards a curfew, the inevitable phone call from a worried parent can cause anxiety and embarrassment. Parents, who often keep a close eye on their children, may catch them sneaking out, reinforcing the idea that staying home is the smarter choice. Teens have the freedom to decide between staying in and enjoying safe activities such as video games, studying, or watching a movie, rather than risking trouble by going out alone late at night.

In conclusion, curfews help keep teenagers out of dangerous situations and reinforce trust between parents and children. By staying home during the late hours, young people can avoid unnecessary trouble, protect their safety, and maintain the respect and confidence of their families.

Those early experiences shape our expectations and influence how we view similar situations later on.

First impressions are difficult to modify because they form the foundation of our perception. The first time we encounter something—whether it is a person, an object, or a place—we learn how important that moment is for us, and it becomes a reference point that is rarely surpassed. This is why the memory of that first happy day remains vivid and unchangeable.

Recognizing the strength of these early moments helps us understand why they are so hard to change and why they matter so much in our lives.
